finding.title: Stored review body is rendered as raw HTML (stored XSS)
finding.description: Review bodies are accepted and stored without HTML sanitization, then rendered using Jinja's safe filter. A reviewer can persist script tags or event-handler markup that executes in every visitor's product-page browser.
finding.evidence: An authenticated POST /products/1/reviews with body '<script>alert(1)</script>' returned 201, and GET /p/MUG-SPECK returned the same script inside <div class="review-body"> without escaping.

reason: It identifies stored review text rendered with the safe filter, causing stored XSS on the product page.

finding.title: Stored display name reaches SQL without parameterization in admin review report
finding.description: A customer can set their display_name through PATCH /account. The report endpoint later interpolates that stored value into a quoted SQL WHERE clause, so a malicious display name can alter the query when a staff member requests the report. Use a bound parameter for the author_name comparison.
finding.evidence: PATCH /account accepts arbitrary display_name values up to 60 characters (shopapi/auth.py:116-125), and shopapi/admin.py:77-81 builds the SQL with f"... '{customer['display_name']}' ...". A value containing a quote and SQL expression therefore reaches SQLite in a staff-triggered request.

reason: The finding describes the second-order SQL injection in reviews_by_customer, where a customer-controlled stored display name is interpolated into the report query.

finding.title: Unsafe pickle deserialization of client-controlled basket cookie
finding.description: The basket cookie is only base64 encoded and has no signature or integrity protection. read_basket passes attacker-controlled decoded bytes to pickle.loads, allowing a forged cookie containing a pickle gadget to execute arbitrary Python code whenever a basket endpoint reads it.
finding.evidence: shopapi/basket.py:15-23 obtains request.cookies['basket'], base64-decodes it, and calls pickle.loads before any validation; with_basket at lines 26-29 creates the cookie without signing it. The broad exception handler runs only after pickle deserialization and cannot undo gadget execution.

reason: It identifies the unauthenticated pickle deserialization of the client-controlled basket cookie in read_basket, enabling code execution.

finding.title: Token refresh accepts unsigned attacker-controlled claims
finding.description: The refresh endpoint decodes the supplied JWT with verify_signature=False, then trusts its sub claim and issues a newly signed token for that user. An attacker can submit an unsigned or arbitrarily signed token naming any existing user ID and obtain a valid access token without knowing the user's credentials or original token.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/refresh with a token whose payload contained {"sub":1} and an invalid signature returned HTTP 200 and a valid-looking token for user 1. The vulnerable decode is auth.py:101-107.

reason: The finding identifies auth.py's refresh endpoint disabling signature verification and issuing a signed token from the untrusted subject claim.

finding.title: SQL injection in product search
finding.description: The q query parameter is concatenated directly into the SQLite LIKE expression. An attacker can change the predicate (and potentially use SQLite UNION expressions) instead of performing a literal search.
finding.evidence: GET /products/search?q=%27%20OR%201%3D1-- returned HTTP 200 with all six products, demonstrating that the supplied quote and predicate altered the query.

reason: It identifies SQL injection in the q parameter of GET /products/search, where user input is concatenated into the SQL query.

finding.title: Order detail endpoint exposes any customer's order
finding.description: show_order calls get_order directly and does not use own_order or otherwise compare customer_id with the authenticated user. Any signed-in customer who guesses an order ID can read another customer's order contents, payment totals, delivery information, and refunds.
finding.evidence: Using a valid Priya customer token, GET /orders/3 returned Tom's delivered order, including its items and payment totals, with HTTP 200. The ownership check exists in own_order at lines 32-36 but is not used by show_order at lines 46-50.

reason: It identifies the IDOR in show_order, which lets any signed-in customer read another customer's order.

finding.title: Trailing-slash variant bypasses staff-only admin guard
finding.description: The global admin authorization hook compares request.path literally against the set of registered rule strings. The refunds endpoint permits both slash forms (strict_slashes=False), but its registered path is compared as the no-slash form; requesting /admin/refunds/ therefore skips the staff check and reaches the privileged refund handler.
finding.evidence: Unauthenticated POST /admin/refunds/ with {"order_id":1,"amount_pence":1} returned HTTP 200 {"ok":true,"refunded_pence":1}, while GET /admin/users without credentials returned 403. Authorization should be enforced by endpoint identity or a blueprint-wide decorator, not exact path-string matching.

reason: It identifies the trailing-slash bypass of the staff-only admin check for /admin/refunds/.

finding.title: Trailing-slash admin refund route bypasses staff authorization
finding.description: The global admin guard compares request.path to the set of registered rule strings. The refund endpoint is registered with strict_slashes=False, so /admin/refunds/ reaches the handler while request.path is not the registered /admin/refunds string. The handler itself has no authorization check, allowing unauthenticated callers to issue refunds against arbitrary orders.
finding.evidence: GET/POST to /admin/refunds without credentials returned 403, but POST /admin/refunds/ with {"order_id":3,"amount_pence":1} returned HTTP 200 and recorded the refund. The guard is in shopapi/__init__.py:36-41 and the vulnerable route is shopapi/admin.py:52-67.

reason: The trailing-slash route bypasses the exact-path staff authorization check, allowing access to the refund handler.

finding.title: Payment-status timeout fails open and marks orders paid
finding.description: When the payment provider status request times out, the exception handler sets status to paid and continues through the paid-order path. A transient provider timeout therefore allows an unpaid order to become processing and sets paid_pence to the order total.
finding.evidence: payments.py:39-44 catches requests.Timeout, assigns status = "paid", and updates the order to processing. The comment explicitly says reconciliation happens later, but fulfillment is enabled immediately without provider confirmation.

reason: It identifies confirm_payment treating a provider timeout as paid, allowing the order to be processed without confirmed payment.

finding.title: JWT signing key is hardcoded and exposed in source
finding.description: SECRET_KEY is a fixed, source-controlled value. Anyone who obtains the repository can forge HS256 access tokens, including tokens for staff users; the key is not required to be supplied through deployment configuration.
finding.evidence: config.py defines SECRET_KEY = "hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d" at line 3, while auth.py:27 and auth.py:42 use it for all JWT signing and verification.

reason: It identifies the hardcoded JWT signing secret in config.py, which can be used to forge tokens.

finding.title: Review bodies are stored and rendered as raw HTML
finding.description: Review text is accepted without sanitization and rendered using Jinja's safe filter. A customer can persist script-capable HTML that executes for every visitor to the product page, creating stored XSS.
finding.evidence: POST /products/1/reviews with body succeeded, and GET /p/MUG-SPECK rendered that exact element in the review body. Input is inserted at products.py:90-91 and rendered unescaped at product.html:13.

reason: It identifies stored review-body XSS caused by rendering unsanitized review text with the safe filter.

finding.title: Passwords are stored as unsalted SHA-256 hashes
finding.description: Password hashing uses a single fast, unsalted SHA-256 digest. A database compromise enables efficient offline dictionary and brute-force cracking, especially because the application seeds predictable demo credentials. Use a password KDF such as Argon2id, scrypt, or bcrypt with a per-password salt.
finding.evidence: hash_password at auth.py:15-17 is hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest(), and the resulting value is stored in users.password_hash by register at lines 77-78 and reset_confirm at lines 158-159.

reason: The finding identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in hash_password.

finding.title: CORS reflects arbitrary origins while allowing credentials
finding.description: Every request Origin is copied into Access-Control-Allow-Origin and credentials are enabled, without an allowlist check. This permits arbitrary web origins to make credentialed cross-origin requests, increasing the impact of any browser-held credentials and violating the stated trust boundary.
finding.evidence: A GET /health with Origin: https://evil.example returned Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://evil.example and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. The reflection is implemented at __init__.py:44-50 and CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS defaults true in config.py:12.

reason: It identifies the arbitrary Origin reflection with credentialed CORS in the after_request handler.

finding.title: Product search is SQL-injection vulnerable
finding.description: The search term is concatenated directly into a SQL LIKE expression instead of being passed as a bound parameter. An attacker can alter the WHERE clause, extract data through UNION/error behavior, or cause database errors.
finding.evidence: The query at products.py:40-42 concatenates q. GET /products/search?q=%27%20OR%20%271%27%3D%271 returned all products rather than only matching products, and a UNION-shaped input caused an HTTP 500.

reason: It identifies SQL injection in the q parameter of GET /products/search, where the query is concatenated into SQL.

finding.title: Token refresh accepts unsigned attacker-controlled JWT claims
finding.description: The refresh endpoint decodes the supplied token with verify_signature=False and only checks that the resulting subject exists. Anyone can construct an unsigned token for any user and obtain a valid signed session token, including for staff accounts.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/refresh with token eyJhbGciOiJub25lIn0.eyJzdWIiOjF9. returned HTTP 200 and a fresh signed token for user id 1. No signature, issuer, or expiration is checked before load_user().

reason: The refresh endpoint disables JWT signature verification, allowing forged tokens to be exchanged for valid signed tokens.

finding.title: Order details do not enforce authentication or ownership
finding.description: The order-detail endpoint calls get_order() directly instead of own_order(), and its require_auth wrapper catches the 401 exception and continues into the handler. Any caller can therefore read any order by numeric ID.
finding.evidence: GET /orders/3 with no Authorization header returned HTTP 200 and the order's items, payment amount, and status. The same request with Priya's token also returned Tom's order 3. The relevant path is orders.show_order -> get_order; own_order is defined but not used here.

reason: It identifies the cross-customer order access in show_order (V01) and also describes require_auth swallowing the 401 and failing open (V22).

finding.title: Product search is SQL injectable
finding.description: The search term is concatenated into a SQL statement rather than passed as a parameter. An attacker can alter the WHERE clause and potentially extract or modify data depending on the SQLite statement context and future query changes.
finding.evidence: GET /products/search?q=' OR 1=1 -- returned all six products (HTTP 200), whereas the same endpoint is intended to match the supplied term. The vulnerable expression is the string concatenation at products.py:40-41.

reason: The finding identifies SQL injection in the concatenated search query in GET /products/search.

finding.title: Stored review HTML is rendered without escaping
finding.description: Review bodies are user-controlled but rendered with Jinja's safe filter. An authenticated user can store script or other active markup that executes for every visitor to the product page.
finding.evidence: POST /products/1/reviews as an authenticated user with body <script>alert(1)</script> returned 201; GET /p/MUG-SPECK then contained the literal <script>alert(1)</script>. The body is inserted with {{ r.body|safe }}.

reason: The finding identifies stored review XSS because user-controlled review bodies are rendered with the safe filter in product.html.

finding.title: Authentication failures are swallowed and handlers still run
finding.description: require_auth catches every Exception, including Flask's HTTPException raised by abort(401), then invokes the protected handler with g.user set to None. Routes that do not immediately dereference g.user become unauthenticated endpoints, as demonstrated by the order-detail route.
finding.evidence: The wrapper catches abort(401, 'sign in required') at lines 53-58 and calls f(*args, **kwargs). GET /orders/1 without a token returned HTTP 200 rather than 401.

reason: The require_auth wrapper catches abort(401) and continues, allowing unauthenticated requests to reach protected handlers.

finding.title: Unsigned client cookie is deserialized with pickle
finding.description: The basket cookie is entirely attacker-controlled and has no MAC or signature. pickle.loads executes arbitrary pickle reducers during request processing, allowing a crafted cookie to execute code as the application process before the value is type-checked.
finding.evidence: Every request to /basket invokes read_basket(), which base64-decodes the basket cookie and calls pickle.loads at basket.py:20. with_basket at lines 26-28 writes the same unsigned format, so there is no integrity key or verification boundary.

reason: It identifies the unsigned base64-encoded pickle cookie being deserialized in read_basket, enabling remote code execution.

finding.title: Payment-status timeout fails open as paid
finding.description: A timeout contacting the payment provider is treated as a successful payment and changes the order to processing with paid_pence equal to the total. A network failure can therefore release goods without confirmed payment.
finding.evidence: confirm_payment catches requests.Timeout at lines 39-42 and assigns status = 'paid'; the following branch updates status and paid_pence at lines 43-45. The comment explicitly says reconciliation happens later, but the order is already released.

reason: It identifies confirm_payment treating a provider timeout as paid and processing the order without confirmed payment.

finding.title: JWT signing key is hardcoded and predictable
finding.description: All HS256 session tokens use a repository-embedded secret. Anyone who obtains the source or a deployed copy can forge tokens and set arbitrary claims, including the staff role used by admin authorization.
finding.evidence: config.py sets SECRET_KEY to the literal hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d, and auth.make_token/user_from_request use it for HS256 verification. Admin authorization trusts the database role from the forged token's subject after token decoding.

reason: It identifies the hardcoded JWT signing secret in config.py, which allows tokens to be forged.

finding.title: Passwords are stored as unsalted SHA-256 digests
finding.description: Password hashing uses a single fast unsalted SHA-256 digest. Database compromise enables rapid offline guessing and makes equal passwords immediately identifiable; a password-specific slow salted KDF such as Argon2id, scrypt, or bcrypt is required for password storage.
finding.evidence: hash_password returns hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() at auth.py:15-16 and the result is stored directly in users.password_hash during registration and reset.

reason: It identifies the unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in hash_password.

finding.title: Credentialed CORS reflects every requesting origin
finding.description: For any Origin header the application reflects that origin and enables credentials. This permits arbitrary web origins to make credentialed cross-origin requests and exposes any authenticated cookie-backed endpoint if such credentials are present.
finding.evidence: curl -H 'Origin: https://evil.example' http://127.0.0.1:39081/products returned Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://evil.example and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. There is no allowlist check before reflection.

reason: The finding identifies the credentialed CORS behavior that reflects any Origin without an allowlist check.

finding.title: Application entry point enables Flask debug mode
finding.description: Running the documented entry point starts Flask with debug=True. If this entry point is exposed outside development, Werkzeug's interactive debugger and verbose exception responses can disclose source, configuration, and potentially permit code execution through the debugger console.
finding.evidence: run.py invokes app.run(host='127.0.0.1', port=5000, debug=True) when executed directly; the repository README documents python run.py as the application startup path.

reason: The finding correctly identifies debug=True in run.py, which enables Flask’s interactive debugger.

finding.title: Approved-host image import follows unvalidated redirects
finding.description: The initial URL is restricted to an allowlisted hostname and that hostname is checked for a public address, but requests.get follows redirects by default. An approved public host can redirect the server to an internal address, which is then fetched without revalidation.
finding.evidence: import_image calls check_url(url) once and then requests.get(url, timeout=10, stream=True) without allow_redirects=False or validating each response URL. check_url only examines the initial parsed hostname at lines 28-35.

reason: The finding identifies the SSRF in import_image/check_url, where redirects are followed without validating the destination.

finding.title: Payment webhook does not validate the settled amount
finding.description: A correctly signed webhook marks an order paid using any amount_pence supplied by the event, without comparing it with the order total or requiring a positive amount. A forged or compromised provider event can mark an underpaid order as fully processing while recording an arbitrary paid amount.
finding.evidence: payment_webhook only checks the order status and then assigns int(event.get('amount_pence', 0)) at lines 69-71. There is no equality or minimum check against order['total_pence']; the signature covers only order_id at lines 53-55, not status or amount.

reason: The webhook signature covers only the order ID, leaving the supplied amount and status unprotected and allowing an underpaid order to be marked paid.

finding.title: Request logging records credentials and other sensitive POST bodies
finding.description: The global request hook logs up to 2,000 characters of every POST, PUT, or PATCH body. Login passwords, reset codes, payment data, gift-card codes, and user-submitted content are consequently written to application logs.
finding.evidence: log_request calls request.get_data(as_text=True)[:2000] for all mutating requests at lines 29-31, with no route or field redaction. This includes POST /auth/login and POST /auth/reset/confirm.

reason: It identifies log_request in shopapi/__init__.py logging request bodies, including credentials, which is V20.

finding.title: Order detail endpoint does not enforce ownership
finding.description: show_order uses get_order rather than own_order. Any authenticated customer can retrieve another customer's order, including item quantities, payment totals, delivery date, and refunds; combined with the fail-open decorator, the tested endpoint also disclosed this data without valid authentication.
finding.evidence: GET /orders/3 with a token for customer id 1 returned HTTP 200 and the order belonging to customer id 2. GET /orders/1 with Authorization: Bearer invalid also returned HTTP 200. The ownership check exists in own_order at lines 32-36 but is not used by show_order.

reason: The finding identifies the order ownership flaw in show_order and also reports that require_auth fails open for invalid tokens.

finding.title: Token refresh accepts unsigned attacker-controlled JWT claims
finding.description: The refresh endpoint decodes the supplied JWT with verify_signature=False and only checks that the resulting subject maps to a user. An attacker can construct an unsigned token containing any known user id, including a staff user id, and receive a newly signed token for that account.
finding.evidence: auth.py:101-107 uses jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False}) and then make_token(user). A request with an unsigned token containing sub=3 returned HTTP 200 and a signed token for the staff account id 3. That token can then authorize /admin routes.

reason: The refresh endpoint disables JWT signature verification and issues a valid token for the subject, enabling account takeover.

finding.title: Product search is vulnerable to SQL injection
finding.description: The search term is concatenated directly into a SQL statement. An attacker can alter the WHERE clause and potentially use SQLite-specific injection to disclose or manipulate data depending on the statement context.
finding.evidence: products.py:40-42 builds SQL with "... LIKE '%" + q + "%' ..." instead of parameters. GET /products/search?q=%25%27%20OR%201%3D1-- (q = %' OR 1=1--) returned all six products, whereas a normal search such as q=mug returns only MUG-SPECK.

reason: The finding correctly identifies SQL injection in the concatenated query in products.search.

finding.title: Client-controlled basket cookie is deserialized with pickle
finding.description: The basket cookie is entirely attacker-controlled and is passed to pickle.loads after base64 decoding. Python pickle deserialization can execute attacker-supplied __reduce__ payloads in the application process. This is reachable without authentication through GET /basket and the basket item endpoints.
finding.evidence: basket.py:15-23 reads request.cookies['basket'] and calls pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw)); with_basket at lines 26-29 writes an unsigned, unencrypted pickle back to the client. No MAC/signature or safe serialization format is used.

reason: It identifies the unsigned, client-controlled pickle deserialization in shopapi/basket.py, which can enable remote code execution.

finding.title: Review bodies are rendered as trusted HTML, enabling stored XSS
finding.description: Review body input is stored without sanitization and is rendered with the Jinja safe filter. A customer can persist script or event-handler markup which executes whenever another user views the product page, including staff moderators.
finding.evidence: products.py:82-91 stores the submitted body directly; templates/product.html:13 renders r.body|safe. There is no sanitizer for review bodies (description_html's bleach processing applies only to product descriptions).

reason: It identifies stored XSS from unsanitized review bodies rendered with the safe filter on the product page.

finding.title: Authentication decorator fails open when authentication fails
finding.description: require_auth catches Exception around both token parsing and abort(401), clears g.user, and then calls the protected view anyway. As a result, routes whose view does not dereference g.user can be accessed without authentication, and other protected routes may fail with an internal error rather than returning 401.
finding.evidence: Code path: require_auth at shopapi/auth.py:48-59 catches abort(401) and returns f(*args, **kwargs). Requesting GET /orders/1 with an invalid Bearer token returned HTTP 200 and order 1's full details, even though show_order calls get_order() rather than checking ownership. This also defeats the intended authentication boundary for any similarly implemented route.

reason: The finding identifies require_auth catching abort(401) and allowing unauthenticated requests through (V22), and its order example also describes reading another customer’s order via get_order (V01).

finding.title: Payment status timeout fails open as paid
finding.description: When the payment provider times out, confirm_payment explicitly sets status='paid' and proceeds as though the provider confirmed payment. A customer can exploit provider/network availability or repeated timeout conditions to obtain an order marked processing without a successful payment.
finding.evidence: payments.py:37-43 catches requests.Timeout and assigns status = "paid"; lines 43-46 then set the order to processing and paid_pence=total_pence. The comment says reconciliation happens later, but fulfillment is enabled immediately.

reason: It identifies confirm_payment treating a provider timeout as paid and processing the order without successful payment.

finding.title: Passwords are stored as unsalted fast SHA-256 hashes
finding.description: Password hashing uses a single unsalted SHA-256 digest, which is unsuitable for password storage. A database compromise permits efficient offline guessing and causes identical passwords to have identical hashes. Password reset and seeded accounts use the same weak scheme.
finding.evidence: hash_password at auth.py:15-16 is hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest(), with no salt or work factor. The users schema stores only this value, and scripts/seed.py:32-33 creates demo accounts using it.

reason: The finding identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in hash_password, matching V09.

finding.title: Request logging records credentials and sensitive request bodies
finding.description: Every POST, PUT, and PATCH body is logged, truncated only at 2,000 characters. This includes login passwords, password-reset codes and new passwords, bearer-like values supplied in JSON, payment data, and other personal information. Anyone with log access can recover credentials or reset codes.
finding.evidence: shopapi/__init__.py:29-31 logs request.get_data(as_text=True) for all state-changing requests without redaction. The login endpoint accepts passwords in POST JSON (auth.py:84-93), and reset confirmation accepts reset codes and new passwords (auth.py:143-159).

reason: It identifies the request logger recording unredacted POST, PUT, and PATCH bodies, including credentials and reset data.

finding.title: Application is launched with Flask debug mode enabled
finding.description: The normal run.py entry point calls app.run(debug=True). If this entry point is used in a reachable environment, Flask's debugger can expose detailed tracebacks and potentially its interactive debugger, which enables code execution when the debugger PIN is compromised or disabled/misconfigured.
finding.evidence: run.py:5-6 invokes app.run(host="127.0.0.1", port=5000, debug=True). This is the documented startup path in README.md:12.

reason: The finding identifies debug=True in run.py, which enables Flask’s interactive debugger.

finding.category: CWE-347: Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature
finding.title: Passwordless token refresh accepts unsigned JWT claims
finding.description: The refresh endpoint disables signature verification and trusts the attacker-supplied sub claim. Anyone can construct an unsigned JWT containing another user's ID and obtain a valid signed access token for that account.
finding.evidence: jwt.decode(token, options={'verify_signature': False}) is used at line 101, then claims.get('sub') is loaded and passed to make_token() at lines 104-107 without validating the original token's signature, issuer, or audience.

reason: It identifies the refresh endpoint accepting unsigned JWT claims and issuing a valid token for the claimed subject.

finding.title: Payment webhook trusts an unauthenticated amount value
finding.description: The webhook signature covers only order_id, not status or amount_pence. Anyone who obtains or can replay a valid order-id signature can submit a paid event with an arbitrary amount, and the handler records that amount as paid without comparing it with the order total or provider data.
finding.evidence: webhook_signature at payments.py:53-55 signs only str(order_id). payment_webhook at lines 69-71 accepts int(event.get('amount_pence', 0)) and writes it directly to paid_pence. There is no check that the amount equals total_pence, is positive, or is authenticated by the signature.

reason: The webhook signature covers only the order ID while the handler trusts the submitted payment status and amount.

finding.title: Unauthenticated basket cookie enables arbitrary code execution
finding.description: The basket cookie is attacker-controlled but is passed directly to pickle.loads without a signature or other authenticity check. A remote unauthenticated attacker can submit a crafted cookie and execute arbitrary Python code when any basket-reading endpoint is requested.
finding.evidence: read_basket() base64-decodes request.cookies['basket'] and calls pickle.loads(raw) at shopapi/basket.py:16-20; the cookie is created with plain pickle.dumps at lines 26-28 and is not authenticated.

reason: It identifies unauthenticated pickle deserialization in shopapi/basket.py read_basket, enabling remote code execution.

finding.title: JWT signing secret is hardcoded in source
finding.description: SECRET_KEY is a fixed literal in the repository. Anyone who obtains the source or a deployment artifact can forge HS256 authentication tokens, including staff tokens, and impersonate any user. The application also has a predictable default webhook secret.
finding.evidence: config.py:3 sets SECRET_KEY = "hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d" and config.py:8 defaults WEBHOOK_SECRET to "whsec-local". JWTs are signed and verified with SECRET_KEY in auth.py:27 and auth.py:42.

reason: It identifies the hardcoded JWT signing secret in config.py, which lets an attacker forge authentication tokens.

finding.category: CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key
finding.title: Authenticated users can read other customers' orders
finding.description: The order detail endpoint authenticates the caller but never verifies that the requested order belongs to that caller. Any logged-in customer who can guess an order ID can retrieve another customer's order contents, payment totals, delivery information, and refunds.
finding.evidence: show_order() returns order_json(get_order(order_id)) at lines 46-49; get_order() queries only by order ID at lines 25-29, while the ownership check exists only in own_order() at lines 32-35 and is not used here.

reason: The finding identifies the IDOR in show_order, which retrieves orders by ID without checking that the caller owns them.

finding.title: Customer display names are injected into the admin review report query
finding.description: A customer can choose an arbitrary display name, and the staff-only report embeds that value directly in SQL. A malicious customer can therefore inject SQL that executes when an administrator requests the customer's review report.
finding.evidence: update_account() stores the user-controlled display_name at shopapi/auth.py:119-125, and reviews_by_customer() interpolates customer['display_name'] into the SQL f-string at shopapi/admin.py:77-81.

reason: The finding describes the second-order SQL injection in reviews_by_customer, where a customer-controlled display name is interpolated into the report query.

finding.title: Product search concatenates the query into SQL
finding.description: The public search endpoint concatenates the q parameter into a SQL statement. An attacker can alter the WHERE clause or use UNION-based input to read unintended database values.
finding.evidence: The SQL at lines 40-42 is built as '... name LIKE %' + q + '% ...' and executed without parameter binding.

reason: The finding identifies SQL injection in the q parameter of the product search query in shopapi/products.py.

finding.title: Approved image URLs can redirect the server to internal destinations
finding.description: The endpoint validates only the initial hostname and DNS result, but requests.get follows redirects by default. An approved public image host can redirect the server to an internal or otherwise restricted URL, bypassing the allowlist and public-IP check.
finding.evidence: check_url() validates the original URL at lines 28-35, while requests.get(url, timeout=10, stream=True) at line 50 follows redirects without validating each destination.

reason: It identifies the redirect-following SSRF in check_url/import_image, where only the initial URL is validated.

finding.title: Review bodies are rendered as trusted HTML
finding.description: Review bodies are user-controlled but rendered with the safe filter. An attacker can submit HTML or script content in a review body; it is stored and executed for visitors to the product page.
finding.evidence: Review body is inserted from request data at shopapi/products.py:82-91, then rendered with {{ r.body|safe }} at product.html:13. The author_name expression at line 14 remains autoescaped.

reason: It identifies stored review text rendered with the safe filter on the product page, enabling stored XSS.

finding.title: Payment status timeout is treated as a successful payment
finding.description: A timeout contacting the payment provider is converted into status='paid'. Network failure therefore lets an order enter processing without confirmation that the customer paid, creating a direct payment bypass.
finding.evidence: The Timeout handler explicitly sets status = 'paid' at lines 39-42, after which lines 43-45 mark the order processing and set paid_pence to total_pence.

reason: The finding identifies confirm_payment treating a provider timeout as paid, allowing an unpaid order to be processed.

finding.title: Hard-coded JWT and webhook signing secret
finding.description: The production configuration contains a fixed SECRET_KEY, and the webhook secret also has a known default. The fixed JWT secret permits token forgery, while the default webhook secret permits forged payment events whenever the environment variable is not set.
finding.evidence: SECRET_KEY is hard-coded as 'hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d' at config.py:3 and is used to sign JWTs in shopapi/auth.py:27; WEBHOOK_SECRET defaults to the publicly visible 'whsec-local' at config.py:8 and is used for webhook authentication at shopapi/payments.py:54-63.

reason: The finding identifies the hard-coded JWT signing secret in config.py, matching V08; the webhook-secret claim is a separate issue and does not match V19’s webhook-signature flaw.

finding.title: Passwords are stored as unsalted SHA-256 hashes
finding.description: Password hashes use fast, unsalted SHA-256 rather than a password-specific KDF. If the database is obtained, passwords can be cracked cheaply with dictionary and GPU attacks, and identical passwords produce identical hashes.
finding.evidence: hash_password() returns hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() at lines 15-16, and that value is stored during registration at lines 77-78.

reason: It identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in hash_password, matching V09.

finding.category: CWE-532: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File
finding.title: Request logging records credentials and other sensitive request bodies
finding.description: Every POST, PUT, and PATCH request body is written to application logs. This includes login passwords, password reset data, bearer-token refresh requests, and potentially payment or personal data, exposing credentials to anyone with log access.
finding.evidence: The before_request hook logs request.get_data(as_text=True)[:2000] for all mutating requests at lines 29-31, with no endpoint or field redaction.

reason: It identifies the request logger in shopapi/__init__.py logging sensitive POST, PUT, and PATCH bodies.

finding.title: Trailing-slash admin refund route bypasses the global staff check
finding.description: The global guard compares request.path for exact equality with registered admin rules. The refund rule allows both slash forms, but the registered rule is compared as /admin/refunds; a request to /admin/refunds/ therefore skips the guard and reaches the privileged refund handler.
finding.evidence: POST /admin/refunds/ without credentials with {"order_id":1,"amount_pence":1} returned HTTP 200 and {"ok":true,"refunded_pence":1}. The guard is in shopapi/__init__.py lines 36-41 and uses exact request.path membership; the route at admin.py:52 has strict_slashes=False.

reason: It identifies the trailing-slash bypass of the staff check on the /admin/refunds route.

finding.title: The basket cookie is an unauthenticated pickle and permits arbitrary code execution
finding.description: The server deserializes a client-controlled, base64-encoded cookie with pickle.loads. The cookie has no signature or encryption, so an attacker can construct a pickle whose deserialization executes attacker-chosen Python code in the web process. Catching exceptions does not make pickle deserialization safe.
finding.evidence: read_basket at lines 18-23 directly passes request.cookies['basket'] to pickle.loads; with_basket at lines 26-29 gives clients the serialized format but does not sign it. /basket is publicly reachable, so an attacker can send a crafted basket cookie before making the request.

reason: It identifies the unauthenticated pickle deserialization in shopapi/basket.py read_basket, which permits remote code execution.

finding.title: require_auth swallows authentication failures and executes the handler anyway
finding.description: The authentication decorator catches Exception around both authentication and abort(401), then always calls the wrapped handler. Consequently endpoints decorated with require_auth can execute without a bearer token; handlers that do not immediately dereference g.user are directly exposed, while others return errors instead of a clean 401.
finding.evidence: GET /orders/1 with no Authorization header returned HTTP 200 and the complete order, even though show_order is decorated with @require_auth. GET /giftcards/HFDEMO10 also returned the card balance without authentication. The failing abort is caught at lines 53-58 and the wrapped function is called unconditionally at line 58.

reason: The require_auth decorator catches the 401 abort and continues into the handler, allowing unauthenticated requests to reach protected routes.

finding.title: Product search is vulnerable to SQL injection
finding.description: The q query parameter is concatenated directly into a SQL statement. An attacker can alter the WHERE clause and retrieve arbitrary product rows (and potentially use SQLite SQL injection primitives depending on the payload).
finding.evidence: GET /products/search?q=%27%20OR%201%3D1-- returned all six products. The query at lines 40-42 uses string concatenation rather than a bound parameter.

reason: The finding identifies SQL injection in the concatenated q parameter in GET /products/search.

finding.title: Order details lack an ownership check
finding.description: show_order calls get_order directly rather than own_order. Because the broken authentication decorator also permits anonymous execution, any caller can enumerate order IDs and read another customer's order contents, payment totals, and refunds.
finding.evidence: GET /orders/1 without authentication returned the order belonging to the seeded customer, including items, paid_pence and refunds. The ownership check exists in own_order at lines 32-36 but is not used by show_order.

reason: The finding identifies the missing ownership check in show_order (V01) and also describes the fail-open authentication decorator (V22).

finding.category: CWE-345: Insufficient Validation of Data Authenticity
finding.title: Webhook accepts an arbitrary payment amount
finding.description: The webhook signature covers only the order ID, not the event status or amount. A validly signed paid event can set paid_pence to any attacker-selected value, including an amount unrelated to the order total, which can corrupt payment and refund accounting.
finding.evidence: webhook_signature() hashes only str(order_id) at lines 53-55; the paid handler then assigns int(event.get('amount_pence', 0)) directly to paid_pence at lines 69-71 without checking it against order.total_pence or provider data.

reason: The webhook signature covers only the order ID while the handler trusts an attacker-selected payment amount.

finding.title: Token refresh accepts unsigned attacker-controlled JWT claims
finding.description: The refresh endpoint decodes the supplied JWT with verify_signature=False, obtains only the subject claim, and issues a new signed session token for that user. A caller can therefore submit an unsigned token naming any existing user and obtain a valid session as that user.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/refresh with the unsigned token eyJhbGciOiJub25lIn0.eyJzdWIiOjF9. returned HTTP 200 and a newly signed token for user id 1. The implementation explicitly disables signature verification at auth.py:101.

reason: It identifies the refresh endpoint’s disabled JWT signature verification, allowing forged claims to be exchanged for a valid session token.

finding.title: Payment status timeouts fail open and mark orders as paid
finding.description: When the payment provider times out, the code sets status to paid instead of leaving the order awaiting payment or retrying. A provider/network outage can therefore turn an unconfirmed order into a processing order and enable fulfillment or subsequent refund flows without payment confirmation.
finding.evidence: The Timeout handler at lines 39-42 assigns status = 'paid'; lines 43-45 then mark the order processing and set paid_pence = total_pence. The comment explicitly says reconciliation happens later, but no compensating state prevents fulfillment during that interval.

reason: The finding identifies confirm_payment treating a provider timeout as paid and processing the order without payment confirmation.

finding.title: Payment webhook signature does not cover the event contents
finding.description: The HMAC is calculated only over order_id. Anyone who obtains or reuses a valid signature for an order can change status and amount_pence without invalidating it, and the handler does not verify that the paid amount equals the order total. A signed event can therefore mark an order paid for an arbitrary amount, including zero.
finding.evidence: webhook_signature at lines 53-55 signs only str(order_id), while payment_webhook trusts event status and int(event.amount_pence) at lines 69-73. The amount is written directly to paid_pence and is never compared with order.total_pence.

reason: The webhook signature covers only the order ID while the handler trusts the event status and amount, allowing a captured signature to be replayed with altered payment details.

finding.title: Passwords are stored as unsalted fast SHA-256 hashes
finding.description: Password hashes are plain SHA-256 digests with no salt or work factor. A database compromise permits efficient offline cracking, including immediate reuse of the same digest for users sharing a password. Passwords should use a memory- or CPU-hard password hashing scheme such as Argon2id, scrypt, or bcrypt.
finding.evidence: hash_password is hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() at lines 15-16, and that value is stored directly during registration and reset at lines 77 and 158-159.

reason: The finding identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in shopapi/auth.py hash_password, matching V09.

finding.title: Request logging records credentials and other sensitive request bodies
finding.description: Every POST, PUT, and PATCH request logs up to 2,000 characters of the raw body. This includes login passwords, password-reset codes and replacement passwords, bearer-adjacent account data, gift-card codes, and payment/order data, creating sensitive-data exposure in application logs.
finding.evidence: The before_request hook at lines 29-33 calls request.get_data(as_text=True) and logs it verbatim. /auth/login and /auth/reset/confirm send passwords in JSON, so those secrets are captured by this logger.

reason: The request logger records raw POST, PUT, and PATCH bodies, including credentials and other sensitive data, matching V20.

finding.title: Review bodies are rendered as trusted HTML
finding.description: Authenticated users can submit arbitrary review body text, which is stored without sanitization. Product pages render review bodies with the Jinja safe filter, allowing stored HTML/JavaScript to execute for every visitor viewing the product page.
finding.evidence: add_review stores the submitted body unchanged at products.py:90-91, and templates/product.html:13 renders {{ r.body|safe }}. A review body such as would be persisted and emitted as active markup.

reason: The finding correctly identifies stored review XSS caused by saving raw review bodies and rendering them with the safe filter.

finding.title: Unauthenticated pickle deserialization in the basket cookie
finding.description: The basket cookie is entirely controlled by the client, but is passed to pickle.loads without authentication or integrity protection. A remote attacker can supply a crafted cookie that executes arbitrary Python code when any basket endpoint calls read_basket().
finding.evidence: read_basket() base64-decodes request.cookies['basket'] and calls pickle.loads(raw) at line 20; with_basket() writes an unsigned pickle back to the client at lines 26-28.

reason: It identifies the unauthenticated pickle deserialization in shopapi/basket.py’s read_basket function.

finding.title: Passwordless JWT refresh accepts attacker-forged claims
finding.description: The refresh endpoint decodes the submitted JWT with signature verification disabled, trusts its sub claim to select a database user, and then signs a fresh token. Anyone can submit a hand-crafted token with the subject of another user, including a staff user, and obtain a valid bearer token for that account.
finding.evidence: jwt.decode(token, options={'verify_signature': False}) is used at line 101, followed by load_user(claims.get('sub')) and make_token(user) at lines 104-107.

reason: The refresh endpoint disables JWT signature verification and reissues a signed token for the forged subject, enabling account takeover.

finding.title: JWT signing key is hard-coded in source
finding.description: The application uses a fixed, source-visible SECRET_KEY for HS256 bearer tokens. Anyone who obtains the repository or source artifact can forge tokens for arbitrary user IDs and roles, compromising every authenticated endpoint.
finding.evidence: SECRET_KEY is assigned the literal value 'hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d' at line 3 and is used for JWT signing and verification in shopapi/auth.py lines 27 and 42.

reason: The finding identifies the hard-coded SECRET_KEY in config.py, which can be used to forge JWTs.

finding.title: Production JWT signing key is hardcoded and predictable
finding.description: SECRET_KEY is a literal repository value and is used to sign and verify all HS256 bearer tokens. Anyone who obtains the source or this deployed configuration can forge tokens for arbitrary user IDs and roles, including staff. The webhook secret also has a permissive hardcoded default at line 8.
finding.evidence: config.py:3 defines SECRET_KEY = "hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d"; auth.py:27 and auth.py:42 use it for JWT signing and verification. The value is not required to come from an environment/secret manager.

reason: The finding identifies the hardcoded JWT signing secret in config.py, which can enable forged tokens.

finding.title: Product search concatenates attacker input into SQL
finding.description: The q query parameter is interpolated directly into a SQL string. An unauthenticated attacker can inject SQL syntax to alter the query and extract data from the SQLite database.
finding.evidence: The query at lines 40-42 builds the LIKE expression using q by string concatenation and executes it without parameters.

reason: It identifies SQL injection in the product search query by concatenating the q parameter into SQL.

finding.title: Review bodies are rendered as trusted HTML
finding.description: Authenticated users can submit arbitrary review text, but the product template marks each review body safe. A malicious reviewer can store HTML or script content that executes for every visitor to the product page.
finding.evidence: products.py:90 stores the submitted body without sanitization, and product.html line 13 renders r.body with the Jinja safe filter.

reason: The finding identifies stored XSS because raw review bodies are rendered with the safe filter in product.html.

finding.title: Passwords are stored as unsalted SHA-256 digests
finding.description: SHA-256 is a fast general-purpose hash and is used without a salt or work factor. A database disclosure enables efficient offline cracking of user passwords, including the staff account if it uses a reused or guessable password.
finding.evidence: hash_password() returns hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() at lines 15-16, and the resulting digest is stored directly in users.password_hash at auth.py:77.

reason: The finding identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password storage in hash_password, matching V09.

finding.title: Trailing-slash admin refund route bypasses staff authorization
finding.description: The global admin guard compares the raw request path against the registered rule strings. The refund rule accepts both slash forms, but only the no-slash form is in admin_paths, so POST /admin/refunds/ skips the staff check and can issue refunds anonymously.
finding.evidence: staff_only_admin() gates only when request.path is in admin_paths at lines 36-41. The route is registered with strict_slashes=False in shopapi/admin.py:52; a test request to /admin/refunds/ returned 200 and created a refund without Authorization.

reason: It identifies the trailing-slash refund route bypassing the staff-only admin check.

finding.title: Staff review report is vulnerable to SQL injection
finding.description: A customer's display name is inserted into a SQL statement using an f-string. A customer can set display_name to SQL syntax, and any staff member viewing the report then causes the injected query to execute.
finding.evidence: The report query contains f"WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}' ORDER BY r.id DESC" at line 80; display_name is user-controlled via shopapi/auth.py:124.

reason: The report interpolates a customer-controlled display_name into its SQL query, matching the second-order SQL injection in reviews_by_customer.

finding.title: Payment timeout fails open as a successful payment
finding.description: If the payment provider times out, the exception handler sets status to paid and marks the order processing with the full total. An attacker or network condition that causes provider requests to time out can obtain fulfillment without a confirmed payment.
finding.evidence: The requests.Timeout handler at lines 39-42 assigns status = 'paid'; lines 43-46 then set paid_pence = total_pence and transition the order to processing.

reason: It identifies the payment-provider timeout being treated as paid, causing the order to be processed without confirmed payment.

finding.title: Refresh accepts unsigned attacker-controlled JWT claims
finding.description: The refresh endpoint explicitly disables signature verification and only checks that the subject names an existing user. An attacker can construct an unsigned token for any user ID and receive a newly signed bearer token for that account.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/refresh with token eyJhbGciOiJub25lIiwidHlwIjoiSldUIn0.eyJzdWIiOjF9. returned HTTP 200 and a valid HS256 token for user 1.

reason: The finding describes the refresh endpoint accepting unsigned JWT claims and issuing a valid token, matching V17.

finding.title: Payment webhook trusts an unvalidated amount
finding.description: After checking only the order ID signature, the webhook writes the event-supplied amount into paid_pence without requiring it to equal the order total or checking that it is positive. A signed paid event can therefore mark an underpaid order as paid or create inconsistent payment state.
finding.evidence: The paid branch assigns int(event.get('amount_pence', 0)) directly to paid_pence at lines 70-71; the signature is computed only over order_id at lines 53-55.

reason: The webhook signature covers only the order ID while the handler trusts the event-supplied amount, matching V19's payment-webhook integrity flaw.

finding.title: Order details are disclosed without checking ownership
finding.description: The route requires a valid token but calls get_order() directly and never compares customer_id with g.user. Any signed-in customer can enumerate order IDs and read another customer's items, payment totals, status, refunds, and delivery date.
finding.evidence: GET /orders/3 with no Authorization header returned HTTP 200 and the seeded order belonging to customer 2. The same route is protected only by @require_auth; own_order(), which performs the ownership check, is not used.

reason: The finding identifies the order-ownership IDOR in show_order, and its claim that the route returns an order without an Authorization header also identifies require_auth failing open.

finding.title: Trailing-slash admin refund route bypasses the staff check
finding.description: Admin authorization compares request.path to a set of canonical Flask rules. The refunds rule is registered with strict_slashes=False, so /admin/refunds/ reaches the handler but does not equal /admin/refunds. The handler has no independent authorization check.
finding.evidence: Unauthenticated POST /admin/refunds/ with {"order_id":1,"amount_pence":1} returned HTTP 200 and created a refund. POST /admin/refunds with the same body returned HTTP 403.

reason: The trailing-slash refunds route bypasses the exact-path staff authorization check, matching V03.

finding.title: Product search is SQL injectable
finding.description: The q parameter is concatenated into a LIKE query. SQL metacharacters can alter the WHERE clause and expose or manipulate query results.
finding.evidence: GET /products/search?q=%27%20OR%201%3D1%20-- returned all six products, whereas the literal search term has no matching product.

reason: The finding correctly identifies SQL injection in the product search query, where the q parameter is concatenated into SQL.

finding.title: Authentication failures are swallowed by require_auth
finding.description: require_auth catches its own abort(401) exception and still invokes the protected view with g.user set to None. Endpoints whose view does not dereference g.user can therefore be called without authentication; notably, order lookup exposes any order and gift-card balance exposes card balances.
finding.evidence: The abort(401) at lines 53-54 is caught by the broad Exception handler at line 55, which then calls f(*args, **kwargs) at line 58. shopapi/orders.py:49 calls get_order() without an ownership check, and shopapi/giftcards.py:16 returns a balance after the bypassed decorator.

reason: It identifies the fail-open require_auth decorator, and also points out that order lookup lacks an ownership check.

finding.title: Stored display names reach an admin SQL query unsafely
finding.description: A customer can set display_name through PATCH /account. The admin report then interpolates that stored value into SQL, allowing a second-order SQL injection when staff request the report.
finding.evidence: A registered user with display_name x' OR 1=1 -- caused GET /admin/reports/reviews?customer_id=5 (as staff) to return an unrelated review. The value is written by shopapi/auth.py:124 and interpolated at this line.

reason: It identifies the second-order SQL injection in reviews_by_customer, where a customer-controlled stored display_name is interpolated into the admin report query.

finding.title: Review bodies are rendered as unsanitized HTML
finding.description: Review submission accepts arbitrary text, but the template marks the body safe. A customer can store script-capable markup that executes in every visitor's browser on the product page.
finding.evidence: Submitting a review body of to POST /products/1/reviews resulted in that exact tag being returned by GET /p/MUG-SPECK. The unsafe output is {{ r.body|safe }}.

reason: It identifies stored XSS from review bodies rendered with |safe in product.html.

finding.title: Client-controlled basket cookie is deserialized with pickle
finding.description: The basket cookie is only base64 encoded, not authenticated or otherwise constrained. pickle.loads executes pickle opcodes before the result is type-checked, so a requester who supplies a crafted basket cookie can execute code in the application process on any basket-reading endpoint.
finding.evidence: read_basket() accepts request.cookies['basket'] and calls pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw)) before checking that the result is a dict. The cookie is generated by with_basket() without a signature or encryption.

reason: The finding identifies unauthenticated pickle deserialization of the client-controlled basket cookie in read_basket, matching the remote-code-execution vulnerability.

finding.title: Passwords are stored as unsalted fast SHA-256 hashes
finding.description: Password hashes use raw SHA-256 with no per-password salt or work factor. A database disclosure permits efficient offline cracking, especially because the seeded/demo password is shared and weakly structured.
finding.evidence: hash_password() is hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest(), and the result is stored directly in users.password_hash. No salt, KDF, or password-hashing library is used.

reason: The finding identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in hash_password, matching V09.

finding.title: JWT signing uses a hardcoded repository secret
finding.description: SECRET_KEY is a fixed, guessable application value in source code. Anyone who obtains the source or a deployed copy can forge HS256 access tokens, including staff-role claims (and the application does not bind the role claim to the database role). Secrets must be supplied through protected deployment configuration and rotated.
finding.evidence: config.py sets SECRET_KEY = 'hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d', and auth.py:27 uses it to sign all bearer tokens. The same configuration pattern sets WEBHOOK_SECRET to the public default 'whsec-local'.

reason: It identifies the hardcoded JWT signing secret in config.py, which enables token forgery.

finding.title: Payment timeout fails open and marks the order paid
finding.description: When the payment provider times out, confirm_payment() unconditionally substitutes the status paid and sets paid_pence to the order total. A transient provider failure therefore allows checkout to proceed without evidence of payment.
finding.evidence: The requests.Timeout handler sets status = 'paid', and the common paid branch changes the order to processing at lines 43-45. The comment explicitly says reconciliation happens later, after the customer has received the paid state.

reason: It identifies confirm_payment treating a provider timeout as successful payment and marking the order paid.

finding.title: Passwordless token refresh permits impersonation of any user
finding.description: The refresh endpoint decodes the supplied JWT with signature verification disabled and then issues a newly signed token for the subject in the untrusted claims. An attacker can choose a known user ID, including the staff account, and obtain a valid token with that user's current database role.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/refresh with JSON {"token":"eyJhbGciOiJub25lIn0.eyJzdWIiOjN9."} returned 200 and a valid signed token for sub 3 (the seeded staff user). The code at auth.py:101 uses jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False}) before loading the subject.

reason: The refresh endpoint disables JWT signature verification and issues a valid token for the untrusted subject, enabling account takeover.

finding.title: Request logging records credentials and other sensitive request bodies
finding.description: Every POST body is logged verbatim up to 2,000 characters. This includes login passwords, registration/reset data, bearer-adjacent secrets in request payloads, and potentially payment or personal information, creating a credential disclosure path through application logs.
finding.evidence: The before_request hook calls request.get_data(as_text=True) for all POST requests. POST /auth/login sends the password in the JSON body, so the configured shopapi logger records it.

reason: The request logger records POST bodies, including credentials, which is the sensitive-data logging issue in V20.

finding.title: Authenticated users can read any order
finding.description: The order detail route authenticates the caller but calls get_order(), which only checks whether the order exists. It never applies own_order() or otherwise compares customer_id with the caller, exposing order contents and refund history across accounts.
finding.evidence: With Priya's valid bearer token, GET /orders/3 returned 200 and the seeded order belonging to Tom, including its items, prices, payment amount, and status. show_order() at orders.py:46-49 calls get_order(order_id) directly.

reason: The finding identifies the IDOR in show_order, which retrieves any order without checking that it belongs to the authenticated customer.

finding.title: Authentication decorator fails open
finding.description: require_auth catches its own abort(401) as a broad Exception, sets g.user to None, and still invokes the protected handler. Handlers that use g.user then produce an unhandled 500, while handlers that do not use it execute without authentication. The gift-card balance endpoint therefore discloses card balances to unauthenticated callers.
finding.evidence: GET /giftcards/HFDEMO10 without Authorization returned 200 with the card balance. GET /account without Authorization reached the handler and returned 500 instead of 401. The unconditional return f(*args, **kwargs) after the except is at auth.py:55-59.

reason: It identifies require_auth catching abort(401) and continuing to the protected handler, matching the fail-open authentication vulnerability.

finding.title: Password reset codes are predictable and have no attempt limit
finding.description: Reset codes are eight decimal digits generated from Python's non-cryptographic Mersenne Twister and reset confirmation has no rate limiting or failed-attempt counter. An attacker can make unlimited online guesses during the 30-minute validity window, and the PRNG output is not suitable for authentication tokens.
finding.evidence: reset_request() creates the code with random.random(), while reset_confirm() compares the supplied code at line 153 and performs no attempt tracking, throttling, or lockout.

reason: It identifies the predictable reset-code generation and unlimited guessing in reset_request/reset_confirm.

finding.title: Payment status timeout fails open as paid
finding.description: When the provider status request times out, the checkout handler explicitly changes the status to paid and proceeds to processing. A provider outage or induced timeout therefore lets an order be fulfilled without confirmation of payment.
finding.evidence: The requests.Timeout handler at payments.py:39-42 sets status = "paid"; lines 43-45 then set the order to processing and paid_pence to total_pence. The documented reconciliation job does not exist in the repository, so the fail-open state is immediately committed.

reason: It identifies confirm_payment treating a provider timeout as paid, allowing orders to be processed without payment.

finding.title: Review bodies are stored XSS
finding.description: Review text is stored without HTML sanitization and rendered with Jinja's safe filter. Any authenticated user can publish markup or script that executes for every visitor of the product page.
finding.evidence: POST /products/1/reviews as Priya with body <script>alert(1)</script> returned 201; GET /p/MUG-SPECK then contained the same script inside the review body. The sink is {{ r.body|safe }} at product.html:13, and add_review() only checks length at products.py:83-91.

reason: It identifies stored XSS in review bodies rendered with |safe on the product page.

finding.title: Client-controlled basket cookie is unsafe-deserialized with pickle
finding.description: The basket cookie is only base64 encoded, not authenticated or otherwise constrained to data values. read_basket() passes attacker-controlled cookie bytes to pickle.loads(), allowing a crafted cookie to execute arbitrary Python code in the application process before the type check.
finding.evidence: GET /basket invokes read_basket() and therefore pickle.loads() on the request's basket cookie at basket.py:15-23. A signed/encrypted server-side session or a JSON value with strict validation is required; the current base64 encoding provides no protection against a malicious pickle payload.

reason: The finding identifies unauthenticated pickle deserialization of the client-controlled basket cookie in read_basket, matching V18.

finding.title: Product search is vulnerable to SQL injection
finding.description: The search term is concatenated directly into a SQLite LIKE expression. SQL metacharacters can alter the WHERE clause and expose or manipulate the query's result set.
finding.evidence: GET /products/search?q=%27%20OR%201%3D1-- returned all 6 products, including products unrelated to the search. The query at products.py:40-42 concatenates q instead of using a bound parameter.

reason: The finding correctly identifies SQL injection in the concatenated search query in shopapi/products.py.

finding.title: Approved-host image import can be redirected to internal URLs
finding.description: The endpoint validates that the initial URL uses an approved public hostname, but requests.get() follows redirects by default. An approved host can redirect the server to localhost, private network addresses, or cloud metadata, turning this staff-accessible importer into SSRF.
finding.evidence: check_url() at images.py:28-35 validates only the parsed initial URL and its DNS result. The subsequent requests.get(url, ...) at line 50 follows HTTP redirects without revalidating each destination. No redirect=False or per-hop destination check is present.

reason: It identifies the redirect-following SSRF in shopapi/images.py’s import_image/check_url flow.

finding.title: Order details are accessible by ID without ownership authorization
finding.description: The authenticated order-details endpoint calls get_order directly, which only checks that the ID exists and never verifies that the order belongs to the requesting customer. Any user who learns another order ID can read its status, totals, items, and refunds.
finding.evidence: shopapi/orders.py:25-29 get_order performs only SELECT ... WHERE id; show_order at :46-49 returns order_json(get_order(order_id)) rather than own_order. The ownership check exists separately in own_order at :32-36 but is not used by this route.

reason: The finding correctly identifies the IDOR in show_order, which retrieves an order without checking that it belongs to the requesting customer.

finding.title: Payment webhook trusts an attacker-controlled settlement amount
finding.description: After signature validation, a paid event's amount_pence is copied directly into paid_pence without checking it is positive or equals the order total (or the provider's settled amount). A validly signed event can mark an order paid for zero or an arbitrary amount; the default webhook secret is also committed in configuration.
finding.evidence: The paid branch executes UPDATE ... paid_pence = int(event.get('amount_pence', 0)) with no amount validation. The signing key defaults to the hardcoded value in config.py:8, so deployments that do not override it permit anyone who can read the source to forge signatures.

reason: The webhook trusts amount_pence without authenticating it as part of the signed data, matching V19; the webhook-secret detail does not match the JWT signing-secret finding V08.

finding.title: Passwords are stored as unsalted SHA-256 hashes
finding.description: Password hashes use a fast, unsalted general-purpose hash. A database disclosure permits efficient dictionary and brute-force cracking, and identical passwords are trivially identifiable across accounts. Passwords should use a memory-hard password KDF with a unique salt.
finding.evidence: hash_password() is hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() at auth.py:15-16, and the result is stored directly in users.password_hash during registration and reset. No salt or work factor is present.

reason: The finding identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password storage in hash_password, matching V09.

finding.title: Request logging records passwords and other secrets
finding.description: All POST, PUT, and PATCH bodies are logged verbatim up to 2,000 characters. Login and registration bodies contain passwords; reset requests contain reset-related data; other logged bodies may contain payment or personal information. These secrets persist in application logs and may be accessible to operators or log aggregators.
finding.evidence: The before_request hook at __init__.py:29-31 calls request.get_data(as_text=True) and logs it without redaction. This applies to /auth/login, /auth/register, and /auth/reset/confirm as well as every other mutating route.

reason: It identifies the request logger in shopapi/__init__.py logging request bodies, including passwords and other secrets.

finding.title: Refresh endpoint accepts unsigned attacker-controlled JWT claims
finding.description: The refresh endpoint decodes the supplied token with signature verification disabled and uses only its sub claim to mint a valid signed token. An attacker can select any existing user ID and obtain a session token without knowing a password or signing key.
finding.evidence: shopapi/auth.py:100-107 calls jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False}), loads claims.sub, and returns make_token(user). A POST /auth/refresh with an alg:none token containing sub=2 returned HTTP 200 and a fresh HS256 token.

reason: The refresh endpoint disables JWT signature verification and uses the attacker-controlled subject claim to mint a valid token.

finding.title: Authentication decorator fails open on authentication errors
finding.description: require_auth catches its own 401 abort (and any other exception), clears g.user, and nevertheless invokes the protected handler. Consequently routes intended to require a signed-in user can execute anonymously.
finding.evidence: shopapi/auth.py:51-58 catches Exception around user_from_request()/abort(401) and returns f(*args, **kwargs). A live unauthenticated GET /giftcards/HFDEMO10 returned HTTP 200 and the gift-card balance, despite shopapi/giftcards.py:10-12 using @require_auth. The same decorator protects account, order mutation, checkout, reviews, redemption, and payment confirmation routes.

reason: It identifies require_auth catching the 401 and continuing into protected handlers, which is the fail-open authentication flaw in V22.

finding.title: Cancellation and return refunds can overlap and exceed the purchase
finding.description: Cancellation validation tracks only cancelled_qty, while return validation tracks only returned_qty. The same item quantity can therefore be cancelled and returned in separate requests, producing two refunds. Neither path checks the aggregate refund total against paid_pence, and concurrent requests can also pass their checks before either update commits.
finding.evidence: cancel_items() validates item['cancelled_qty'] at orders.py:62-68 and issues a refund at lines 69-70; return_items() independently validates item['returned_qty'] at lines 88-94 and issues another refund at lines 95-96. There is no cross-check against the other quantity or existing refunds.

reason: It identifies the return_items flaw that ignores cancelled_qty, allowing already-refunded cancelled items to be returned and refunded again.

finding.title: Product search is SQL injectable
finding.description: The q query parameter is concatenated into a LIKE expression instead of being passed as a bound parameter. Attackers can alter the WHERE clause, extract unintended catalogue data, or trigger database errors.
finding.evidence: shopapi/products.py:40-42 constructs SQL as "... name LIKE '%" + q + "%' OR sku LIKE '%" + q + "%' ..." and executes it directly.

reason: The finding identifies SQL injection in the q parameter of shopapi/products.py search, matching V11.

finding.title: Payment webhook signature does not cover the payment amount or status
finding.description: The HMAC is calculated only over order_id. A request with a valid signature for an order can change amount_pence independently, including setting paid_pence to zero or an amount greater than the order total, and the handler accepts it without provider-side verification.
finding.evidence: webhook_signature() at payments.py:53-55 signs only str(order_id), while payment_webhook() at lines 69-71 trusts event.status and int(event.amount_pence) separately. The configured fallback secret is the hardcoded value whsec-local in config.py:8, making the signing key recoverable from the source/deployment defaults.

reason: It identifies that the webhook signature covers only the order ID while the handler trusts the supplied status and amount.

finding.title: Stored review content is rendered as raw HTML
finding.description: Review bodies are user-supplied but rendered with Jinja's safe filter. An authenticated reviewer can store script/event-handler markup that executes for anyone viewing the product page, causing persistent XSS.
finding.evidence: shopapi/templates/product.html:13 renders {{ r.body|safe }}. shopapi/products.py:82-91 accepts and stores review body without HTML sanitization (only length validation).

reason: The finding identifies stored XSS from unsanitized review bodies rendered with `|safe` on the product page.

finding.title: Trailing-slash admin refund path bypasses staff authorization
finding.description: The global admin check compares request.path to the set of route rules exactly. The refund endpoint permits both slash forms, but only the no-slash rule is in the set, so /admin/refunds/ reaches the handler without the staff check.
finding.evidence: shopapi/__init__.py:26 and :36-41 use exact request.path membership in admin_paths. shopapi/admin.py:51-53 declares /refunds with strict_slashes=False. An unauthenticated POST /admin/refunds/ with {"order_id":1,"amount_pence":1} returned HTTP 200 and performed a refund.

reason: The trailing-slash refund route bypasses the exact-path staff authorization check described in V03.

finding.title: JWT signing key is hardcoded in source
finding.description: SECRET_KEY is a fixed repository value. Anyone with source access (including a leaked package or deployment artifact) can mint valid HS256 bearer tokens for arbitrary users and roles; the key is not required to be supplied through deployment secrets.
finding.evidence: config.py:3 sets SECRET_KEY = "hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d". shopapi/auth.py:27 signs tokens with this key and :42 trusts it for every bearer request.

reason: It identifies the hardcoded SECRET_KEY in config.py, which can be used to forge signed tokens.

finding.title: Unauthenticated basket cookie enables pickle deserialization RCE
finding.description: The basket cookie is entirely client-controlled and is base64-decoded then passed to pickle.loads. A crafted cookie can execute arbitrary Python during every basket request, without authentication or a server-side signing key.
finding.evidence: shopapi/basket.py:15-23 reads request.cookies['basket'] and calls pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw)); /basket is public at :44-46. with_basket at :26-29 also issues unsigned pickle data, so there is no integrity protection.

reason: The finding identifies unauthenticated pickle deserialization of the client-controlled basket cookie in read_basket, enabling remote code execution.

finding.title: Passwords are stored as unsalted fast SHA-256 hashes
finding.description: Password hashing uses a single unsalted SHA-256 digest, which is optimized for speed and vulnerable to offline dictionary/rainbow-table cracking after a database compromise. A password-specific slow KDF such as Argon2id, scrypt, or bcrypt should be used.
finding.evidence: shopapi/auth.py:15-20 implements hash_password as hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() and compares the result directly; registration at :77 stores this value.

reason: It identifies the unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in shopapi/auth.py.

finding.title: Admin review report is SQL injectable through stored display names
finding.description: A customer's display_name is interpolated into a SQL string without escaping or parameter binding. A malicious display name can break out of the string and alter the report query when a staff member requests that customer's report; the admin path bypass above makes this particularly dangerous.
finding.evidence: shopapi/admin.py:74-80 loads customer-controlled display_name and builds f"... WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}' ORDER BY ...". Display names are accepted from registration/update and are not SQL-escaped.

reason: It identifies the second-order SQL injection in reviews_by_customer, where a customer-controlled display name is interpolated into the report query.

finding.title: SQL injection in product search endpoint
finding.description: The /products/search endpoint concatenates the q query parameter directly into a SQL LIKE clause using string concatenation rather than parameterized queries. An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL through the q parameter, bypass filters, extract data from other tables, or drop tables.
finding.evidence: GET /products/search?q='%20OR%201%3D1-- returns all 6 products (HTTP 200) instead of filtering by name. Code at line 41: "SELECT * FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%'" + q + "%' ..."

reason: It identifies SQL injection in the q parameter of GET /products/search, where the query is concatenated into SQL.

finding.title: Stored XSS via review body rendered with |safe in Jinja2 template
finding.description: Review bodies submitted by authenticated users through POST /products/<id>/reviews are stored in the database and rendered in the HTML template with the |safe filter, which bypasses Jinja2's auto-escaping. A malicious review containing JavaScript executes in any visitor's browser when viewing the product page.
finding.evidence: POST /products/1/reviews with {body: '<script>alert(1)</script>'} returned 201. Subsequent GET /p/MUG-SPECK returns the raw <script> tag unescaped inside the review-body div.

reason: It identifies stored XSS from raw review text rendered with |safe in product.html.

finding.title: Token refresh endpoint accepts forged JWTs (verify_signature=False)
