finding.description: The /auth/refresh endpoint decodes incoming JWTs with jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False}), accepting any arbitrary claims payload regardless of signature. It then creates a new signed Bearer token for whichever user ID appears in the sub claim, enabling privilege escalation.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/refresh with fabricated JWT payload {sub: 1, role: 'staff'} returned HTTP 200 with a valid signed Bearer token for user 1. Decoding the response confirms sub=1 and a proper HS256 signature.

reason: It identifies the refresh endpoint accepting unsigned JWTs and exchanging them for valid signed tokens.

finding.title: Hardcoded JWT signing secret in source code
finding.description: SECRET_KEY used to sign and verify JWTs is hardcoded as a plaintext string ('hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d'). Anyone with repository access can forge valid tokens for any user identity and role, completely undermining authentication.
finding.evidence: Line 3: SECRET_KEY = \"hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d\" – fixed plaintext string used for both jwt.encode() and jwt.decode() throughout auth.py.

reason: It identifies the hardcoded SECRET_KEY in config.py, which can be used to forge JWTs.

finding.title: Weak password-reset tokens generated with predictable PRNG
finding.description: Password-reset tokens use random.random() (Mersenne Twister, predictable) producing only 8-digit numeric codes (~27 bits of entropy). An attacker who intercepts or leaks a single token can brute-force all codes in minutes. The reset_confirm endpoint performs plain string comparison against this weak token.
finding.evidence: Line 135: token = '%08d' % int(random.random() * 10**8). No cryptographic randomness source (os.urandom/secrets) is used. Space limited to 10^8 possibilities.

reason: It identifies the predictable random.random() password-reset codes and their small brute-forceable space in reset_request/reset_confirm.

finding.title: Payment status timeout fails open as paid
finding.description: When the payment provider times out, confirm-payment explicitly sets status to paid and proceeds to processing. A transient outage or induced timeout therefore lets a customer obtain an order without confirmed payment.
finding.evidence: shopapi/payments.py:37-43 catches requests.Timeout, logs it, and sets status = "paid"; :44 then updates the order to processing and paid_pence = total_pence.

reason: The finding identifies confirm_payment treating a provider timeout as paid and processing the order without confirmed payment.

finding.title: User account enumeration via login endpoint
finding.description: Login returns different error messages for non-existent accounts ('no account with that email') versus wrong passwords ('wrong password'). An attacker can enumerate registered email addresses by probing the login endpoint with different payloads.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/login with nonexistent@example.com returned {'error': 'no account with that email'}. Same endpoint with priya.shah@mail.test but wrong password returned {'error': 'wrong password'}.

reason: The finding identifies login email enumeration caused by distinct errors for unknown accounts and incorrect passwords.

finding.title: Open CORS reflects any Origin with credentials enabled
finding.description: The cors after_request handler sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin to the requesting Origin without validating against a whitelist, while simultaneously setting Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. Any attacker-controlled site can make credentialed cross-origin requests to the application.
finding.evidence: GET /health with Origin: https://evil.example.com returned Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true and Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://evil.example.com.

reason: The after_request handler reflects arbitrary Origin values while allowing credentials, matching the CORS vulnerability in shopapi/__init__.py.

finding.title: Order details exposed via IDOR (insecure direct object reference)
finding.description: GET /orders/<order_id> retrieves and returns full order details using get_order(), which only checks existence—not that the requesting user owns it. Any authenticated user can view another user's orders including items, prices, payment status, and delivery dates.
finding.evidence: Logged in as Priya Shah (user_id=1), GET /orders/3 (owned by user_id=2) returned full order details: items=[BLANKET-WOOL x1], total_pence=4500, delivered_on='2026-10-24'. Compare to /orders list endpoint (line 42) which correctly filters by customer_id.

reason: It identifies the IDOR in show_order, where GET /orders/<id> uses get_order without checking that the requester owns the order.

finding.title: Insecure deserialization of basket cookie via pickle
finding.description: Basket cookies are deserialized using pickle.loads() on fully user-controlled binary data. While post-deserialization validation restricts results to dict type, certain pickle exploit chains can satisfy isinstance(data, dict) while still triggering code execution during unpickling. The cookie has no integrity protection beyond base64 encoding.
finding.evidence: Line 20: data = pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw)). Accepts user-controlled binary from cookie header. Result validation only checks isinstance(data, dict).

reason: It identifies the unsigned, user-controlled pickle deserialization in shopapi/basket.py that can enable remote code execution.

finding.title: Plaintext passwords logged in request bodies for mutating methods
finding.description: The log_request before_request handler logs the full body text of POST, PUT, and PATCH requests up to 2000 characters. This captures passwords from /auth/register, /auth/login, and sensitive PII from other forms.
finding.evidence: Line 31: log.info('%s %s %s', request.method, request.path, request.get_data(as_text=True)[:2000]) – captures complete JSON body including the password field during registration and login.

reason: The finding identifies log_request logging POST, PUT, and PATCH bodies, including passwords, which is V20.

finding.title: Payment confirmation marks unpaid order as paid on provider timeout
finding.description: When confirm-payment times out contacting the provider, the code assumes the payment succeeded (status='paid') and immediately transitions the order to 'processing' (shippable). Network failures, provider outages, or delays cause unpaid orders to ship without actual payment. Losses reconciled overnight per the comment.
finding.evidence: Lines 39-42: except requests.Timeout … status = 'paid', followed by UPDATE SET status='processing' (lines 44-45). No retry or pending state.

reason: It identifies confirm_payment treating a provider timeout as paid and processing the order without payment.

finding.title: Gift card redemption has TOCTOU race condition
finding.description: The redeem endpoint reads the gift card balance, validates against it, then updates the balance—all without a transaction. Two concurrent requests from the same user can read the same balance, both pass validation, and both debit the card, resulting in negative effective balance.
finding.evidence: Lines 36-43: Balance is read (line 36), validated (line 39), updated later (line 43) without BEGIN TRANSACTION. Parallel POST /giftcards/redeem requests could double-spend.

reason: The redeem function reads and validates the balance before updating it, allowing concurrent redemptions to overspend the gift card.

finding.title: Webhook signature only covers order_id, not event payload
finding.description: The webhook HMAC signature is computed from order_id only. An attacker who learns order_ids (via IDOR or elsewhere) can forge valid webhook signatures with arbitrary status and amount_pence values, marking unpaid orders as paid or forging refund amounts.
finding.evidence: Line 55: hmac.new(secret, str(order_id).encode(), hashlib.sha256). Event data (status, amount_pence) is not part of the signed input but is trusted after signature verification (lines 69-71).

reason: The webhook signature covers only the order ID, leaving status and amount fields unsigned and replayable.

finding.title: SQL injection in admin review report via display_name
finding.description: The admin reports/reviews endpoint constructs SQL using f-string interpolation with customer['display_name']. Attackers register with crafted display_names containing SQL metacharacters and trigger injection through this endpoint. Staff authorization protects the route but the token refresh vulnerability makes staff access trivially obtainable.
finding.evidence: Line 80: f\"WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}' ORDER BY r.id DESC\". Tested: registered user with display_name \"' OR '1'='1\", then requested /admin/reports/reviews?customer_id=14 which returned ALL reviews (7 rows) instead of just that customer's.

reason: It identifies the second-order SQL injection in the admin review report and also explicitly points to the forged-token refresh vulnerability.

finding.title: Passwords hashed with unsalted SHA-256
finding.description: Passwords are hashed using plain hashlib.sha256 with no salt, no iterations, and no pepper. All users with the same password have identical hashes, making rainbow table attacks practical. This also means the bcrypt/argon2 password_hash column design is wasted.
finding.evidence: Line 16: return hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest(). No salt or key stretching applied. Identical passwords produce identical hashes across users.

reason: The finding identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in shopapi/auth.py, matching V09.

finding.title: Flask debug mode enabled (debug=True)
finding.description: run.py runs Flask with debug=True, which enables the interactive debugger accessible via the console and exposes detailed traceback information. On a network-accessible deployment this could allow remote code execution via the debugger PIN feature.
finding.evidence: Line 6: app.run(host='127.0.0.1', port=5000, debug=True).

reason: The finding identifies debug=True in run.py, matching the planted Flask debug-mode vulnerability.

finding.title: JWT signing secret is hardcoded in source
finding.description: SECRET_KEY has a fixed source-controlled value. Anyone who obtains the repository can mint valid HS256 tokens for any existing user, bypassing password authentication and impersonating accounts.
finding.evidence: config.py:3 sets SECRET_KEY to "hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d" and auth.py:27 signs all bearer tokens with it; auth.py:42 trusts the same key for every request.

reason: The finding identifies the hardcoded JWT signing secret in config.py, which enables forged tokens.

finding.title: Password reset refreshes unsigned attacker-controlled JWTs
finding.description: The refresh endpoint decodes the supplied token with signature verification disabled and only checks that its subject belongs to a user. An attacker can submit an unsigned token naming any existing user and receive a valid signed session token for that account.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/refresh with an alg:none token whose payload is {"sub":1} returned 200 and a signed token; that token was accepted by GET /account. The vulnerable decode is at shopapi/auth.py:101-107.

reason: It identifies the refresh endpoint accepting unsigned attacker-controlled tokens and issuing valid signed tokens for arbitrary users.

finding.title: Unsigned basket cookie enables arbitrary pickle deserialization
finding.description: The basket cookie is entirely controlled by the client and is deserialized with pickle without a signature or integrity check. A crafted cookie can execute arbitrary Python code in the web process when any basket endpoint reads it.
finding.evidence: shopapi/basket.py:20 calls pickle.loads on request.cookies['basket']; shopapi/basket.py:27 creates the cookie without signing it. A base64-encoded pickle containing an os.system reducer was accepted by GET /basket (HTTP 200), demonstrating the attacker-controlled deserialization path.

reason: It identifies the unsigned, attacker-controlled basket cookie being unpickled in shopapi/basket.py, enabling remote code execution.

finding.title: Stored review XSS
finding.description: Authenticated users can submit review bodies that are later inserted into the product page with the Jinja safe filter. A reviewer can therefore execute JavaScript in every visitor’s browser.
finding.evidence: POST /products/1/reviews as a normal customer with body '<script>alert(document.domain)</script>' succeeded; GET /p/MUG-SPECK then returned that script verbatim inside the review-body div. Input is stored at shopapi/products.py:90 and rendered with |safe at shopapi/templates/product.html:13.

reason: It identifies stored review text rendered with |safe on the product page, enabling stored XSS.

finding.title: Order detail endpoint lacks ownership authorization
finding.description: The order detail route calls get_order directly instead of own_order, so any authenticated customer who guesses an order ID can read another customer’s order, items, payment totals, refunds, and delivery information.
finding.evidence: Authenticated Priya Shah requested GET /orders/3 and received Tom Okafor’s delivered order, including its BLANKET-WOOL item and payment totals. shopapi/orders.py:46-49 returns get_order(order_id) without checking customer_id.

reason: It identifies the IDOR in show_order, which returns an order without verifying that the requester owns it.

finding.title: Trailing-slash admin refund route bypasses staff check
finding.description: The global admin guard compares request.path to the set of exact route rules. The refund route disables strict slashes, so /admin/refunds/ reaches the handler while not matching the guard’s /admin/refunds path.
finding.evidence: A customer bearer token POSTed to /admin/refunds/ with an order and amount and received 200 with a refund recorded. The bypass is in shopapi/__init__.py:26-41; the slash-tolerant privileged handler is shopapi/admin.py:52-67.

reason: The exact-path admin guard is bypassed by the trailing-slash form of the slash-tolerant refund route.

finding.title: Product search is vulnerable to SQL injection
finding.description: The search term is concatenated directly into the SQL statement. An unauthenticated caller can alter the WHERE clause and potentially extract or modify database data depending on the database engine and query context.
finding.evidence: GET /products/search?q=%27+OR+1%3D1+-- returned all six products. The query is built by concatenating q at shopapi/products.py:40-42.

reason: The finding identifies SQL injection in the q parameter concatenated into the query by shopapi/products.py search.

finding.title: Payment status timeout fails open as paid
finding.description: If the payment provider times out, the exception handler sets status to paid and the order is moved to processing with paid_pence equal to the order total. A provider outage or induced timeout therefore allows fulfilment without confirmed payment.
finding.evidence: shopapi/payments.py:37-44 catches requests.Timeout, assigns status = 'paid', and updates the order to processing and fully paid. The comment explicitly describes the timeout as an expected provider condition.

reason: It identifies confirm_payment in shopapi/payments.py treating a provider timeout as paid and processing the order without confirmed payment.

finding.title: Editable local install of hf_payments bypasses supply chain controls
finding.description: The editable install (-e packages/hf_payments) pulls whatever source code exists at that path, bypassing version pinning and hash verification from the dependency index. Combined with lack of --require-hashes on regular deps, this reduces supply chain integrity assurance.
finding.evidence: Line 6: -e packages/hf_payments. Local pyproject.toml uses flit-core with dynamic version from git, confirming mutable local dependency.

reason: The editable install is a local development dependency, not the public-index dependency-confusion issue in V07, and the finding does not establish that the local source is attacker-controlled.

finding.title: Stored display name reaches an admin SQL query unsafely
finding.description: A customer controls display_name and can store SQL syntax in it. The staff review-report query interpolates that stored value into SQL, enabling a second-order SQL injection when staff view the report.
finding.evidence: A customer was able to set display_name to x' OR 1=1 -- via PATCH /account; the subsequent staff GET /admin/reports/reviews?customer_id=1 returned reviews matching the injected predicate. The vulnerable f-string is shopapi/admin.py:77-82.

reason: It identifies the second-order SQL injection in the admin review report using a customer-controlled stored display_name.

finding.title: Passwords use fast unsalted SHA-256
finding.description: Password hashes are generated with bare SHA-256 and no per-user salt or work factor. A database disclosure permits efficient offline cracking and makes identical passwords trivially identifiable.
finding.evidence: shopapi/auth.py:15-20 hashes passwords as hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() and compares the result directly. The same scheme is used to seed all demo accounts in scripts/seed.py:32-33.

reason: The finding identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in shopapi/auth.py’s hash_password function.

finding.title: Approved-host image fetch follows redirects without revalidation
finding.description: The URL allowlist and public-IP check apply only to the initial hostname. requests.get follows redirects by default, so an approved CDN or supplier URL that redirects to an internal address can make the server fetch internal resources.
finding.evidence: shopapi/images.py:28-35 validates only u.hostname, while shopapi/images.py:50 calls requests.get(url, ...) with the default redirect behavior and no validation of each redirect destination.

reason: It identifies the SSRF in shopapi/images.py where redirects are followed without validating the destination.

finding.title: Application entry point enables Flask debug mode
finding.description: Running the documented application entry point starts Flask with debug=True. In a deployed or accidentally exposed instance this can disclose stack traces and enable the Werkzeug interactive debugger, which can lead to code execution.
finding.evidence: run.py:5-6 calls app.run(host='127.0.0.1', port=5000, debug=True); there is no environment-gated production check.

reason: The finding identifies debug=True in run.py, matching the planted debug-mode vulnerability.

finding.title: Payment webhook trusts attacker-controlled payment amount
finding.description: After checking only a signature derived from the order ID, the webhook marks an awaiting order as processing and copies event.amount_pence into paid_pence without checking it against the order total or provider-side payment record. A validly accepted underpayment can therefore release the order.
finding.evidence: shopapi/payments.py:63 authenticates only webhook_signature(order_id), while lines 69-71 accept any paid event amount and write it directly to paid_pence. No comparison with orders.total_pence or a provider lookup is performed.

reason: The webhook authenticates only the order ID, then trusts the supplied payment amount without verifying it against the signed body or provider record.

finding.title: Product search is SQL injectable
finding.description: The q parameter is concatenated into a SQL LIKE expression instead of being bound as a parameter. This permits unauthenticated SQL injection and disclosure or manipulation depending on the database driver and query payload.
finding.evidence: GET /products/search?q=%27%20OR%201%3D1-- returned HTTP 200 with all six products, whereas the same endpoint normally limits results to matching rows. The vulnerable concatenation is at shopapi/products.py:368-369.

reason: It identifies SQL injection in the q parameter of GET /products/search, where the query is concatenated into SQL.

finding.title: Dependencies resolved from internal PyPI index without hash verification
finding.description: Requirements prioritize pypi.hartleyfinch.internal as the primary index with pypi.org as extra-index. No --require-hashes flag is used, meaning package contents are not cryptographically verified against known-good checksums. If the internal PyPI server is compromised, supply-chain injection is possible.
finding.evidence: Line 1: --index-url https://pypi.hartleyfinch.internal/simple (primary). No --require-hashes anywhere. Third-party deps lack hash pinning.

reason: It identifies the requirements configuration using public PyPI as an extra index without hash pinning, which is the dependency-confusion risk in V07, though its emphasis on compromise of the internal index is different.

finding.title: Order detail endpoint exposes any customer's order
finding.description: show_order calls get_order directly instead of own_order, so any authenticated user can read an order by enumerating its integer ID.
finding.evidence: GET /orders/3 with no Authorization header returned HTTP 200 and the other customer's order, including items, payment totals, status, and refund data. The missing ownership check is in show_order at shopapi/orders.py:271-273; the list and mutation endpoints use customer scoping.

reason: The finding identifies the missing ownership check in show_order, and its evidence that a request without a token succeeds also indicates the fail-open authentication check.

finding.title: Review bodies are stored and rendered as unrestricted HTML
finding.description: Review body input is stored without HTML sanitisation and rendered with the Jinja safe filter. A customer can therefore persist script markup that executes for every visitor to the product page.
finding.evidence: Authenticated POST /products/1/reviews with body `<script>alert(document.domain)</script>` returned 201; GET /p/MUG-SPECK then contained the same executable script. The input is stored at shopapi/products.py:418-419 and rendered with |safe at shopapi/templates/product.html:10.

reason: It identifies stored XSS in review bodies rendered with |safe on the product page.

finding.title: Refresh accepts unsigned attacker-selected identity claims
finding.description: The refresh endpoint decodes a supplied JWT with signature verification disabled and only checks that the referenced user exists. An attacker can submit an unsigned token with another user's sub claim and receive a freshly signed token for that account, including staff accounts.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/refresh with an unsigned JWT containing {"sub":3,"exp":future} returned HTTP 200 and a valid signed token whose claims identify user 3, the staff account. The disabled verification is at shopapi/auth.py:163-171.

reason: It identifies the refresh endpoint accepting unsigned attacker-selected identity claims and issuing a valid token.

finding.title: Staff review report interpolates a user-controlled display name into SQL
finding.description: A customer's display_name is copied into a SQL f-string. Any customer can set that name through /account, and a staff member viewing the report then causes the injected SQL to execute.
finding.evidence: I registered a user with display_name `x' OR 1=1 -- ` and requested /admin/reports/reviews?customer_id=4 as staff; the response returned the review matching the injected OR condition. The f-string is at shopapi/admin.py:767-770.

reason: It describes the second-order SQL injection in reviews_by_customer, where a customer-controlled display_name is interpolated into the report query.

finding.title: Passwords are stored with unsalted fast SHA-256
finding.description: Password hashes are bare SHA-256 digests with no salt or work factor. A database compromise permits highly efficient offline cracking, including reuse of the demo password across accounts.
finding.evidence: hash_password is exactly hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() at shopapi/auth.py:79-80, and the resulting value is stored in users.password_hash during registration and reset.

reason: The finding identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in hash_password, matching V09.

finding.title: Basket cookie deserialisation enables server-side code execution
finding.description: The basket cookie is attacker-controlled, only base64 encoded, and is passed directly to pickle.loads. Python pickle supports callable reduction objects, so a request can execute arbitrary code in the web process before the type check.
finding.evidence: read_basket decodes request.cookies['basket'] and calls pickle.loads at shopapi/basket.py:436-444. No signature, encryption, or safe data format is used; the cookie is created from pickle.dumps at lines 447-449.

reason: It identifies the unsigned, attacker-controlled basket cookie being unpickled in read_basket, enabling remote code execution.

finding.title: Request logging records credentials and secrets
finding.description: Every POST, PUT, and PATCH body is written to the application log, including login passwords, password reset submissions, bearer-adjacent sensitive data, gift-card codes, and payment/webhook payloads. Anyone with log access can recover those values.
finding.evidence: The before_request hook calls request.get_data(as_text=True) and logs up to 2000 bytes at shopapi/__init__.py:29-31. Authentication and reset endpoints accept passwords and reset codes in JSON bodies, so those values are captured verbatim.

reason: The request logger records POST, PUT, and PATCH bodies, including passwords and reset codes, exposing sensitive data in logs.

finding.title: Payment status timeout fails open as paid
finding.description: A timeout while querying the payment provider is converted into status='paid' and the order is moved to processing. A provider outage or induced timeout can therefore fulfil unpaid orders.
finding.evidence: The timeout handler at shopapi/payments.py:654-657 explicitly assigns status = 'paid', and lines 658-660 persist processing and paid_pence=total_pence. No provider confirmation or later compensating action is required before fulfilment.

reason: It identifies confirm_payment treating a provider-status timeout as paid and processing the order without payment.

finding.title: JWT signing key is hardcoded and shared by default
finding.description: The application uses a source-controlled constant as SECRET_KEY. Anyone who obtains the repository or package can mint valid HS256 bearer tokens for any user; there is no startup requirement for a deployment-specific secret.
finding.evidence: config.py:3 sets SECRET_KEY to `hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d`, and shopapi/auth.py:91/106 uses it to sign and verify all access tokens. The live refresh exploit also demonstrates that a newly signed token grants the selected user's current privileges.

reason: It identifies the hardcoded SECRET_KEY in config.py, which allows attackers with access to the source to forge valid tokens.

finding.title: Password reset codes are brute-forceable without throttling
finding.description: Reset codes are six-to-eight digit values generated with the non-cryptographic random module, and confirmation has no attempt limit, lockout, or rate limit. An attacker can repeatedly guess a live code during its 30-minute validity window.
finding.evidence: Codes are generated with random.random() at shopapi/auth.py:199, stored for 30 minutes at lines 200-203, and compared directly at lines 213-218. There is no failed-attempt counter or request throttling in either reset route.

reason: It identifies the predictable reset codes generated with random.random() and the lack of attempt limits that makes them brute-forceable.

finding.title: Token refresh accepts unsigned attacker-controlled JWT claims
finding.description: The refresh endpoint decodes the supplied JWT with signature verification disabled and only checks that the claimed subject maps to a user. Anyone can construct an unsigned token naming any existing user and obtain a valid signed session token for that user, including a staff account.
finding.evidence: auth.py:101 uses jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False}), then loads claims.sub and issues a new token. POST /auth/refresh with an unsigned JWT containing {"sub":1} returned HTTP 200 and a fresh HS256 token without any prior authentication.

reason: It identifies the refresh endpoint accepting unsigned JWT claims and issuing a valid token for the claimed user.

finding.title: Authentication decorator fails open when abort raises
finding.description: require_auth catches every Exception, including the abort(401) it raises for missing or invalid credentials, and then calls the protected view anyway with g.user set to None. This makes protected endpoints execute without authentication; endpoints that do not dereference g.user can disclose or modify data, while others return an unintended 500.
finding.evidence: The except block at lines 55-58 suppresses the authentication failure. GET /orders/1 with no Authorization header returned HTTP 200 and the complete order belonging to user 1. GET /giftcards/HFDEMO10 with no credentials also returned HTTP 200 and the card balance.

reason: It identifies require_auth catching abort(401) and continuing into protected routes without authentication, which is the fail-open vulnerability.

finding.title: Payment webhook uses a known default secret and trusts client-supplied amount
finding.description: WEBHOOK_SECRET falls back to a source-visible constant, and the webhook signature covers only order_id. After producing that signature, a caller can mark an order paid for any amount without comparing it to the order total or provider-side payment record.
finding.evidence: config.py:8 sets WEBHOOK_SECRET to `whsec-local`; shopapi/payments.py:668-670 signs only order_id and lines 684-686 assign int(event.amount_pence) without validation. Using HMAC(`whsec-local`, `4`) I POSTed {order_id:4,status:'paid',amount_pence:1} to /webhooks/payments and received 200; /orders/4 then showed status processing and paid_pence 1 despite total_pence 1200.

reason: The webhook signs only the order ID while trusting the supplied status and amount, allowing a valid signature to be replayed with altered payment details.

finding.title: Checkout never reserves or decrements inventory
finding.description: Checkout creates order items from the basket without checking product stock or updating it. Repeated or concurrent checkouts can therefore sell any quantity regardless of the catalogue's stock limit.
finding.evidence: basket_json reads product price but not stock at shopapi/basket.py:453-462; checkout then inserts every item at lines 490-494 without a stock predicate or stock update. The live catalogue exposes finite stock values through /products, but checkout does not enforce them.

reason: The checkout inventory-overselling issue is a real weakness in shopapi/basket.py but is distinct from the keyed return/refund flaw.

finding.title: JWT signing key is hardcoded in source
finding.description: SECRET_KEY is a fixed, repository-visible string. Anyone who obtains the source or deployment package can forge HS256 access tokens, including tokens for staff users (and the refresh endpoint independently worsens this). The key should be supplied from a protected deployment secret and rotated.
finding.evidence: config.py:3 sets SECRET_KEY = "hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d" with no environment or secret-manager lookup. make_token and user_from_request use this key for all bearer tokens.

reason: It identifies the hardcoded JWT signing secret in config.py that can be used to forge tokens.

finding.title: Order detail endpoint exposes any order
finding.description: show_order calls get_order rather than own_order, so it does not verify that the authenticated requester owns the requested order. Combined with the fail-open decorator this is directly unauthenticated, and even with a valid account it is an IDOR across customers.
finding.evidence: GET /orders/1 without credentials returned HTTP 200 with order 1's items, total, payment amount, and delivery data. The route uses get_order(order_id) at line 49, whereas the ownership-checking helper is own_order().

reason: The finding identifies the IDOR in show_order (V01) and also describes the fail-open authentication decorator allowing unauthenticated access (V22).

finding.title: Trailing-slash admin refund route bypasses global staff check
finding.description: The application protects admin routes by comparing request.path to the set of registered rule strings. The refund route explicitly accepts both slash forms (strict_slashes=False), but only the canonical rule is in admin_paths. A request to the trailing-slash variant therefore skips staff_only_admin and reaches the privileged refund operation without authentication.
finding.evidence: POST /admin/refunds/ with no Authorization header and JSON {"order_id":3,"amount_pence":1} returned HTTP 200 {"ok":true,"refunded_pence":1}. The route is declared at admin.py:52 with strict_slashes=False, while the global check in shopapi/__init__.py:36-41 compares exact request.path values.

reason: The trailing-slash refund route bypasses the exact-path staff check, matching the admin access-control flaw in V03.

finding.title: Production installation trusts an unaudited private index and unhashed packages
finding.description: The production requirements use a private package index before PyPI, allow fallback to public PyPI, and provide no hashes. The separately published hf-payments package has an unpinned requests dependency and a build requirement of setuptools>=61, allowing dependency or build-tool drift and supply-chain substitution during deployment.
finding.evidence: requirements.txt:13-19 configures the private index plus public extra index with version pins but no hashes; packages/hf_payments/pyproject.toml:31 and :34 leave requests and setuptools range-resolved. The deployment README directs production to install this file.

reason: It identifies the public extra index alongside the internal hf-payments package and lack of hash pinning, which creates dependency-confusion risk.

finding.title: Product search is SQL injectable
finding.description: The search term is concatenated directly into a SQL LIKE expression instead of being passed as a parameter. An attacker can alter the WHERE clause, extract information through SQL behavior, or cause query errors.
finding.evidence: products.py:40-42 builds SQL using q directly. GET /products/search?q=%27%20OR%201%3D1%20-- returned all six products rather than only matching products, demonstrating WHERE-clause injection.

reason: The finding identifies SQL injection in the search query built from the q parameter in shopapi/products.py.

finding.title: Customer display names reach an admin SQL query unescaped
finding.description: The moderation report interpolates customer.display_name into a SQL string. A customer can set their own display name through the account endpoint, then a staff member viewing the report causes that stored value to be interpreted as SQL.
finding.evidence: admin.py:80 constructs f"WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}' ORDER BY...". display_name is user-controlled via auth.py:119-125 and is not SQL-escaped or parameterized.

reason: The finding describes the second-order SQL injection in the admin reviews report using a customer-controlled stored display name.

finding.title: Review bodies are stored and rendered as unsafe HTML
finding.description: Review text is accepted from authenticated users and stored, but the template renders it with |safe. A reviewer can persist arbitrary HTML/JavaScript in product pages, causing stored XSS for every visitor and potentially staff users.
finding.evidence: products.py:83-91 inserts the supplied body without sanitization; product.html:13 renders r.body|safe. The review limit is only a length check and does not remove markup or scripts.

reason: It identifies stored XSS from unsanitized review text rendered with |safe in product.html.

finding.title: Payment status timeout fails open to paid
finding.description: When the payment provider times out, the endpoint sets status = "paid" and transitions the order to processing instead of leaving it awaiting payment. A provider outage or induced timeout therefore permits fulfillment without confirmed payment.
finding.evidence: payments.py:39-42 catches requests.Timeout and assigns status = "paid"; lines 43-46 then mark the order processing and paid_pence equal to total_pence.

reason: It identifies the payment confirmation timeout being treated as paid, allowing an order to be processed without confirmed payment.

finding.title: CORS reflects arbitrary origins while allowing credentials
finding.description: Every request Origin is copied into Access-Control-Allow-Origin and credentials are enabled. A malicious web page can make credentialed cross-origin requests to this API; this is especially dangerous if browser-managed credentials are later introduced and is not a valid restricted CORS policy.
finding.evidence: GET /health with Origin: https://evil.example returned Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://evil.example and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. The code performs unconditional reflection at lines 45-50 and config.py:12 enables credentials.

reason: It identifies the unconditional Origin reflection with credentials in the CORS after_request handler.

finding.title: Request logging records sensitive POST bodies
finding.description: The request hook logs up to 2,000 characters of every POST/PUT/PATCH body. This includes login passwords, password-reset codes and new passwords, bearer-like secrets, payment data if added to requests, and personal information, exposing them to application log readers and retained log systems.
finding.evidence: shopapi/__init__.py:30-31 calls request.get_data(as_text=True) and logs it for every mutating request. The login and reset endpoints accept passwords/codes in JSON bodies at auth.py:84-93 and 129-159.

reason: It identifies the request logger in shopapi/__init__.py logging sensitive request bodies, matching V20.

finding.title: Payment webhook trusts attacker-supplied amount
finding.description: The webhook signature covers only the order_id, not the event status or amount. Anyone able to produce/replay a valid order-id signature can submit a paid event with an arbitrary amount, and the server stores that amount as paid_pence without checking it against the order total or provider response.
finding.evidence: webhook_signature() at lines 53-55 signs only str(order_id). payment_webhook at lines 69-71 accepts event.amount_pence via int() and writes it directly to paid_pence. The test request shape in tests/test_shop.py:103-104 demonstrates that amount is supplied independently from the signature.

reason: The webhook signs only the order ID while trusting the supplied status and amount, allowing a valid signature to be replayed with altered payment data.

finding.title: Authentication decorator fails open after authentication errors
finding.description: require_auth catches the exception raised by abort(401), clears g.user, and still invokes the protected handler. Protected endpoints that do not perform their own user check can therefore execute without authentication.
finding.evidence: The except block at shopapi/auth.py:55-58 catches authentication failures and calls the wrapped handler. GET /orders/1 without an Authorization header returned HTTP 200; GET /account without authentication reached the handler and returned HTTP 500 rather than 401.

reason: It identifies require_auth in shopapi/auth.py catching abort(401) and allowing unauthenticated requests to reach protected handlers.

finding.title: Password reset codes use predictable non-cryptographic randomness without throttling
finding.description: Reset codes are generated with random.random(), which is not suitable for security tokens, and the confirmation endpoint has no attempt limit or lockout. An attacker can repeatedly guess the eight-digit code during its 30-minute validity window, while a predictable PRNG state can further reduce the search space.
finding.evidence: auth.py:135 generates the code from random.random() rather than secrets/system randomness; reset_confirm compares guesses at lines 149-153 and has no rate-limit or attempt counter.

reason: It identifies the predictable reset-code generation and lack of attempt limits in reset_request/reset_confirm.

finding.title: Trailing-slash admin refund route bypasses staff authorization
finding.description: The staff-only before_request check compares request.path to the registered route strings. The refund route accepts both slash forms via strict_slashes=False, but only the no-slash form is in admin_paths, so /admin/refunds/ reaches the privileged handler without authorization.
finding.evidence: POST /admin/refunds/ with {"order_id":3,"amount_pence":1} and no authentication returned HTTP 200 and created a refund, while an unauthenticated request to GET /admin/users returned HTTP 403. The route is defined at shopapi/admin.py:52-67.

reason: It identifies the trailing-slash /admin/refunds/ route bypassing the staff-only check.

finding.title: Client-controlled basket cookie is deserialized with pickle
finding.description: The basket cookie is controlled by the client and is passed to pickle.loads after only Base64 decoding. A malicious pickle can execute attacker-supplied Python code whenever a basket endpoint processes the cookie.
finding.evidence: read_basket at shopapi/basket.py:15-23 reads request.cookies['basket'] and calls pickle.loads without a signature or MAC. The cookie is generated with pickle.dumps at lines 26-29, but client input is not authenticated before deserialization.

reason: The finding identifies unauthenticated deserialization of the client-controlled basket cookie with pickle in read_basket, enabling remote code execution.

finding.title: Order details lack an ownership check
finding.description: show_order calls get_order directly instead of own_order. Any request reaching the endpoint can retrieve another customer's order details, including items, payment amounts, refunds, and delivery information.
finding.evidence: own_order with the customer ownership check is defined at shopapi/orders.py:32-36, but show_order calls get_order at line 49. GET /orders/1 without authentication returned HTTP 200 with the complete order record.

reason: The finding identifies the ownership-check bypass in show_order, and its unauthenticated-access evidence also describes the fail-open authentication bug.

finding.title: Token refresh accepts unsigned attacker-controlled claims
finding.description: The refresh endpoint disables JWT signature verification, trusts the unverified sub claim, and issues a newly signed token for that user. An attacker can therefore obtain a valid session token for any existing account, including staff accounts.
finding.evidence: shopapi/auth.py:101 calls jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False}) and lines 104-107 load the user and issue a new token. POST /auth/refresh with the unsigned token eyJhbGciOiJub25lIiwidHlwIjoiSldUIn0.eyJzdWIiOjF9. returned HTTP 200 and a signed token for user 1.

reason: The finding identifies refresh disabling JWT signature verification and issuing a signed token for the unverified subject, matching V17.

finding.title: Stored display names are interpolated into the admin review-report SQL query
finding.description: A customer can set a display name containing SQL syntax through the account endpoint. The admin review report later inserts that stored value into an f-string SQL query, allowing the customer to cause SQL errors or inject report-query SQL when staff view the report.
finding.evidence: update_account stores the user-controlled display_name at shopapi/auth.py:119-125, and reviews_by_customer interpolates customer['display_name'] into SQL at shopapi/admin.py:77-80 instead of binding it as a parameter.

reason: It identifies the second-order SQL injection in reviews_by_customer, where a customer-controlled stored display name is interpolated into the report query.

finding.title: Payment-provider timeouts mark orders as paid
finding.description: When the payment-status request times out, the exception handler assigns status='paid' and the normal success path changes the order to processing and records the full order total as paid. A provider outage can therefore cause fulfillment of an unpaid order.
finding.evidence: shopapi/payments.py:39-45 catches requests.Timeout, sets status to paid, and updates the order to processing with paid_pence=total_pence without provider confirmation.

reason: It identifies the payment timeout in confirm_payment being treated as success, causing an unpaid order to be marked paid and processed.

finding.title: Product search is vulnerable to SQL injection
finding.description: The search term is concatenated directly into the SQL statement. An unauthenticated attacker can alter the query, trigger database errors, or attempt UNION-based access to other tables.
finding.evidence: shopapi/products.py:40-42 concatenates q into the SQL query. GET /products/search?q=%27%20UNION%20SELECT%20id%2Cemail%2Cpassword_hash%2C0%2C0%2C0%20FROM%20users-- returned HTTP 500, demonstrating that attacker-controlled SQL reached SQLite.

reason: It identifies the concatenated search query in GET /products/search as SQL injection.

finding.title: Stored XSS in product reviews
finding.description: Authenticated users can submit arbitrary review bodies, which are stored without sanitization and rendered with Jinja's safe filter. Submitted HTML or script content can execute in every visitor's browser on the product page.
finding.evidence: shopapi/products.py:82-91 stores the review body directly. shopapi/templates/product.html:13 renders r.body with {{ r.body|safe }}.

reason: The finding identifies stored review XSS caused by saving review bodies raw and rendering them with the safe filter.

finding.title: Image importer follows redirects without revalidating the destination
finding.description: The importer validates only the initial approved hostname and its resolved addresses. requests.get follows redirects by default, so an approved public image host can redirect the server to an internal address or cloud metadata endpoint, which is not checked again.
finding.evidence: check_url at shopapi/images.py:28-35 validates only the original URL, while line 50 calls requests.get(url, timeout=10, stream=True) with default redirect handling and no final-URL validation.

reason: It identifies the SSRF in shopapi/images.py: the initial URL is validated, but redirects can reach unchecked internal addresses.

finding.title: Gift-card redemption permits concurrent double spending
finding.description: Redemption checks the balance, records a redemption, and updates the balance in separate operations without a conditional debit or row lock. Concurrent requests can both pass the balance check and redeem more than the card's original value.
finding.evidence: shopapi/giftcards.py:36-43 reads the card balance, computes new_balance, inserts the redemption, and later writes the balance. There is no atomic UPDATE ... WHERE balance_pence >= amount guard or locking transaction.

reason: The finding identifies the race condition in gift-card redemption where concurrent requests can overspend the balance.

finding.title: Password-reset codes use weak randomness and have no guessing controls
finding.description: Reset codes are generated with the non-cryptographic random.random() PRNG and remain valid for 30 minutes. Confirmation has no failed-attempt counter, throttling, or lockout, permitting unlimited online guesses against the eight-digit code.
finding.evidence: shopapi/auth.py:135 generates the code with random.random(); lines 149-154 validate only existence, expiry, and equality. No attempt limit or rate limiting is applied to /auth/reset/confirm.

reason: It identifies the predictable reset-code generation and lack of guessing limits in reset confirmation.

finding.title: Payment webhook signature does not cover status or amount
finding.description: The webhook HMAC authenticates only order_id. The status and amount_pence fields are trusted separately, so a valid signature can be replayed or paired with a modified amount, and the amount is recorded without comparison to the order total.
finding.evidence: webhook_signature at shopapi/payments.py:53-55 signs only str(order_id), while payment_webhook at lines 69-71 stores int(event.get('amount_pence', 0)) directly and does not compare it with total_pence.

reason: The webhook authenticates only the order ID, allowing status and amount to be altered or replayed without being covered by the signature.

finding.title: Passwords are stored as unsalted SHA-256 hashes
finding.description: Password hashing uses a fast, unsalted SHA-256 digest rather than an adaptive password-hashing algorithm such as Argon2id, scrypt, or bcrypt. A database compromise enables efficient offline cracking.
finding.evidence: hash_password at shopapi/auth.py:15-16 returns hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest(), and registration stores it at lines 77-78.

reason: It identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in hash_password, matching V09.

finding.title: Hardcoded JWT signing secret enables token forgery
finding.description: HS256 JWTs use a fixed source-controlled secret. Anyone who obtains the repository or deployed source can forge tokens for arbitrary user IDs and roles, bypassing authentication and potentially impersonating staff.
finding.evidence: config.py:3 defines SECRET_KEY = 'hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d'; shopapi/auth.py:27 signs tokens and lines 42-45 validate them using this value.

reason: It identifies the hardcoded JWT signing secret in config.py, which can be used to forge tokens.

finding.title: Application starts Flask's development debugger by default
finding.description: The provided executable entry point runs Flask with debug=True. If exposed in a deployment, unhandled exceptions can disclose sensitive internals through the Werkzeug debugger and may enable code execution if its console protection is bypassed.
finding.evidence: run.py:6 calls app.run(host='127.0.0.1', port=5000, debug=True).

reason: It identifies debug=True in run.py, which enables the Flask development debugger.

finding.title: Request logging records passwords and other sensitive request bodies
finding.description: Every POST, PUT, and PATCH body is logged, including login and registration passwords, reset codes, new passwords, and personal or payment-related data. These secrets may be retained in logs and exposed to log readers or aggregators.
finding.evidence: shopapi/__init__.py:29-31 logs request.get_data(as_text=True)[:2000] for every mutating request. Authentication and reset endpoints accept credentials in these bodies at shopapi/auth.py:66-93 and :143-159.

reason: The finding identifies log_request recording request bodies, including credentials, matching V20.

finding.title: Authentication failures are swallowed, allowing protected handlers to execute
finding.description: require_auth catches abort(401) and other authentication exceptions, sets g.user to None, and still invokes the protected handler. Protected handlers that do not immediately dereference g.user can therefore be reached without authentication.
finding.evidence: The decorator aborts at lines 53-54 when no user exists, but the broad except at lines 55-57 catches the exception and execution continues to f(*args, **kwargs). GET /orders/1 without an Authorization header returned HTTP 200 with the complete order record.

reason: The require_auth decorator catches abort(401) and continues to the protected handler, allowing unauthenticated access.

finding.title: Token refresh accepts unsigned attacker-controlled JWT claims
finding.description: The refresh endpoint disables JWT signature verification and uses the untrusted sub claim to load a user before issuing a newly signed token. An attacker who knows a user ID can mint a valid session token for that account, including staff accounts.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/refresh reaches jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False}) and then load_user(claims.get('sub')) before make_token(user). The existing token must be cryptographically validated, or refresh must use a separately validated refresh-token mechanism.

reason: It identifies the unsigned-token verification flaw in the /auth/refresh endpoint that lets an attacker obtain a signed token for another user.

finding.title: Default webhook secret enables forged payment events
finding.description: WEBHOOK_SECRET falls back to the source-controlled value whsec-local. Deployments that do not override it allow anyone who knows the application source/defaults to generate valid webhook signatures and alter payment state.
finding.evidence: config.py:8 sets WEBHOOK_SECRET = os.environ.get('WEBHOOK_SECRET', 'whsec-local'); shopapi/payments.py:53-64 uses it to authenticate payment webhooks.

reason: The source-controlled default webhook secret is a separate real weakness that enables forged signatures, distinct from V19’s flaw of signing only the order ID and trusting the remaining webhook body.

finding.title: Unauthenticated insecure deserialization of the basket cookie
finding.description: The basket cookie is client-controlled, unsigned, and directly passed to pickle.loads. A crafted pickle can execute arbitrary code in the web process when any basket endpoint reads the cookie.
finding.evidence: read_basket() calls pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw)) at line 20, while with_basket() stores a bare pickle at lines 26-28 without a MAC or authenticated encryption. Basket endpoints such as GET /basket invoke read_basket without authentication.

reason: The finding identifies unauthenticated unpickling of the client-controlled basket cookie in read_basket, which can enable remote code execution.

finding.title: Product search is vulnerable to SQL injection
finding.description: The q query parameter is concatenated directly into the SQL statement, allowing an attacker to alter the WHERE clause and retrieve unintended product records.
finding.evidence: The query is built by concatenating q into both LIKE expressions rather than binding it. GET /products/search?q=%27%20OR%201%3D1-- returned all six products instead of a normal matching subset.

reason: The finding identifies SQL injection in the q parameter of GET /products/search, where user input is concatenated into the query.

finding.title: Order details lack an ownership check
finding.description: The order detail endpoint calls get_order() directly instead of own_order(), so an authenticated customer can retrieve another customer's order details. Because require_auth also fails open, the endpoint is currently accessible without authentication.
finding.evidence: show_order() returns order_json(get_order(order_id)); the ownership check exists only in own_order(). GET /orders/1 without credentials returned status, item quantities and prices, payment amount, and refunds.

reason: The finding identifies the missing ownership check in show_order (V01) and also describes require_auth failing open (V22).

finding.title: Trailing-slash refund route bypasses staff authorization
finding.description: The global admin authorization compares request.path against exact route strings. The refund route accepts both slash forms, but only /admin/refunds is in the collected route set; the handler has no in-handler authorization check.
finding.evidence: The route is declared strict_slashes=False at shopapi/admin.py:52 while staff_only_admin checks exact membership at lines 36-40. POST /admin/refunds/ without credentials with {"order_id":1,"amount_pence":1} returned HTTP 200 and created a refund.

reason: It identifies the trailing-slash route bypassing the exact-path staff authorization check for /admin/refunds.

finding.title: Stored cross-site scripting in product reviews
finding.description: Review bodies are stored without sanitization and rendered with Jinja's safe filter. An authenticated user can submit markup or script that executes for visitors viewing the product page.
finding.evidence: add_review() inserts the supplied body directly at shopapi/products.py:90-91, and product.html renders r.body|safe at line 13.

reason: It identifies stored XSS from unsanitized review bodies rendered with |safe on the product page.

finding.title: Stored display names reach an administrative SQL query without parameterization
finding.description: A customer can set a display name containing SQL syntax. When staff later request the review report for that customer, the stored name is interpolated into SQL, allowing the customer-controlled value to alter the report query and disclose other reviews.
finding.evidence: update_account() stores display_name with a parameterized update, but reviews_by_customer() constructs f"WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}' ORDER BY r.id DESC" at lines 77-80. A name such as ' OR 1=1-- changes the SQL predicate.

reason: The finding identifies second-order SQL injection in reviews_by_customer via the customer-controlled stored display_name.

finding.title: Checkout ignores product stock
finding.description: Checkout calculates totals from the client basket and creates order items without checking or decrementing product stock. A customer can therefore order arbitrary quantities up to the basket limit even when inventory is zero or insufficient.
finding.evidence: basket_json at shopapi/basket.py:32-41 reads prices but not stock, and checkout inserts the order and items at lines 69-73 without a stock validation or inventory update.

reason: Checkout appears to create orders without validating or decrementing inventory, a real business-logic flaw not listed among the keyed vulnerabilities.

finding.title: Payment provider timeout fails open as paid
finding.description: When the payment provider times out, confirm_payment() treats the order as paid and moves it to processing. An outage or induced timeout can therefore allow an unpaid order to proceed.
finding.evidence: The requests.Timeout handler assigns status = "paid" at lines 39-42, and lines 43-45 set status to processing and paid_pence equal to total_pence.

reason: The finding describes confirm_payment treating a provider timeout as paid and processing the order, matching V23.

finding.title: JWT signing key is hardcoded in source
finding.description: SECRET_KEY is a fixed literal committed to the repository. Anyone who obtains the source or deployed package can forge HS256 tokens for arbitrary users and roles, including staff.
finding.evidence: config.py:3 sets SECRET_KEY = "hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d"; shopapi/auth.py:27 signs tokens and shopapi/auth.py:42 verifies them with this value.

reason: The finding identifies the hardcoded SECRET_KEY in config.py, which enables forging signed JWTs.

finding.title: Passwords are stored using unsalted SHA-256
finding.description: Passwords are stored as fast, unsalted general-purpose hashes rather than a salted password KDF. A database compromise permits efficient offline dictionary attacks and identical passwords have identical hashes.
finding.evidence: hash_password() returns hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() at lines 15-16; the result is stored during registration at lines 77-78 and reset at lines 158-159.

reason: The finding identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in shopapi/auth.py hash_password.

finding.title: Payment webhook signature does not bind status or amount
finding.description: The webhook MAC covers only order_id, while status and amount_pence are trusted from the unsigned JSON body. A party able to obtain or replay a valid signature for an order can change a payment to paid with a zero or partial amount.
finding.evidence: webhook_signature() hashes only str(order_id) at lines 53-55. The paid branch trusts event.get('status') and int(event.get('amount_pence', 0)) and sets processing at lines 69-71 without comparing the amount to total_pence or binding those fields into the MAC.

reason: The webhook MAC covers only the order ID, leaving the payment status and amount unbound and trusted from the request body.

finding.title: Login enables account enumeration and has no brute-force protection
finding.description: Login returns distinct responses for nonexistent and existing accounts and contains no rate limiting or lockout, allowing attackers to identify valid accounts and repeatedly guess passwords.
finding.evidence: A missing user returns "no account with that email" at lines 89-90, whereas an existing user with a wrong password returns "wrong password" at lines 91-92.

reason: The finding identifies the login endpoint’s distinct responses for unknown users versus wrong passwords and its lack of rate limiting or lockout.

finding.title: Payment webhook has a predictable default signing secret
finding.description: WEBHOOK_SECRET falls back to the hardcoded value whsec-local. Any deployment that omits the environment override allows an attacker to forge payment events and change order state.
finding.evidence: config.py:8 defines os.environ.get("WEBHOOK_SECRET", "whsec-local"); payment_webhook() authenticates events using that setting at shopapi/payments.py:53-64.

reason: A predictable default webhook secret is a real weakness, but it is distinct from the listed JWT secret and the webhook signature’s failure to cover the body.

finding.title: Password reset codes are predictable and have no attempt limiting
finding.description: Reset codes use Mersenne-Twister random.random(), have only eight decimal digits, remain valid for 30 minutes, and failed guesses are neither rate-limited nor counted. Attackers can brute-force the reset code or potentially predict it.
finding.evidence: reset_request() generates the code with int(random.random() * 10**8) at lines 135-136. reset_confirm() only compares the supplied code at lines 149-154 and has no throttling, attempt counter, or lockout.

reason: It identifies predictable, short password-reset codes generated with random.random() and lacking attempt limits in reset_request/reset_confirm.

finding.title: Request logging records passwords and reset codes
finding.description: Every mutating request body is logged, including login passwords and password-reset codes. Log retention or access can therefore expose credentials and account-recovery secrets.
finding.evidence: log_request() logs request.get_data(as_text=True)[:2000] for all POST, PUT, and PATCH requests at lines 29-31. The login and reset endpoints accept their secrets in those bodies.

reason: The finding identifies log_request logging request bodies containing credentials, matching V20.

finding.title: Dependency installation permits public-index dependency confusion
finding.description: pip is configured with an internal index and public PyPI as an extra index, without constraining hf-payments to the internal source. A malicious public package with the same distribution name and a winning version could execute code during installation or use.
finding.evidence: requirements.txt lines 1-2 set --index-url to the internal repository and --extra-index-url to pypi.org. Line 7 installs hf-payments by name, and packages/hf_payments/pyproject.toml identifies the local distribution with that same name.

reason: The requirements configure public PyPI as an extra index while installing the internal hf-payments package by name, enabling dependency confusion.

finding.title: Unauthenticated basket cookie is deserialized with pickle
finding.description: The basket cookie is only base64 encoded and is not authenticated before being passed to pickle.loads. An attacker can send a crafted cookie whose pickle payload executes arbitrary Python code in the application process during any request that reads the basket.
finding.evidence: raw = request.cookies.get(COOKIE); data = pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw))

reason: The unauthenticated basket cookie is unpickled from attacker-controlled data, enabling remote code execution.

finding.title: Product search concatenates the query into SQL
finding.description: The public search parameter is inserted directly into a SQL statement. SQL metacharacters can change the query and potentially expose or modify database data, depending on the SQLite statement context.
finding.evidence: "SELECT * FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%" + q + "%' OR sku LIKE '%" + q + "%' ORDER BY name LIMIT 50"

reason: The finding identifies SQL injection in shopapi/products.py search by concatenating the query parameter into SQL.

finding.title: Checkout ignores and does not decrement product stock
finding.description: Checkout creates order items from the basket without checking current inventory or decrementing stock. Customers can repeatedly order unlimited quantities, including products whose stock is zero.
finding.evidence: basket_json() reads price and quantity but never checks p['stock']; checkout() inserts the order and order_items at lines 69-73 and performs no stock update anywhere in the transaction.

reason: Checkout’s failure to validate or decrement stock enables inventory overselling, a real business-logic weakness not listed in the key.

finding.title: Order details can be read by any authenticated customer
finding.description: show_order loads an order by the supplied ID but never checks that it belongs to the authenticated user. Any customer who can guess or learn another order ID can read its status, prices, items, payment totals, and refunds.
finding.evidence: return jsonify(order_json(get_order(order_id)))

reason: The finding identifies the IDOR in show_order, which loads an order by ID without checking that it belongs to the authenticated customer.

finding.title: Cancellation and return quantities can both be refunded
finding.description: Cancellation and return flows track quantities independently. The same units can therefore be cancelled and later returned, producing multiple refunds for the same merchandise.
finding.evidence: cancel_items() validates only cancelled_qty at lines 65-67, while return_items() validates only returned_qty at lines 91-93. Neither validation subtracts units already cancelled or returned.

reason: The return validation ignores cancelled quantities, allowing already-refunded cancelled units to be returned and refunded again.

finding.title: Customer-controlled display names reach an admin SQL query
finding.description: A customer can set display_name through the account endpoint, and the reports endpoint interpolates that value into SQL. A malicious customer name can therefore inject SQL when staff request the review report for that customer.
finding.evidence: f"WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}' ORDER BY r.id DESC"

reason: The finding identifies the second-order SQL injection in reviews_by_customer, where a customer-controlled display_name is interpolated into the admin report query.

finding.title: Review bodies are rendered as trusted HTML
finding.description: Authenticated users can submit arbitrary review text, but the product template renders it with the safe filter. A reviewer can store markup or script that executes for visitors to the product page, including staff or other customers.
finding.evidence: {{ r.body|safe }}

reason: The product template renders stored review bodies with the safe filter, allowing stored XSS.

finding.title: Token refresh trusts an unsigned user identity
finding.description: The refresh endpoint explicitly disables signature verification and then issues a signed token for the user ID in the attacker-supplied claims. User IDs are sequential, so an attacker can submit an unsigned token naming another account and obtain a valid token for that account (including staff).
finding.evidence: claims = jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False}); user = load_user(claims.get("sub")); return jsonify(token=make_token(user))

reason: The refresh endpoint disables signature verification and issues a valid token for the attacker-supplied user identity, including staff accounts.

finding.title: JWT signing key is hardcoded in source
finding.description: The application uses a source-controlled constant as the HS256 signing key. Anyone who obtains the repository can mint valid tokens for arbitrary users, including staff users, and access all bearer-token protected functionality.
finding.evidence: SECRET_KEY = "hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d"

reason: The finding identifies the hardcoded JWT signing secret in config.py, which allows token forgery.

finding.title: Payment-status timeout is treated as successful payment
finding.description: If the payment provider times out, the endpoint fails open by setting status to paid and processing the order without receiving confirmation. A customer can cause or exploit provider/network timeouts to obtain fulfillment without a verified payment.
finding.evidence: except requests.Timeout: ... status = "paid"

reason: The finding identifies confirm_payment treating a provider timeout as successful payment and processing the order without confirmation.

finding.title: Passwords are stored as unsalted SHA-256 hashes
finding.description: Password hashes use a fast, unsalted general-purpose hash. A database compromise permits efficient offline cracking and identical passwords produce identical hashes; a password KDF such as Argon2id, scrypt, or bcrypt with a unique salt is required for resistant storage.
finding.evidence: return hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest()

reason: The finding identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password storage in shopapi/auth.py's hash_password function.

finding.title: Authentication failures are swallowed by the auth decorator
finding.description: abort(401) raises an exception that is caught by the broad handler, after which the protected view is still called with g.user set to None. This bypasses the intended authentication gate; the gift-card balance view then returns data without using g.user, allowing unauthenticated balance lookups when a card code is known.
finding.evidence: except Exception: ... g.user = None; return f(*args, **kwargs)

reason: The finding identifies require_auth swallowing abort(401) and allowing unauthenticated requests through, which is V22.

finding.title: Passwordless token refresh accepts unsigned JWT claims
finding.description: The refresh endpoint disables signature verification and trusts the supplied sub claim before issuing a newly signed token. An unauthenticated attacker can submit an unsigned JWT naming any existing user and obtain a valid token for that account, including a staff account.
finding.evidence: claims = jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False}); user = load_user(claims.get("sub")); return jsonify(token=make_token(user))

reason: The refresh endpoint disables JWT signature verification and issues a signed token for the supplied subject, enabling account takeover.

finding.title: Hard-coded JWT signing secret
finding.description: The application uses a source-controlled, fixed value as the HS256 signing key. Anyone who obtains the repository can mint valid authentication tokens, including tokens for staff accounts.
finding.evidence: SECRET_KEY = "hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d"

reason: The finding identifies the hardcoded SECRET_KEY in config.py, which allows anyone with the source to forge JWTs.

finding.title: Order detail endpoint exposes other customers' orders
finding.description: The authenticated order-detail endpoint calls get_order directly and never checks that the order belongs to the requesting user. Any logged-in customer who guesses an order ID can read another customer's items, payment totals, status, and refunds.
finding.evidence: return jsonify(order_json(get_order(order_id)))

reason: It identifies the IDOR in show_order, where get_order is used without checking that the order belongs to the requesting customer.

finding.title: Webhook signature does not cover the event payload
finding.description: The HMAC authenticates only the order ID, not the status or amount. Anyone able to obtain or replay a valid signature for an order can alter amount_pence or status while retaining the same signature, allowing an order to be marked paid for an arbitrary amount. In the supplied production config, the fallback webhook secret is also a source-visible constant.
finding.evidence: webhook_signature(order_id) signs only str(order_id); event status and amount_pence are accepted separately; config.py defaults WEBHOOK_SECRET to whsec-local

reason: The finding identifies that the webhook HMAC covers only the order ID while status and amount are trusted separately, matching V19.

finding.title: Product search is vulnerable to SQL injection
finding.description: The public search query is concatenated into a SQL statement instead of being bound as a parameter. An attacker can alter the WHERE clause and extract or manipulate data through the search endpoint.
finding.evidence: "SELECT * FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%" + q + "%' OR sku LIKE '%" + q + "%' ORDER BY name LIMIT 50"

reason: The finding identifies SQL injection in the product search query, where user input is concatenated into SQL.

finding.title: Unauthenticated unsafe deserialization of basket cookie
finding.description: The basket cookie is entirely client-controlled and is passed to pickle.loads without authentication or a restricted unpickler. A crafted cookie can execute arbitrary Python code when any visitor requests /basket.
finding.evidence: data = pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw))

reason: The client-controlled basket cookie is unpickled without authentication, enabling remote code execution.

finding.title: Payment timeout is treated as successful payment
finding.description: If the payment provider times out, the application unconditionally changes the order to processing and records the full total as paid. A provider outage or induced timeout can therefore create unpaid orders that are fulfilled.
finding.evidence: except requests.Timeout: ... status = "paid"; the paid branch sets status = 'processing' and paid_pence = total_pence

reason: It identifies the payment timeout in confirm_payment being treated as paid, allowing orders to be fulfilled without payment.

finding.title: Stored review content is rendered as trusted HTML
finding.description: Review bodies are accepted from authenticated users and later rendered with the Jinja safe behavior in the product template. A reviewer can store script or event-handler markup that executes for users viewing the product page.
finding.evidence: The review body is inserted at line 90 and rendered as {{ r.body|safe }} in shopapi/templates/product.html line 14.

reason: Review bodies are stored raw and rendered with Jinja’s |safe filter, enabling stored XSS.

finding.title: Approved-host image import follows unrestricted redirects
finding.description: The URL is checked against the approved host and public DNS result once, then requests.get follows redirects by default. An approved host can redirect the server to an internal or metadata-service address, allowing staff-triggered SSRF and retrieval of internal responses.
finding.evidence: check_url(url) validates the initial URL, then requests.get(url, timeout=10, stream=True) follows redirects without allow_redirects=False or validating each destination

reason: It identifies the redirect-following SSRF in shopapi/images.py, where only the initial URL is validated.

finding.title: Payment webhook signature does not cover payment amount or status
finding.description: The HMAC is calculated only over order_id, while the handler trusts attacker-controlled status and amount_pence fields. Any party able to obtain or reuse a valid order signature can change the credited amount, including crediting an order as paid for zero or an arbitrary amount.
finding.evidence: webhook_signature(order_id) signs only str(order_id), but lines 247-249 trust event status and int(event.get("amount_pence", 0))

reason: The webhook HMAC covers only the order ID while the handler trusts the supplied status and amount, allowing a valid signature to be replayed with altered payment details.

finding.title: Customer display names enable second-order SQL injection in review reports
finding.description: A staff report interpolates a customer's mutable display_name directly into SQL. A customer can set a display name containing SQL syntax; when staff request that customer's report, the injected expression is executed and can disclose review data beyond the selected customer.
finding.evidence: f"WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}' ORDER BY r.id DESC"

reason: The finding identifies the second-order SQL injection in reviews_by_customer, where a customer-controlled display_name is interpolated into the report query.

finding.title: SQL injection in admin reviews report via display_name
finding.description: The /admin/reports/reviews endpoint constructs a SQL query using an f-string embedding customer['display_name'] directly into the WHERE clause on line 80. While the initial customer lookup on line 74 uses parameterized queries, once an attacker registers or modifies a user account with a display_name containing SQL injection payloads, the second query becomes vulnerable.
finding.evidence: After registering a user with display_name="' UNION SELECT 1,2,password_hash,NULL,NULL,NULL,NULL,NULL FROM users--", accessing GET /admin/reports/reviews?customer_id=8 caused HTTP 500 (SQL syntax error).

reason: It identifies the second-order SQL injection in reviews_by_customer using the customer’s stored display_name in an f-string.

finding.title: Passwords stored with unsalted, unstretched SHA-256
finding.description: All passwords are hashed with bare hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() on line 16 — no per-user salt, no pepper, and no work-factor stretching (bcrypt, scrypt, argon2, or PBKDF2). The seed script confirms all demo accounts use the same password 'demo-password-1', making rainbow-table lookup trivial. Even unique passwords with typical entropy are vulnerable to fast GPU-based brute force.
finding.evidence: hash_password() at line 16: return hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest(). scripts/seed.py:33 seeds all users with hash_password('demo-password-1').

reason: It identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in hash_password, matching V09.

finding.title: Stored XSS in review body rendered without encoding
finding.description: Review bodies submitted via POST /products/<id>/reviews are stored verbatim and later rendered in product.html on line 13 with {{ r.body|safe }}, which explicitly bypasses Jinja2 auto-escaping. The description_html function sanitizes product descriptions but review bodies skip this step entirely.
finding.evidence: Posted POST /products/1/reviews with body '<script>alert(document.cookie)</script>', rating=5. Subsequent GET /p/MUG-SPECK returned the raw script tag inside <div class="review-body">.

reason: It identifies stored XSS because review bodies are stored raw and rendered with |safe in product.html.

finding.title: JWT token refresh ignores signature verification
finding.description: The /auth/refresh endpoint decodes JWTs with options={'verify_signature': False} on line 101, meaning any client can forge a token with arbitrary claims (user ID, role) regardless of the actual signing key.
