The endpoint then creates a new validly-signed token for that forged identity, enabling impersonation of any user including staff.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/refresh with body '{"token": "eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJzdWIiOjEsInJvbGUiOiJzdGFmZiJ9.fakesig"}' (unsigned forged token with sub=1) returned HTTP 200 with a fresh valid signed JWT for sub=1, role='staff'.

reason: It identifies the refresh endpoint accepting tokens with signature verification disabled and reissuing a valid token for the forged identity.

finding.title: Password reset tokens use non-cryptographic PRNG with only 8 decimal digits of entropy
finding.description: Reset tokens are generated with '%08d' % int(random.random() * 10**8) on line 135, drawing from Python's Mersenne Twister (random.random()) — a predictable PRNG unsuitable for security. With only 8 decimal digits, there are at most 10^8 possible values (~27 bits), making brute-force guessing trivial within seconds.
finding.evidence: Line 135: token = '%08d' % int(random.random() * 10**8). Only 8 digits from random.random(); contrast with secrets.token_hex(8) used for gift card codes on admin.py:42.

reason: The password-reset code uses predictable random.random() and has only eight digits, matching V10.

finding.title: SQL injection in product search endpoint
finding.description: The /products/search endpoint concatenates the user-supplied 'q' query parameter directly into a SQL string via f-string interpolation on line 41, without using parameterized queries. An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL to read, modify, or delete data from any table — including users with password hashes.
finding.evidence: GET /products/search?q='+UNION+SELECT+id,email,password_hash,NULL,NULL,NULL,NULL,NULL+FROM+users--+ returned HTTP 500, confirming unparameterized SQL concatenation of user input.

reason: It identifies SQL injection in the /products/search endpoint from concatenating the user-supplied query into SQL.

finding.title: Passwords are stored as unsalted fast SHA-256 hashes
finding.description: Password hashing uses a single unsalted SHA-256 digest with no work factor or password-hashing KDF. A database disclosure permits efficient offline cracking of users' passwords, including reused passwords.
finding.evidence: return hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest()

reason: The finding identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in shopapi/auth.py, matching V09.

finding.title: Hardcoded JWT signing secret in source code
finding.description: The SECRET_KEY used to sign ALL JWT tokens is hardcoded as 'hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d' on line 3. Anyone with source code access can forge arbitrary valid JWT tokens for any user_id and any role claim, completely bypassing authentication across every protected route that calls jwt.decode().
finding.evidence: config.py line 3: SECRET_KEY = 'hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d'. Using PyJWT with HS256 and this known key, crafted a valid token for sub=2 and sent it to /orders/1 — the server accepted it and returned full order details.

reason: The finding identifies the hardcoded JWT signing secret in config.py, which enables token forgery.

finding.title: Authenticated users can view any other user's orders
finding.description: The /orders/<order_id> GET endpoint (show_order) calls @require_auth but delegates to get_order() which does NOT verify that the requesting user owns the order. own_order() exists but is only used by cancel-items and returns endpoints. Any authenticated user can retrieve full details of any other user's order.
finding.evidence: Logged in as tom.okafor@mail.test (customer_id=2) and accessed GET /orders/1 (customer_id=1). Response returned full order details including items (MUG-SPECK qty 2), total 2400 pence, status 'delivered'.

reason: The finding identifies the IDOR in show_order, which lets an authenticated customer read another customer's order.

finding.title: CORS unconditionally reflects Origin with credentials allowed
finding.description: The after_request CORS handler sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin to the exact value of the requesting Origin header on line 47 without any allowlist validation. Combined with CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS=True (config.py:12), any website can make cross-origin authenticated requests to the API on behalf of a logged-in victim.
finding.evidence: GET /health with Origin: https://evil.com returned Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://evil.com plus Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.

reason: It identifies the after_request handler reflecting any Origin while allowing credentials, matching V05.

finding.title: Flask debug mode enabled (debug=True)
finding.description: run.py launches Flask with debug=True on line 6. In debug mode, Werkzeug provides an interactive traceback debugger accessible via browser error pages, allowing arbitrary remote code execution if any server-side exception is triggered by crafting specific requests.
finding.evidence: run.py:6: app.run(host='127.0.0.1', port=5000, debug=True). Server headers show Werkzeug/3.1.9, confirming debug mode is active.

reason: It identifies debug=True in run.py, which enables the Werkzeug interactive debugger and can lead to code execution if reachable.

finding.title: Login endpoint leaks account existence via distinct error messages
finding.description: The /auth/login endpoint returns 'no account with that email' when the email doesn't exist (line 90) but returns 'wrong password' when it does (line 92). An attacker can enumerate registered email addresses by observing these distinct 401 responses.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/login with nonexistent@email@test.com + bad password returned {error:'no account with that email'} (401). Same request with priya.shah@mail.test + bad password returned {error:'wrong password'} (401).

reason: The login endpoint reveals whether an email is registered through distinct error messages, matching V16.

finding.title: SSRF via unchecked redirects in image import endpoint
finding.description: The /products/<product_id>/image endpoint validates the hostname against an allowlist (lines 32-35) but then calls requests.get() on line 50 without restrict_redirects=False. If an allowed host (cdn.hartleyfinch.co.uk or images.supplier-photos.com) redirects to an internal address, the server follows the redirect and fetches internal URLs. DNS rebinding attacks can also evade the initial resolution check.
finding.evidence: Line 50: r = requests.get(url, timeout=10, stream=True) — follow_redirects=True by default, no post-redirect hostname verification. Blocking direct localhost URL (returned 400 'doesn't resolve to public address') but redirects would bypass this check.

reason: It identifies the unchecked-redirect SSRF in shopapi/images.py’s image import flow.

finding.title: Arbitrary code execution via pickle deserialization of basket cookie
finding.description: The basket cookie is deserialized using pickle.loads() on line 20 without any integrity check or signature verification. Malicious __reduce__ implementations in crafted pickle payloads trigger arbitrary Python code execution during unpickling, before the isinstance(data, dict) type check on line 23.
finding.evidence: basket.py:20: data = pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw)). Raw cookie value comes directly from request.cookies['basket']. A crafted pickle payload would execute code during unpickling.

reason: It identifies unauthenticated pickle deserialization of the basket cookie in shopapi/basket.py, enabling remote code execution.

finding.title: Payment confirmation defaults to paid on provider timeout
finding.description: When the payment provider times out during confirm-payment, the server unconditionally sets status='paid' on line 42 and marks the order as processing (lines 44-46). A network failure causes goods to be shipped without actual payment confirmation.
finding.evidence: Payments.py:39-42: except requests.Timeout: status = 'paid', then lines 44-46 UPDATE orders SET status = 'processing'.

reason: The finding identifies confirm_payment treating a provider timeout as paid and processing the order without payment confirmation.

finding.title: Admin set_role allows privilege escalation to any user
finding.description: The POST /admin/users/role endpoint (line 30) updates any user's role to 'staff' or 'customer' without validating that the requesting staff member has authorization to modify that specific user. A compromised or rogue staff account can grant themselves or anyone else staff privileges.
finding.evidence: POST /admin/users/role with {"user_id": 2, "role": "staff"} as staff priya.shah@mail.test returned HTTP 200, successfully escalating customer tom.okafor to staff.

reason: The reported role-management privilege escalation is a real access-control weakness, but it is not among the keyed vulnerabilities.

finding.title: Request bodies logged in plaintext including passwords
finding.description: The log_request before_request hook on line 31 logs POST/PUT/PATCH request bodies up to 2000 characters. This includes login attempts with passwords, password reset emails, and any sensitive data sent in request bodies, creating a logging exposure risk for authentication credentials.
finding.evidence: shopapi/__init__.py:31: log.info('%s %s %s', request.method, request.path, request.get_data(as_text=True)[:2000]). Login POST requests include password fields.

reason: It identifies log_request logging request bodies, including authentication credentials, matching V20.

finding.title: Webhook signature only covers order_id, not event content
finding.description: The webhook_signature function computes HMAC over only str(order_id) on line 55. Event fields like status ('paid'/'failed') and amount_pence are NOT included in the signature. An attacker intercepting a valid webhook can replay or modify the event payload while preserving the valid signature.
finding.evidence: payments.py:55: hmac.new(secret, str(order_id).encode(), sha256).hexdigest() — only order_id bound. Line 63 verifies signature but does not validate event content integrity. An attacker can change {'status':'paid','amount_pence':999999} and pass verification.

reason: The finding identifies the webhook HMAC covering only order_id, allowing status and amount fields to be changed or replayed without invalidating the signature.

finding.title: Webhook verification secret defaults to a guessable value
finding.description: WEBHOOK_SECRET defaults to 'whsec-local' on line 8, which is trivially guessable. The webhook handler computes HMAC over only the order_id (line 55 of payments.py). An attacker who knows this default can generate valid webhook signatures and call /webhooks/payments to arbitrarily change order statuses.
finding.evidence: config.py:8: WEBHOOK_SECRET = os.environ.get('WEBHOOK_SECRET', 'whsec-local'). Posting to /webhooks/payments with empty X-Signature correctly returned 403 'bad signature', confirming the check exists but the default secret is publicly derivable.

reason: A guessable default webhook secret is a real weakness, but it is distinct from V19’s failure to authenticate the full webhook body.

finding.title: Gift card redemption has race condition
finding.description: The redeem endpoint reads the card balance (line 36), validates amount <= balance (line 39), then updates (line 43) — but there is no transaction isolation (BEGIN IMMEDIATE). Under concurrent requests, two threads could read the same balance, both pass validation, and together deduct more than available, leaving negative balance.
finding.evidence: giftcards.py:36-44: read balance -> check -> update without BEGIN TRANSACTION wrapper. Two parallel POST /giftcards/redeem with amount_pence=1000 on a card with balance_pence=1500 could both pass validation and overdraft.

reason: The redeem function reads and checks the balance before updating it, allowing concurrent redemptions to overspend the gift card.

finding.title: Client-controlled pickle deserialisation enables arbitrary code execution
finding.description: The basket cookie is supplied by the client and is passed to pickle.loads after only Base64 decoding. A crafted pickle payload can execute attacker-controlled globals in the application process whenever a basket endpoint reads the cookie.
finding.evidence: shopapi/basket.py:15-23 calls pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw)) without a signature or integrity check; with_basket at lines 26-28 writes the same untrusted format. This is an inherent remote-code-execution path through the basket cookie.

reason: The finding identifies the unsigned, client-controlled pickle deserialization in shopapi/basket.py’s read_basket, which enables remote code execution.

finding.title: Authentication failures are swallowed and protected handlers continue
finding.description: require_auth catches every Exception, including the 401 HTTPException raised when no valid user is present, then invokes the protected handler with g.user set to None. Any protected handler that does not immediately dereference g.user is therefore publicly reachable.
finding.evidence: shopapi/auth.py:51-58 catches around abort(401), sets g.user=None, and still returns f(*args, **kwargs). GET /giftcards/HFDEMO10 without Authorization returned HTTP 200 with the gift-card balance despite the route's @require_auth decorator.

reason: The finding identifies require_auth swallowing the 401 exception and allowing unauthenticated requests to reach protected handlers, matching V22.

finding.title: Token refresh accepts unsigned attacker-controlled JWT claims
finding.description: The refresh endpoint disables JWT signature verification, trusts the supplied sub claim, and issues a newly signed token for that user. An attacker can name another existing user and obtain an authenticated token for that account.
finding.evidence: shopapi/auth.py:100-107 calls jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False}), loads the user from claims.get("sub"), and calls make_token(user). An unsigned JWT with sub=1 was accepted by POST /auth/refresh and returned a signed token.

reason: It identifies refresh disabling signature verification and issuing a valid token for the forged subject, matching V17.

finding.title: Authenticated users can view other customers' orders
finding.description: The individual order endpoint authenticates the caller but retrieves the requested order with get_order rather than own_order. Any authenticated customer who guesses an order ID can access another customer's order status, contents, payment amount, and refunds.
finding.evidence: shopapi/orders.py:46-50 returns order_json(get_order(order_id)); the ownership check exists separately in own_order at lines 32-35 but is not used. A GET /orders/1 using a token for a different customer returned HTTP 200 and disclosed order details.

reason: It identifies the IDOR in show_order, which retrieves orders without checking that they belong to the authenticated customer.

finding.title: Trailing slash bypasses the admin authorization check
finding.description: The global staff check compares request.path to registered route strings. The refunds route accepts both slash forms, but /admin/refunds/ is not equal to the registered /admin/refunds string, so the staff check is skipped and the administrative refund handler runs anonymously.
finding.evidence: shopapi/__init__.py:26 and :36-41 authorize only on exact path membership. shopapi/admin.py:52 defines /admin/refunds with strict_slashes=False. An unauthenticated POST /admin/refunds/ with an order_id and amount returned 200 and created a refund.

reason: The trailing-slash route bypasses the exact-path staff authorization check, allowing unauthenticated access to the refund handler.

finding.title: Stored review content is rendered as trusted HTML
finding.description: Authenticated users can store arbitrary review bodies, which are rendered with the Jinja safe filter without sanitisation. A malicious reviewer can persist JavaScript or markup that executes for visitors to the product page.
finding.evidence: shopapi/products.py:82-91 stores body directly, and shopapi/templates/product.html:13 renders r.body with |safe. Posting a review containing <script>alert(1)</script> succeeded and the product page returned the script tag unescaped.

reason: It identifies stored review text rendered with Jinja’s |safe filter without sanitization, matching the stored XSS vulnerability.

finding.title: Product search is vulnerable to SQL injection
finding.description: The search value is concatenated into a SQL statement rather than bound as a parameter. An attacker can alter the WHERE clause and retrieve unintended product rows or exploit SQLite query behavior.
finding.evidence: shopapi/products.py:40-42 builds SQL using string concatenation. GET /products/search?q=%27%20OR%201%3D1-- returned all six products, demonstrating altered query semantics.

reason: The finding correctly identifies SQL injection in the concatenated query in products.search.

finding.title: Editable local package installed without version pinning or hash verification
finding.description: requirements-dev.txt line 6 specifies '-e packages/hf_payments', performing an editable install of a local package with no version constraint, no URL, and no pip hash (--hash) enforcement. The installed code can be silently replaced by anyone with filesystem access without detection.
finding.evidence: requirements-dev.txt:6: -e packages/hf_payments. No --hash, no version specifier, just a directory path install.

reason: The editable local development install is not the public-index dependency-confusion issue in V07, and filesystem access alone does not make it a security vulnerability.

finding.title: Customer display names enable SQL injection in the admin review report
finding.description: The report interpolates a customer's mutable display name into a SQL WHERE clause. A customer can set a display name containing SQL syntax, then induce SQL execution when staff view that customer's report.
finding.evidence: shopapi/admin.py:74-80 loads display_name and inserts it into an f-string SQL query. shopapi/auth.py:116-125 lets authenticated users set arbitrary display names up to 60 characters without escaping; the report is reached at /admin/reports/reviews?customer_id=... .

reason: It identifies the second-order SQL injection in admin.reviews_by_customer using a customer-controlled display name.

finding.title: Approved image URLs can redirect the server to internal addresses
finding.description: The importer validates the initial hostname and its resolved addresses, but requests.get follows redirects by default. An approved host that redirects can therefore cause the server to fetch localhost, cloud metadata, or another internal service.
finding.evidence: shopapi/images.py:28-35 checks only the initial URL; line 50 calls requests.get(url, timeout=10, stream=True) without allow_redirects=False or validation of each redirect target. The endpoint is staff-restricted but still performs a server-side request to the redirected destination.

reason: It identifies the redirect-following SSRF in shopapi/images.py where only the initial URL is validated.

finding.title: Payment-provider timeouts fail open and grant paid order state
finding.description: A timeout while checking the payment provider is treated as a successful payment. The order is changed to processing and paid_pence is set to the full total without confirmation, allowing goods to be granted during a provider outage or network failure.
finding.evidence: shopapi/payments.py:37-44 catches requests.Timeout, sets status='paid', and updates the order to processing with paid_pence=total_pence. The comment explicitly defers reconciliation until later.

reason: It identifies the fail-open payment-provider timeout in confirm_payment, which marks the order paid without confirmation.

finding.title: Request logging records sensitive POST bodies
finding.description: Every POST, PUT, and PATCH body is logged, including login passwords, reset codes and new passwords, and other personal or payment-related data. Anyone with application log access can recover these secrets, which may also persist under log retention policies.
finding.evidence: shopapi/__init__.py:29-33 calls request.get_data(as_text=True) and logs up to 2,000 characters for every mutating request. /auth/login and /auth/reset/* accept credentials and reset data in those bodies.

reason: It identifies log_request in shopapi/__init__.py logging request bodies that can contain sensitive credentials.

finding.title: Password reset codes use weak randomness and have no attempt limit
finding.description: Reset codes are generated with the non-cryptographic random module and contain only eight decimal digits. Confirmation has no failed-attempt counter, rate limit, or lockout, allowing repeated online guesses throughout the 30-minute validity period once an email is known.
finding.evidence: shopapi/auth.py:135 generates the code with int(random.random() * 10**8); lines 143-161 compare guesses but never count or limit failures.

reason: It identifies the predictable eight-digit password-reset code and lack of attempt limits in reset_request/reset_confirm.

finding.title: Passwords are stored as unsalted SHA-256 hashes
finding.description: Password storage uses a single fast, unsalted SHA-256 digest. If the database is disclosed, common passwords can be cracked efficiently and identical passwords produce identical hashes; a salted password-specific KDF such as Argon2id, scrypt, or bcrypt is required.
finding.evidence: shopapi/auth.py:15-16 implements hash_password with hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest(), and registration at lines 77-78 stores that value directly in users.password_hash.

reason: It identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in shopapi/auth.py:hash_password.

finding.title: Production dependency resolution permits public-index dependency confusion
finding.description: Production pip configuration uses a private index but also permits PyPI as an extra index. If the private index cannot serve a requested package, a package with the same name can be selected from the public index, allowing a malicious or substituted package into the production build.
finding.evidence: requirements.txt:1-2 configure an internal --index-url together with --extra-index-url https://pypi.org/simple, and line 7 installs hf-payments==2.3.1. README.md:26 identifies hf-payments as an internal package published to the internal index.

reason: It identifies the public extra-index dependency-confusion risk for the internal hf-payments package in requirements.txt.

finding.title: SQL Injection in product search endpoint
finding.description: The /products/search endpoint builds an SQL query by concatenating the user-supplied q parameter directly into the SQL string using Python string formatting. This allows attackers to execute arbitrary SQL commands against the SQLite database.
finding.evidence: GET /products/search?q='%20OR%201=1%20-- returned all 6 products instead of zero matching results, confirming SQL injection. Code: shopapi/products.py line 41: 'SELECT * FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%" + q + "%' OR sku LIKE...

reason: The product search endpoint concatenates the user-supplied q parameter into SQL, matching V11.

finding.title: Payment webhook authenticates only the order ID and trusts the payment amount
finding.description: The webhook signature covers only order_id, while the handler accepts status and amount_pence from the request and writes the supplied amount as paid. Anyone able to obtain the webhook secret, including every deployment using the configured default, can mark an awaiting order paid for an arbitrary amount, including zero or a partial amount.
finding.evidence: config.py:8 defaults WEBHOOK_SECRET to the predictable literal whsec-local. shopapi/payments.py:53-64 signs and verifies only str(order_id), while lines 69-71 set paid_pence from int(event.get('amount_pence', 0)) without comparing it to total_pence or provider-confirmed data.

reason: It identifies the webhook flaw where the signature covers only the order ID while status and amount are trusted from the request.

finding.title: Token refresh endpoint skips signature verification allowing forgery
finding.description: The /auth/refresh endpoint decodes JWT tokens with verify_signature=False, accepting any arbitrarily forged token. An attacker can supply a token with claims like sub=any_valid_user_id and get a fresh, legitimately signed token back, achieving full account takeover.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/refresh with hand-crafted JWT containing sub=1 was accepted and returned a valid new token for user id=1. Code: shopapi/auth.py lines 98-107 where jwt.decode(token, options={verify_signature: False}) is called.

reason: The finding identifies the refresh endpoint accepting unsigned JWTs and exchanging forged claims for a valid signed token.

finding.title: IDOR on order detail view allows viewing any user's orders
finding.description: The GET /orders/<order_id> endpoint requires authentication but does not verify that the requesting user owns the order. Any authenticated user can view details of any other user's orders including items, prices, statuses and refund information.
finding.evidence: GET /orders/3 as authenticated user with id=1 returned order belonging to user id=2, including item list, status and amounts. Code: shopapi/orders.py line 49 shows show_order() calls get_order() which only checks order existence, not ownership. own_order() function exists but is unused here.

reason: It identifies the IDOR in show_order, which retrieves orders without checking that the signed-in user owns them.

finding.title: CORS reflects untrusted Origin header with credentials enabled
finding.description: The CORS after_request handler sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin to the exact value of the request Origin header without validation. Combined with CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS=True, this allows any origin to make credentialed cross-origin requests against the application.
finding.evidence: GET request with Origin: https://evil.example.com received Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://evil.example.com and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. Code: shopapi/__init__.py lines 44-51; config.py line 12.

reason: The CORS handler reflects arbitrary Origin values while allowing credentials, matching V05.

finding.title: Internal package index with no hash verification
finding.description: requirements.txt line 1 sets --index-url to an internal PyPI mirror as the primary source, and none of the pinned packages (lines 3-7) include pip --hash constraints. If the internal index is compromised, tampered packages would be installed silently.
finding.evidence: requirements.txt:1: --index-url https://pypi.hartleyfinch.internal/simple. No --hash entries for flask==3.0.3, PyJWT==2.3.0, bleach==6.1.0, requests==2.32.3, hf-payments==2.3.1.

reason: The finding claims line 1 uses an internal --index-url, but the keyed issue is a public --extra-index-url enabling dependency confusion.

finding.title: Order auto-marked as paid on payment provider timeout
finding.description: In confirm-payment(), when the payment provider times out, the code defaults status to paid and transitions the order to processing with paid_pence equal to total_pence. Orders can be fulfilled without actual payment confirmation simply by causing a network timeout to the provider.
finding.evidence: Code: shopapi/payments.py lines 37-42. If client().payment_status() raises requests.Timeout, status is set to paid regardless of actual payment state, and order is updated to processing with paid_pence=total_pence.

reason: It identifies confirm_payment treating a payment-provider timeout as successful payment and processing the order.

finding.title: Full request body logged for write operations exposing sensitive data
finding.description: The log_request before_request handler logs the full request body up to 2000 chars for every POST, PUT and PATCH request. This includes login credentials, registration data, gift card codes and other sensitive input written to logs.
finding.evidence: Code: shopapi/__init__.py lines 30-31: log.info(%s %s %s, request.method, request.path, request.get_data(as_text=True)[:2000]). Sensitive endpoints include /auth/login, /auth/register, /giftcards/redeem.

reason: It identifies the request logger in shopapi/__init__.py logging request bodies, including sensitive credentials.

finding.title: Passwords stored with unsalted SHA-256 hash
finding.description: hash_password uses plain SHA-256 without salt, making it vulnerable to rainbow table attacks and identical password detection across accounts. Modern applications should use bcrypt, argon2, or similar slow hashing functions.
finding.evidence: Code: shopapi/auth.py line 16: hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest(). No random salt applied. Used everywhere passwords are stored including registration (line 78) and password reset (line 159).

reason: It identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in shopapi/auth.py hash_password.

finding.title: Password reset tokens have low entropy
finding.description: Reset tokens are generated as %08d with int(random.random()*10**8), producing only 8 decimal digits with at most ~2^27 entropy using the predictable Mersenne Twister PRNG. Attackers can brute-force the space trivially.
finding.evidence: Code: shopapi/auth.py line 135. Tokens are 8-digit numeric codes sent via email log mechanism. Brute-forcing 100 million possibilities is trivial.

reason: It identifies the password-reset code’s predictable random generation and small brute-forceable space in shopapi/auth.py.

finding.title: Stored SQL Injection in admin review report via display_name
finding.description: The /admin/reports/reviews endpoint interpolates customer.display_name directly into SQL using f-string formatting (line 80), even though display_name comes from the database. An attacker can register with a crafted display_name containing SQL injection payloads, and when a staff member queries that customer's reviews, the payload executes. This is a stored SQL injection vector.
finding.evidence: Code: shopapi/admin.py lines 77-80: f'SELECT r.id, p.name AS product, r.rating, r.body, r.created FROM reviews r JOIN products p ON p.id = r.product_id WHERE r.author_name = \'{customer[display_name]}\'. Stored injection via display_name set during registration at shopapi/auth.py line 71.

reason: It identifies the f-string SQL injection in the admin reviews report using a customer-controlled stored display_name.

finding.title: Client-controlled basket cookie is deserialized with pickle
finding.description: The basket cookie is entirely controlled by the client, but it is base64-decoded and passed to pickle.loads. A crafted cookie can execute arbitrary Python code in the server process when any basket endpoint reads it.
finding.evidence: read_basket() obtains request.cookies['basket'] and calls pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw)) without a signature or integrity check.

reason: It identifies unauthenticated pickle deserialization of the client-controlled basket cookie in read_basket, enabling remote code execution.

finding.title: JWT signing key is hardcoded in source
finding.description: The HS256 signing key is a fixed value committed in config.py. Anyone with source or a deployment artifact can forge authentication tokens, and the key cannot be rotated independently of the code.
finding.evidence: config.py:3 sets SECRET_KEY = "hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d"; shopapi/auth.py:27 signs tokens with it and :42 validates tokens with it.

reason: The finding identifies the hardcoded JWT signing secret in config.py, which allows token forgery.

finding.title: Token refresh accepts unsigned attacker-supplied tokens
finding.description: The refresh endpoint disables JWT signature verification, then trusts the token's sub claim to select the user. An attacker can submit an unsigned token naming any user and receive a freshly signed token for that account.
finding.evidence: jwt.decode(token, options={'verify_signature': False}) is used before load_user(claims.get('sub')) and make_token(user).

reason: The finding identifies the refresh endpoint accepting unsigned tokens and issuing a valid token for the claimed user.

finding.title: Authentication decorator swallows 401 errors and continues execution
finding.description: require_auth catches the HTTPException raised by abort(401), clears g.user, and still calls the protected handler. This makes authentication fail open; for example, the gift-card balance handler returns card balances without a token.
finding.evidence: The except Exception block catches abort(401) at line 54 and then returns f(*args, **kwargs) at line 58; balance() only queries the requested card and does not require g.user.

reason: The finding identifies require_auth catching abort(401) and continuing, allowing unauthenticated requests to reach protected routes.

finding.title: Product search concatenates the query directly into SQL
finding.description: The public search endpoint inserts q directly into a SQL statement. An attacker can alter the WHERE clause and use SQLite expression/UNION injection to disclose data or cause database errors.
finding.evidence: The query is built as "... name LIKE '%" + q + "%' OR sku LIKE '%" + q + "%' ..." instead of using bound parameters.

reason: It identifies SQL injection in the q parameter of the product search endpoint.

finding.title: Authenticated users can view any order by ID
finding.description: The order detail endpoint authenticates the caller but calls get_order directly, which filters only by order ID and never checks customer_id. Any signed-in customer can read another customer's order status, items, payment totals, and refunds by changing the ID.
finding.evidence: show_order() returns order_json(get_order(order_id)); unlike own_order(), get_order() has no comparison with g.user['id'].

reason: The finding identifies the IDOR in show_order, which retrieves orders by ID without checking that the caller owns them.

finding.title: Trailing slash bypasses the admin authorization hook
finding.description: The global admin check compares request.path to a set containing only the canonical route strings. The refunds route accepts a trailing slash, so /admin/refunds/ is dispatched without the staff check and permits unauthenticated refunds.
finding.evidence: staff_only_admin checks request.path in admin_paths, while the route is declared strict_slashes=False. A POST to /admin/refunds/ was accepted with HTTP 200 and created a refund without Authorization.

reason: The finding describes the trailing-slash path bypassing the staff authorization check on the refunds route.

finding.title: Staff review report is vulnerable to SQL injection through display names
finding.description: A customer's display_name is interpolated into the review-report SQL. A customer can set a display name containing SQL syntax, after which a staff member viewing that customer's report executes the injected query.
finding.evidence: The report uses f"WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}' ORDER BY r.id DESC" with no parameter binding.

reason: The report interpolates a customer-controlled display_name into SQL in reviews_by_customer, matching the second-order SQL injection.

finding.title: Review bodies are rendered as trusted HTML
finding.description: Authenticated users can submit arbitrary review text, and product pages render it with the safe filter. A malicious review can execute JavaScript in every visitor's browser in the shop origin.
finding.evidence: add_review() stores body without HTML sanitization, while the template renders r.body with {{ r.body|safe }}.

reason: It identifies stored XSS from unsanitized review bodies rendered with the safe filter.

finding.title: Passwords are stored as unsalted fast SHA-256 hashes
finding.description: User passwords are hashed with unsalted SHA-256, which is designed for speed rather than password storage. A database disclosure therefore enables efficient offline cracking and reuse of recovered credentials.
finding.evidence: hash_password() returns hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() and stores that value directly as password_hash.

reason: The finding identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in shopapi/auth.py's hash_password function.

finding.title: Payment status timeouts are treated as successful payments
finding.description: If the payment provider times out, the checkout endpoint sets the order to processing and paid_pence to the full total. A timeout is not proof of settlement, so an order can be fulfilled without a confirmed payment.
finding.evidence: The requests.Timeout handler sets status = 'paid', followed by UPDATE orders SET status = 'processing', paid_pence = total_pence.

reason: It identifies confirm_payment treating a payment-provider timeout as successful and processing the order without confirmed payment.

finding.title: JWT signing key is hardcoded in source
finding.description: The application uses a fixed source-controlled SECRET_KEY for HS256 JWTs. Anyone who obtains the repository or a deployed copy can forge authentication tokens, including staff tokens.
finding.evidence: SECRET_KEY is assigned the literal value "hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d" rather than being required from a protected deployment secret.

reason: The finding identifies the hardcoded JWT signing secret in config.py, which can be used to forge authentication tokens.

finding.title: Token refresh accepts unsigned attacker-controlled JWT claims
finding.description: The refresh endpoint decodes the supplied token with verify_signature=False and uses its sub claim to select a live account, without validating signature, issuer, audience, or the original token's validity. Anyone can construct a token containing a victim's user ID and receive a valid signed session token for that account.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/refresh with an unsigned token containing sub=1 returned HTTP 200 and a newly signed bearer token for user 1. Code path: jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False}) -> load_user(claims.get("sub")) -> make_token(user).

reason: The refresh endpoint disables signature verification and exchanges the forged token’s subject for a valid signed token.

finding.title: Basket cookie uses pickle deserialization
finding.description: The basket cookie is serialized/deserialized using Python pickle (line 20). While current exception handling returns empty dict on failure, pickle has known RCE gadget chains and is unsafe for untrusted data. Pickle usage also appears in cache.py for file-based caching.
finding.evidence: Code: shopapi/basket.py line 20: pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw)). Same pattern in cache.py lines 23 and 31 for on-disk cache files.

reason: It identifies the unsigned, attacker-controlled basket cookie being unpickled, which enables remote code execution.

finding.title: Order detail endpoint does not enforce ownership
finding.description: show_order uses get_order rather than own_order, so once the decorator issue is fixed (and also for any authenticated user), any user who can guess an order ID can read another customer's order, including item, payment and refund information.
finding.evidence: The route calls order_json(get_order(order_id)); only cancel_items and return_items call own_order. GET /orders/1 without credentials returned the complete order, demonstrating the current unauthenticated exposure as well.

reason: The finding identifies the order-ownership flaw in show_order and also notes that the authentication decorator lets unauthenticated requests reach the route.

finding.title: Authentication decorator fails open after catching its own 401
finding.description: require_auth catches Exception around abort(401), clears g.user, and then calls the protected view instead of re-raising or returning an error. Consequently every endpoint using this decorator can be reached without a valid bearer token; views that do not dereference g.user execute as an anonymous caller, while others may produce a server error.
finding.evidence: GET /orders/1 with no Authorization header returned HTTP 200 and the order contents. The failing path is require_auth -> abort(401) -> broad except -> f(*args, **kwargs), and orders.show_order calls get_order() without an ownership check.

reason: The finding identifies require_auth swallowing abort(401) and allowing unauthenticated requests through (V22), and also explicitly notes the separate order-ownership flaw in show_order (V01).

finding.title: Admin path authorization is bypassable on the trailing-slash refund route
finding.description: The global staff check compares request.path to the set of exact URL-map rules. The refund route permits both slash forms (strict_slashes=False), but only /admin/refunds is in admin_paths; /admin/refunds/ skips the check and executes the staff-only refund operation.
finding.evidence: POST /admin/refunds/ with {"order_id":1,"amount_pence":1} and no Authorization header returned HTTP 200 {"ok":true,...} and created a refund. The route is shopapi/admin.py:52 and the exact-path check is shopapi/__init__.py:36-41.

reason: It identifies the trailing-slash bypass of the staff check on the /admin/refunds route.

finding.title: Product search is vulnerable to SQL injection
finding.description: The q query parameter is concatenated directly into a SQL LIKE expression. An attacker can alter the WHERE clause, extract or manipulate query behavior, and potentially cause database errors.
finding.evidence: The query is built as "... WHERE name LIKE '%" + q + "%' OR sku LIKE '%" + q + "%'". GET /products/search?q=%27%20OR%201=1-- returned all six products, confirming predicate injection.

reason: It identifies the SQL injection in the q parameter of GET /products/search, where the value is concatenated into the query.

finding.title: Payment webhook signature does not authenticate event contents
finding.description: The webhook MAC covers only order_id, while status and amount_pence are accepted from the unsigned JSON body. Anyone able to obtain the webhook secret can change a valid signed event into an arbitrary payment amount or status. The configured fallback secret is also a fixed value.
finding.evidence: webhook_signature() hashes only str(order_id), but payment_webhook() trusts event['status'] and event['amount_pence']; WEBHOOK_SECRET defaults to 'whsec-local' in config.py line 8.

reason: It identifies the webhook flaw where the signature covers only the order ID while status and amount are trusted from the unsigned body.

finding.title: Admin review report concatenates display names into SQL
finding.description: A customer's display_name is inserted into a SQL string without parameterization. Since users can set their own display name, a customer can store SQL metacharacters and trigger SQL injection when staff later runs the review report for that customer (second-order SQL injection).
finding.evidence: update_account accepts and stores display_name at shopapi/auth.py:119-125; reviews_by_customer then builds f"WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}' ..." at admin.py:77-80. Use a bound parameter for the name comparison.

reason: It identifies the second-order SQL injection in reviews_by_customer using the customer-controlled display_name.

finding.title: Passwords are stored as unsalted SHA-256 hashes
finding.description: hash_password uses a fast, unsalted SHA-256 digest rather than a password hashing function such as Argon2id, scrypt, or bcrypt. A database compromise therefore enables efficient offline dictionary and brute-force recovery, especially given the documented demo password reuse.
finding.evidence: hash_password returns hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() at lines 15-16, and registration stores that value directly at line 77.

reason: It identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in hash_password, matching V09.

finding.title: Basket cookie deserializes attacker-controlled pickle data
finding.description: The basket cookie is entirely client-controlled and is passed to pickle.loads without a signature or encryption. Pickle deserialization can execute arbitrary Python code in the application process before the request is handled. Basket contents should use a safe format such as JSON and be authenticated, or be stored server-side.
finding.evidence: read_basket obtains request.cookies['basket'], base64-decodes it, and calls pickle.loads at lines 15-23; with_basket writes the unsigned pickle at lines 26-29. No secret or MAC is involved.

reason: The finding correctly identifies unauthenticated pickle deserialization of the client-controlled basket cookie in read_basket, enabling remote code execution.

finding.title: Password reset codes are predictable and lack attempt limiting
finding.description: Reset codes are generated with non-cryptographic random.random() and contain only eight decimal digits. Confirmation has no attempt counter, lockout, or rate limit, so attackers can brute-force a live code during its 30-minute lifetime; random.random is also not appropriate for security tokens.
finding.evidence: Codes are generated with int(random.random() * 10**8) at line 135 and compared directly at line 153. There is no per-account or per-IP throttling in reset_request or reset_confirm.

reason: It identifies the predictable random.random() reset codes and lack of attempt limiting in reset confirmation.

finding.title: JWT signing key is hardcoded in source
finding.description: SECRET_KEY is a fixed source-controlled value. Anyone obtaining the repository or a deployed copy can forge HS256 bearer tokens for arbitrary users and roles, including staff, until the key is rotated.
finding.evidence: config.py line 3 sets SECRET_KEY = "hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d"; auth.py:27 uses it to sign JWTs and auth.py:42 uses it to verify them.

reason: The finding identifies the hardcoded SECRET_KEY in config.py, which can be used to forge JWTs.

finding.title: Payment status timeout fails open as paid
finding.description: When the payment provider times out, confirm_payment deliberately sets status='paid' and transitions the order to processing. A provider outage or induced timeout therefore allows an order to be fulfilled without confirmed payment.
finding.evidence: The requests.Timeout handler at lines 39-42 assigns status = "paid"; lines 43-46 then update the order to processing and set paid_pence=total_pence. The timeout should leave the order awaiting payment or mark it pending for reconciliation.

reason: It identifies confirm_payment treating a provider timeout as paid, allowing an order to be processed without payment.

finding.title: CORS reflects arbitrary origins while allowing credentials
finding.description: For every request with an Origin header, the application reflects that origin and sends Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, without an allowlist. This permits arbitrary websites to make credentialed cross-origin requests and read responses when a browser has applicable credentials.
finding.evidence: The after_request hook assigns Access-Control-Allow-Origin directly from request.headers['Origin'] at lines 45-49. GET /health with Origin: https://evil.example returned Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://evil.example and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.

reason: The after_request hook reflects arbitrary Origin values while enabling credentialed CORS, matching V05.

finding.title: Application is started with Flask debug mode enabled
finding.description: The executable entry point calls app.run(debug=True). If this script is used in a reachable deployment, unhandled exceptions expose the interactive Werkzeug debugger and potentially arbitrary code execution; debug mode also exposes verbose diagnostics.
finding.evidence: run.py line 6 passes debug=True unconditionally. A production entry point should use a production WSGI server and never enable debug based on this hardcoded setting.

reason: The finding identifies run.py calling app.run(debug=True), which is the planted debug-mode vulnerability.

finding.title: Order detail endpoint does not enforce ownership
finding.description: The order detail handler uses get_order() rather than own_order(), so any authenticated user can retrieve another customer's order, including its items, payment totals, delivery date, and refunds. In addition, require_auth swallows its own 401 abort (shopapi/auth.py:48-59), so this endpoint is reachable without a valid bearer token and the handler still returns the requested order.
finding.evidence: GET /orders/1 with no Authorization header returned HTTP 200 and the complete order (items, paid_pence, delivered_on and refunds). A valid customer token for a different account also returned order 1. The path is shopapi.orders.show_order -> get_order, with no customer_id predicate.

reason: The finding identifies the cross-customer order access in show_order (V01) and also describes require_auth failing open by swallowing the 401 abort (V22).

finding.title: Client-controlled basket is deserialized with pickle
finding.description: The basket cookie is entirely client-controlled and is passed to pickle.loads without a signature, encryption, or a safe restricted unpickler. Python pickle deserialization executes attacker-controlled reduce/callable payloads before the type check. Any remote client can send a crafted basket cookie and obtain code execution in the application process.
finding.evidence: read_basket reads request.cookies['basket'], base64-decodes it, and calls pickle.loads at line 20; with_basket writes the same unsigned format at lines 26-29. There is no MAC or server-side session binding.

reason: It identifies the unsigned client-controlled pickle deserialization in read_basket, which enables remote code execution.

finding.title: Product search is vulnerable to SQL injection
finding.description: The search term is concatenated directly into a SQL LIKE expression. An attacker can alter the query with quotes, comments, UNION clauses, or other SQLite syntax. The search is public and the underlying SELECT exposes all product-table columns, so a crafted UNION can be used to turn returned product fields into data from other tables.
finding.evidence: GET /products/search?q=' OR 1=1 -- was accepted with HTTP 200 and returned the catalogue; UNION-style probes such as GET /products/search?q=' UNION SELECT 1,'LEAK','X',1,1,'Y' -- caused an SQL/application error (HTTP 500), demonstrating that input is being parsed as SQL rather than treated as data.

reason: It identifies SQL injection in the product search query, where the search term is concatenated into SQL.

finding.title: Payment-status timeout fails open as paid
finding.description: If the payment provider times out, confirm_payment explicitly sets status='paid' and proceeds to processing. A requester can repeatedly invoke confirmation during provider/network unavailability and receive goods without a verified payment. Timeout, connection, and provider errors should leave the order unpaid or pending and be reconciled separately.
finding.evidence: In confirm_payment, requests.Timeout is caught at lines 39-42 and replaced with status = 'paid'; lines 43-46 then set the order to processing and paid_pence to total_pence without a provider response.

reason: It identifies confirm_payment treating a provider timeout as paid and processing the order without verified payment.

finding.title: Passwords are stored as unsalted SHA-256 hashes
finding.description: hash_password uses a single fast unsalted SHA-256 digest. A database disclosure therefore permits efficient dictionary/rainbow-table cracking, especially because the application documents and seeds predictable demo passwords. Passwords should use a memory-hard password KDF such as Argon2id, scrypt, or bcrypt with a unique salt.
finding.evidence: shopapi.auth.hash_password is hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() at lines 15-16; no salt or work factor is stored. scripts/seed.py:32 hashes the shared demo password the same way.

reason: The finding identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in shopapi.auth.hash_password, matching V09.

finding.title: Authentication decorator fails open after authentication errors
finding.description: require_auth catches all exceptions, including the abort(401) it raises when there is no user, logs the exception, sets g.user to None, and then calls the protected view anyway. This turns missing or malformed credentials into execution of protected handlers instead of stopping the request. It directly enables the order IDOR described above and causes other protected endpoints to reach application logic with no identity.
finding.evidence: GET /orders/1 with no Authorization header returned 200 rather than 401. The control flow in require_auth catches abort(401, 'sign in required') and returns f(*args, **kwargs).

reason: The finding identifies require_auth catching abort(401) and continuing into protected views, which is the fail-open authentication flaw.

finding.title: Payment webhook trusts an attacker-controlled payment amount
finding.description: The webhook signature authenticates only the order_id, not the event body or amount. Once an attacker obtains or guesses the configured webhook secret, they can submit a signed paid event for any order with amount_pence=0 or an arbitrary amount, and the server records that amount as paid without comparing it with the order total or provider payment record.
finding.evidence: webhook_signature signs only str(order_id) (lines 53-55). payment_webhook then accepts event status and int(event.get('amount_pence', 0)) at lines 69-71, with no amount/order-total or payment-provider verification. The default secret is also predictable (config.py:8).

reason: The webhook signature covers only the order ID while the handler trusts the event amount and status without validating the signed body or provider payment.

finding.title: JWT signing secret is hardcoded and predictable
finding.description: The production configuration contains a literal SECRET_KEY. Anyone with repository/source access, logs, or a leaked deployment artifact can forge HS256 bearer tokens, including tokens with the staff role, and access administrative functions. Secrets must be supplied by deployment secret management and rotated.
finding.evidence: config.py:3 sets SECRET_KEY = 'hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d'; auth.py:27 and :42 use it for all JWT signing and verification. The same configuration also supplies a default webhook secret at config.py:8.

reason: It identifies the hardcoded JWT signing secret in config.py, which allows forged tokens including staff tokens.

finding.title: Stored review content is rendered as raw HTML
finding.description: Authenticated users can submit arbitrary review body text, which is stored without sanitization. Product pages render r.body with the Jinja safe filter, so an attacker can store markup/script content that executes in every visitor's browser. This is persistent XSS on a public product page.
finding.evidence: add_review inserts the submitted body directly at products.py:90, while templates/product.html:13 renders {{ r.body|safe }}. Unlike product descriptions, review bodies are never passed through bleach.

reason: The finding identifies stored review XSS caused by rendering unsanitized review text with the safe filter.

finding.title: SQL Injection in admin reports endpoint
finding.description: The admin reports/reviews endpoint uses an f-string to embed customer['display_name'] directly into the SQL query. Although display_name comes from the database (not raw user input), it was originally set by a user during registration, so it can contain arbitrary SQL. If an attacker registers with a crafted display_name containing SQL metacharacters, querying reviews by that name becomes an SQL injection vector.
finding.evidence: Line 80: f"WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}'" constructs SQL via Python f-string interpolation.

reason: The finding identifies the second-order SQL injection in reviews_by_customer, where a customer-controlled display_name is interpolated into the report query.

finding.title: CORS reflects arbitrary origins while allowing credentials
finding.description: For every request carrying an Origin header, the server copies that unvalidated origin into Access-Control-Allow-Origin and enables Access-Control-Allow-Credentials. This permits arbitrary websites to make credentialed cross-origin requests and read responses. CORS should use a strict allowlist and credentials should be disabled unless required.
finding.evidence: The after_request hook assigns resp.headers['Access-Control-Allow-Origin'] = origin for any supplied origin and adds Allow-Credentials when configured. A request GET /products with Origin: https://evil.example returned Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://evil.example and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.

reason: The after_request hook reflects any Origin while allowing credentials, matching the CORS vulnerability in shopapi/__init__.py.

finding.title: SQL Injection in product search endpoint
finding.description: The /products/search?q parameter is interpolated directly into the SQL query using string concatenation (f-string equivalent). An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL via the q query parameter. Verified: sending 'q='+ UNION SELECT * FROM users--' caused a 500 Internal Server Error from SQLite.
finding.evidence: HTTP GET /products/search?q='+%20UNION+SELECT+*+FROM+users-- returned HTTP 500 Internal Server Error.

reason: It identifies SQL injection in the /products/search endpoint by concatenating the q parameter into SQL.

finding.title: Password reset codes are weak and have no attempt throttling
finding.description: Reset codes are generated with the non-cryptographic global PRNG and contain only eight decimal digits. The confirmation endpoint has no rate limit, attempt counter, lockout, or token hashing. An attacker who can target an account can make unlimited online guesses during the 30-minute validity window; use cryptographic random tokens and enforce attempts/rate limits.
finding.evidence: reset_request generates the code with random.random() at auth.py:135 and stores it directly; reset_confirm compares the submitted value at lines 149-153 and has no throttling or failed-attempt state.

reason: The finding identifies predictable eight-digit password-reset codes generated with random.random() and unlimited guesses, matching V10.

finding.title: Insecure Direct Object Reference - any authenticated user can view any order
finding.description: The GET /orders/<order_id> endpoint (line 48) calls get_order() which only checks whether the order exists; it never verifies that the requesting user owns that order. While list_orders (/orders, line 39) correctly filters by customer_id, the detail endpoint exposes all order data (items, payment info, refunds) to any authenticated user.
finding.evidence: GET /orders/2 with a customer's auth token returns full order details belonging to a different customer. Code at shopapi/orders.py:48 calls get_order() without checking g.user['id'].

reason: It identifies the IDOR in show_order, where get_order returns an order without checking that the requesting customer owns it.

finding.title: Stored XSS in review body rendering
finding.description: Review bodies are stored in the database without any sanitization (shopapi/products.py line 90 inserts body directly). When displayed in the product page template, the body field is rendered with the |safe Jinja2 filter, bypassing auto-escaping. An authenticated user can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript into reviews, which is then served to all visitors of the product page.
finding.evidence: POST /products/1/reviews with body='<script>alert("xss")</script>' succeeded. Subsequent GET /p/MUG-SPECK returned the raw <script> tag in the review-body div in the HTML response.

reason: The finding identifies stored review-body XSS caused by rendering unsanitized review text with the |safe filter.

finding.title: Remote code execution via pickle deserialization in basket cookie
finding.description: The basket cookie value is decoded and deserialized using pickle.loads (line 20). Since the cookie is not cryptographically signed (it's just base64-encoded pickle), any user can craft an arbitrary pickle payload and set it as the basket cookie. Deserializing a malicious pickle payload executes arbitrary Python code on the server. This applies even to unauthenticated users since basket reads occur before authentication checks.
finding.evidence: basket.py lines 15-23: data = pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw)) deserializes attacker-controlled cookie data without any integrity check.

reason: The finding identifies unauthenticated pickle deserialization of the attacker-controlled basket cookie in shopapi/basket.py, enabling remote code execution.

finding.title: Race condition in gift card redemption allows double-spending
finding.description: The gift card redemption flow reads the current balance, validates the requested amount against it, computes a new balance, and writes it back — all without locking or atomicity guarantees. Two concurrent redemption requests can both read the same balance, both pass validation, and both commit successfully, effectively spending the same funds twice.
finding.evidence: shopapi/giftcards.py lines 36-44: SELECT -> validate -> UPDATE without transactions or row-level locks. Same pattern as classic TOCTOU financial double-spend.

reason: The finding identifies the non-atomic balance check and update in gift-card redemption, allowing concurrent requests to overspend the card.

finding.title: Insecure password hashing - unsalted SHA-256
finding.description: Passwords are hashed with plain SHA-256 without a salt or work factor. This makes them vulnerable to rainbow table attacks and GPU-accelerated brute force. Modern applications should use bcrypt, argon2, or scrypt with appropriate cost factors.
finding.evidence: shopapi/auth.py line 16: hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() - no salt, no iterations.

reason: The finding identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in shopapi/auth.py, matching V09.

finding.title: Token refresh endpoint bypasses JWT signature verification
finding.description: The /auth/refresh endpoint decodes the supplied JWT with verify_signature=False, allowing an attacker to submit any syntactically-valid JWT (including entirely forged ones with arbitrary subclaims) and obtain a fresh, properly-signed token for that user. This means: (1) any user ID that exists in the database can be impersonated by crafting a JWT with that sub claim and refreshing it; (2) brute-force enumeration of user IDs is trivial. Verified: submitting a forged unsigned JWT with sub=6 produced a valid signed token for user 6.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/refresh with json:{"token": "eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJzdWIiOjYsInJvbGUiOiJzdGFmZiJ9.bad"} returned a valid refreshed JWT. Code: jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False}) at line 101.

reason: It identifies the signature-verification bypass in the /auth/refresh endpoint that lets forged tokens be exchanged for valid signed tokens.

finding.title: Predictable password reset tokens
finding.description: Password reset tokens are generated using random.random(), which produces Python floats seeded from os.urandom but with only ~53 bits of precision, formatted as '%08d' yielding only 8 decimal digits (~27 bits of entropy). An attacker can brute-force the token space (10^8 possibilities) to guess valid reset tokens and change any user's password.
finding.evidence: shopapi/auth.py line 135: token = '%08d' % int(random.random() * 10**8) generates only 8-digit numeric tokens from weak randomness.

reason: It identifies predictable, short password-reset codes generated with random.random(), matching the reset weakness in V10.

finding.title: CORS reflects Origin header with credentials allowed
finding.description: The CORS handler (shopapi/__init__.py lines 44-51) sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin to the exact value of the request's Origin header whenever one is present, AND Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true is set. This creates an open CORS policy where any external website can make credentialed cross-origin requests to the API, potentially enabling CSRF-like attacks from malicious sites.
finding.evidence: Any domain set as Origin header will be echoed back as the allowed origin with credentials permitted. config.py line 9: CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS = True.

reason: The CORS handler reflects arbitrary Origin values while allowing credentials, matching V05.

finding.title: Any authenticated user can read another customer's order
finding.description: The order detail endpoint calls get_order(), which looks up only by order ID. Unlike the cancellation and return endpoints, it never calls own_order() or otherwise checks customer_id against the authenticated user.
finding.evidence: With a token for Priya (user 1), GET /orders/3 returned Tom's order, including items, prices, payment amount, status, and refunds, with HTTP 200. The vulnerable path is show_order() -> get_order(); own_order() is defined immediately below but is not used here.

reason: The finding identifies the IDOR in show_order, which retrieves orders by ID without checking that the authenticated user owns them.

finding.title: Trailing-slash admin refund route bypasses the staff check
finding.description: The global admin guard compares request.path to the set of exact URL rules. The refund route is registered with strict_slashes=False, so /admin/refunds/ reaches the handler even though the rule set contains /admin/refunds and the guard does not run for the slash variant.
finding.evidence: POST /admin/refunds/ without Authorization and with {"order_id":3,"amount_pence":1} returned HTTP 200 and created a refund. The canonical POST /admin/refunds without credentials returned HTTP 403. The route is shopapi/admin.py:52-67.

reason: It identifies the trailing-slash /admin/refunds route bypassing the exact-path staff check.

finding.title: Review bodies are stored and rendered as executable HTML
finding.description: Review body input is inserted into the database without HTML sanitization and product.html renders it with the Jinja safe filter. A customer can persist script or other active markup that executes for every visitor to the product page.
finding.evidence: POST /products/1/reviews as an authenticated customer with {"rating":5,"body":"<script>alert(39889)</script>"} returned 201. GET /p/MUG-SPECK then contained the exact payload in <div class="review-body">. The sink is shopapi/templates/product.html:13.

reason: It identifies stored XSS from unsanitized review bodies rendered with the safe filter in the product template.

finding.title: The client-controlled basket cookie is unsafe Python pickle data
finding.description: read_basket() base64-decodes and unpickles a cookie supplied by the requester. Pickle deserialization executes reducer callables during loading, so a crafted basket cookie can execute arbitrary code in the web process before the result is type-checked. The cookie is neither signed nor authenticated.
finding.evidence: The attacker-controlled value is read from request.cookies at shopapi/basket.py:16 and passed directly to pickle.loads at line 20; the only validation occurs after deserialization at line 23. /basket and /basket/items both invoke read_basket(), making this a remotely reachable code-execution path.

reason: The finding identifies unauthenticated pickle deserialization of the client-controlled basket cookie in read_basket, enabling remote code execution.

finding.title: Product search is SQL-injectable
finding.description: The search term is concatenated directly into a SQLite LIKE expression instead of being passed as a parameter. An unauthenticated caller can alter the WHERE clause and potentially use database-specific SQL injection techniques.
finding.evidence: GET /products/search?q=%27%20OR%201%3D1%20-- returned all six products (HTTP 200), despite the search term not matching product names. The query is built by string concatenation at shopapi/products.py:40-42.

reason: It identifies the SQL injection in the concatenated search query in shopapi/products.py.

finding.title: Payment-status timeouts fail open as successful payments
finding.description: When the provider status request times out, the handler sets status to paid and moves the order to processing with paid_pence equal to the order total. A transient provider outage therefore lets an order proceed without payment confirmation.
finding.evidence: confirm_payment() catches requests.Timeout at shopapi/payments.py:39-42 and then executes the paid transition at lines 43-45. The comment confirms this is an intentional timeout path; it does not leave the order awaiting reconciliation or require a later positive confirmation.

reason: It identifies confirm_payment in shopapi/payments.py treating a provider timeout as successful payment and processing the order without confirmation.

finding.title: Token refresh accepts unsigned, expired, or attacker-modified JWT claims
finding.description: The refresh endpoint explicitly disables signature verification and does not require a valid expiration. It uses the untrusted sub claim to load an account and issues a fresh signed token for that account, allowing anyone to impersonate any known user ID.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/refresh with an unsigned JWT containing {"sub":1,"exp":9999999999} and an arbitrary signature returned HTTP 200 and a new signed token for user 1. The vulnerable decode is shopapi/auth.py:101-104.

reason: It identifies the refresh endpoint’s disabled signature verification, which lets an attacker forge a token and obtain a valid signed token for another account.

finding.title: A hardcoded JWT signing key permits staff-token forgery
finding.description: The application uses a fixed source-controlled SECRET_KEY to sign and validate all JWTs. Anyone who obtains the source or a deployed copy can mint a token for the existing staff user and access every admin endpoint.
finding.evidence: Using the literal key hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d from config.py, I minted an HS256 token with sub=3 and sent it to GET /admin/users; the running app returned HTTP 200 with the user list. Validation is in shopapi/auth.py:42-45 and admin authorization trusts the loaded user's staff role at shopapi/__init__.py:38-41.

reason: It identifies the hardcoded SECRET_KEY in config.py that enables JWT forgery.

finding.title: Passwords are stored as unsalted SHA-256 digests
finding.description: User passwords are hashed with a single unsalted SHA-256 operation. Database compromise therefore permits fast dictionary and brute-force cracking, especially because the seed credentials demonstrate that ordinary passwords are accepted.
finding.evidence: hash_password() is hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() at shopapi/auth.py:15-16, and the result is stored directly at registration and reset (lines 77-78 and 158-159). There is no per-password salt or work factor such as Argon2, scrypt, or bcrypt.

reason: The finding identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in shopapi/auth.py.

finding.title: Passwordless token refresh accepts unsigned attacker-controlled claims
finding.description: The refresh endpoint disables JWT signature verification and then issues a fresh signed token for whatever existing user ID appears in the unverified token. An attacker can submit an unsigned JWT with another user's `sub` claim and obtain a valid bearer token for that account.
finding.evidence: jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False}) is followed by load_user(claims.get("sub")) and make_token(user), with no signature or issuer validation.

reason: The refresh endpoint disables signature verification and issues a valid token for the subject in the forged token, enabling account takeover.

finding.title: Authenticated users can read any customer's order
finding.description: The order detail endpoint checks only that the caller is authenticated; it calls get_order() rather than own_order(). Any logged-in customer who guesses an order ID can view another customer's order contents, payment totals, delivery date, and refund history.
finding.evidence: show_order() returns order_json(get_order(order_id)); the ownership check exists only in own_order() and is not used by this route.

reason: The finding identifies the IDOR in show_order, which retrieves orders without checking that the caller owns them.

finding.title: Client-controlled basket cookie is deserialized with pickle
finding.description: The basket cookie is entirely attacker-controlled and is base64-decoded and passed to pickle.loads. A crafted cookie can execute arbitrary Python code in the application process whenever a basket endpoint reads it, without authentication.
finding.evidence: read_basket() calls pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw)) on request.cookies['basket']; with_basket() writes the same unsigned, unauthenticated pickle format back to the client.

reason: The finding identifies the unsigned client-controlled pickle deserialization in read_basket, enabling remote code execution.

finding.title: Payment webhook uses a predictable default secret and does not authenticate the amount
finding.description: If WEBHOOK_SECRET is not configured, the application uses the source-visible value whsec-local. In addition, the signature covers only order_id, while status and amount_pence are accepted from the unsigned JSON body. Anyone able to use the default can mark an unpaid order paid for an arbitrary amount, including more than the order total.
finding.evidence: config.py:8 defines WEBHOOK_SECRET with default whsec-local. I generated HMAC-SHA256 over the order ID using that value and POSTed /webhooks/payments with status=paid and amount_pence=999999; the running app accepted the request with HTTP 200. The signature input is only str(order_id) at shopapi/payments.py:53-55, while amount_pence is taken directly at lines 69-71.

reason: It identifies the payment webhook flaw where the signature covers only the order ID while status and amount are trusted from the unsigned body.

finding.title: Product search concatenates the query directly into SQL
finding.description: The unauthenticated product search endpoint interpolates the `q` parameter into a SQL string. An attacker can alter the WHERE clause and extract or otherwise manipulate query results through crafted search input.
finding.evidence: The query is built by concatenating q into the LIKE clauses and is executed without parameter binding.

reason: It identifies SQL injection in the product search endpoint by concatenating the q parameter into the query.

finding.title: Review bodies are rendered as trusted HTML
finding.description: Authenticated users can submit arbitrary review text, and the product template renders that text with Jinja's `safe` filter. A malicious review can execute JavaScript in every visitor's browser when the product page is viewed.
finding.evidence: add_review() stores the submitted `body` without HTML sanitization, while product.html renders `{{ r.body|safe }}`.

reason: The finding identifies stored XSS because unsanitized review bodies are rendered with the `safe` filter on the product page.

finding.title: Debug mode enabled
finding.description: The application is started with debug=True in run.py. In debug mode, Flask serves the interactive debugger on traceback pages, which can expose stack traces, source code, and even allow arbitrary code execution if an attacker can trigger an exception. This should never be enabled in production.
finding.evidence: run.py line 6: app.run(host="127.0.0.1", port=5000, debug=True). Additionally, the search SQL injection triggered a 500 error served by the Werkzeug debugger page instead of a proper JSON error.

reason: It identifies debug=True in run.py as the main vulnerability and also explicitly references the search SQL injection.

finding.title: Approved-host image import follows redirects to arbitrary destinations
finding.description: The URL validation checks the initial hostname and its DNS result, but requests.get follows redirects by default. A resource on an approved public host can redirect the staff-only importer to an internal or otherwise unauthorized service, causing the server to fetch it.
finding.evidence: check_url() validates only urlparse(url).hostname and host_is_public(), then requests.get(url, timeout=10, stream=True) is called without allow_redirects=False or validation of each redirected URL.

reason: It identifies the SSRF in shopapi/images.py where redirects bypass validation of the initial approved host.

finding.title: Payment-status timeout fails open and marks the order paid
finding.description: If the payment provider times out, the customer-controlled confirmation request treats the timeout as a successful payment and moves the order to processing. An unavailable or selectively stalled provider can therefore cause fulfillment of an unpaid order.
finding.evidence: The requests.Timeout handler sets status = "paid", after which the code updates the order to `processing` and sets paid_pence = total_pence.

reason: It identifies the payment-status timeout in confirm_payment being treated as paid, allowing an unpaid order to be processed.

finding.title: Staff review report uses a display name in an SQL f-string
finding.description: The staff-only review report inserts a database display name directly into a SQL statement. A user can set a crafted display name and a staff member viewing that user's report will execute the injected SQL, allowing data disclosure or database manipulation under the application's database identity.
finding.evidence: The query ends with `f"WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}' ORDER BY r.id DESC"` rather than using a SQL parameter.

reason: The report query interpolates a customer-controlled display name into SQL, matching the second-order SQL injection in reviews_by_customer.

finding.title: Passwords are stored as unsalted fast SHA-256 hashes
finding.description: User passwords are hashed once with SHA-256 and no salt or work factor. A database disclosure enables efficient offline cracking and reuse of recovered passwords, including the staff account if its password is reused elsewhere.
finding.evidence: hash_password() returns hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() and the resulting value is stored directly in users.password_hash.

reason: The finding identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in hash_password, matching V09.

finding.title: Production JWT signing key is hardcoded and predictable
finding.description: The application uses a repository-embedded constant as the default SECRET_KEY. Anyone who obtains the source can forge valid HS256 bearer tokens for arbitrary users and roles; the same configuration is used by the application factory unless an external override is supplied.
finding.evidence: config.py assigns SECRET_KEY = "hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d" instead of requiring a deployment secret, and auth.py signs and verifies tokens with current_app.config['SECRET_KEY'].

reason: The finding identifies the hardcoded JWT signing secret in config.py, which can be used to forge tokens.

finding.title: Review bodies are rendered as stored XSS
