finding.description: Authenticated users can submit arbitrary review body text, which is persisted without sanitization and rendered using Jinja's safe filter. Visiting the product page executes HTML/script-capable review content in every viewer's browser.
finding.evidence: products.py:82-91 accepts and stores body without HTML sanitization; product.html:13 renders {{ r.body|safe }}. The same template also explicitly bypasses escaping for this attacker-controlled stored value.

reason: It identifies stored XSS from unsanitized review bodies rendered with |safe in the product template.

finding.title: Trailing-slash admin refund route bypasses staff authorization
finding.description: Authorization is applied by comparing request.path to the set of exact admin route rules. The refund route is declared strict_slashes=False, so /admin/refunds/ reaches the handler but is not equal to the collected /admin/refunds rule. The handler itself has no authorization check, allowing unauthenticated refunds.
finding.evidence: __init__.py:26-41 checks only exact request.path values. admin.py:52 declares /admin/refunds strict_slashes=False and lines 54-67 perform the refund without checking g.user. POST /admin/refunds/ with no Authorization header returned HTTP 200 {"ok":true,"refunded_pence":1}.

reason: It identifies the trailing-slash route bypass of the staff authorization check on the admin refund endpoint.

finding.title: Admin review report concatenates display names into SQL
finding.description: The customer's display_name, which is user-controlled through PATCH /account, is interpolated into the report query. A customer can set a quote-containing display name and cause SQL syntax/injection when staff later view the report; the report should use a bound parameter.
finding.evidence: admin.py:77-81 uses f"WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}' ..." instead of a parameterized value. display_name is updated from request data at auth.py:116-125.

reason: It identifies the second-order SQL injection in admin.py’s reviews_by_customer report using the customer-controlled display_name.

finding.title: Product search is SQL-injectable
finding.description: The q query parameter is concatenated directly into a SQL LIKE expression. An unauthenticated caller can alter the WHERE clause and retrieve products outside the intended search (and potentially exploit SQLite expression injection).
finding.evidence: products.py:40-43 constructs SQL with "... LIKE '%" + q + "%' ...". GET /products/search?q=%27%20OR%201%3D1-- returned the full catalogue (all six products) rather than a matching result.

reason: The finding identifies SQL injection in the q parameter of GET /products/search, matching V11.

finding.title: Request logging records submitted passwords and reset codes
finding.description: The global request hook logs the raw body of every POST request. Login, registration, password reset, and payment-related requests therefore place credentials, reset codes, and other sensitive request data into application logs accessible to log readers and potentially retained or exported elsewhere.
finding.evidence: For every POST the hook executes `request.get_data(as_text=True)[:2000]` and passes it to log.info(); the authentication endpoints accept passwords and reset codes in POST JSON bodies.

reason: The request logger records POST bodies containing passwords and reset codes, matching the sensitive-data logging vulnerability.

finding.title: Token refresh accepts unsigned attacker-chosen JWT claims
finding.description: The refresh endpoint decodes the submitted JWT with signature verification disabled, then trusts its sub claim to select an account and issues a valid signed token. Anyone who knows or guesses a user ID can mint a session token without a password or valid JWT signature.
finding.evidence: auth.py:100 calls jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False}); line 104 loads claims['sub'] and line 107 signs a fresh token. POST /auth/refresh with an unsigned token containing sub=3 and an expired exp returned HTTP 200 and a valid staff token.

reason: It identifies the refresh endpoint’s disabled signature verification, which lets an attacker forge a token for any account.

finding.title: JWT signing key is hardcoded and predictable
finding.description: SECRET_KEY is committed as a fixed source-code value. Anyone obtaining the repository can forge HS256 authentication tokens, including staff-role claims, and the application has no requirement that a deployment override it.
finding.evidence: config.py:3 sets SECRET_KEY = "hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d". auth.py:27 and 42 use this value for all JWT signing and verification.

reason: It identifies the hardcoded JWT signing secret in config.py, which enables token forgery.

finding.title: Passwords are stored as unsalted fast SHA-256 hashes
finding.description: Password hashing uses a single unsalted SHA-256 digest, making database compromise vulnerable to rapid offline dictionary/rainbow-table cracking. Password verification also uses a normal equality comparison rather than a password-hashing verifier.
finding.evidence: auth.py:15-20 implements hash_password with hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() and compares the resulting digest directly; registration stores that value at lines 77-78.

reason: It identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in shopapi/auth.py’s hash_password function.

finding.title: Payment status timeout fails open as paid
finding.description: If the payment provider times out, the endpoint unconditionally sets status to paid and moves the order to processing. A provider outage or induced timeout therefore lets checkout proceed without confirmation of payment.
finding.evidence: payments.py:37-44 catches requests.Timeout and sets status = "paid" before updating the order to processing and paid_pence = total_pence.

reason: It identifies the payment-provider timeout being treated as paid, allowing an order to proceed without payment.

finding.title: SQL injection in product search
finding.description: The /products/search endpoint concatenates the untrusted 'q' query parameter directly into SQL LIKE clauses on line 41, providing no parameterization or escaping. An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL to read, modify, or delete any data from the database.
finding.evidence: GET /products/search?q='%20OR%201%3D1-- returned all 6 products instead of filtered results. GET /products/search?q='%20UNION%20SELECT%20id,email,password_hash,1,1,1%20FROM%20users-- triggered HTTP 500, confirming raw SQL error propagation.

reason: The finding identifies SQL injection in the /products/search endpoint caused by concatenating the untrusted q parameter into SQL.

finding.title: CORS reflects arbitrary origins while allowing credentials
finding.description: Every request Origin is reflected into Access-Control-Allow-Origin, and credentials are enabled by default. Any malicious origin can make credentialed cross-origin API requests in browsers if the application uses browser credentials, exposing authenticated responses and enabling state-changing requests.
finding.evidence: __init__.py:44-50 copies the unvalidated Origin into Access-Control-Allow-Origin and emits Allow-Credentials when config enables it; config.py:12 sets CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS = True.

reason: It identifies the arbitrary-Origin reflection with credentialed CORS in the after_request handler.

finding.title: Stored XSS via review bodies rendered unsanitized with |safe filter
finding.description: Review bodies are stored as-is and rendered with |safe filter on line 13 of the template, bypassing Jinja2's auto-escaping. An attacker can post a review body containing HTML/JavaScript (e.g., ), which executes in any viewer's browser when viewing the product page. Additionally, product descriptions use |safe on line 8 (though bleach.clean sanitizes markdown first, the review body has no sanitization). Display names ARE auto-escaped by Jinja2, but the review body is not.
finding.evidence: Multiple reviews with and bodies visible in GET /p/MUG-SPECK response HTML under class='review-body' divs, confirming unsanitized rendering.

reason: The finding identifies stored review text rendered with |safe without sanitization, matching V13.

finding.title: User-controlled pickle deserialization in basket cookie
finding.description: Basket cookies are base64-encoded Python pickle objects. Line 20 calls pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw)) where 'raw' comes entirely from request.cookies.get('basket'), which is set by the client. While exceptions are caught and return an empty basket, pickle deserialization of untrusted data is a known attack vector that can enable remote code execution through crafted opcodes targeting the application's dependencies. The exception handling may not catch all exploit scenarios.
finding.evidence: Line 20: pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw)) where raw originates from request.cookies.get(COOKIE), controlled entirely by the user.

reason: The finding identifies unauthenticated pickle deserialization of the client-controlled basket cookie in read_basket, enabling remote code execution.

finding.title: Server-Side Request Forgery via HTTP redirect following in image import
finding.description: check_url validates that the initial URL hostname is in IMAGE_HOSTS and resolves to a public IP (lines 32-35), but requests.get(url, timeout=10, stream=True) on line 50 follows HTTP redirects automatically (the default behavior of the requests library). An attacker supplying a URL from an approved host (e.g., cdn.hartleyfinch.co.uk/hijack.png) that issues a 3xx redirect to an internal/private address (e.g., 169.254.169.254 for cloud metadata, or 127.0.0.1 for local services) bypasses all validation on the final destination.
finding.evidence: Line 32 checks u.hostname against IMAGE_HOSTS; line 50: requests.get(url, timeout=10, stream=True) follows redirects to any destination without re-validation.

reason: The finding describes the redirect-following SSRF in shopapi/images.py, where only the initial URL is validated.

finding.title: Payment confirmation treats provider timeout as success (fail-open)
finding.description: When the payment provider call times out in confirm_payment (line 39), the handler defaults status to 'paid' (line 42) and proceeds to mark the order as 'processing', advancing the shipment pipeline. If network conditions cause frequent timeouts, or if an attacker deliberately causes the provider to time out, customers receive goods without paying. The comment explicitly acknowledges 'Reconciliation runs overnight', leaving a window where unpaid orders ship.
finding.evidence: Lines 39-42: except requests.Timeout → current_app.logger.warning(...) → status = 'paid', then db.execute("UPDATE orders SET status = 'processing', paid_pence = total_pence"). Orders advance to shipping without verified payment.

reason: It identifies confirm_payment treating a provider timeout as paid, matching V23.

finding.title: CORS reflects any Origin with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials enabled
finding.description: The after_request CORS hook sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin to whatever the client sends as the Origin header (line 47). When CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS is True (config.py line 12), it also sets Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true (line 50). Combined, this allows any malicious website to make authenticated cross-origin requests on behalf of logged-in users, defeating CSRF protections entirely. The safe approach would be a fixed whitelist of allowed origins.
finding.evidence: GET /health with Origin: https://evil.com returned Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://evil.com AND Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, confirming reflected origin with credentials enabled.

reason: The after_request hook reflects arbitrary Origin values while allowing credentials, matching the CORS vulnerability.

finding.title: Token refresh endpoint accepts forged JWTs (signature verification disabled)
finding.description: The /auth/refresh endpoint decodes the provided token with verify_signature=False (line 101). Any attacker can craft any JWT payload specifying arbitrary 'sub' (user ID) and 'role' claims, and the endpoint will create a fresh, properly signed token for that identity. This allows complete auth bypass — an unauthenticated attacker can impersonate any user including staff. Even though the broader @require_auth bug exposes all routes, fixing that alone would leave this root cause exploitable.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/refresh with forged JWT {sub:3, role:'staff'} returned HTTP 200 and a new valid, properly signed token. Using that token, GET /admin/users returned the full user list, confirming staff-level access was obtained.

reason: It identifies signature verification disabled in /auth/refresh, allowing forged tokens to be exchanged for signed tokens, and also explicitly notes the fail-open @require_auth bug.

finding.title: SQL injection in admin reviews report via interpolated display_name
finding.description: The /admin/reports/reviews endpoint uses Python f-string interpolation to embed customer['display_name'] directly into the SQL WHERE clause on line 80. While customer_id is safely parameterized, the displayed name extracted from the database is then interpolated unsafely. Since the broader @require_auth bug exposes admin routes to unauthenticated attackers, and since display_name is user-controllable via registration (auth.py line 77) and update_account (auth.py line 124), an attacker can store a SQL-injection payload as their display name and trigger injection against the admin API.
finding.evidence: Customer with id=11 had display_name "' UNION SELECT 1,'test',password_hash,'x','x' FROM users--". GET /admin/reports/reviews?customer_id=11 returned rows containing password hashes from the users table instead of legitimate reviews for that user.

reason: It identifies the second-order SQL injection in admin.reviews_by_customer, and also explicitly describes the fail-open require_auth bug.

finding.title: Passwords hashed with saltless SHA-256
finding.description: hash_password on line 16 uses plain hashlib.sha256() with no salt and zero iterations. Identical passwords across different users produce identical hashes, enabling rainbow table attacks. A single leaked database reveals all passwords. bcrypt, argon2id, or PBKDF2 with per-user random salt and ≥100k iterations should be used instead.
finding.evidence: Line 16: return hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() — single-pass SHA-256, no salt, no iterations.

reason: It identifies unsalted, single-pass SHA-256 password storage in hash_password.

finding.title: @require_auth decorator silently bypasses authentication due to broad except Exception handler
finding.description: The require_auth wrapper (lines 48-59) calls abort(401) when user_from_request returns None, but that HTTPException is caught by the bare 'except Exception' block on line 55. The handler logs the error, sets g.user = None, and then PROCEEDS TO EXECUTE THE FUNCTION anyway (line 58: return f(*args, **kwargs)). This means every endpoint decorated with @require_auth is accessible without authentication. All authenticated operations — reading other users' orders, viewing giftcard balances, adding items to basket, posting reviews, redeeming gift cards — are fully unauthenticated.
finding.evidence: GET /orders/1 without Authorization header returned HTTP 200 with full order details. GET /orders/2 returned another user's order. POST /basket/items {'sku': 'CARAFE', 'qty': 1} without auth returned HTTP 200 and added item.

reason: The finding correctly identifies the broad exception handler swallowing the 401 and allowing unauthenticated requests to continue.

finding.title: Flask debug=True enabled in entry point
finding.description: The run script starts Flask with debug=True (line 6). In production exposure, this enables the interactive Werkzeug debugger traceback pages, which provide an inline Python console accessible through error pages, enabling remote code execution via crafted URLs that trigger exceptions. While bound to 127.0.0.1, accidental network exposure would allow full RCE.
finding.evidence: run.py line 6: app.run(host="127.0.0.1", port=5000, debug=True)

reason: It identifies debug=True in run.py, which enables the Werkzeug interactive debugger.

finding.title: Password reset tokens use non-cryptographic randomness
finding.description: Reset tokens are generated as '%08d' % int(random.random() * 10**8) on line 135, producing only 8 decimal digits from Python's Mersenne Twister PRNG (~26.6 bits of entropy). This is trivially brute-forceable (only 10^8 possible values, and many fewer unique values given random.random()'s precision). An attacker trying codes sequentially could recover any reset token in seconds.
finding.evidence: Line 135: token = '%08d' % int(random.random() * 10**8) — only 8 digits from non-crypto random module (secrets.token_hex recommended instead).

reason: The finding identifies predictable, brute-forceable password-reset codes generated with random.random() in reset_request.

finding.title: Account enumeration via distinguishable login error messages
finding.description: The login endpoint returns 'no account with that email' (line 90) when the user doesn't exist, but 'wrong password' (line 92) when the user exists but credentials don't match. Attackers can enumerate valid email addresses in the system by observing these different error responses.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/login with nonexistent@mail.test → {"error":"no account with that email"}. POST /auth/login with priya.shah@mail.test + wrong password → {"error":"wrong password"}.

reason: The finding identifies account enumeration through distinguishable login errors, which is part of the login weakness in V16.

finding.title: Hardcoded JWT signing key in source code
finding.description: SECRET_KEY is hardcoded as 'hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d' (line 3). Anyone with source code access can forge valid JWT tokens for any user identity, completely undermining session integrity. This severely compounds the /auth/refresh vulnerability and means leaking this single file breaks all authentication.
finding.evidence: config.py line 3: SECRET_KEY = "hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d"

reason: It identifies the hardcoded JWT signing secret in config.py, which allows attackers with source access to forge tokens.

finding.title: Request body content logged verbatim including sensitive data
finding.description: The log_request before_request hook writes the full request body (first 2000 characters) to the log for POST/PUT/PATCH requests (line 31). This captures password fields during registration and login, personal data from form submissions, and other sensitive information in plaintext logs, violating data minimization principles and privacy regulations. Additionally, failed login attempts and other security-relevant events are not explicitly monitored or alerted.
finding.evidence: Line 31: log.info("%s %s %s", request.method, request.path, request.get_data(as_text=True)[:2000]) — logs all POST/PUT/PATCH request bodies verbatim.

reason: The finding identifies verbatim logging of request bodies in log_request, matching V20; its note about unmonitored failed logins also matches part of V21.

finding.title: Authentication failures fail open
finding.description: require_auth catches the 401 HTTPException raised when no valid user exists, logs it, sets g.user to None, and still invokes the protected handler. Any protected endpoint that does not immediately dereference g.user can therefore be used anonymously.
finding.evidence: GET /orders/1 without an Authorization header returned HTTP 200 and the complete order. The exception handler at lines 55-58 catches all exceptions and calls f(*args, **kwargs) after the failed check.

reason: The finding identifies require_auth catching the 401 exception and allowing unauthenticated requests to reach protected routes.

finding.title: Token refresh accepts unsigned attacker-controlled JWTs
finding.description: The refresh endpoint disables JWT signature verification and uses only the attacker-supplied sub claim to load a user. An attacker can name any existing account and obtain a newly signed access token for it.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/refresh with an unsigned JWT containing {"sub":1} returned HTTP 200 and a fresh signed token. Lines 101-105 decode with verify_signature=False and do not require proof of possession of a valid refresh token.

reason: It identifies the refresh endpoint accepting unsigned tokens and issuing a valid signed token for the attacker-selected account.

finding.title: Unauthenticated basket cookie is deserialized with pickle
finding.description: The basket cookie is client-controlled and has no integrity protection, but read_basket base64-decodes it and passes it to pickle.loads. A crafted cookie can execute arbitrary Python code when any endpoint reads the basket, including the public basket endpoint.
finding.evidence: read_basket at lines 15-23 calls pickle.loads on request.cookies['basket']; GET /basket at lines 44-46 invokes it without authentication or a signature check.

reason: It identifies the unsigned, client-controlled basket pickle deserialization in read_basket, which can enable remote code execution.

finding.title: Trailing-slash admin route bypasses staff authorization
finding.description: The global admin check compares request.path against exact registered route strings. The refunds route accepts both slash forms via strict_slashes=False, but the alternate form is not in admin_paths, allowing an unauthenticated caller to execute the staff-only refund handler.
finding.evidence: POST /admin/refunds/ with no Authorization header and {"order_id":1,"amount_pence":1} returned HTTP 200 and created a refund. The route is declared at shopapi/admin.py:52 with strict_slashes=False, while the check uses exact request.path membership at lines 36-41.

reason: It identifies the trailing-slash /admin/refunds/ route bypassing the exact-path staff authorization check.

finding.title: Product search is vulnerable to SQL injection
finding.description: The search term is concatenated into a SQL statement rather than passed as a bound parameter, allowing query predicates to be altered by a requester.
finding.evidence: The query at lines 40-42 interpolates q into both LIKE clauses. GET /products/search?q=%27%20OR%201%3D1-- returned all six products instead of a literal search result.

reason: The finding identifies SQL injection in GET /products/search caused by concatenating the search term into the query.

finding.title: Order lookup does not enforce ownership
finding.description: show_order calls get_order rather than own_order and never compares customer_id with the authenticated user. Any caller who knows an order ID can read another customer's order details, including totals, payment amount, items, and refunds.
finding.evidence: GET /orders/1 without authentication returned HTTP 200 with the order contents because authentication also fails open. Even after fixing that decorator, the handler at lines 46-49 still invokes get_order directly instead of the ownership-checking own_order helper.

reason: The finding primarily identifies the order ownership bypass in show_order (V01) and also describes require_auth failing open (V22).

finding.title: Review bodies are rendered as trusted HTML
finding.description: Review text is stored without sanitization and rendered with Jinja's safe filter. A user can submit HTML or script content that executes for visitors viewing the product page.
finding.evidence: add_review stores body directly at shopapi/products.py:82-91, and product.html renders r.body using {{ r.body|safe }} at line 13.

reason: It identifies the stored XSS caused by saving review text raw and rendering it with the safe filter.

finding.title: Staff review report is vulnerable to stored SQL injection
finding.description: The review report interpolates a customer's display_name into a SQL string. display_name is user-editable through /account, so a customer can store SQL syntax that is executed when staff request the report.
finding.evidence: Lines 77-81 construct the query with f"... WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}' ...". update_account at shopapi/auth.py:116-125 writes the untrusted display_name.

reason: The report interpolates a customer-controlled display_name into SQL, matching the second-order SQL injection in reviews_by_customer.

finding.title: Payment status timeout marks orders as paid
finding.description: A timeout contacting the payment provider is treated as a successful payment. The order is then moved to processing and paid_pence is set to total_pence, allowing fulfillment during provider outages or induced timeouts.
finding.evidence: confirm_payment catches requests.Timeout at lines 39-42 and assigns status = 'paid'; lines 43-46 then update the order to processing and paid_pence = total_pence.

reason: It identifies confirm_payment treating a provider timeout as paid, allowing unpaid orders to be processed.

finding.title: Passwords are stored as unsalted SHA-256 hashes
finding.description: Passwords are processed with one unsalted SHA-256 operation rather than a password-specific KDF. A database disclosure permits fast offline dictionary and brute-force cracking, with identical passwords producing identical hashes.
finding.evidence: hash_password at lines 15-16 returns hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest(). Registration and reset store this value at lines 77-78 and 158-159; no salt or work factor is used.

reason: The finding identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in shopapi/auth.py, matching V09.

finding.title: Staff can issue gift cards to themselves
finding.description: The /admin/giftcards endpoint allows a staff member to specify an arbitrary owner_id in the JSON body (line 45). Since owner_id defaults to null if not provided, a staff member can self-issue high-value gift cards (up to £500 per call, line 40). While the audit log records this action (line 46), there is no prevention against abuse. Staff can accumulate significant value by repeatedly issuing gift cards to themselves.
finding.evidence: POST /admin/giftcards with {"amount_pence": 50000, "owner_id": 3} (where user 3 is the calling staff member) returned HTTP 201 with code=HFDDDB5D497C and balance_pence=50000.

reason: This identifies a separate weakness in /admin/giftcards allowing staff to issue value to themselves, not the race condition in V15’s gift-card redemption.

finding.title: Password reset codes use weak randomness and have no attempt limit
finding.description: Reset codes are generated with non-cryptographic random.random(), are only eight decimal digits, and can be tried repeatedly for 30 minutes without throttling or an attempt counter. This permits online guessing of reset codes, especially from multiple clients.
finding.evidence: reset_request generates the code with int(random.random() * 10**8) at lines 135-136. reset_confirm compares the submitted code at lines 149-154 but records no failed attempts and applies no rate limit.

reason: It identifies the predictable reset codes and lack of attempt limits in reset_request/reset_confirm.

finding.title: Hardcoded predictable JWT signing secret
finding.description: HS256 JWTs use a source-controlled constant as their signing key. Anyone who obtains the source or knows the published configuration can forge access tokens, including tokens for other users or staff accounts.
finding.evidence: config.py:3 sets SECRET_KEY = 'hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d'; auth.py:23-27 signs tokens with it and auth.py:41-45 validates bearer tokens with the same value.

reason: The finding identifies the hardcoded JWT signing secret in config.py, which can be used to forge tokens.

finding.title: Login endpoint enables account enumeration
finding.description: The endpoint returns distinct responses for nonexistent accounts and existing accounts with incorrect passwords, allowing attackers to confirm registered email addresses.
finding.evidence: login returns "no account with that email" at line 90 when the user is absent and "wrong password" at line 92 when the account exists.

reason: The login endpoint reveals whether an email is registered through distinct error responses, matching V16.

finding.title: Payment webhook authenticates only the order ID
finding.description: The webhook HMAC covers only order_id, while status and amount_pence are trusted from the unsigned request body. Anyone able to generate or reuse a valid order signature can mark an order paid with an arbitrary amount, and the source-controlled default webhook secret makes signature generation feasible when configuration is not overridden.
finding.evidence: webhook_signature at lines 53-55 signs only str(order_id), while payment_webhook trusts event.status and event.amount_pence at lines 69-73. config.py:8 defaults WEBHOOK_SECRET to the known value whsec-local.

reason: It identifies the webhook flaw where the HMAC covers only the order ID while status and amount are trusted from the body.

finding.title: Request logging records sensitive credentials and personal data
finding.description: The global request logger writes mutating request bodies to application logs without redaction. Logs can therefore contain login and registration passwords, reset codes and passwords, refresh tokens, payment data, and other customer information.
finding.evidence: log_request at lines 28-31 logs request.get_data(as_text=True)[:2000] for every POST, PUT, and PATCH request, including /auth/login, /auth/refresh, and /auth/reset/confirm.

reason: The finding identifies log_request logging request bodies, including sensitive credentials, which matches V20.

finding.title: Stored SQL injection in staff review report
finding.description: reviews_by_customer interpolates customer display_name into SQL. A customer can set this through PATCH /account and a staff report request then executes the resulting SQL fragment.
finding.evidence: PATCH /account accepts punctuation in display_name; GET /admin/reports/reviews?customer_id=... reaches the f-string at lines 77-81 without parameterization.

reason: It identifies the second-order SQL injection in reviews_by_customer using a customer-controlled display_name.

finding.title: Image import follows redirects beyond the approved-host check
finding.description: The initial URL is restricted to approved public hosts, but requests.get follows redirects by default. An approved host that redirects to an internal or otherwise unapproved address can make the staff image-import endpoint fetch that address, bypassing the intended SSRF boundary.
finding.evidence: check_url validates only the initial parsed URL and its DNS result at lines 28-35; line 50 calls requests.get(url, timeout=10, stream=True) without allow_redirects=False or validation of each redirect destination.

reason: It identifies the redirect-following SSRF in shopapi/images.py, where only the initial URL is validated.

finding.title: SQL injection in product search
finding.description: The search term is concatenated directly into a SQL LIKE expression instead of being bound as a parameter. An unauthenticated caller can alter the WHERE clause.
finding.evidence: GET /products/search?q=%27%20OR%201%3D1-- returned HTTP 200 and all six catalogue products, demonstrating predicate bypass.

reason: The finding identifies SQL injection in the concatenated query parameter in GET /products/search.

finding.title: Persistent cross-site scripting in product reviews
finding.description: Review bodies are stored without HTML sanitization and rendered with Jinja's safe filter. Any authenticated user can persist markup that executes for product-page visitors.
finding.evidence: POST /products/<product_id>/reviews accepts body up to 2000 characters at products.py:82-92, and product.html line 13 emits r.body|safe.

reason: It identifies stored XSS from review bodies rendered with the safe filter on the product page.

finding.title: Unauthenticated pickle deserialization of basket cookie
finding.description: The basket cookie is client-controlled and unsigned, yet passed to pickle.loads. A crafted cookie can invoke attacker-controlled pickle reductions during any basket-reading request, resulting in code execution.
finding.evidence: read_basket decodes request.cookies['basket'] and calls pickle.loads at line 20; with_basket only base64-encodes pickle data and provides no signature.

reason: The finding correctly identifies unauthenticated pickle deserialization of the basket cookie in read_basket, enabling remote code execution.

finding.title: Checkout does not enforce or reserve inventory
finding.description: Checkout creates order lines from the client-controlled basket without checking stock or decrementing/reserving inventory. Repeated checkouts can therefore sell more units than the product stock indicates.
finding.evidence: checkout inserts the order and order_items at lines 69-73 using basket quantities. There is no stock predicate, stock update, or reservation anywhere in the checkout transaction.

reason: The finding describes a separate inventory-enforcement flaw in checkout, not the unsafe pickle deserialization in basket.read_basket (V18).

finding.title: Application entry point enables Flask debug mode
finding.description: The documented application startup path unconditionally enables Flask's interactive debugger. If the service is exposed through port forwarding or a proxy, unhandled exceptions can disclose source and the Werkzeug debugger can provide code execution.
finding.evidence: run.py:6 calls app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=5000, debug=True), and README.md documents running this entry point.

reason: The finding correctly identifies debug=True in run.py as enabling Flask’s interactive debugger.

finding.title: Payment timeout is treated as successful payment
finding.description: When provider status times out, confirm_payment assigns status='paid' and transitions the order to processing with paid_pence equal to the order total. An outage or induced timeout therefore marks an order paid without confirmation.
finding.evidence: The requests.Timeout handler at lines 39-42 assigns paid; lines 43-46 update status to processing and paid_pence to total_pence.

reason: It identifies confirm_payment treating a provider timeout as successful payment and processing the order without confirmation.

finding.title: Authenticated users can view other customers' orders
finding.description: show_order calls get_order, which selects solely by order ID, rather than own_order. A signed-in user who guesses another order ID can retrieve status, totals, items, and refund history.
finding.evidence: GET /orders/<order_id> is protected only by require_auth at lines 46-49; get_order lines 25-29 has no customer_id predicate, while IDs are sequential.

reason: It identifies the IDOR in show_order, which fetches orders by ID without checking that they belong to the signed-in customer.

finding.title: Passwords stored as unsalted fast SHA-256 hashes
finding.description: Password hashes are plain SHA-256 digests with no salt or work factor. Database disclosure permits rapid offline dictionary and brute-force recovery.
finding.evidence: hash_password at lines 15-16 is hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest(), and registration stores it directly at line 78.

reason: The finding identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in hash_password.

finding.title: Hardcoded JWT signing secret permits token forgery
finding.description: SECRET_KEY is a fixed repository-visible string used as the HS256 key for bearer JWTs. Anyone obtaining source can mint tokens with arbitrary user IDs and claims, bypassing authentication and authorization.
finding.evidence: config.py line 3 sets SECRET_KEY to a fixed string; auth.py lines 27 and 42 use it to sign and validate HS256 tokens.

reason: The finding identifies the hardcoded JWT signing secret in config.py, which enables token forgery.

finding.title: Stored display-name SQL injection in admin report
finding.description: A customer-controlled display_name is interpolated into a SQL string. Updating an account name and then requesting the review report can inject SQL through the f-string.
finding.evidence: PATCH /account accepts the attacker-controlled display_name (shopapi/auth.py:120-125); /admin/reports/reviews then interpolates customer['display_name'] at line 80. Bind the value as a SQL parameter.

reason: The finding identifies the second-order SQL injection in reviews_by_customer, where a customer-controlled display_name is interpolated into the admin report query.

finding.title: Trailing-slash refund route bypasses staff authorization
finding.description: The admin authorization hook compares request.path to exact route rules. The refunds route allows a trailing slash, so /admin/refunds/ is accepted but does not equal the collected /admin/refunds rule; the handler runs without staff authorization.
finding.evidence: Unauthenticated POST /admin/refunds/ reached the refund handler and returned HTTP 404 {"error":"no such order"} rather than 403. With a valid order it can call issue_refund without checking g.user.

reason: The trailing-slash refund route bypasses the exact-path staff authorization check.

finding.title: Product search SQL injection
finding.description: The search query is concatenated directly into the SQL statement, allowing an unauthenticated requester to alter the WHERE clause or append SQL expressions.
finding.evidence: GET /products/search?q=%27%20UNION%20SELECT%201,2,3,4,5,6,7-- reaches the concatenation at line 41; use parameterized LIKE values instead.

reason: It identifies the concatenated query parameter in GET /products/search, which is the SQL injection in V11.

finding.title: Passwordless token refresh accepts unsigned JWT claims
finding.description: The refresh endpoint explicitly disables signature verification, trusts the supplied sub claim, and signs a fresh token for that user. Anyone can submit a token encoding a known user ID (including staff) and obtain a valid session.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/refresh with an unsigned JWT payload {"sub":3} returned a valid staff JWT in testing. Require a valid signed refresh token and verify issuer/audience/expiry and token type.

reason: It identifies the refresh endpoint accepting unsigned claims and issuing a valid signed token for the supplied subject.

finding.title: Unauthenticated pickle deserialization from basket cookie
finding.description: The basket cookie is entirely client-controlled and is passed to pickle.loads without authentication or signing. A crafted cookie can execute attacker-chosen pickle gadget code when any basket endpoint reads it.
finding.evidence: read_basket() base64-decodes request.cookies['basket'] and calls pickle.loads at line 20 before any authentication. Use JSON with validation and an integrity-protected server-side/session representation instead.

reason: It identifies unauthenticated pickle deserialization in shopapi/basket.py’s read_basket function, matching the remote-code-execution vulnerability.

finding.title: Stored XSS in product reviews
finding.description: Review bodies are user-controlled and rendered with |safe, so HTML and event handlers persist and execute for every visitor to the product page.
finding.evidence: An authenticated POST /products//reviews with body '' is rendered by GET /p/MUG-SPECK. Escape review text (or sanitize with a strict HTML policy) before rendering.

reason: The finding identifies stored XSS from raw review text rendered with |safe in product.html.

finding.title: Trailing-slash admin refund bypasses staff check
finding.description: Admin protection compares request.path against a set of exact route strings. The refunds endpoint permits a trailing slash but the hook does not protect that alternate path, allowing unauthenticated refunds.
finding.evidence: Unauthenticated POST /admin/refunds/ with {"order_id":1,"amount_pence":1} returned 200 and created a refund, while the hook only checks exact membership in admin_paths. Protect by endpoint/blueprint or normalize paths.

reason: The exact-path admin check misses the trailing-slash refunds route, allowing the endpoint to bypass the staff check.

finding.title: Payment timeout fails open as paid
finding.description: When the payment provider times out, the exception handler unconditionally sets status to 'paid'. An attacker can cause or exploit provider unavailability to move an unpaid order into processing without payment.
finding.evidence: confirm_payment catches requests.Timeout at lines 39-42 and assigns status='paid', then line 44 marks the order processing and sets paid_pence. Timeouts must remain pending and be reconciled securely.

reason: It identifies confirm_payment treating a provider timeout as paid, allowing an order to be processed without payment.

finding.title: Order detail lacks ownership check
finding.description: The authenticated order detail handler calls get_order() rather than own_order(), so any signed-in customer can retrieve another customer's order, items, payment/refund details by changing the numeric ID.
finding.evidence: GET /orders/<order_id> is authenticated but line 49 uses get_order directly; replace with own_order (or an equivalent customer_id predicate).

reason: The finding identifies the IDOR in show_order, where get_order is used without checking that the order belongs to the authenticated customer.

finding.title: Passwords stored as unsalted SHA-256
finding.description: Password hashes use fast unsalted SHA-256, making database compromise vulnerable to efficient offline cracking. Use a modern adaptive password KDF such as Argon2id, scrypt, or bcrypt with per-password salts.
finding.evidence: hash_password() directly returns hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() at line 16.

reason: It identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in hash_password, matching V09.

finding.title: Passwordless token refresh accepts unsigned attacker-controlled JWT claims
finding.description: The refresh endpoint disables JWT signature verification and uses the unverified subject claim to issue a newly signed token. An attacker can name any existing user, including a staff user, and obtain a valid bearer token for that account.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/refresh with {"token":"eyJhbGciOiJub25lIn0.eyJzdWIiOjN9."} returned HTTP 200 and a signed token containing sub=3 and role=staff. The code at lines 101-107 decodes without verification and then calls make_token().

reason: The refresh endpoint disables signature verification and issues a signed token from the attacker-controlled subject claim.

finding.title: Internal PyPI index without hash pinning creates supply chain risk
finding.description: The primary package index (line 1) points to https://pypi.hartleyfinch.internal/simple, with pypi.org/simple only as extra-index-url. No --require-hashes directive is present. If the internal index is compromised, MITMed, or its TLS terminated insecurely, an attacker could substitute any dependency with a malicious version. Additionally, while direct dependencies are pinned by version, transitive dependencies are not pinned or checksummed. The editable install in requirements-dev.txt (-e packages/hf_payments) also masks potential code changes in local packages.
finding.evidence: requirements.txt line 1: --index-url https://pypi.hartleyfinch.internal/simple with no --require-hashes. Transitive dependencies unpinned.

reason: It identifies the public extra index in requirements.txt alongside the internal package setup and lack of hash pinning, which are the dependency-confusion risk described by V07.

finding.title: Payment webhook trusts attacker-chosen amount
finding.description: The webhook signature covers only order_id, not status or amount_pence. Anyone able to produce/replay a valid order-id signature (and the provider itself) can mark an order paid for an arbitrary amount; the handler never checks amount against the order total or paid amount.
finding.evidence: At lines 53-55 the HMAC input is only str(order_id); line 70 writes int(event.amount_pence) directly to paid_pence. Sign the complete canonical event and validate amount equals the expected total.

reason: The webhook signature covers only the order ID while the handler trusts the supplied status and amount, matching V19.

finding.title: Authentication failures are swallowed and protected handlers continue executing
finding.description: require_auth catches the abort(401) raised for a missing or invalid user, sets g.user to None, and still invokes the protected handler. Any protected endpoint that does not immediately dereference g.user can therefore be used anonymously, and other endpoints may fail with an uncontrolled server error instead of returning 401.
finding.evidence: The broad except at lines 55-58 catches the authentication abort and calls f(*args, **kwargs). GET /orders/1 without Authorization returned HTTP 200.

reason: The finding identifies require_auth swallowing abort(401) and allowing unauthenticated requests to reach protected handlers.

finding.title: Product search is vulnerable to SQL injection
finding.description: The q parameter is concatenated directly into the SQL statement rather than passed as a bound parameter, allowing an attacker to alter the WHERE clause and retrieve unintended records.
finding.evidence: GET /products/search?q=%27%20OR%201%3D1-- returned all six products. The query at lines 40-42 directly concatenates q into SQL.

reason: The finding identifies SQL injection in the q parameter of GET /products/search, matching V11.

finding.title: Order detail endpoint exposes orders without ownership validation
finding.description: The detail handler calls get_order() rather than own_order(), so it does not check that the requester owns the order. Combined with the swallowed authentication failure, the endpoint is also reachable without credentials.
finding.evidence: GET /orders/1 without an Authorization header returned HTTP 200 with order items, prices, payment totals, delivery date, and refunds.

reason: The finding identifies the ownership-check failure in show_order (V01) and also describes the swallowed authentication failure that lets unauthenticated requests reach the route (V22).

finding.title: Trailing-slash admin refund route bypasses the staff authorization check
finding.description: The global check compares request.path to registered route rules. The refunds route accepts both slash forms via strict_slashes=False, but only /admin/refunds is in admin_paths; /admin/refunds/ therefore reaches the staff-only handler without the check.
finding.evidence: POST /admin/refunds/ with no authentication returned HTTP 200 and created a refund, while POST /admin/refunds returned HTTP 403.

reason: It describes the trailing-slash /admin/refunds/ route bypassing the staff authorization check.

finding.title: Staff review report builds SQL from an attacker-controlled display name
finding.description: A customer can set display_name through PATCH /account. When staff request that customer's review report, the stored name is interpolated into an SQL f-string, allowing crafted input to alter the report query in a privileged request context.
finding.evidence: Line 80 uses f"WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}'" without parameterization; update_account at lines 116-125 stores the customer-controlled value.

reason: It identifies the second-order SQL injection in reviews_by_customer, where a customer-controlled display name is interpolated into the report query.

finding.title: Hardcoded JWT signing secret
finding.description: The application uses a fixed source-controlled SECRET_KEY for JWT signing. Anyone who obtains the repository can forge authentication tokens (and the refresh flaw makes staff impersonation especially direct). Load a high-entropy secret from deployment secrets and rotate it.
finding.evidence: config.py line 3 sets SECRET_KEY = 'hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d'; auth.py:27 uses it for HS256 tokens.

reason: It identifies the hardcoded SECRET_KEY in config.py, which lets anyone with the source forge JWTs.

finding.title: Unsigned client-controlled pickle basket cookie enables remote code execution
finding.description: The basket cookie is only base64 encoded and is deserialized with pickle without a signature, server-side session identifier, or restricted unpickler. An attacker can submit a malicious pickle payload and trigger arbitrary code execution whenever a basket endpoint reads it.
finding.evidence: read_basket() passes base64.urlsafe_b64decode(request.cookies['basket']) directly to pickle.loads() at lines 15-23; with_basket() creates the unauthenticated cookie at lines 26-29.

reason: It identifies the unsigned, client-controlled pickle deserialization in shopapi/basket.py that enables remote code execution.

finding.title: Payment status timeout fails open and marks an order as paid
finding.description: When the payment provider times out, the exception handler treats the result as paid. The following branch moves the order to processing and sets paid_pence to the order total without confirmation from the provider.
finding.evidence: The requests.Timeout handler at lines 39-42 assigns status='paid'; lines 43-45 then update the order to processing and paid_pence=total_pence.

reason: It identifies confirm_payment in shopapi/payments.py treating a provider timeout as paid and processing the order without payment confirmation.

finding.title: Stored review content is rendered as trusted HTML
finding.description: Authenticated users can submit arbitrary review bodies, and the product template applies Jinja's safe filter when rendering them. A malicious reviewer can persist markup or script that executes for users viewing the product page.
finding.evidence: add_review stores body without sanitization at products.py lines 82-92, while product.html line 13 renders r.body|safe.

reason: The finding identifies unsanitized review bodies rendered with Jinja’s safe filter, matching the stored XSS in V13.

finding.title: JWT signing key is hardcoded and shared by deployments
finding.description: The HS256 signing key is embedded in source rather than supplied through protected deployment configuration. Anyone obtaining the source or deployed artifact can forge bearer tokens for arbitrary users and roles.
finding.evidence: config.py line 3 sets SECRET_KEY to the literal hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d; auth.py lines 27 and 42 use it for signing and validation.

reason: It identifies the hardcoded SECRET_KEY in config.py, which can be used to forge JWTs.

finding.title: Passwords are stored as unsalted fast SHA-256 hashes
finding.description: Passwords are hashed directly with SHA-256 without a salt or password-specific work factor. A database compromise permits efficient offline dictionary and brute-force recovery, and identical passwords have identical hashes.
finding.evidence: hash_password() returns hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() at lines 15-16; no password KDF such as Argon2, scrypt, or bcrypt is used.

reason: It identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in shopapi/auth.py’s hash_password function.

finding.title: Password reset codes use weak randomness and have no online guessing protection
finding.description: Reset codes are generated with the non-cryptographic random.random() PRNG and contain only eight decimal digits. Confirmation has no attempt counter, throttling, or lockout during the 30-minute validity window, allowing repeated guesses.
finding.evidence: reset_request() uses int(random.random() * 10**8) at line 135; reset_confirm() directly compares the submitted code at line 153 and has no failed-attempt tracking or rate limiting.

reason: It identifies the weak random reset codes and lack of attempt limits in reset_request/reset_confirm.

finding.title: Concurrent gift-card redemptions can double spend the balance
finding.description: Redemption reads the balance, computes a new value, inserts a redemption, and performs an unconditional update in separate operations. Concurrent requests can both pass the balance check and record spending against the same starting balance, while the last update overwrites the balance.
finding.evidence: Lines 39-43 check card.balance_pence, calculate new_balance, insert a redemption, and unconditionally update the card. There is no transaction locking or conditional update that verifies the observed balance.

reason: The finding describes the race condition in giftcards.py redeem, where concurrent redemptions can overwrite the balance based on the same prior read.

finding.title: Image import can follow redirects to an unvalidated destination
finding.description: The URL check validates the initial hostname against an allowlist and checks its initial DNS answers, but requests.get follows redirects by default and the redirected destination is not passed through check_url. An approved host that redirects, or is compromised, can therefore make the staff-only importer fetch internal or otherwise unintended resources.
finding.evidence: check_url() validates only the parsed initial URL at lines 28-35, while line 50 calls requests.get(url, timeout=10, stream=True) without allow_redirects=False or revalidating each redirect.

reason: It identifies the redirect-following SSRF in shopapi/images.py, where only the initial URL is validated.

finding.title: Request logging records passwords, reset codes, and bearer tokens
finding.description: The global logger records the first 2,000 characters of every write request body. Login passwords, reset confirmation codes and replacement passwords, and refresh tokens are all sent in those bodies and are consequently copied into application logs and log aggregators.
finding.evidence: log_request() calls request.get_data(as_text=True)[:2000] for all POST, PUT, and PATCH requests at lines 29-31; the listed auth endpoints accept secrets in their JSON bodies.

reason: The finding identifies log_request logging request bodies, including passwords and reset secrets, matching V20.

finding.title: Payment webhook uses a predictable default secret and trusts the supplied amount
finding.description: When WEBHOOK_SECRET is unset, signatures use the source-visible default whsec-local. In addition, the authenticated message covers only the order ID: the handler accepts any amount_pence and records it without comparing it with the order total or a provider transaction.
finding.evidence: config.py line 8 supplies the fallback secret. payments.py lines 53-64 authenticate a signature over only order_id, and lines 69-71 write event.amount_pence directly to paid_pence without validation.

reason: It identifies the webhook flaw where the signature covers only the order ID while the supplied amount is trusted.

finding.title: SQL injection in product search
finding.description: The /products/search endpoint interpolates the 'q' query parameter directly into a SQL string via Python string concatenation. An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL, demonstrated by a UNION SELECT that extracts password hashes from the users table.
finding.evidence: GET /products/search?q=a'%20UNION%20SELECT%201,email,password_hash,4,5,6,7%20FROM%20users--%20 returned rows containing email addresses and SHA-256 password hashes from the users table.

reason: It identifies SQL injection in the q parameter of GET /products/search, matching V11.

finding.title: Dependency installation lacks artifact hash verification and uses multiple indexes
finding.description: Version pins alone do not authenticate the package artifacts selected by the installer. The build uses an internal index plus public PyPI and provides no hashes, so a compromised mirror or substituted artifact can enter the build without integrity verification.
finding.evidence: requirements.txt lines 1-2 configure an internal index and pypi.org, while lines 3-7 contain version pins but no --hash entries.

reason: The requirements file combines an internal index with public PyPI and has no hash pinning, matching the dependency-confusion and artifact-integrity risk in V07.

finding.title: Returns can refund more than the amount paid after prior refunds
finding.description: The return path computes a refund solely from the returned item quantities and prices. It does not account for existing refunds or cap cumulative refunds against paid_pence, so a prior goodwill or cancellation refund can be followed by a full item return refund exceeding the payment.
finding.evidence: return_items() calculates total at lines 86-94 and calls issue_refund() at line 96 without summing existing refunds; the separate admin path explicitly performs that cumulative check at admin.py lines 61-64.

reason: It identifies the return_items flaw that can refund items already refunded through cancellation, allowing duplicate refunds.

finding.title: JWT refresh accepts unsigned/forged tokens, allowing arbitrary privilege escalation
finding.description: The /auth/refresh endpoint decodes the supplied token with verify_signature=False, ignoring the JWT signature entirely. An attacker crafts any arbitrary JWT payload (e.g. sub=3 role=staff), sends it to /auth/refresh, and receives a new JWT that is legitimately signed with the app's secret key. This completely bypasses authentication.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/refresh with a forged JWT produced a fresh, server-signed token for user id=3 (staff). The forged token was verified working via subsequent API calls to protected endpoints like /admin/users.

reason: It identifies the refresh endpoint accepting tokens with signature verification disabled, allowing forged tokens to be exchanged for valid signed tokens.

finding.title: Order marked paid without verifying payment status
finding.description: On /orders/<id>/confirm-payment, if the external payment provider times out (requests.Timeout caught at line 39), the code unconditionally sets status to 'paid' (line 42). This means an order can be transitioned to 'processing' without confirming that payment was actually received, allowing free orders under network failure conditions.
finding.evidence: Code at shopapi/payments.py:39-42 catches requests.Timeout and sets status='paid'. Tested against /orders/{id}/confirm-payment endpoint during timeout scenarios.

reason: It identifies the timeout path in confirm_payment that treats an unverified payment as paid.

finding.title: Passwords hashed with unsalted SHA-256
finding.description: hash_password() applies plain SHA-256 without a salt or work factor (no bcrypt, scrypt, or argon2). This makes stored password hashes trivially crackable with precomputed rainbow tables or fast GPU-based brute force.
finding.evidence: shopapi/auth.py:16: return hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest(). Seed script uses a known weak password (demo-password-1) across all test accounts.

reason: It identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in hash_password, matching V09.

finding.title: SQL injection in admin reviews-by-customer report
finding.description: The display_name of the looked-up user is interpolated via f-string directly into the SQL query. While this requires admin access, if any user (including customers) registers with a display_name containing a quote character, the resulting query becomes malformed and injectable when an admin invokes this endpoint.
finding.evidence: shopapi/admin.py:78-81 constructs SQL as f"WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}'". The display_name is settable by any user through /account PATCH with no sanitization.

reason: It identifies the second-order SQL injection in reviews_by_customer, where a customer-controlled display_name is interpolated into the report query.

finding.title: Full request body logged in plaintext for authenticated mutations
finding.description: All POST/PUT/PATCH request bodies are logged verbatim (up to 2000 bytes), including sensitive data such as passwords during registration/login/reset, payment amounts, gift card codes, and personally identifiable information. Log access therefore grants exposure of credentials and personal data.
finding.evidence: shopapi/__init__.py:30-31: log.info('%s %s %s', request.method, request.path, request.get_data(as_text=True)[:2000]) captures full JSON body.

reason: The request logger records POST, PUT, and PATCH bodies, including sensitive credentials and personal data.

finding.title: Password reset tokens have insufficient entropy
finding.description: Reset tokens are generated as '%08d' % int(random.random() * 10**8), yielding at most 10^8 possibilities (~27 bits of entropy). Python's random module uses Mersenne Twister, which is deterministic and predictable. An attacker can brute-force reset codes offline and hijack any account's password reset flow.
finding.evidence: Code: token = '%08d' % int(random.random() * 10**8). Only 8 decimal digits of randomness from PRNG.

reason: It identifies the predictable, short password-reset code generated with random.random() in reset_request.

finding.title: Unvalidated CORS allows credential-leaking cross-origin requests
finding.description: The after_request hook echoes the request Origin header directly back as Access-Control-Allow-Origin (no allowlist). Combined with CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS=True (config.py line 12), any website can make credentialed cross-origin requests to the app and read responses, enabling CSRF-like attacks with stolen cookies.
finding.evidence: Config at config.py:12 sets CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS=True. Code at shopapi/__init__.py:47 sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin=request.headers.get('Origin') without validation. Verified by sending requests from a different Origin header.

reason: The after_request hook reflects any Origin and allows credentials, matching the CORS vulnerability in V05.

finding.title: Insecure Direct Object Reference on order details endpoint
finding.description: GET /orders/<id> shows any order to any authenticated user regardless of ownership. The get_order() function does not check if the requesting user is the order's owner. Customers can view complete details of other users' orders including items, prices, and refund history.
finding.evidence: With priya's auth token (user_id=1), GET /orders/3 returned the full order details for order belonging to user 2 (Tom Okafor), confirmed with HTTP 200 response containing items and pricing.

reason: It identifies the IDOR in show_order, where GET /orders/<id> uses get_order without checking order ownership.

finding.title: SQL injection in product search endpoint
finding.description: The /products/search endpoint interpolates the user-supplied 'q' query parameter directly into a SQL query string using Python string concatenation, rather than using parameterized queries. An attacker can execute arbitrary SQL against the SQLite database.
finding.evidence: Code: shopapi/products.py line 41: "SELECT * FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%" + q + "%' OR sku LIKE '%" + q + "%' ORDER BY name LIMIT 50". Sending ?q=' UNION SELECT 1,name,password_hash,4,5,6,7 FROM users-- returns HTTP 500 (SQLiteSyntaxError confirming SQL injection).

reason: It identifies SQL injection in the /products/search endpoint caused by concatenating the user-supplied query into SQL.

finding.title: SQL injection in admin reviews report via display_name
finding.description: The /admin/reports/reviews endpoint builds its SQL query using an f-string that embeds customer['display_name'] (retrieved earlier from the database). While the initial lookup is parameterized, an attacker who registers or updates their display_name to contain SQL metacharacters (e.g., "') OR 1=1--") will cause SQL injection when staff view their reviews. Since the STAFF role guard is checked elsewhere, an authenticated staff member can trigger this, but the root cause is that user-controlled display_name reaches the SQL interpreter unsafely.
finding.evidence: Code: shopapi/admin.py lines 74-80: customer display_name is fetched via parameterized query, then embedded in f-string: f"WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}'". An attacker registering with display_name containing quotes/sql can poison this.

reason: It identifies the second-order SQL injection in admin.reviews_by_customer, where a customer-controlled display_name is interpolated into the report query.

finding.title: JWT signature verification disabled in token refresh
finding.description: The /auth/refresh endpoint decodes the supplied JWT with verify_signature=False, meaning any forged token accepted as input produces a fresh valid token. An attacker can supply any sub value in a self-signed JWT to assume any user's identity, provided that user_id exists in the database.
finding.evidence: Code: shopapi/auth.py line 101: jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False}). Tested: sending a forged token with sub=1 produced a valid session token for Priya Shah (user id 1).

reason: The refresh endpoint disables JWT signature verification, allowing forged tokens to be exchanged for valid signed tokens.

finding.title: Unsalted SHA-256 password hashing
finding.description: Passwords are hashed with plain SHA-256 without a per-user salt. This is vulnerable to rainbow table attacks and precomputation. Modern applications should use bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2id with built-in salting.
finding.evidence: Code: shopapi/auth.py lines 15-16: def hash_password(password): return hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest(). No salt is generated or stored alongside the hash.

reason: The finding identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in shopapi/auth.py's hash_password function.

finding.title: Request bodies (including passwords) logged in plaintext
finding.description: The log_request before_request handler writes the full body of every POST, PUT, and PATCH request to the log, truncating only to 2000 characters. This includes password fields in login/registration/reset requests and any other sensitive data submitted by users.
finding.evidence: Code: shopapi/__init__.py line 31: log.info("%s %s %s", request.method, request.path, request.get_data(as_text=True)[:2000]). Login requests contain passwords which are thus written to server logs.

reason: The finding identifies log_request logging POST, PUT, and PATCH request bodies, including passwords, to the application logs.

finding.title: Arbitrary code execution via pickle-deserialized basket cookie
finding.description: The basket cookie is a base64-encoded pickle object that is unpickled without any integrity check. An attacker can craft a malicious pickle payload containing arbitrary Python expressions. When the server deserializes this cookie, it will execute the attacker's code (e.g., os.system('rm -rf /')).
finding.evidence: Code: shopapi/basket.py line 20: data = pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw)). The pickle format supports arbitrary object instantiation and method calls. Any authenticated or anonymous user controls this cookie.

reason: The finding identifies the unsigned pickle deserialization of the attacker-controlled basket cookie in shopapi/basket.py, which enables remote code execution.

finding.title: User enumeration via login endpoint error messages
finding.description: The login endpoint returns different error messages for non-existent accounts ('no account with that email') versus known accounts with wrong passwords ('wrong password'), allowing attackers to enumerate registered email addresses through automated testing.
finding.evidence: Code: shopapi/auth.py lines 90 and 92 return distinct error strings. Verified against running app: posting to /auth/login with nonexistent@email.test returns {"error":"no account with that email"} while correct email + wrong password returns {"error":"wrong password"}.

reason: The login endpoint reveals whether an email is registered through distinct error messages, matching V16.

finding.title: Weak pseudo-random password reset tokens
finding.description: Password reset tokens are generated using Python's random.random(), which is not cryptographically secure and only produces values seeded by process start time. Combined with the format "%08d" (8 decimal digits), there are only 100 million possible codes, trivially brute-forced. Also, the timing comparison in reset_confirm uses == which could leak information, though SQLite handles this differently.
finding.evidence: Code: shopapi/auth.py line 135: token = "%08d" % int(random.random() * 10**8). Only ~10^8 possible values from insecure PRNG.

reason: It identifies the predictable, short password-reset codes generated with random.random() in reset_request.

finding.title: Insecure Direct Object Reference on order details endpoint
finding.description: The /orders/<int:order_id> endpoint uses get_order() instead of own_order(), allowing any authenticated user to view the complete details of ANY order in the system (including other customers' orders), regardless of ownership.
finding.evidence: Code: shopapi/orders.py line 49 calls get_order(order_id) which only verifies the order exists. Compare with line 36 own_order() which checks ownership. Tested: GET /orders/3 (owned by customer 2) succeeded for customer 1's auth context.

reason: It identifies the IDOR in show_order, where get_order() allows a customer to view another customer's order.

finding.title: Hardcoded SECRET_KEY in source code
finding.description: The Flask SECRET_KEY used for signing JWT tokens and session cookies is hardcoded in the source file ('hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d'). Anyone with repository access can forge valid JWT tokens and impersonate any user.
finding.evidence: Code: config.py line 3: SECRET_KEY = "hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d". Combined with the weak hash algorithm (HS256 in PyJWT), this key being public effectively breaks authentication entirely.

reason: The finding identifies the hardcoded SECRET_KEY in config.py, which can be used to forge signed tokens.

finding.title: CORS reflects Origin with credentials enabled
finding.description: The CORS handler dynamically sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin to the requesting Origin header, and CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS is True. This allows any website to make cross-origin authenticated requests to this API, leaking user data and allowing actions on behalf of victims.
finding.evidence: Code: shopapi/__init__.py lines 44-51 reflect Origin; config.py line 11 sets CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS = True. Verified: requesting /products with Origin: https://evil.com returns Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true with the evil origin.

reason: The finding identifies the CORS handler reflecting arbitrary Origin values while allowing credentials, matching V05.

finding.title: SQL injection in product search endpoint
finding.description: The /products/search endpoint builds its SQL query using string concatenation with the raw user-supplied 'q' parameter. An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL, as confirmed by sending `'+OR+1=1--` which returned all products regardless of the search term. Error responses when injection fails may leak database schema details.
finding.evidence: GET /products/search?q='+OR+1=1-- returned all 6 products instead of zero matches. Confirmed SQLi in shopapi/products.py:41: `"SELECT * FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%" + q + "%' OR sku LIKE '%" + q + "%' ORDER BY name LIMIT 50"`

reason: It identifies SQL injection in the raw q parameter used by the product search query in shopapi/products.py.

finding.title: SQL injection in admin reviews endpoint
finding.description: The /admin/reports/reviews endpoint embeds the customer display_name directly into a SQL query using an f-string. Because display_name comes from the database (stored during registration without sanitization), but any registered user can control their own display_name, this creates a second-order SQL injection path. A user who registers with a display_name containing SQL can then inject arbitrary SQL through this admin endpoint.
finding.evidence: A registered user (display_name=`x'; DROP TABLE reviews; --`) was created at POST /auth/register. This name is later embedded unsafely in: `f"WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}'"` on line 80. While the endpoint requires staff access, the underlying display_name value is attacker-controlled via registration.

reason: The finding identifies the second-order SQL injection in admin.reviews_by_customer, where an attacker-controlled stored display_name is interpolated into the report query.

finding.title: Refresh token endpoint accepts forged tokens via verify_signature=False
finding.description: The /auth/refresh endpoint decodes JWTs with verify_signature=False, meaning any attacker can forge a token with sub=<any_user_id>, swap it for a valid signed token, and impersonate that user. Verified by creating a fake JWT with algorithm='none', sub=3 (staff), and refreshing it to get a legitimate signed staff token. This bypasses all authentication entirely.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/refresh with token `eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJub25lIn0...` (forged, algorithm=none) returned HTTP 200 and a valid signed JWT. Using that returned token, GET /admin/users succeeded as staff, confirming privilege escalation.

reason: The refresh endpoint disables JWT signature verification, allowing forged tokens to be exchanged for valid signed tokens.

finding.title: Debug mode enabled in application entry point
finding.description: The application runs with debug=True, which enables the interactive Werkzeug debugger. If exposed, an attacker can execute arbitrary Python code on the server through the debugger console.
finding.evidence: Code: run.py line 6: app.run(host="127.0.0.1", port=5000, debug=True). While bound to localhost, this is unsafe for production and leaks detailed stack traces on errors.

reason: run.py enables debug=True, matching the planted vulnerability of exposing the Werkzeug interactive debugger.

finding.title: Missing authorization on individual order view (IDOR)
finding.description: The GET /orders/<id> endpoint only checks authentication (via @require_auth) but never verifies the requesting user owns the order. In contrast, own_order() correctly validates customer_id. Any authenticated user can view another user's full order history, items, refund details, and amounts.
finding.evidence: Logged in as customer admin2@hartleyfinch.co.uk (user_id=5), sent GET /orders/2 which returned order belonging to Priya Shah (user_id=1), including status, total_pence=2400, and item details.

reason: It identifies the IDOR in show_order, where any authenticated customer can view another customer's order.

finding.title: Passwords hashed with unsalted SHA-256
finding.description: hash_password() uses plain SHA-256 without a per-user salt. This makes rainbow table attacks feasible and identical passwords produce identical hashes. Modern practices require bcrypt, scrypt, or argon2.
finding.evidence: shopapi/auth.py:16: `return hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest()`. The seed script shows all demo users share password 'demo-password-1' producing the same hash, confirming no salting.

reason: It identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in hash_password, matching V09.

finding.title: Account enumeration via login response
finding.description: The login endpoint returns 'no account with that email' (401) versus 'wrong password' (401) for different failure modes. While both return 401, the JSON error message differs, allowing attackers to enumerate valid email addresses. Combined with the lack of rate limiting, this enables credential stuffing against known accounts.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/login with nonexistent@example.com returned {"error":"no account with that email"} while POST with priya.shah@mail.test and wrong password returned {"error":"wrong password"}. No rate limiting exists on the login endpoint.

reason: The finding identifies the login email-enumeration behavior and lack of rate limiting in auth.py.

finding.title: Hardcoded JWT secret key
finding.description: SECRET_KEY is hardcoded as a static string ('hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d') in config.py. This key is used to sign all JWT tokens. Anyone who reads this source code can forge authentication tokens for any user (including staff/admin roles), completely bypassing authentication. It also means the key is shared across all instances.
finding.evidence: config.py:3: `SECRET_KEY = "hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d"`. Used in auth.py:27 for jwt.encode() and auth.py:42 for jwt.decode().

reason: The finding identifies the hardcoded JWT signing secret in config.py, which enables token forgery.

finding.title: Stored XSS via unescaped review body
finding.description: Review comments are stored verbatim and rendered with Jinja2's |safe filter, bypassing auto-escaping. An attacker-posted review containing HTML/JavaScript executes in other users' browsers when they view the product page. The description_html() function only sanitizes the product description_md field, not the review body itself.
finding.evidence: POST /products/1/reviews with body `<script>alert('xss')</script>` succeeded (201). GET /p/MUG-SPECK then rendered `<script>alert('xss')</script>` inside `<div class="review-body">`, confirming execution. Found in template line 13: `{{ r.body|safe }}`.

reason: It identifies stored XSS from raw review text rendered with `|safe` in the product template.

finding.title: Weak password reset tokens
finding.description: Reset tokens are generated with '%08d' % int(random.random() * 10**8), producing values between 00000000 and 99999999 — only ~10^8 possibilities. Since random.random() uses Python's Mersenne Twister (predictable given state) and the space is tiny, an attacker can brute-force the reset code or predict it. The 30-minute window compounds this risk.
finding.evidence: shopapi/auth.py:135: `token = "%08d" % int(random.random() * 10**8)`. This produces an 8-digit numeric token from a weak PRNG with only 100 million possible values.

reason: The reset code uses random.random() to generate a short, brute-forceable token, matching V10.

finding.title: JWT signature verification disabled on /auth/refresh enables impersonation
finding.description: The /auth/refresh endpoint decodes JWTs with verify_signature=False at line 101. Any crafted JWT payload is accepted regardless of signature validity. The endpoint trusts whatever sub claim appears in the forged token to look up and re-issue a real session for that user.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/refresh with unsigned forged JWT containing sub=1 returned HTTP 200 with a freshly signed valid JWT for user 1. GET /account confirmed identity as user 1 (Priya Shah).

reason: It identifies the refresh endpoint accepting unsigned tokens and issuing valid tokens for the forged subject, matching V17.

finding.title: SQL injection in product search endpoint
finding.description: The /products/search endpoint builds its SQL query by concatenating the user-supplied q parameter directly into the string at line 41. No parameterization is used, allowing an attacker to inject arbitrary SQL including UNION-based attacks.
finding.evidence: GET /products/search?q=%27%20OR%201%3D1%20-- returned all 6 products instead of zero results.

reason: It identifies SQL injection in the q parameter of GET /products/search, matching V11.

finding.title: Stored XSS via review body rendered unescaped in product pages
