finding.description: Review bodies submitted via POST /products/id/reviews are stored after minimal validation but not sanitized. The Jinja2 template renders review bodies with the safe filter at product.html line 13, bypassing autoescaping. An attacker can inject script tags or javascript: URIs.
finding.evidence: POST /products/1/reviews with body=<script>alert(1)</script> succeeded with 201. GET /p/MUG-SPECK returned HTML containing the raw script tag inside div.review-body.

reason: It identifies stored review-body XSS caused by rendering unsanitized review text with the safe filter.

finding.title: Auth decorator swallows HTTPException, allowing unauthenticated access to protected endpoints
finding.description: The @require_auth decorator wraps authentication in a try/except Exception block. When abort(401) raises Flask HTTPException at line 54, it is caught by except Exception, g.user is set to None, and execution continues to the route handler. Endpoints not referencing g.user return data unauthenticated; those referencing g.user crash with 500 errors.
finding.evidence: GET /orders/1 with no Authorization header returned HTTP 200 with full order data. GET /orders with no auth returned 500 Internal Server Error due to AttributeError when accessing g.user id.

reason: The finding identifies require_auth catching the HTTPException from abort(401) and continuing unauthenticated, which is V22.

finding.title: SQL injection in admin review lookup via unsanitized display_name
finding.description: The /admin/reports/reviews endpoint constructs its SQL query using Python f-string interpolation with customer display_name at line 80. While this requires staff authentication, the display_name value was originally user-controlled input (settable via PATCH /account) and stored without sanitization.
finding.evidence: Set user 1 display_name to SQL injection payload via PATCH /account. GET /admin/reports/reviews?customer_id=1 as staff triggered HTTP 500 Internal Server Error.

reason: It identifies the second-order SQL injection in reviews_by_customer, where a customer-controlled display_name is interpolated into the admin report query.

finding.title: Payment confirmation marks order as paid when provider times out
finding.description: When the external payment provider does not respond within the timeout period, the confirm_payment handler sets status=paid at line 42 and unconditionally updates the order to processing with paid_pence equal to total_pence. If the payment actually failed but only the network timed out, the customer receives goods without paying.
finding.evidence: Code at payments.py lines 37-45: except requests.Timeout branch sets status=paid then falls through to if status==paid update to processing with full amount credited.

reason: It identifies the timeout path in confirm_payment that treats an unverified payment as paid and processes the order.

finding.title: Insecure Direct Object Reference - order details accessible to any authenticated user
finding.description: The show_order function calls get_order which selects ANY order by ID without verifying the requesting user owns the order. Any authenticated user can view another user's order details including items, prices, payment amounts, refund history, and delivery dates.
finding.evidence: Authenticated as user 1, GET /orders/1 returned complete details of Priya Shah's order. Even without Authorization header, the auth decorator bug allowed unauthenticated access returning full order data.

reason: The finding identifies the order-ownership IDOR in show_order and also explicitly describes the fail-open authentication decorator.

finding.title: Passwords hashed with unsalted single-pass SHA-256
finding.description: Password hashing at line 16 uses hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() with no salt, pepper, or iterative stretching. This enables offline brute-force and rainbow table attacks across all users simultaneously.
finding.evidence: def hash_password(password): return hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() - single-pass SHA-256, no salt, no work factor.

reason: The finding identifies unsalted, single-pass SHA-256 password storage in hash_password, matching V09.

finding.title: Flask debug mode enabled in production deployment
finding.description: debug=True is passed to app.run() at line 6, enabling Werkzeug interactive debugger and auto-reloader. If an exception occurs, the debugger presents an interactive Python console that could allow remote code execution if the PIN is guessable.
finding.evidence: app.run(host=127.0.0.1, port=5000, debug=True)

reason: The finding identifies debug=True in run.py, which enables the Werkzeug interactive debugger.

finding.title: Sensitive request bodies including plaintext passwords logged to server logs
finding.description: At line 31, all POST/PUT/PATCH request bodies are logged in full (truncated to 2000 characters) via log.info(). Registration requests contain plaintext passwords, exposing credentials in log output accessible to operators or monitoring systems.
finding.evidence: log.info with request.get_data(as_text=True)[:2000] captures entire request body including passwords sent during registration.

reason: It identifies the request logger recording POST, PUT, and PATCH bodies, including plaintext passwords, in server logs.

finding.title: Unrestricted CORS with credentials allowed from any origin
finding.description: The CORS middleware at lines 44-50 echoes back the requester Origin header unconditionally as Access-Control-Allow-Origin and sets Access-Control-Allow-Credentials true. Any website can make authenticated cross-origin requests.
finding.evidence: GET /products with Origin https://evil.example.com returned headers Access-Control-Allow-Origin https://evil.example.com and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials true.

reason: It identifies the CORS handler reflecting arbitrary origins while allowing credentials.

finding.title: Password reset token has only ~27 bits of entropy from non-cryptographic RNG
finding.description: The reset token at line 135 is generated with 8-digit decimal number producing max 100 million possibilities using the random module which is deterministic and not cryptographically secure. Combined with a 30-minute validity window, brute-force recovery is feasible.
finding.evidence: token = %08d % int(random.random() * 10**8) produces only 8 digits (~27 bits entropy). With 30-minute expiry, exhaustive search is feasible over network.

reason: The finding identifies the predictable, short password-reset code generated with random.random(), which is V10.

finding.title: Secret key hardcoded in source code
finding.description: SECRET_KEY is a static string committed to the repository. Since JWT tokens use HS256 with this key, anyone reading the source code can forge valid JWT tokens for any user with any role.
finding.evidence: SECRET_KEY = hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d visible in plain text in config.py line 3.

reason: The finding identifies the hardcoded JWT signing secret in config.py, which allows tokens to be forged.

finding.title: Unsafe pickle deserialization of browser-controlled cookie data
finding.description: The basket cookie at line 20 is deserialized with pickle.loads from data controlled by the browser. Pickle supports arbitrary object instantiation, meaning a crafted cookie payload can trigger remote code execution. No integrity check validates the cookie before loading.
finding.evidence: pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw)) at line 20 reads raw data from browser-controlled basket cookie without HMAC or signature verification.

reason: It identifies the unsigned, browser-controlled pickle deserialization in shopapi/basket.py that can enable remote code execution.

finding.title: Unauthenticated pickle deserialization from the basket cookie
finding.description: The basket cookie is client-controlled and unsigned, but is decoded with pickle.loads(). A crafted cookie can execute attacker-controlled Python code whenever a basket endpoint reads it.
finding.evidence: read_basket() base64-decodes request.cookies['basket'] and calls pickle.loads() at shopapi/basket.py:15-23. with_basket() writes an ordinary base64-encoded pickle at lines 26-28 without authentication or signing. The public GET /basket endpoint invokes read_basket().

reason: It identifies unauthenticated pickle deserialization in shopapi/basket.py's read_basket function, enabling remote code execution.

finding.title: User enumeration via distinct login error messages
finding.description: The login endpoint returns different error messages for non-existent emails versus wrong password for existing accounts, allowing attackers to enumerate valid email addresses.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/login with nonexistent@nobody.com returned error no account with that email. POST with priya.shah@mail.test + bad password returned wrong password.

reason: The finding identifies email enumeration through distinct login errors in auth.login, which is part of V16.

finding.title: Trailing-slash admin refund route bypasses staff authorization
finding.description: The global admin check compares the literal request path to registered route rules. The refund route accepts a trailing slash due to strict_slashes=False, but the trailing-slash path is not in the exact rule set, allowing the handler to run without the staff check.
finding.evidence: shopapi/__init__.py:26-41 builds admin_paths from route rules and checks request.path for exact membership. shopapi/admin.py:51-53 registers /admin/refunds with strict_slashes=False, while goodwill_refund() performs a refund at lines 55-67 without its own authorization check.

reason: It identifies the trailing-slash bypass of the staff check on /admin/refunds, allowing goodwill_refund to run without authorization.

finding.title: Authentication failures are swallowed, allowing protected handlers to continue
finding.description: require_auth catches the 401 exception raised when authentication fails and then invokes the protected handler with g.user set to None. Protected handlers that do not immediately dereference g.user are therefore reachable without authentication.
finding.evidence: The broad except at shopapi/auth.py:55-58 catches abort(401) from line 54 and returns f() anyway. A request without Authorization to GET /orders/3 returned HTTP 200 with order details, while the same flaw exposes GET /giftcards/HFDEMO10.

reason: The require_auth decorator catches the 401 exception and continues into protected handlers with g.user=None, matching the fail-open authentication flaw.

finding.title: Stored display names enable second-order SQL injection in the staff report
finding.description: A customer's stored display_name is interpolated into a SQL query when staff request the review report. A customer can save SQL syntax as their display name and have it interpreted later in the administrative query.
finding.evidence: display_name is accepted and stored by update_account() at shopapi/auth.py:119-125. reviews_by_customer() inserts customer['display_name'] into an f-string SQL WHERE clause at shopapi/admin.py:77-80 instead of binding it.

reason: The finding identifies the second-order SQL injection in reviews_by_customer, where a customer-controlled display_name is interpolated into the report query.

finding.title: Stored XSS in review bodies
finding.description: Review bodies are stored without sanitization and rendered as trusted HTML, allowing an authenticated user to inject script or event-handler markup that executes for visitors viewing the product page.
finding.evidence: add_review() inserts the submitted body directly at shopapi/products.py:90-91. shopapi/templates/product.html renders the review body with the Jinja safe filter, so the stored value is not escaped.

reason: The review identifies stored XSS from raw review bodies rendered with the Jinja safe filter.

finding.title: Product search is vulnerable to SQL injection
finding.description: The q parameter is concatenated directly into the SQL statement instead of being bound as a parameter, allowing an attacker to alter the WHERE clause and retrieve unintended records.
finding.evidence: shopapi/products.py:40-42 constructs SQL by concatenating q into LIKE expressions. GET /products/search?q=%27%20OR%201%3D1%20-- returned all six products instead of only matching products.

reason: The finding identifies SQL injection in the concatenated q parameter in GET /products/search.

finding.title: Order detail endpoint does not enforce ownership
finding.description: The order detail handler uses get_order() rather than own_order(), so an authenticated customer can retrieve another customer's order details. Combined with the fail-open authentication decorator, unauthenticated callers can also retrieve them.
finding.evidence: show_order() at shopapi/orders.py:46-49 returns order_json(get_order(order_id)); the ownership check exists only in own_order() at lines 32-36 and is not called. GET /orders/3 without credentials returned the order's items, totals, delivery date and refunds.

reason: It identifies the ownership bypass in show_order (V01) and also describes the fail-open authentication decorator (V22).

finding.title: Returns ignore previously cancelled quantities
finding.description: The return validation compares returned quantity only with the original quantity and ignores cancelled_qty. Units already cancelled and refunded can therefore be returned and refunded a second time after delivery.
finding.evidence: cancel_items() increments cancelled_qty at shopapi/orders.py:65-68. return_items() accepts a return when returned_qty + qty <= item.qty at lines 90-93 and refunds qty * price at lines 94-96, without subtracting cancelled_qty.

reason: The finding identifies return_items allowing refunds for quantities previously cancelled, matching V14.

finding.title: Payment timeout fails open and marks orders as paid
finding.description: A timeout from the payment provider is explicitly converted to status='paid', after which the order is moved to processing and credited for its full total. Provider outages or induced timeouts can create unpaid fulfillable orders.
finding.evidence: confirm_payment() catches requests.Timeout and sets status = 'paid' at shopapi/payments.py:39-42. Lines 43-46 then set the order to processing and paid_pence=total_pence.

reason: It identifies confirm_payment treating a provider timeout as paid, allowing unpaid orders to be processed.

finding.title: Hardcoded JWT signing secret
finding.description: The JWT signing key is fixed in source code. Anyone who obtains the source or package can forge tokens, including tokens claiming the staff role.
finding.evidence: config.py:3 sets SECRET_KEY = 'hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d'; shopapi/auth.py uses it for both token signing at line 27 and verification at line 42.

reason: The finding identifies the hardcoded SECRET_KEY in config.py that can be used to forge JWTs.

finding.title: Token refresh accepts unsigned and expired JWTs
finding.description: The refresh endpoint disables signature verification and does not require a valid expiration claim. Anyone can fabricate an unsigned token containing an existing user ID and obtain a newly signed token with that user's role.
finding.evidence: shopapi/auth.py:101 calls jwt.decode(token, options={'verify_signature': False}); the untrusted sub is used to load a user at line 104 and make_token() issues a fresh token at line 107.

reason: The refresh endpoint disables JWT signature verification and uses the untrusted subject to issue a valid token.

finding.title: Checkout does not enforce or decrement stock
finding.description: Checkout creates order items from the client-controlled basket and current prices without checking product stock or updating it. Repeated customers can therefore place orders for unavailable quantities and oversell inventory indefinitely.
finding.evidence: basket_json() reads product rows and calculates totals at shopapi/basket.py:32-41 but never checks stock. checkout() inserts order items at lines 69-73 and no stock update occurs anywhere in that flow.

reason: The finding describes a distinct inventory-overselling weakness in checkout, not the basket-cookie deserialization issue in V18.

finding.title: Image import follows redirects to unvalidated destinations
finding.description: The image importer validates only the initial URL's hostname and public DNS result. requests.get() follows redirects by default, so an approved host that redirects can make the server fetch an internal or metadata address.
finding.evidence: check_url() validates only the original parsed URL at shopapi/images.py:28-35, then import_image() calls requests.get(url, timeout=10, stream=True) at line 50 without allow_redirects=False or revalidating redirect targets.

reason: It identifies the SSRF in shopapi/images.py where redirects can reach unvalidated destinations.

finding.title: Passwords are stored using unsalted SHA-256
finding.description: Passwords are hashed with a fast unsalted digest and no work factor. A database compromise therefore enables rapid offline cracking of common or reused passwords.
finding.evidence: hash_password() returns hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() at shopapi/auth.py:15-16, and check_password() compares raw digests at lines 19-20.

reason: It identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in hash_password, matching V09.

finding.title: Payment webhook authenticates only the order ID and trusts the amount
finding.description: The webhook signature covers only order_id. Once a signature is accepted, the request can supply any status amount and the handler stores amount_pence without comparing it to the order total or a provider-verified transaction.
finding.evidence: webhook_signature() signs only str(order_id) at shopapi/payments.py:53-55; payment_webhook() verifies that value at line 63 and assigns int(event.get('amount_pence', 0)) directly to paid_pence at lines 69-71.

reason: It identifies the webhook flaw where the signature covers only the order ID while the handler trusts the supplied payment amount and status.

finding.title: Concurrent gift-card redemptions can overspend a card
finding.description: Redemption reads the balance, checks the requested amount, computes a new balance, and later writes it without a row lock or conditional balance update. Concurrent requests can both pass the check and record redemptions against the same balance.
finding.evidence: shopapi/giftcards.py:36-43 performs the balance check, calculates new_balance, inserts the redemption, and unconditionally updates the card. The SQLite connection has no transaction-level conditional update protecting this sequence.

reason: It identifies the race condition in gift-card redemption where concurrent requests can overspend the balance.

finding.title: JWT Signature Verification Disabled on Token Refresh
finding.description: The /auth/refresh endpoint decodes incoming JWTs with verify_signature=False, accepting any token regardless of signature, origin, or tampering. Attackers can forge arbitrary claims (including sub=3 for admin role) and receive freshly signed valid tokens for those users.
finding.evidence: Line 101: jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False}). Live test: POST /auth/refresh with forged JWT payload {'token':'eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJzdWIiOjMsInJvbGUiOiJzdGFmZiJ9.'} returned a newly signed valid token for sub=3 (admin).

reason: The finding identifies refresh decoding JWTs with signature verification disabled, allowing forged tokens to be exchanged for valid signed tokens.

finding.title: Request logging records passwords and other sensitive request data
finding.description: The request hook logs complete POST, PUT, and PATCH bodies, including plaintext login and registration passwords, reset codes and new passwords, and potentially payment data. Anyone with log access can recover these secrets.
finding.evidence: shopapi/__init__.py:28-31 calls request.get_data(as_text=True)[:2000] for every write request with no endpoint-specific redaction.

reason: It identifies the request logger in shopapi/__init__.py logging sensitive POST, PUT, and PATCH bodies.

finding.title: Account Enumeration via Login Error Messages
finding.description: The login endpoint returns different error messages depending on whether the email exists ('no account with that email') versus having the correct email but wrong password ('wrong password'). This allows attackers to enumerate valid registered email addresses through simple probing.
finding.evidence: Live test: POST /auth/login with nonexistent@test.com returned {"error":"no account with that email"}. With admin@hartleyfinch.co.uk + wrong password returned {"error":"wrong password"}. Lines 90 and 92 produce distinct responses.

reason: The finding identifies login email enumeration through distinct responses for unknown emails and incorrect passwords.

finding.title: Predictable default webhook secret permits forged payment events
finding.description: When WEBHOOK_SECRET is not configured, the application uses the publicly guessable value whsec-local. An attacker can calculate valid webhook signatures and forge payment events.
finding.evidence: config.py:8 uses os.environ.get('WEBHOOK_SECRET', 'whsec-local'). The webhook derives its only signature from this secret and the attacker-supplied order ID at shopapi/payments.py:53-55.

reason: A publicly guessable default webhook secret enables forged payment events, which is a real weakness distinct from V19’s signature-scope and replay flaws.

finding.title: Arbitrary Code Execution via Pickle Deserialization in Basket Cookie
finding.description: The basket cookie value is deserialized using pickle.loads() without any integrity protection or sandboxing. An attacker who can craft a malicious cookie can achieve remote code execution when the server deserializes it. The cookie is set via with_basket() after add_item(), making exploitation straightforward.
finding.evidence: Line 20: data = pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw)). read_basket() deserializes whatever the client sends. Line 27: pickle.dumps() creates the cookie value.

reason: It identifies the unauthenticated pickle deserialization of the client-controlled basket cookie in read_basket, enabling remote code execution.

finding.title: Broken Authentication: require_auth Decorator Caught All Exceptions Including abort()
finding.description: The require_auth wrapper catches all exceptions including the HTTPException raised by abort(401), then falls through to execute the view function with g.user=None. This means every endpoint decorated with @require_auth effectively has NO authentication. Endpoints like /account or /orders crash when they try to access g.user['id'] (causing 500 errors), but endpoints that don't reference g.user (like /giftcards/<code>) serve data completely unauthenticated.
finding.evidence: Lines 48-59: except Exception block catches abort(401)'s HTTPException, sets g.user=None, then calls f(*args, **kwargs). Live test: GET /giftcards/HFDEMO10 without Authorization header returned {"balance_pence":1000} (HTTP 200). GET /account without auth returns HTTP 500.

reason: It identifies require_auth catching abort(401) and continuing unauthenticated, the fail-open vulnerability in V22.

finding.title: SQL Injection in Product Search
finding.description: The product search endpoint directly concatenates the user-controlled 'q' parameter into an SQL query without parameterization. An attacker can extract arbitrary data from the database, including password hashes.
finding.evidence: Line 40-41: String concatenation '%...' + q + '...'%' in LIKE clause. Live test: GET /products/search?q='+OR+1=1-- returned all products instead of matching results.

reason: It identifies SQL injection in the concatenated q parameter in GET /products/search.

finding.title: Password reset codes lack brute-force protection
finding.description: Reset codes are eight decimal digits generated with the non-cryptographic random module, remain valid for 30 minutes, and have no attempt counter or rate limiting. Repeated guesses can eventually reset an account password.
finding.evidence: shopapi/auth.py:135 generates the code with random.random() and an eight-digit format; reset_confirm() checks guesses at lines 143-161 without counting failures or applying rate limits.

reason: It identifies the predictable reset-code generation and lack of attempt limits in reset_request/reset_confirm.

finding.title: Stored XSS via Unescaped Review Content
finding.description: Review bodies are rendered using Jinja2's |safe filter, which completely disables auto-escaping. Any HTML or JavaScript submitted in a review will execute in visitors' browsers. Author names on line 14 are similarly vulnerable.
finding.evidence:
Line 13:
{{ r.body|safe }}
. Pre-existing test data includes a review with body containing which renders as raw script tags in the product page response.

reason: It identifies stored review-body XSS from rendering raw review text with the |safe filter.

finding.title: Weak Password Reset Tokens
finding.description: Password reset tokens are generated using Python's random.random() (Mersenne Twister PRNG), producing at most 100 million possible values (%08d). These are easily brute-forceable. Should use secrets.token_hex(6) or similar CSPRNG with sufficient entropy.
finding.evidence: Line 135: token = '%08d' % int(random.random() * 10**8)

reason: The finding identifies the predictable random.random() password-reset code in auth.py, matching V10.

finding.title: SQL Injection in Admin Reviews Report via Display Name
finding.description: The customer display_name is interpolated directly into a SQL query via Python f-string when querying reviews. While this route requires staff authentication, the require_auth decorator is globally broken (see separate finding), making it reachable by unauthenticated attackers. Even authenticated, any compromised staff member can perform full database attacks.
finding.evidence: Line 80: f"WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}' ...". Live test: Accessing admin/reports/reviews?customer_id=4 with a user whose display_name contains SQL metacharacters caused an HTTP 500 error from SQLite parse failure.

reason: It identifies the second-order SQL injection in reviews_by_customer, where a customer-controlled display name is interpolated into the report query.

finding.title: Hardcoded Secret Key
finding.description: The JWT signing SECRET_KEY is hardcoded as a literal string in source code. Anyone reading the repository knows the signing key, enabling them to forge arbitrary valid JWTs. Combined with the disabled signature verification on /auth/refresh, this enables complete authentication takeover.
finding.evidence: Line 3: SECRET_KEY = 'hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d'

reason: The finding identifies the hardcoded signing secret in config.py (V08) and also describes the signature-verification bypass in /auth/refresh (V17).

finding.title: Debug Mode Enabled
finding.description: The application is started with debug=True, exposing Werkzeug's interactive Python debugger in exception pages (allowing arbitrary code execution via the debugger console) and returning verbose stack traces to clients instead of safe JSON error responses.
finding.evidence: Line 6: app.run(host='127.0.0.1', port=5000, debug=True). Live test: various unauthorized requests returned HTTP 500 with HTML stack trace pages instead of JSON error responses.

reason: It identifies debug=True in run.py, which exposes the Werkzeug interactive debugger and verbose error details.

finding.title: Insecure Password Hashing (No Salt, Single Iteration)
finding.description: Passwords are hashed using bare SHA-256 without salt and without iteration count. Vulnerable to rainbow tables and GPU-based dictionary attacks. Identical passwords across users share the same hash, defeating uniqueness.
finding.evidence: Line 16: hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest()

reason: It identifies the unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in shopapi/auth.py.

finding.title: Sensitive Request Bodies Logged Without Sanitization
finding.description: Full request bodies (up to 2000 characters) are logged for every state-changing request. This captures sensitive information such as passwords during registration/login, gift card codes, payment details, and personal identifiers.
finding.evidence: Line 31: log.info('%s %s %s', request.method, request.path, request.get_data(as_text=True)[:2000])

reason: The request logger records up to 2,000 characters of state-changing request bodies, including passwords and other sensitive data.

finding.title: Payment Confirmation Bypass via Timeout Assumption
finding.description: When the payment provider times out during confirm-payment, the system automatically assumes status='paid' and marks the order as processing. An attacker who can cause intentional timeouts (e.g., via connection exhaustion) can confirm unpaid orders. The comment explicitly states this is assumed pending overnight reconciliation.
finding.evidence: Lines 39-42: except requests.Timeout: status = 'paid'. Order is marked processing and paid before actual confirmation.

reason: It identifies the timeout in confirm_payment being treated as paid, allowing an order to be processed without payment.

finding.title: Server-Side Request Forgery via Image Import Following Redirects
finding.description: Image import fetches external URLs using requests.get() which follows HTTP redirects by default. A whitelisted host can redirect to internal network addresses (e.g., http://localhost, http://169.254.169.254). DNS rebinding may also bypass hostname checks.
finding.evidence: Line 50: requests.get(url, timeout=10, stream=True) — default behavior follows Location headers. Hostname validation at check_url() only covers the starting URL.

reason: It identifies the SSRF in image import where requests follows redirects after only the initial URL is validated.

finding.title: Unrestricted CORS with Credentials Allowed
finding.description: The application reflects any Origin header back as Access-Control-Allow-Origin and includes Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. This permits any malicious website to make authenticated cross-origin requests to the API using session cookies. While JWT auth is primarily header-based (not cookie-based), the combination with the broken require_auth decorator makes this worse.
finding.evidence: Lines 44-50: origin reflected back verbatim with credentials enabled. Live test: GET /health with Origin: https://evil.example.com returned Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://evil.example.com and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.

reason: It identifies the unrestricted credentialed CORS behavior in the after_request hook.

finding.title: JWT signature verification disabled on token refresh
finding.description: The /auth/refresh endpoint decodes tokens with options={'verify_signature': False}. An attacker can forge a token with any 'sub' claim and get a valid session token for that user. Tested: POST /auth/refresh with an arbitrary signed payload returned a valid token for sub=1.
finding.evidence: Line 101: jwt.decode(token, options={'verify_signature': False}). HTTP test: POST /auth/refresh with a fake JWT {'sub':1} yielded token for user id 1.

reason: It identifies the refresh endpoint disabling JWT signature verification, allowing forged tokens to be exchanged for valid signed tokens.

finding.title: SQL injection in product search
finding.description: The search endpoint constructs SQL using string concatenation with the untrusted query parameter 'q'. An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL through the LIKE clause.
finding.evidence: Line 41: "SELECT * FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%' || q || '%'" via string concat. Confirmed via HTTP: GET /products/search?q=' OR 1=1-- returns all products.

reason: It identifies SQL injection from concatenating the untrusted search parameter into the product search query.

finding.title: No ownership check on order detail endpoint
finding.description: GET /orders/<int:order_id> calls get_order() which does not check that the requesting user owns the order. The own_order() helper exists but is unused here. Any authenticated user can view any other user's order details including refund history.
finding.evidence: Line 49: return jsonify(order_json(get_order(order_id))) uses get_order() without ownership check. HTTP test: authenticated user 4 retrieved order 3 belonging to user 2.

reason: It identifies the missing ownership check in show_order on GET /orders/<id>, allowing customers to read other users’ orders.

finding.title: Unsafe pickle deserialization of basket cookie
finding.description: read_basket() uses pickle.loads() on data from the client-controlled basket cookie. Pickle is inherently unsafe - an attacker can craft a malicious pickle payload to achieve arbitrary code execution on the server.
finding.evidence: Line 20: pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw)). Cookie value is fully controlled by the client.

reason: The client-controlled basket cookie is deserialized with pickle in read_basket, enabling remote code execution.

finding.title: SQL injection in admin reviews-by-customer endpoint
finding.description: The display_name is interpolated directly into the SQL query via f-string. Since customer names come from the users table, an attacker can create a display_name containing SQL to extract arbitrary data.
finding.evidence: Line 80: f"WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}'". A user can register with display_name like: Robert'); DROP TABLE reviews;--

reason: It identifies the f-string SQL injection in the admin reviews-by-customer report using a customer-controlled display name.

finding.title: Password hashing lacks salt
finding.description: hash_password() uses raw SHA-256 without any random salt. Identical passwords produce identical hashes, enabling rainbow table attacks and making it trivial to detect password reuse across accounts.
finding.evidence: Line 16: hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest(). No salt is generated or combined with the password.

reason: The finding correctly identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in hash_password.

finding.title: Hardcoded SECRET_KEY
finding.description: The JWT signing secret is hardcoded in the source code as a known value. Anyone with access to the repository can forge valid authentication tokens for any user.
finding.evidence: Line 3: SECRET_KEY = 'hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d'.

reason: It identifies the hardcoded JWT signing secret in the configuration, which can be used to forge tokens.

finding.title: Debug mode enabled
finding.description: Flask debug=True enables interactive debugger and auto-reload, which exposes stack traces and arbitrary code execution in development. Should not be used in production.
finding.evidence: Line 6: app.run(host='127.0.0.1', port=5000, debug=True)

reason: The finding identifies debug=True in run.py, which enables the interactive debugger.

finding.title: Weak password reset token
finding.description: Reset tokens are generated using Python's random.random() (a PRNG, not cryptographically secure) and formatted as only 8 decimal digits (%08d). Attackers can brute-force these codes within seconds.
finding.evidence: Line 135: '%08d' % int(random.random() * 10**8). This produces an 8-digit number from a weak PRNG.

reason: The reset codes use predictable random.random() values and are only eight digits, matching the weak password-reset code vulnerability.

finding.title: Unsafe pickle deserialization in cache layer
finding.description: cache.get() uses pickle.load() to read cached files. While cache files are currently created only by the app, the pickle format is vulnerable to deserialization attacks if any cache file can be modified by an attacker.
finding.evidence: Line 23: pickle.load(f) reads cache files from CACHE_DIR.

reason: The finding flags pickle loading in the app-controlled cache layer, which is decoy D5.

finding.title: CORS reflects Origin header without allowlist
finding.description: The CORS handler echoes back any Origin header as Access-Control-Allow-Origin when credentials are allowed. Combined with the wildcard origin this enables cross-origin request forgery from any website that can make credentialed requests.
finding.evidence: Lines 45-50: resp.headers['Access-Control-Allow-Origin'] = origin with CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS=True. Allows any site to send credentialed requests.

reason: The CORS handler reflects any Origin while allowing credentials, matching the unrestricted credentialed CORS vulnerability.

finding.title: Request body logged verbatim
finding.description: POST/PUT/PATCH request bodies are logged in full (up to 2000 characters). Sensitive data like passwords, payment details, or personal information sent in JSON request bodies will appear in log files.
finding.evidence: Line 31: log.info('%s %s %s', request.method, request.path, request.get_data(as_text=True)[:2000])

reason: The request logger records up to 2,000 characters of POST, PUT, and PATCH bodies, potentially exposing passwords and other sensitive data in logs.

finding.title: Cross-site scripting via unsanitized review body
finding.description: Review bodies are stored in the database without sanitization and rendered in the product HTML template using Jinja2's |safe filter. An attacker who posts a review can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript.
finding.evidence: Template line 13: {{ r.body|safe }}. Body comes from reviews table, inserted at products.py line 90 without escaping.

reason: It identifies stored review content rendered with |safe without sanitization, matching V13.

finding.title: Any authenticated user can read another customer's order
finding.description: The single-order endpoint calls get_order() directly instead of own_order(), so it checks that the order exists but never verifies that its customer_id matches the authenticated user. Order contents, payment amounts, delivery data, and refunds are exposed across accounts.
finding.evidence: With a valid bearer token for customer id 1, GET /orders/3 returned HTTP 200 and the order belonging to customer id 2 (BLANKET-WOOL, paid_pence 4500). The protected mutation endpoints use own_order(), but show_order does not.

reason: It identifies the IDOR in show_order, which returns an order without checking that it belongs to the authenticated customer.

finding.title: Account enumeration via login error message
finding.description: The login endpoint returns different error messages: 'no account with that email' vs 'wrong password'. An attacker can enumerate valid email addresses by observing which error they receive.
finding.evidence: Lines 89-90: Different JSON errors for missing user vs wrong password. Also true for /auth/reset/request (line 140) - always returns ok=True regardless of whether the email exists, but the timing difference may leak information.

reason: The finding identifies email enumeration through distinct login errors, which is explicitly part of V16.

finding.title: Staff Can Escalate Arbitrary Users to Staff Role
finding.description: Any authenticated staff member can change any user's role to 'staff' via /admin/users/role. There is no restriction preventing self-promotion or escalation of accounts. Due to the globally broken @require_auth decorator, this endpoint may also be reachable by unauthenticated attackers.
finding.evidence: Line 27-33: set_role() accepts role='staff' and updates any user_id without restriction. Live test: POST /admin/users/role with user_id=2 and role='staff' succeeded while authenticated as another staff member.

reason: The main finding is an unlisted privilege-escalation issue in set_role, and its note about unauthenticated access identifies the broken require_auth decorator (V22).

finding.title: Token refresh accepts unsigned attacker-controlled JWT claims
finding.description: The refresh endpoint decodes the supplied token with verify_signature=False and uses its sub claim to load an account. An attacker can construct an unsigned token naming any user, including staff, and receive a newly signed valid token for that account. Expiration is also not enforced during this decode.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/refresh with an unsigned token whose payload contained {"sub":3,"exp":1793582730} returned HTTP 200 and a signed token whose claims identified sub 3 and role staff. No original valid signature was required.

reason: It identifies the refresh endpoint accepting unsigned JWT claims and issuing a valid token for the claimed account.

finding.title: Trailing-slash admin refund route bypasses the staff check
finding.description: The global admin guard compares request.path to the set of exact route rules. The refund route is registered with strict_slashes=False, allowing both slash variants, but the slash variant is not in admin_paths. Consequently an unauthenticated caller can reach the goodwill refund handler.
finding.evidence: POST /admin/refunds/ with no Authorization header and {"order_id":3,"amount_pence":1} returned HTTP 200 with {"ok":true,"refunded_pence":1}. POST /admin/refunds (without the slash) correctly returned HTTP 403.

reason: The trailing-slash refund route bypasses the exact-path staff check, matching V03.

finding.title: JWT signing key is hardcoded in source
finding.description: SECRET_KEY is a fixed source-controlled value. Anyone who obtains the source or repository can forge HS256 authentication tokens, impersonate users, and bypass role checks. The application also uses this key for every JWT across environments unless configuration overrides it.
finding.evidence: config.py assigns SECRET_KEY = "hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d" rather than requiring a deployment secret. JWTs in auth.py are signed and verified directly with this value.

reason: It identifies the hardcoded JWT signing secret in the configuration, which allows token forgery.

finding.title: Product search is vulnerable to SQL injection
finding.description: The q parameter is concatenated into a SQL LIKE expression instead of being passed as a bound parameter. A public unauthenticated request can alter the WHERE clause and retrieve records outside the intended search.
finding.evidence: GET /products/search?q=%27%20OR%201%3D1%20-- returned HTTP 200 with all six catalogue products, demonstrating that the supplied search value changed the SQL predicate.

reason: The finding identifies SQL injection in the products search route caused by concatenating the q parameter into the query.

finding.title: Admin set_role can escalate any user to staff
finding.description: The admin set_role endpoint lets any staff member change the role of ANY user, including escalating arbitrary customers to staff. There is no validation that user_id belongs to the intended target or any restrictions on escalation.
finding.evidence: Line 30: db.execute('UPDATE users SET role = ? WHERE id = ?', (data['role'], data.get('user_id'))). Any staff can change any user to staff role.

reason: The set_role endpoint's ability to let staff promote arbitrary users is a separate privilege-escalation weakness not listed in the key.

finding.title: Review bodies are rendered as unsanitized HTML
finding.description: Authenticated users can submit arbitrary review body text, which is stored without sanitization. The product template renders r.body with the Jinja safe filter, allowing stored HTML/JavaScript to execute for every visitor to the product page. This is a persistent XSS affecting customers and potentially staff browsers.
finding.evidence: POST /products/<product_id>/reviews accepts body values up to 2,000 characters and inserts them unchanged at products.py:90. The subsequent product page renders the same value with {{ r.body|safe }} at templates/product.html:13.

reason: It identifies stored XSS from unsanitized review bodies rendered with the safe filter in the product template.

finding.title: Password reset codes use weak randomness and have no brute-force protection
finding.description: Reset codes are generated with the non-cryptographic random.random() PRNG as an 8-digit decimal code. The confirmation endpoint has no attempt limit, lockout, or rate limiting, so an attacker can repeatedly guess valid codes during the 30-minute window and take over accounts.
finding.evidence: reset_request() generates the code with int(random.random() * 10**8), and reset_confirm() compares a user-supplied code directly without recording or limiting failed attempts.

reason: It identifies predictable random.random() reset codes and the lack of attempt limits that makes them brute-forceable.

finding.title: Payment provider timeout fails open and marks orders paid
finding.description: When payment_status() times out, the exception handler sets status = "paid" and continues through the success path. A provider outage or induced timeout therefore changes an unpaid order to processing and sets paid_pence equal to the order total without confirmation of payment.
finding.evidence: The requests.Timeout handler at lines 39-42 explicitly assigns status = "paid"; lines 43-45 then set the order to processing and paid_pence = total_pence. The comment says reconciliation happens later, but the customer receives the goods before payment is confirmed.

reason: It identifies the payment provider timeout being treated as paid in confirm_payment, allowing an unpaid order to be processed.

finding.title: Arbitrary code execution via deserialization of untrusted pickle data
finding.description: The basket cookie is a base64-encoded Python pickle blob. An attacker can craft a malicious pickle payload in their browser cookie, and when the server calls pickle.loads(), arbitrary code is executed by the deserialization machinery via __reduce__ hooks.
finding.evidence: Basket cookie is serialized/deserialized with pickle in basket.py lines 20 and 27. An attacker can set the basket cookie to a crafted pickle payload which triggers RCE on the server side.

reason: The finding correctly identifies unauthenticated pickle deserialization of the basket cookie in shopapi/basket.py as remote code execution.

finding.title: JWT token refresh accepts unsigned/forged tokens
finding.description: The /auth/refresh endpoint decodes JWT tokens with verify_signature=False, allowing any actor to craft a forged token with arbitrary claims and obtain a valid signed session token.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/refresh with unsigned token eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOjEsInJvbGUiOiJhZG1pbiJ9.invalid returned a valid signed JWT. Line: jwt.decode(token, options={verify_signature: False}).

reason: It identifies the refresh endpoint accepting forged tokens because JWT signature verification is disabled.

finding.title: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) in image import
finding.description: Although host_is_public() checks DNS resolution results, it does not prevent DNS rebinding attacks where the initial resolve returns a public IP but subsequent requests connect to an internal address. An attacker can supply an approved host that resolves internally.
finding.evidence: Line 50: requests.get(url, timeout=10, stream=True). After check_url() validation, the URL is fetched without further DNS checks during the request.

reason: The finding describes a real DNS-rebinding SSRF risk in image import, but V02 is specifically the redirect-following bypass of URL validation.

finding.title: SQL injection in product search endpoint
finding.description: The search endpoint concatenates user-supplied search term directly into a SQL LIKE clause without parameterization.
finding.evidence: Request to /products/search?q=%20UNION+SELECT+1,email,password_hash,4,5,6,7,8,9,10+FROM+users--%20 returned HTTP 500 confirming SQL injection. Affected line: SELECT * FROM products WHERE name LIKE '% + q + %' (line 41).

reason: It identifies SQL injection in the q parameter of GET /products/search in shopapi/products.py.

finding.title: Payment webhook trusts an arbitrary payment amount
finding.description: After checking only an order-id-derived signature, the webhook accepts event.amount_pence without comparing it to the order total or requiring a valid payment-provider transaction. A signed or compromised webhook can mark a full order as processing while recording any amount, including zero or a small underpayment.
finding.evidence: The paid branch writes int(event.get("amount_pence", 0)) directly to paid_pence and changes status to processing. There is no check against orders.total_pence or payment_id.

reason: The webhook signature covers only the order ID while the handler trusts the supplied amount and status, allowing a captured signature to be replayed with altered payment details.

finding.title: Payment confirmation treats provider timeout as success
finding.description: When the external payment provider times out, the application marks the order as processed without verifying actual payment status.
finding.evidence: payments.py lines 39-42: except requests.Timeout: sets status = paid. Order status becomes processing and paid_pence is updated even if the payment never actually succeeded.

reason: It identifies the payment confirmation timeout being treated as paid, allowing an order to be processed without verified payment.

finding.title: SQL injection in admin reviews report via f-string interpolation
finding.description: The admin reports/reviews endpoint interpolates display_name directly into a SQL query using an f-string. A user registering with a SQL-injection display_name can trigger arbitrary SQL when an admin views their review history.
finding.evidence: Line 80: f WHERE r.author_name = {customer[display_name]}. Attacker registers with special display_name, admin queries /admin/reports/reviews?customer_id=<id>, triggering SQL injection.

reason: It identifies the second-order SQL injection in admin.reviews_by_customer via the customer-controlled display_name interpolated into the report query.

finding.title: Unsalted SHA-256 password hashing
finding.description: Passwords are hashed with plain SHA-256 without salt, vulnerable to precomputed rainbow table attacks and offline brute-force cracking.
finding.evidence: shopapi/auth.py line 16: hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest(). No salt is added. scripts/seed.py confirms same weak hashing for all accounts.

reason: It identifies the unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in shopapi/auth.py.

finding.title: SECRET_KEY hardcoded in source code
finding.description: The Flask SECRET_KEY used for signing JWT tokens is hardcoded in config.py, allowing anyone with repo access to forge authentication tokens.
finding.evidence: config.py line 3: SECRET_KEY = hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d. Used in jwt.encode/jwt.decode in shopapi/auth.py lines 27 and 42.

reason: The hardcoded SECRET_KEY in config.py can be used to forge signed authentication tokens.

finding.title: Account enumeration via distinct login error messages
finding.description: Login returns different errors for nonexistent email vs wrong password, allowing attackers to enumerate valid accounts.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/login with nonexistent email returns no account with that email; valid email plus wrong password returns wrong password.

reason: The login route reveals whether an email is registered through distinct error messages, matching V16.

finding.title: CORS reflects Origin with credentials allowed
finding.description: CORS handler sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin to the requester's Origin header value and allows credentials, enabling cross-origin authenticated requests from any domain.
finding.evidence: shopapi/__init__.py lines 44-51: resp.headers[Access-Control-Allow-Origin] = origin with CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS = true (config.py line 12).

reason: The finding identifies the arbitrary Origin reflection with credentials enabled in the CORS after-request handler.

finding.title: Unauthenticated pickle deserialization enables remote code execution
finding.description: The basket cookie is fully controlled by the client, but its base64-decoded contents are passed to pickle.loads without any signature or integrity check. A crafted cookie can execute arbitrary Python code whenever a public endpoint reads the basket.
finding.evidence: read_basket() at shopapi/basket.py:15-23 calls pickle.loads on request.cookies['basket']; GET /basket invokes it at lines 44-46 and does not require authentication. Replace pickle with a safe format such as JSON and authenticate or integrity-protect the value.

reason: It identifies unauthenticated pickle deserialization in shopapi/basket.py read_basket, matching the remote-code-execution vulnerability.

finding.title: Weak pseudo-random password reset tokens
finding.description: Password reset tokens use random.random() which is not cryptographically secure. Tokens are only 8 decimal digits, easily bruteforceable.
finding.evidence: shopapi/auth.py line 135: token = %08d % int(random.random() * 10**8). Python docs warn random module is not suitable for security. Only up to 100 million possible values.

reason: It identifies the predictable random.random() password-reset code and its small brute-forceable value space in reset_request.

finding.title: Webhook authentication falls back to a publicly known default secret
finding.description: WEBHOOK_SECRET defaults to the source-controlled value whsec-local when the environment variable is absent. In a deployment that does not explicitly override it, anyone who knows the code can generate valid X-Signature values for arbitrary order IDs and submit payment events.
finding.evidence: config.py uses os.environ.get("WEBHOOK_SECRET", "whsec-local"), while payments.py derives the accepted HMAC directly from that setting. The repository contains the fallback value and no startup check requiring a production secret.

reason: A publicly known fallback webhook secret is a real weakness, but it differs from V19’s body-unbound HMAC and replay issue.

finding.title: Token refresh accepts unsigned attacker-controlled claims
finding.description: The refresh endpoint disables JWT signature verification and only checks whether the supplied subject belongs to an existing user. An attacker can submit an unsigned token naming another user and obtain a newly signed token for that account.
finding.evidence: auth.py:101 calls jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False}); lines 104-107 load claims['sub'] and issue a fresh token. An unsigned JWT with payload {"sub":1} was accepted by POST /auth/refresh and returned HTTP 200 with a signed token. Verify the signature, algorithm, issuer and intended refresh-token claims before using the subject.

reason: It identifies the refresh endpoint accepting unsigned token claims and issuing a valid signed token for the claimed account.

finding.title: Authentication failures are swallowed and protected handlers continue
finding.description: require_auth catches all exceptions, including Flask's abort(401), clears g.user, and then invokes the protected handler. Protected handlers therefore execute without authentication and may disclose data or fail with an internal error instead of rejecting the request.
finding.evidence: The wrapper at auth.py:51-58 unconditionally calls f after catching the abort at line 54. In the running application, GET /account without credentials returned HTTP 500 rather than 401, and GET /orders/1 without credentials reached its handler. Only catch token parsing errors and let authentication failures propagate.

reason: The require_auth decorator catches abort(401) and continues into the protected handler, allowing unauthenticated requests through.

finding.title: Review bodies are rendered as trusted HTML, enabling stored XSS
finding.description: Authenticated users can submit arbitrary review text, which is stored without sanitization and rendered through Jinja's safe filter. Script-capable markup will execute for visitors viewing the product page.
finding.evidence: products.py:82-91 stores the submitted body directly; product.html:13 renders r.body|safe. POST /products/<product_id>/reviews can therefore persist markup that executes on GET /p/<sku>. Escape review text or sanitize it with a narrowly defined HTML policy before rendering.

reason: The finding identifies stored XSS from raw review text rendered with the safe filter in product.html.

finding.title: Product search is vulnerable to SQL injection
finding.description: The q parameter is concatenated into the SQL statement rather than bound as a parameter. Attackers can alter the WHERE clause and potentially retrieve unintended product data.
finding.evidence: products.py:40-42 constructs SQL by concatenating q into two LIKE expressions. GET /products/search?q=%27%20OR%201%3D1-- returned all products in the running application. Bind the wildcard value as a SQL parameter.

reason: It identifies the SQL injection in products.search caused by concatenating the q parameter into the query.

finding.title: Payment-provider timeout fails open as paid
finding.description: A timeout while querying the payment provider is treated as confirmation of payment. The order is moved to processing and paid_pence is set to the total despite no successful provider response.
finding.evidence: payments.py:37-42 catches requests.Timeout and sets status = "paid"; lines 43-45 then update the order to processing and set paid_pence = total_pence. A timeout must leave the order awaiting payment or mark it for reconciliation, not release it.

reason: It identifies the payment-status timeout being treated as paid in confirm_payment, allowing an unpaid order to be processed.

finding.title: Customer display names are interpolated into an admin SQL query
finding.description: A customer-controlled display name is inserted into the review-report WHERE clause without parameterization. A name containing quotes or SQL syntax can alter the query when staff request the report.
finding.evidence: admin.py:74 loads the user-selected display_name and line 80 builds f"WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}' ORDER BY r.id DESC". Display names are accepted from registration and account updates at auth.py:71 and 119-125. Use a bound parameter and preferably identify reviews by author_id rather than copied names.

reason: The finding describes customer-controlled display_name being interpolated into the admin review report SQL query, matching the second-order SQL injection in reviews_by_customer.

finding.title: Order detail endpoint does not verify ownership
finding.description: show_order requires the flawed authentication decorator but calls get_order instead of own_order, so it never compares the requested order's customer_id with the authenticated user. Any caller who reaches the handler can retrieve another customer's order details.
finding.evidence: orders.py:32-36 contains the ownership check in own_order(), but show_order at lines 46-49 directly returns order_json(get_order(order_id)). GET /orders/1 without an Authorization header returned HTTP 200 with the order record in the running application.

reason: The finding identifies the ownership bypass in show_order (V01) and also notes that the fail-open authentication decorator lets unauthenticated requests reach it (V22).

finding.title: Passwords are stored using unsalted fast SHA-256
finding.description: Passwords are hashed with a single unsalted SHA-256 digest, with no salt or work factor. A database disclosure permits highly efficient dictionary and brute-force recovery, and equal passwords have equal hashes.
finding.evidence: auth.py:15-20 directly computes and compares hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest(). Use a password-specific KDF such as Argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt with a unique salt per password.

reason: The finding identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in shopapi/auth.py, matching V09.

finding.title: Payment webhook authenticates only the order ID and trusts the amount
finding.description: The HMAC covers only str(order_id), not the event status or amount. Anyone who can produce or obtain a valid signature for an order can change the amount and mark an awaiting order as processing; the handler never checks that the amount equals the order total.
finding.evidence: webhook_signature at payments.py:53-55 signs only order_id, while lines 69-71 trust event.status and int(event.amount_pence) and write that value to paid_pence. Sign the complete canonical event and require the authenticated provider amount to match the order total.

reason: The webhook signature covers only the order ID while status and amount are trusted, allowing a captured signature to be replayed with altered payment details.

finding.title: Trailing-slash admin route bypasses staff authorization
finding.description: The staff gate compares request.path with exact route strings. The refunds route accepts both slash variants, but only /admin/refunds is in the route set, so /admin/refunds/ reaches the staff-only handler without the check.
finding.evidence: staff_only_admin at __init__.py:36-41 checks exact membership in admin_paths; admin.py:52 declares /admin/refunds with strict_slashes=False. POST /admin/refunds/ without authentication returned HTTP 200 and created a refund in the running application.

reason: It identifies the exact-path staff check bypassed by the trailing-slash variant of /admin/refunds.

finding.title: Password reset codes are weakly generated and have no online guessing controls
finding.description: Reset codes are eight decimal digits generated with the non-cryptographic random module. Confirmation has no failed-attempt counter, rate limit or lockout during the 30-minute validity period, allowing repeated online guesses.
finding.evidence: auth.py:135 uses random.random() to create the code; auth.py:149-154 checks only expiry and equality, and the reset routes contain no throttling. Generate a CSPRNG token and enforce per-account/IP attempt and rate limits.

reason: It identifies predictable random.random()-generated reset codes with no attempt limit, matching V10.

finding.title: Request logging stores passwords and other sensitive request bodies
finding.description: The global request hook logs up to 2,000 bytes of every mutating request body, including login and registration passwords, reset codes and replacement passwords, and other personal or payment data. Anyone with log access can recover these secrets.
finding.evidence: __init__.py:28-31 calls request.get_data(as_text=True) and logs it for every POST, PUT and PATCH. This includes bodies sent to /auth/login and /auth/reset/confirm. Redact security-sensitive fields or do not log request bodies.

reason: The request logger records mutating request bodies, including passwords and reset secrets, matching V20.

finding.title: Login errors disclose whether an email is registered
finding.description: The login endpoint returns different responses for an unknown email and a wrong password, allowing attackers to enumerate valid customer and staff accounts before attempting attacks.
finding.evidence: auth.py:89-92 returns "no account with that email" for a missing user and "wrong password" for an existing user. POST /auth/login with those cases produces distinguishable 401 response bodies. Return a generic authentication failure and rate-limit attempts.

reason: The finding identifies email enumeration in the login endpoint, which is part of V16.

finding.title: JWT signing key is hardcoded in source
finding.description: HS256 tokens use a fixed source-controlled key shared by all deployments. Anyone who obtains the repository or an artifact containing it can forge valid customer or staff authentication tokens.
finding.evidence: config.py:3 sets SECRET_KEY to a literal; auth.py:27 signs tokens and auth.py:42 validates them with that value. Load a unique high-entropy key from deployment secret storage and rotate it safely.

reason: It identifies the hardcoded JWT signing secret in config.py that enables token forgery.

finding.title: Authentication failures are swallowed and protected handlers continue
finding.description: require_auth catches its own abort(401) (and any other exception), sets g.user to None, and still calls the handler. Consequently endpoints decorated with @require_auth are reachable without a valid token; handlers that do not dereference g.user disclose protected data, while others may fail with a 500 instead of returning 401.
finding.evidence: The wrapper catches Exception at lines 55-58 and unconditionally returns f(*args, **kwargs). GET http://127.0.0.1:49933/orders/1 returned 200 with order 1 belonging to a customer, and GET /giftcards/HFDEMO10 returned 200 with the gift-card balance, without Authorization.

reason: The require_auth wrapper catches abort(401) and continues to protected handlers, allowing unauthenticated requests through.

finding.title: Trailing-slash admin refund route bypasses the global staff check
finding.description: The before_request hook compares request.path with the registered rule strings. The refund rule is registered as /admin/refunds with strict_slashes=False, but Flask also accepts /admin/refunds/. That accepted path is not in admin_paths, allowing the refund handler to run without the staff check.
finding.evidence: POST http://127.0.0.1:49933/admin/refunds/ with {"order_id":1,"amount_pence":1} returned 200 and created a refund, without Authorization. The normal /admin/users path returned 403 unauthenticated.

reason: It identifies the trailing-slash /admin/refunds route bypassing the staff-only check.

finding.title: Forged basket quantities can create negative-value orders
finding.description: Checkout trusts quantities from the deserialized client cookie and does not reapply the 1-20 quantity constraint or require a positive total. A forged basket can use negative or excessive quantities to reduce the order total or create nonsensical order lines.
finding.evidence: basket.py:35-41 multiplies client-supplied qty values, and checkout at lines 64-73 inserts the resulting total and quantities without validation. The cookie is unsigned and client-controlled at lines 26-28. Revalidate every line and total server-side, or store the basket server-side.

reason: It identifies a real forged-quantity business-logic flaw in checkout, not the unsafe pickle deserialization vulnerability in the key.

finding.title: Staff image import can be abused for SSRF through redirects or DNS rebinding
finding.description: The endpoint checks the initial hostname and one DNS resolution, then requests the URL with redirects enabled by default. An approved host can redirect to an internal destination, or a hostname can resolve differently at fetch time, causing the server to retrieve unintended internal resources.
finding.evidence: images.py:28-35 validates only the initial URL and resolution; line 50 calls requests.get without allow_redirects=False or validation of redirect targets. Re-resolve and validate every hop, disable redirects, and enforce IP and scheme restrictions on the actual connection.

reason: It identifies the SSRF in images.py: the initial URL is validated, but redirects can lead requests.get to internal destinations.

finding.title: Refresh accepts unsigned attacker-controlled JWT claims
finding.description: The refresh endpoint decodes the supplied token with signature verification disabled and only checks that the claimed user ID exists. An attacker can submit an unsigned token naming any user, including staff, and receive a freshly signed valid token for that account.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/refresh with the unsigned token eyJhbGciOiJub25lIiwidHlwIjoiSldUIn0.eyJzdWIiOjMsImV4cCI6MX0. returned 200 and a signed token for user 3, whose database role is staff.

reason: It identifies the refresh endpoint accepting unsigned JWT claims and issuing a valid signed token for the claimed account.

finding.title: Production dependency installation trusts an internal index without artifact hashes
finding.description: The production requirements configure an internal package index as primary and PyPI as an extra index, and install the custom payment package without hashes. A compromised index or ambiguous package resolution can introduce attacker-controlled code into the build, and the installer does not verify artifact contents.
finding.evidence: requirements.txt:1-2 set the internal and extra indexes; lines 3-7 contain version pins but no --hash entries, including hf-payments==2.3.1. Use a reviewed lockfile with hashes and an explicitly trusted, controlled repository.

reason: It identifies the public PyPI extra index and un-hashed hf-payments dependency as creating dependency-confusion risk.

finding.title: Product search is SQL-injectable
finding.description: The search string is concatenated directly into a SQL LIKE expression instead of being passed as a bound parameter. This permits changing the query and potentially extracting or modifying database data depending on the database context.
finding.evidence: GET /products/search?q=%27%20OR%201%3D1%20-- returned all six products. The query is assembled by string concatenation at lines 40-42.

reason: It identifies the concatenated search query in GET /products/search, which is the SQL injection described by V11.

finding.title: Payment-provider timeouts fail open as paid orders
finding.description: When payment_status raises requests.Timeout, the code sets status to paid and continues the successful-payment path. A provider outage or induced timeout therefore creates a processing order with paid_pence equal to the total without confirmation of payment.
finding.evidence: confirm_payment catches requests.Timeout at lines 39-42 and assigns status = "paid"; lines 43-45 then mark the order processing and paid.

reason: It identifies the payment confirmation timeout being treated as paid in confirm_payment.

finding.title: Passwords are stored as unsalted SHA-256 hashes
finding.description: Password hashing uses a single fast unsalted SHA-256 digest. Database compromise therefore enables efficient dictionary and rainbow-table cracking; a password KDF such as Argon2id, scrypt, or bcrypt with a unique salt should be used.
finding.evidence: hash_password returns hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() at lines 15-16, and that value is stored in users.password_hash during registration and reset.

reason: The finding identifies the unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in shopapi/auth.py’s hash_password function.

finding.title: Order detail does not enforce ownership
finding.description: show_order calls get_order rather than own_order, so any request that reaches the handler can retrieve another customer's order, including payment and refund history.
finding.evidence: GET http://127.0.0.1:49933/orders/1 returned order 1 and its financial details without authentication. The ownership check exists in own_order at lines 32-35 but is not used by show_order.

reason: It identifies the ownership bypass in show_order, and the unauthenticated request evidence also indicates the authentication decorator fails open.

finding.title: JWT signing key is hardcoded and predictable
finding.description: SECRET_KEY is committed in source rather than supplied as a deployment secret. Anyone with the repository can forge HS256 authentication tokens, including tokens for staff users.
finding.evidence: config.py line 3 sets SECRET_KEY to the literal hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d, and auth.py uses it for all JWT signing and verification.

reason: The finding identifies the hardcoded JWT signing secret in config.py, which can be used to forge tokens.

finding.title: Request logging records credentials and other sensitive POST bodies
finding.description: Every POST, PUT, and PATCH body is logged verbatim up to 2,000 bytes. This includes login passwords, password-reset codes and replacement passwords, bearer-like secrets in request bodies, and personal data, exposing them to log readers and log archives.
finding.evidence: The before_request hook logs request.get_data(as_text=True) at line 31 without endpoint-specific redaction; /auth/login and /auth/reset/confirm accept passwords in those bodies.

reason: The finding identifies log_request logging request bodies, including credentials, matching V20.

finding.title: Review bodies are rendered as trusted HTML
finding.description: Review bodies are accepted from authenticated users and stored without sanitization, then rendered with Jinja's safe filter. A reviewer can persist arbitrary HTML and script content for every visitor of the product page.
finding.evidence: POST /products/1/reviews as the demo customer with body <script>alert(1)</script> returned 201; GET /p/MUG-SPECK then included the same script inside review-body.

reason: It identifies stored XSS from unsanitized review bodies rendered with the safe filter in product.html.

finding.title: Payment webhook secret falls back to a known default
finding.description: Deployments without WEBHOOK_SECRET use the source-controlled value whsec-local. Knowledge of the repository or default configuration is sufficient to calculate valid webhook signatures and alter payment state, especially because the event contents are not signed.
finding.evidence: config.py:8 defines WEBHOOK_SECRET = os.environ.get("WEBHOOK_SECRET", "whsec-local"); payments.py:53-64 uses it for HMAC verification. Fail startup when the secret is absent and provision a unique high-entropy secret per deployment.

reason: The known default webhook secret is a separate real weakness not listed in the key, while the finding also notes V19’s unsigned event contents.

finding.title: Payment webhook signs only the order ID, not the event contents
finding.description: The HMAC covers only str(order_id). The status and amount_pence fields are outside the signed data, so anyone able to produce a signature for an order can change the payment amount or event semantics. The paid transition accepts any supplied amount without comparing it to the order total.
finding.evidence: webhook_signature at lines 53-55 hashes only order_id; lines 69-71 trust event.status and event.amount_pence and write the latter directly to paid_pence.

reason: The webhook signature covers only the order ID, leaving the status and amount unprotected.

finding.title: Order detail endpoint exposes any authenticated customer's order
finding.description: The list endpoint filters by customer_id and mutation endpoints call own_order(), but show_order() calls get_order() directly. Any signed-in customer can therefore read another customer's order, including its items, prices, payment totals, and refund history.
finding.evidence: Code path: show_order() at shopapi/orders.py:46-50 uses get_order() rather than own_order(). With the token returned by POST /auth/login for priya.shah@mail.test, GET /orders/3 returned order 3 belonging to the other demo customer (HTTP 200, containing the blanket item and total 4500).

reason: The finding identifies the IDOR in show_order, which uses get_order instead of restricting access to the customer's own order.

finding.title: Review bodies are stored and rendered as trusted HTML
finding.description: Review bodies are accepted from authenticated users without HTML sanitization and rendered with Jinja's safe filter. A customer can store script-capable markup that executes whenever another user views the product page, resulting in stored XSS.
finding.evidence: add_review() inserts the body at shopapi/products.py:90, while templates/product.html:13 renders r.body with |safe. POST /products/1/reviews with body '' returned 201; GET /p/MUG-SPECK subsequently returned that tag unchanged in the HTML.

reason: The finding describes stored review-body XSS caused by rendering unsanitized user content with |safe.

finding.title: Product search is SQL-injectable
finding.description: The search query concatenates the q parameter directly into a SQL string. An unauthenticated attacker can alter the WHERE clause, trigger SQL errors, and potentially use UNION/error-based techniques to read database contents.
finding.evidence: search() at shopapi/products.py:40-42 constructs SQL with string concatenation. GET /products/search?q=%25%27%20UNION%20SELECT%201%2C2%2C3%2C4%2C5%2C6%20--%20 caused an HTTP 500, demonstrating that attacker-controlled SQL syntax reaches SQLite.

reason: The finding identifies SQL injection in the concatenated q parameter in products.search.

finding.title: Refresh endpoint accepts unsigned attacker-supplied JWT claims
finding.description: The refresh endpoint decodes the supplied token with verify_signature=False and only checks that the claimed user exists. An attacker can construct an unsigned JWT containing another user's sub, then receive a newly signed valid token for that account (including staff accounts). Refresh must validate the original signature and normal token claims.
finding.evidence: auth.py:99-107 explicitly disables signature verification before loading claims and calling make_token(). The normal request validator at auth.py:42 correctly verifies signatures, but the refresh path bypasses that check. The only authorization condition is existence of claims.sub.

reason: The refresh endpoint disables JWT signature verification and issues a valid token based on the untrusted subject claim.

finding.title: Payment-status timeout fails open as paid
finding.description: When the payment provider times out, confirm_payment() sets status to paid and advances the order to processing instead of leaving it pending or requiring reconciliation. A provider outage or induced timeout therefore lets a customer obtain fulfillment without a confirmed payment.
finding.evidence: payments.py:37-43 catches requests.Timeout and assigns status = "paid"; lines 43-46 then set the order to processing and paid_pence = total_pence. The comment explicitly says reconciliation happens later, but fulfillment is enabled immediately.

reason: It identifies the timeout path in confirm_payment treating an unconfirmed payment as paid and enabling fulfillment.

finding.title: Build trusts an additional private package index without hash pinning
finding.description: Production installation uses a private index plus public PyPI, with no hashes. If the private index is unavailable or resolution differs, a package name can be satisfied by an unintended public artifact; package integrity is not independently verified. The local payment package also leaves its requests dependency unpinned.
finding.evidence: requirements.txt lines 1-2 configure both https://pypi.hartleyfinch.internal/simple and https://pypi.org/simple, while lines 3-7 pin only direct requirements and provide no --hash values. packages/hf_payments/pyproject.toml line 6 declares dependencies = ["requests"] without a version bound.

reason: The finding identifies dependency confusion from combining the internal package index with public PyPI without hash pinning.

finding.title: JWT signing key is hardcoded and predictable
finding.description: SECRET_KEY is committed in source as a fixed short string. Anyone who obtains the repository or deployment artifact can forge every HS256 bearer token, including tokens asserting staff roles (the refresh vulnerability also makes the impact easier to exploit). The key should be supplied from a protected deployment secret and rotated.
finding.evidence: config.py:3 sets SECRET_KEY = "hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d". auth.py:27 and auth.py:42 use this value for all JWT signing and verification.

reason: It identifies the hardcoded JWT signing secret in config.py, which can be used to forge tokens.
