finding.title: Client-controlled basket cookie is deserialized with pickle
finding.description: The basket cookie is completely client-controlled and is passed to pickle.loads after only base64 decoding. Python pickle deserialization can execute arbitrary code during loading; an attacker can send a malicious basket cookie to any endpoint that reads it, achieving server-side code execution.
finding.evidence: basket.py:15-23 reads request.cookies['basket'], base64-decodes it, and calls pickle.loads without a signature or authenticated encryption. show_basket(), add_item(), and checkout() all call read_basket().

reason: It identifies unauthenticated pickle deserialization of the client-controlled basket cookie in shopapi/basket.py, enabling remote code execution.

finding.title: CORS reflects arbitrary origins while allowing credentials
finding.description: For every request containing Origin, the application reflects that origin and sets Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. This permits any website to be treated as an approved credentialed origin. The API currently uses bearer tokens rather than a cookie session, but the configuration is unsafe and would expose any credential-bearing endpoints or future cookie-authenticated endpoints cross-origin.
finding.evidence: __init__.py:44-50 copies the unvalidated Origin header into Access-Control-Allow-Origin and enables credentials from config.py:12. GET /products with Origin: https://evil.example returned Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://evil.example and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.

reason: The finding correctly identifies the arbitrary Origin reflection with credentials in the CORS after_request handler.

finding.title: Stored display name enables SQL injection in admin review report
finding.description: The report query interpolates a database-controlled display_name into SQL. A customer can set display_name through PATCH /account, then a staff request to the report causes that value to be interpreted as SQL, allowing query manipulation and disclosure of unrelated reviews.
finding.evidence: PATCH /account stores attacker-controlled names (auth.py:116-125); admin.py:77-80 builds WHERE r.author_name = '<display_name>' via f-string. A name such as x' OR 1=1 -- changes the query. Use a placeholder.

reason: It identifies the second-order SQL injection in reviews_by_customer, where a customer-controlled display name is interpolated into the admin report query.

finding.title: SQL injection in product search
finding.description: The q query parameter is concatenated directly into a SQL LIKE expression. An unauthenticated caller can terminate the string and inject SQL predicates, bypassing the intended search and potentially disclosing data.
finding.evidence: GET /products/search?q=%27%20OR%201=1-- reaches products.py:40-41, where q is concatenated into the SQL query; the running application returns the product catalogue for this injected search instead of a literal match. Use parameter binding.

reason: It identifies SQL injection in the q parameter of the product search route, where the value is concatenated into the SQL query.

finding.title: Payment webhook authentication is based on a hardcoded/default secret and does not authenticate event contents
finding.description: Webhook signatures cover only the order ID, not status or amount_pence. Anyone able to obtain the committed default WEBHOOK_SECRET can submit a valid signed paid event with an arbitrary amount, and the handler accepts that amount as paid without comparing it with the order total or provider transaction. The default secret must not be used in production, and the signed payload and amount must be verified.
finding.evidence: config.py:8 defaults WEBHOOK_SECRET to "whsec-local". payments.py:53-55 signs only str(order_id); lines 69-71 accept event status=paid and set paid_pence to int(event.amount_pence), with no amount validation.

reason: The webhook signature covers only the order ID while the handler trusts the supplied status and amount, matching V19.

finding.title: Any authenticated customer can read another customer's order
finding.description: show_order() calls get_order(), which looks up only the supplied order ID and never verifies that the order belongs to the authenticated user. A customer can enumerate order IDs and retrieve other customers' order contents, payment amounts, and refund history.
finding.evidence: show_order() at lines 46-49 returns order_json(get_order(order_id)); get_order() at lines 25-29 queries SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = ? without customer_id, while the ownership check exists separately in own_order() at lines 32-36 but is not used here.

reason: The finding identifies the IDOR in show_order, which retrieves an order by ID without checking that it belongs to the authenticated customer.

finding.title: Client-controlled basket cookie is deserialized with pickle
finding.description: The basket cookie is entirely controlled by the client, but it is passed to pickle.loads(). A crafted cookie can execute arbitrary Python code in the web application's process when any basket endpoint reads it.
finding.evidence: read_basket() obtains request.cookies['basket'] at line 16 and calls pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw)) at line 20 without authentication or signing; show_basket() calls read_basket() at line 46.

reason: It identifies the unsigned, client-controlled pickle deserialization in shopapi/basket.py's read_basket function, enabling remote code execution.

finding.title: Authentication failures are swallowed and protected handlers still execute
finding.description: require_auth catches the abort(401) raised for an unauthenticated request and then invokes the wrapped handler anyway. This defeats the authentication decorator; for example, the gift-card balance endpoint can be called without credentials and returns card balances. Other protected handlers may run with g.user unset and expose error behavior.
finding.evidence: Lines 52-54 call abort(401) when g.user is None, but the broad except at lines 55-58 catches that exception, sets g.user to None, and returns f(*args, **kwargs). The balance endpoint at shopapi/giftcards.py:10-16 is decorated with @require_auth but does not otherwise use g.user.

reason: It identifies require_auth swallowing abort(401) and allowing unauthenticated requests to reach protected handlers, matching V22.

finding.title: Unauthenticated pickle deserialization from basket cookie
finding.description: The basket cookie is client-controlled and is base64-decoded then passed to pickle.loads without authentication. A malicious pickle can execute attacker-chosen Python code whenever /basket, /basket/items, or checkout reads the basket.
finding.evidence: basket.py:15-23 executes pickle.loads on request.cookies[basket]; /basket invokes read_basket without authentication. A malicious pickle encoded as the basket cookie is deserialized on GET /basket before the type check. Use validated JSON or server-side state, never unpickle client input.

reason: The finding identifies unauthenticated unpickling of the client-controlled basket cookie in read_basket, matching the remote-code-execution vulnerability.

finding.title: Product search concatenates the query directly into SQL
finding.description: The unauthenticated search endpoint inserts the q parameter into a SQL statement without parameter binding or escaping. An attacker can alter the WHERE clause or extract unintended product data.
finding.evidence: Lines 40-42 construct SQL by concatenating q into a LIKE pattern and execute the resulting string.

reason: It identifies SQL injection in the q parameter of shopapi/products.py’s product search query.

finding.title: Stored cross-site scripting in review bodies
finding.description: Authenticated users can submit arbitrary review body HTML, and the product template renders persisted bodies with Jinja's safe filter. Script elements and event-handler attributes therefore execute for every visitor viewing the product.
finding.evidence: POST /products/1/reviews with body returned 201 using a valid Bearer token. GET /p/MUG-SPECK returned that exact HTML inside review-body, confirming stored XSS through template line 13. Escape or sanitize review text.

reason: It identifies stored XSS from raw review text rendered with |safe in the product template.

finding.title: Admin review report is vulnerable to SQL injection through display names
finding.description: The review report interpolates a database-stored display name into SQL. A user can register or change a display name containing SQL syntax, then a staff member viewing the report causes that syntax to be executed. The staff-only gate does not remove the injection risk because the attacker controls the stored value.
finding.evidence: At lines 73-74 customer data is loaded from the user-controlled account record, and line 80 builds `WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}'` with an f-string instead of a bound parameter.

reason: It identifies the second-order SQL injection in admin.py’s reviews_by_customer report, where a customer-controlled stored display name is interpolated into SQL.

finding.title: Review bodies are rendered as trusted HTML
finding.description: Authenticated users can submit arbitrary review text, which is stored and later rendered with the Jinja safe filter. A malicious review can execute JavaScript in every visitor's browser on the product page, including staff or customers who have an active session.
finding.evidence: products.py:82-91 accepts and stores body without HTML sanitization; product.html line 13 renders r.body with `|safe`.

reason: The finding identifies stored review text rendered with `|safe` in product.html, matching the stored XSS vulnerability.

finding.title: Passwords are stored as unsalted fast SHA-256 hashes
finding.description: Passwords are hashed with a single unsalted SHA-256 operation. If the database is exposed, common and reused passwords can be recovered efficiently with precomputed or GPU-based cracking, enabling account takeover.
finding.evidence: hash_password() returns hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() at lines 15-16; no per-user salt or password-specific KDF is used.

reason: The finding describes unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in hash_password, matching V09.

finding.title: Payment status timeouts fail open and mark orders paid
finding.description: When the payment provider request times out, confirm-payment treats the timeout as a successful payment and transitions the order to processing with paid_pence equal to the order total. A provider outage or induced timeout therefore allows fulfillment without confirmed payment.
finding.evidence: The requests.Timeout handler at lines 39-42 sets status = 'paid'; lines 43-45 then set status to processing and paid_pence = total_pence.

reason: It identifies confirm_payment treating a provider timeout as payment success and processing the order without confirmed payment.

finding.title: Refresh endpoint accepts unsigned attacker-controlled JWT claims
finding.description: The refresh endpoint decodes the supplied token with verify_signature=False, then trusts its sub claim to select a real user and issues a newly signed token. An attacker can construct an unsigned token naming any user ID and obtain a valid session token for that account without knowing the signing secret.
finding.evidence: Lines 101-107 explicitly disable signature verification and call make_token for the loaded sub. POST /auth/refresh with an unsigned token containing {"sub":1} returned HTTP 200 and a freshly signed bearer token.

reason: It identifies the refresh endpoint's disabled signature verification, which lets forged token claims obtain a valid signed session.

finding.title: Authentication decorator fails open when authentication aborts
finding.description: require_auth catches every Exception, including the abort(401) it raises when no valid bearer token is present, logs it, sets g.user to None, and then invokes the protected view anyway. Protected handlers that do not immediately dereference g.user can therefore be reached without authentication, while others produce an internal error instead of a 401.
finding.evidence: Lines 52-58 catch abort/other exceptions and unconditionally return f(*args, **kwargs). A request without credentials to GET /account reaches the view and returns HTTP 500 rather than 401, demonstrating that the authentication failure is swallowed.

reason: It identifies require_auth swallowing abort(401) and allowing unauthenticated requests to reach protected routes.

finding.title: Passwords are stored as unsalted fast SHA-256 hashes
finding.description: Password hashing uses a single unsalted SHA-256 digest with no work factor or password-hashing scheme. A database disclosure enables efficient offline dictionary and brute-force cracking, and identical passwords produce identical hashes.
finding.evidence: hash_password at lines 15-16 is hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest(), and registration stores that value at line 78.

reason: The finding identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in hash_password, matching V09.

finding.title: JWT signing key is hardcoded in source
finding.description: SECRET_KEY is a fixed, repository-visible string. Anyone who obtains the source or a deployment artifact can forge HS256 tokens for arbitrary user IDs and roles, bypassing authentication and staff authorization.
finding.evidence: config.py line 3 sets SECRET_KEY = "hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d"; auth.py lines 27 and 42 use it for all JWT signing and verification.

reason: The finding identifies the hardcoded JWT signing secret in config.py, which can be used to forge tokens.

finding.title: Admin review report builds SQL with a user-controlled display name
finding.description: The reviews report interpolates customer.display_name directly into a SQL string. Display names are set by customers through the account update endpoint, so a customer can store quote/SQL syntax and trigger SQL injection when staff request the report for that customer.
finding.evidence: admin.py lines 78-80 construct f"WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}' ORDER BY r.id DESC". The value originates from auth.py lines 119-125, where any authenticated user can update display_name.

reason: The report interpolates a customer-controlled display name into SQL, matching the second-order SQL injection in reviews_by_customer.

finding.title: Order details disclose any customer's order
finding.description: The authenticated show_order handler calls get_order directly instead of own_order, so any signed-in customer can retrieve another customer's order, items, payment totals, and refunds by changing the numeric ID.
finding.evidence: A token for Priya (customer id 1) successfully received GET /orders/3, an order seeded for customer id 2, with HTTP 200 and its item and payment data. Code path: show_order line 49 uses get_order(order_id), while own_order performs the ownership check.

reason: It identifies the IDOR in show_order, which retrieves any order without checking that it belongs to the signed-in customer.

finding.title: Order details are exposed without ownership authorization
finding.description: The authenticated order detail route calls get_order directly rather than own_order. get_order checks only whether the order exists and does not compare customer_id with the requesting user, so any caller can read another customer's order, line items, and refunds. Due to the failing authentication decorator, unauthenticated callers can also reach this route.
finding.evidence: show_order at lines 46-49 returns order_json(get_order(order_id)); the ownership check exists separately in own_order at lines 32-36 but is not used. GET /orders/1 with no Authorization header returned HTTP 200 and the complete order including SKU, prices, and refund data.

reason: The finding identifies the IDOR in show_order (V01) and also describes unauthenticated access caused by the fail-open authentication decorator (V22).

finding.title: Admin authorization is bypassed with a trailing slash
finding.description: The global admin guard compares request.path to the set of exact rule strings. The refunds route is registered strict_slashes=False, so /admin/refunds/ reaches the admin handler but does not equal the guarded /admin/refunds path. The handler itself has no authorization check.
finding.evidence: Unauthenticated POST /admin/refunds/ with {"order_id":1,"amount_pence":1} returned HTTP 200 and created a refund, whereas GET /admin/users without credentials returned 403. Guard code is lines 26-41 and handler is shopapi/admin.py lines 52-67.

reason: It identifies the trailing-slash bypass of the staff-only admin guard on /admin/refunds, matching V03.

finding.title: Refresh accepts unsigned, attacker-controlled JWT claims
finding.description: The refresh endpoint decodes the submitted token with verify_signature=False and only checks that the claimed subject exists. An attacker can construct an unsigned token naming any user (including staff), then obtain a valid signed token for that account.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/refresh with an unsigned JWT carrying sub=3 returned HTTP 200 and a valid HS256 token whose user is seeded staff account id 3. Code lines 99-107 explicitly disable signature verification.

reason: It identifies the refresh endpoint accepting unsigned tokens and issuing a valid token for the claimed user.

finding.title: Hardcoded JWT signing secret permits token forgery
finding.description: The production configuration contains a fixed, repository-visible SECRET_KEY used to sign and verify all HS256 authentication tokens. Anyone who obtains the source or deployment artifact can forge tokens for arbitrary user IDs and roles.
finding.evidence: config.py line 3 sets SECRET_KEY to the literal hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d; auth.py lines 27 and 42 use it for JWT signing and validation.

reason: The finding identifies the hardcoded JWT signing secret in config.py, which can be used to forge tokens.

finding.title: Unauthenticated basket cookie deserialization enables pickle code execution
finding.description: The basket cookie is attacker-controlled and is passed directly to pickle.loads after base64 decoding. A crafted pickle can execute arbitrary Python code in the web process whenever any visitor requests /basket or another basket operation.
finding.evidence: Code path shopapi/basket.py lines 15-23 reads request.cookies['basket'] and calls pickle.loads with no signature, encryption, or type-safe serialization. /basket is public at lines 44-46, so no authentication is needed to trigger deserialization.

reason: It identifies the unsigned base64-encoded pickle deserialization in shopapi/basket.py that enables remote code execution.

finding.title: Order detail endpoint does not enforce ownership
finding.description: The order-detail handler retrieves an order by ID with get_order() rather than own_order(). Any authenticated user who can guess or obtain another order ID can read its items, prices, payment totals, delivery information, and refunds.
finding.evidence: show_order() at lines 46-49 calls get_order(order_id), while own_order() at lines 32-36 checks customer_id. GET /orders/1 without authentication returned HTTP 200 with the complete order record (the authentication decorator bug also made this directly demonstrable).

reason: It identifies the IDOR in show_order, which retrieves orders by ID without checking ownership.

finding.title: Trailing-slash admin refund route bypasses staff authorization
finding.description: The staff-only hook compares request.path to the exact registered rule. The refund route accepts a trailing slash because strict_slashes=False, but /admin/refunds/ is not in the collected admin_paths set, so the handler executes without the staff check.
finding.evidence: staff_only_admin() checks exact membership at lines 36-41; the route is registered with strict_slashes=False in shopapi/admin.py:52. An unauthenticated POST /admin/refunds/ with {"order_id":1,"amount_pence":1} returned HTTP 200 and performed a refund, whereas the non-slash route was protected.

reason: It describes the trailing-slash /admin/refunds/ route bypassing the exact-path staff authorization check.

finding.title: Token refresh accepts unsigned attacker-controlled JWT claims
finding.description: The refresh endpoint disables JWT signature verification and uses the untrusted sub claim to select a database user before issuing a newly signed token. An attacker can therefore obtain a valid token for any existing user, including staff users, without credentials.
finding.evidence: Line 101 calls jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False}); lines 104-107 load the user from claims.sub and call make_token(). POST /auth/refresh with an unsigned JWT containing sub=1 returned HTTP 200 and a valid signed token.

reason: It identifies the refresh endpoint’s disabled signature verification, which lets forged claims obtain a valid signed token for any user.

finding.title: Stored display names are interpolated into an admin SQL query
finding.description: The reviews report constructs SQL using an f-string containing customer.display_name rather than a bound parameter. Display names are attacker-controlled at registration/update, so a crafted name can alter the query when an admin report is requested (and the admin trailing-slash bypass makes the report reachable without staff authorization).
finding.evidence: admin.py lines 74-80 load a user-selected display name and interpolate it into WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}'. Names are accepted from registration line auth.py:71 and account updates lines 119-125.

reason: It identifies the second-order SQL injection in reviews_by_customer, where a customer-controlled display name is interpolated into the report query.

finding.title: Product search is vulnerable to SQL injection
finding.description: The q query parameter is concatenated into a SQL statement rather than passed as a bound parameter, allowing an attacker to alter the WHERE clause and potentially retrieve unintended data.
finding.evidence: search() builds the statement by concatenating q at lines 40-42. GET /products/search?q=%27%20OR%201=1-- returned HTTP 200 with all products.

reason: The finding correctly identifies SQL injection in the concatenated q parameter in products.search.

finding.title: Staff review report is vulnerable to SQL injection through stored display names
finding.description: A customer-controlled display name is interpolated into the review-report SQL query. A customer can store a name containing SQL syntax, which is later interpreted when staff request that customer's report.
finding.evidence: reviews_by_customer() constructs f"WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}' ORDER BY r.id DESC" at lines 77-81. Registration and account updates allow users to control display_name, and no parameter binding is used.

reason: The finding describes the second-order SQL injection in reviews_by_customer via a customer-controlled stored display name.

finding.title: Unsafe deserialization of attacker-controlled basket cookie
finding.description: The basket cookie is client-controlled and is passed directly to pickle.loads() without a signature or other integrity check. A crafted cookie can execute arbitrary Python code whenever a basket endpoint reads it.
finding.evidence: read_basket() decodes the request cookie and calls pickle.loads() at lines 15-23. with_basket() creates the cookie with pickle.dumps() at lines 26-28 but does not authenticate it; GET /basket invokes read_basket().

reason: It identifies the unauthenticated pickle deserialization of the client-controlled basket cookie in read_basket, enabling remote code execution.

finding.title: Authentication failures are swallowed and protected handlers continue
finding.description: require_auth catches all exceptions, including Flask's 401 HTTPException from abort(), sets g.user to None, and still invokes the protected handler. Protected endpoints that do not immediately dereference g.user can therefore be accessed without authentication, while others may produce a 500 instead of a 401.
finding.evidence: The wrapper catches Exception at lines 55-57 and unconditionally calls f(*args, **kwargs) at line 58. An unauthenticated GET /giftcards/HF123 reached the protected handler and returned its resource lookup response (404 for a nonexistent card) instead of 401; the same pattern also allowed GET /orders/1 to return order data.

reason: The finding identifies require_auth swallowing abort(401) and continuing into protected handlers, which is the fail-open authentication flaw.

finding.title: Passwords are stored using unsalted SHA-256
finding.description: Passwords are hashed with a fast, unsalted general-purpose digest rather than a password-specific work factor such as Argon2, scrypt, or bcrypt. A database disclosure enables efficient offline cracking and identical passwords have identical hashes.
finding.evidence: hash_password() returns hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() at lines 15-16, and check_password() compares the same fast digest at lines 19-20.

reason: The finding identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in hash_password, matching V09.

finding.title: Stored review content is rendered as raw HTML
finding.description: Authenticated users can submit review bodies that are stored without sanitization and rendered with the Jinja safe filter. A malicious reviewer can persist script or event-handler markup that executes for visitors to the product page.
finding.evidence: add_review() stores body directly at shopapi/products.py:90-91, and product.html line 13 renders {{ r.body|safe }}.

reason: The finding identifies stored XSS because unsanitized review bodies are rendered with the Jinja safe filter.

finding.title: JWT signing secret is hardcoded in application configuration
finding.description: HS256 authentication tokens use a fixed source-controlled secret. Anyone who obtains the source or configuration can forge tokens for arbitrary users and roles.
finding.evidence: config.py:3 sets SECRET_KEY = "hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d"; shopapi/auth.py:27 and :42 use it to sign and verify JWTs.

reason: The finding identifies the hardcoded JWT signing secret in config.py, which enables token forgery.

finding.title: Cancellation and return quantities are tracked independently, permitting duplicate refunds
finding.description: Return validation considers only returned_qty and the original quantity, not quantities previously cancelled. The same units can therefore be cancelled and refunded while processing, then returned and refunded again after delivery.
finding.evidence: cancel_items() increments cancelled_qty and issues a refund at lines 65-70. return_items() separately permits returned_qty + requested quantity <= item.qty at lines 90-96 and never subtracts cancelled_qty.

reason: The finding identifies the return_items flaw: cancelled quantities are excluded from the return limit, enabling duplicate refunds.

finding.title: Payment webhook signature does not cover status or amount
finding.description: The webhook HMAC authenticates only the order ID. Status and amount_pence are trusted after signature validation, and the amount is not checked against the order total. A party able to produce or obtain a valid order signature can replay it with altered payment data.
finding.evidence: webhook_signature() signs only str(order_id) at lines 53-55. payment_webhook() trusts event.status and int(event.amount_pence) at lines 69-73 without including those fields in the MAC or comparing the amount to total_pence.

reason: It identifies the webhook HMAC covering only the order ID while status and amount can be altered or replayed.

finding.title: Password reset codes are weak and unrestricted to online guessing
finding.description: Reset codes are only eight decimal digits, generated with non-cryptographic random.random(), valid for 30 minutes, and checked without attempt limits, throttling, lockout, or invalidation after failed guesses. An attacker can make unlimited online guesses during the validity period.
finding.evidence: reset_request() generates the code with int(random.random() * 10**8) and gives it a 30-minute expiry at lines 135-136. reset_confirm() compares the supplied code at lines 149-154 without recording or limiting failures.

reason: It identifies the predictable, short password-reset codes and lack of attempt limits in reset_request/reset_confirm.

finding.title: Image import follows redirects without revalidating destinations
finding.description: The image importer validates only the initial hostname and its resolved addresses. requests.get() follows redirects by default, so an approved host that redirects can cause the server to fetch an internal or otherwise unauthorized destination.
finding.evidence: check_url() validates only the original parsed URL at lines 28-35, then import_image() calls requests.get(url, timeout=10, stream=True) at line 50 with redirects enabled and no validation of r.url or redirect hops.

reason: It identifies the SSRF in images.py where redirects can bypass validation of the initial URL and reach internal destinations.

finding.title: Request logging records credentials and sensitive request bodies
finding.description: The global request logger records up to 2,000 characters of every POST, PUT, and PATCH body without redaction. Passwords, reset codes, replacement passwords, and payment-related data can consequently persist in logs accessible to operators or log readers.
finding.evidence: log_request() calls request.get_data(as_text=True)[:2000] at lines 29-31 for all modifying requests; login, registration, and reset endpoints accept secrets in those bodies.

reason: The finding identifies log_request writing unredacted modifying-request bodies, including credentials, to logs.

finding.title: The application entry point enables Flask debug mode
finding.description: Starting the normal entry point enables Flask's interactive debugger and verbose exception behavior. If this entry point is exposed through a deployment proxy, an exception can disclose source and potentially expose the debugger console.
finding.evidence: run.py:6 invokes app.run(..., debug=True).

reason: The finding identifies debug=True in run.py, enabling Flask’s interactive debugger.

finding.title: Payment-provider timeout fails open and marks orders as paid
finding.description: A timeout while checking the provider is treated as a successful payment. The order is then moved to processing and paid_pence is set to the full total, allowing an unpaid order to be fulfilled during provider outages or induced timeouts.
finding.evidence: The requests.Timeout handler at lines 39-42 sets status = "paid"; lines 43-45 then update the order to processing and set paid_pence = total_pence.

reason: The finding identifies confirm_payment treating a provider timeout as paid and processing the order without payment.

finding.title: Predictable default webhook secret is enabled by default
finding.description: When WEBHOOK_SECRET is not configured, payment webhooks use the publicly known value whsec-local. Anyone who knows this default can forge signed payment events and mark awaiting-payment orders as paid.
finding.evidence: config.py:8 uses os.environ.get("WEBHOOK_SECRET", "whsec-local"); shopapi/payments.py:53-55 uses it for HMAC validation and lines 69-74 update orders based on the event.

reason: The predictable default webhook secret is a real weakness not listed in the key; V19 concerns the HMAC’s incomplete coverage and replay protection, not the secret’s default value.

finding.title: Trailing-slash admin refund route bypasses the global staff check
finding.description: The staff gate compares request.path to a set of exact route strings. The refund route explicitly accepts both slash forms, but only the no-slash form is included in admin_paths. A caller can use /admin/refunds/ to reach the staff-only handler without the gate, and the handler itself has no authorization check.
finding.evidence: admin.py:52 declares @bp.post('/refunds', strict_slashes=False), while create_app builds admin_paths from the canonical rule and checks exact request.path at lines 37-40. POST /admin/refunds/ with no Authorization header returned HTTP 200 and created a refund (confirmed against the running app).

reason: It identifies the trailing-slash /admin/refunds/ route bypassing the exact-path staff check.

finding.title: Product search is vulnerable to SQL injection
finding.description: The search term is concatenated directly into a SQL LIKE expression instead of being passed as a bound parameter. An attacker can alter the WHERE clause and retrieve arbitrary rows, and potentially use the database query for further data extraction depending on SQLite query constraints.
finding.evidence: products.py:40-41 constructs SQL using q directly. GET /products/search?q=%27%20OR%201%3D1-- returned HTTP 200 with all six products, demonstrating that the supplied term changed query semantics.

reason: The finding identifies SQL injection in the search function by concatenating the query parameter into SQL.

finding.title: Review bodies are rendered as trusted HTML without sanitization
finding.description: Authenticated users can submit arbitrary review body text, and the product template renders it with |safe. A malicious review can therefore execute script in the browser of every visitor to the affected product page, creating persistent stored XSS. The same issue is not mitigated by the product description sanitizer because reviews take a separate unsanitized path.
finding.evidence: products.py:83-91 only trims and length-checks body before storing it; product.html:13 renders r.body|safe. The review is displayed on the public /p/<sku> page at product.html:10-14, so a submitted HTML/script payload becomes persistent content for unauthenticated visitors.

reason: It identifies stored XSS from unsanitized review bodies rendered with |safe in product.html.

finding.title: Payment timeout is treated as successful payment
finding.description: When the payment provider times out, confirm_payment comments that reconciliation will run later but sets status to 'paid' and then transitions the order to processing. A provider outage or induced timeout therefore lets an order proceed without confirmation of payment; the code has no compensating state or later rollback in this path.
finding.evidence: payments.py:37-44 catches requests.Timeout and assigns status = 'paid' before updating the order to processing and setting paid_pence = total_pence. The provider client uses network requests and can raise Timeout at hf_payments/__init__.py:18-20, so a timeout directly produces a fulfilled-paid state.

reason: It identifies confirm_payment treating a provider timeout as paid and processing the order without payment.

finding.title: Authentication decorator fails open when authentication is missing or invalid
finding.description: require_auth catches Exception around both authentication and abort(401), clears g.user, and then invokes the protected view anyway. Consequently, any protected handler that does not immediately dereference g.user can be accessed without authentication. This also turns invalid authentication into unauthenticated execution rather than consistently returning 401.
finding.evidence: The wrapper catches the HTTPException raised by abort(401) at lines 53-58 and still returns f(*args, **kwargs). A request with no Authorization header to GET /orders/1 returned HTTP 200 and the complete order, even though the route at shopapi/orders.py:46 is decorated with @require_auth.

reason: It identifies require_auth swallowing abort(401) and continuing into protected routes, which is the fail-open authentication flaw.

finding.title: SQL injection in admin reviews-by-customer endpoint
finding.description: The /admin/reports/reviews endpoint at line 80 embeds customer['display_name'] (a value read from the database) directly into an f-string SQL query. A staff user who registers or updates their display_name to contain SQL metacharacters can execute arbitrary queries when an admin views reports for that user.
finding.evidence: Registered a user with display_name "' UNION SELECT 'r.id','product','r.rating','r.body','r.created' FROM reviews--". As staff, GET /admin/reports/reviews?customer_id=24 returned columns labeled r.id, r.product etc. from the reviews table, confirming SQL injection via the display_name.

reason: It identifies the second-order SQL injection in reviews_by_customer, where a customer-controlled display_name is interpolated into the report query.

finding.title: SQL injection in product search endpoint
finding.description: The /products/search endpoint at line 41 concatenates the user-supplied 'q' parameter directly into a SQL string using Python string concatenation. An unauthenticated attacker can inject arbitrary SQL via the q parameter to read or modify database contents.
finding.evidence: GET /products/search?q=' OR 1=1-- returned all 6 products instead of filtered results (no matching query term), confirming the WHERE clause was bypassed. Additionally, GET /products/search?q=%27%20UNION%20SELECT%20id,email,password_hash,display_name,role,NULL%20FROM%20users-- caused an HTTP 500 from SQLite column mismatch, indicating injected SQL reached the database.

reason: The finding identifies SQL injection in the `/products/search` endpoint caused by concatenating the user-supplied query into SQL.

finding.title: Remote code execution via insecure pickle deserialization of basket cookie
finding.description: read_basket() at line 20 calls pickle.loads() on a base64-decoded browser cookie value with no verification or sandboxing. Pickle deserialization executes __reduce__ methods, allowing arbitrary Python code execution. Any crafted pickle payload sent as the 'basket' cookie will be executed on the server.
finding.evidence: pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw)) is called on every request on user-controlled data from the 'basket' cookie. The except Exception block returns {} silently, but any exception-free malicious payload executes code during unpickling before the try/except catches it.

reason: The finding identifies unauthenticated pickle deserialization of the user-controlled basket cookie in read_basket, matching V18.

finding.title: Password reset codes use non-cryptographic randomness and have no attempt throttling
finding.description: Reset codes are generated with Python's Mersenne Twister random.random(), which is not suitable for security tokens. The confirmation endpoint has no attempt counter, lockout, or rate limit, while codes remain valid for 30 minutes. This makes online guessing materially easier and allows abusive reset attempts against accounts.
finding.evidence: auth.py:135 generates an eight-digit code using random.random(), and auth.py:151-153 only checks expiry and equality; there is no failed-attempt tracking or throttling.

reason: The finding identifies predictable reset-code generation with no attempt limit in reset_request/reset_confirm, matching V10.

finding.title: Payment webhook does not validate the settled amount
finding.description: The signed webhook authenticates only order_id and accepts any event amount_pence. A validly signed event with amount zero or an amount below the order total still changes an awaiting order to processing and records that arbitrary amount as paid. Payment amount and order identity should be bound into the signed message and checked against the order total/provider record.
finding.evidence: payments.py:53-55 signs only str(order_id), while lines 69-71 accept event status 'paid' and write int(event.get('amount_pence', 0)) without checking it against order['total_pence']. Thus a signed paid event with amount_pence 0 is accepted as a processing order with no recorded payment.

reason: The webhook signature covers only the order ID, while the handler trusts the event amount and status without validating them against the order or signed payload.

finding.title: Token refresh accepts forged tokens due to signature bypass
finding.description: The /auth/refresh endpoint at line 101 decodes JWTs with verify_signature=False, completely bypassing cryptographic signature validation. It only checks if the 'sub' claim references an existing user. An attacker can forge any user's claims (including role=staff), pass the forged token to /auth/refresh, and receive a freshly-signed, legitimate JWT impersonating that user.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/refresh with a fabricated token containing sub=1, role=staff, fake signature returned HTTP 200 with a new valid signed JWT for user 1 as staff. The forged token had no valid HS256 signature but was accepted because verify_signature=False.

reason: The finding identifies the signature-verification bypass in POST /auth/refresh that lets forged tokens be exchanged for valid signed tokens.

finding.title: Stored XSS via unescaped review body rendering
finding.description: Review bodies are rendered in the Jinja2 template with the |safe filter at line 13 ('{{ r.body|safe }}'), which disables HTML escaping. The add_review handler does NOT call bleach.clean() on the body text before inserting it. Attackers can inject script tags and other HTML to perform stored XSS against any visitor viewing the product page.
finding.evidence:
POST /products/1/reviews with body '' succeeded (HTTP 201). Subsequent GET /p/MUG-SPECK returned
, confirming unsanitized stored XSS visible to all visitors.

reason: The finding identifies stored XSS from raw review bodies rendered with |safe in product.html.

finding.title: JWT signing key is hardcoded and predictable in application source
finding.description: SECRET_KEY is a fixed source-controlled value rather than a deployment secret. Anyone who obtains the repository can mint valid HS256 tokens. Since tokens contain a user id and are accepted by user_from_request after signature verification, this permits impersonation of any existing account, including the staff account, until the key is changed and tokens expire.
finding.evidence: config.py:3 sets SECRET_KEY = 'hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d'. auth.py:27 signs tokens with it and auth.py:42 accepts any valid token signed with it. The same configuration also supplies a default webhook secret at config.py:8, making forged payment callbacks possible if the default remains deployed.

reason: It identifies the hardcoded JWT signing secret in config.py, which lets anyone with the source forge valid tokens.

finding.title: CORS reflects Origin header with credentials enabled
finding.description: The app at line 47 sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin to the requesting Origin verbatim (not from a whitelist) while also setting Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true (since CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS is True in config.py). This allows any third-party website to make authenticated cross-origin requests, effectively nullifying Same-Origin Policy protections.
finding.evidence: GET /health with header 'Origin: https://evil.com' returned Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://evil.com AND Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, confirming any origin is accepted with credentials.

reason: It identifies the app’s wildcard Origin reflection combined with credentials enabled in the CORS after_request handler.

finding.title: Password hashing uses unsalted plain SHA-256
finding.description: hash_password() at line 16 uses hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() with no salt. All users with identical passwords produce identical hashes across the entire database, enabling rainbow table attacks, offline brute-force, and cross-user password correlation from breached databases.
finding.evidence: seed.py line 33 shows all demo accounts use hash_password('demo-password-1'), hashed with plain SHA-256 with no salt. No bcrypt, scrypt, or argon2 usage found anywhere in the codebase.

reason: It identifies hash_password in shopapi/auth.py using unsalted, fast SHA-256 instead of a slow salted password hash.

finding.title: Weak and predictable password reset tokens
finding.description: Reset tokens at line 135 are generated as '%08d' % int(random.random() * 10**8), producing only 8 decimal digits (0 to 99,999,999) from Python's Mersenne Twister PRNG. The 100-million space is trivially brute-forceable within the 30-minute token window, and MT state can be predicted given enough observations.
finding.evidence: The token space is only 10^8 values (~26.6 bits of entropy). Brute-forcing takes at most 100M POST requests to /auth/reset/confirm, feasible within the 30-minute expiration window.

reason: It identifies the predictable, brute-forceable reset code generated with random.random() in reset_request.

finding.title: Insecure deserialization (pickle) of cached files
finding.description: cache.get() at line 23 loads files from CACHE_DIR using pickle.load(). Combined with the basket cookie pickle RCE (which provides filesystem write access), an attacker can plant malicious .pickle files under CACHE_DIR that trigger RCE on the next cache hit for that key. Cache keys are predictable (e.g., 'products-name-ASC').
finding.evidence: Lines 22-23: open(path, 'rb') followed by pickle.load(f). Files are stored under CACHE_DIR (default '.cache/') with keys derived from query parameters like 'products-{sort}-{order}'. Once any code execution foothold exists, targeted cache poisoning is possible.

reason: It flags cache-file pickle loading, which is the D5 decoy because the cache files are app-written in a protected directory and are not attacker-controlled.

finding.title: Sensitive request body data logged at INFO level
finding.description: The log_request hook at line 31 logs the full request body (up to 2000 chars) for all POST, PUT, PATCH requests at INFO level. This captures plaintext login credentials (email, password), password reset codes, gift card amounts, and other sensitive data in server logs.
finding.evidence: @app.before_request calls log.info('%s %s %s', request.method, request.path, request.get_data(as_text=True)[:2000]) for all mutating requests. Login payloads containing plaintext passwords are recorded.

reason: It identifies log_request logging sensitive POST, PUT, and PATCH request bodies, including passwords and reset codes.

finding.title: Order detail endpoint lacks ownership check (IDOR)
finding.description: The GET /orders/<int:order_id> endpoint at lines 46-49 uses get_order(order_id) which only verifies that the order exists, without checking that g.user['id'] matches order['customer_id']. In contrast, cancel_items and return_items correctly use own_order() for authorization. Any authenticated user can view details of any other user's orders, including items, prices, refund history, and delivery status.
finding.evidence: Logged in as user 23 (test@evil.com), GET /orders/1 returned full details of order owned by Priya Shah (user 1), including items (MUG-SPECK x2), total_pence, paid_pence, and status. GET /orders/2 similarly revealed Tom Okafor's order.

reason: It identifies the IDOR in show_order, where GET /orders/<id> uses get_order without checking order ownership.

finding.title: Payment confirmation marks order paid on provider timeout
finding.description: When the payment provider API raises requests.Timeout at line 39, confirm_payment defaults status to 'paid' at line 42, marking the order as 'processing' regardless of whether the actual payment was authorized. An attacker can exploit this by blocking or delaying the payments API, forcing false-positive payments.
finding.evidence: Code at shopapi/payments.py lines 39-42: 'except requests.Timeout: ... status = "paid"'. If PAYMENTS_URL is unreachable, slow, or blocked, any customer can force orders into 'processing' status without paying.

reason: It identifies confirm_payment treating a provider timeout as successful payment, allowing an unpaid order to be processed.

finding.title: SQL injection in product search
finding.description: The /products/search endpoint concatenates the untrusted 'q' query parameter directly into a SQL string. An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL via the URL-encoded query string.
finding.evidence: Code path: GET /products/search?q=' OR 1=1 -- . Against running app: request to /products/search?q=%27%20OR%201%3D1%20-- returned all 6 products instead of zero matches.

reason: It identifies SQL injection in shopapi/products.py’s GET /products/search endpoint by concatenating the untrusted q parameter into SQL.

finding.title: Debug mode enabled in application startup
finding.description: app.run at run.py line 6 enables Flask debug mode (debug=True), which exposes Werkzeug's interactive debugger console and detailed stack traces. An attacker could potentially use the debugger to execute arbitrary Python code via the console.
finding.evidence: run.py line 6: app.run(host='127.0.0.1', port=5000, debug=True). With debug=True, the Werkzeug debugger provides an interactive Python shell accessible via the debugger URL pattern.

reason: It identifies debug=True in run.py, which enables the Werkzeug debugger and can expose code execution.

finding.title: Hardcoded JWT signing secret in source code
finding.description: SECRET_KEY is set to a plaintext constant 'hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d' in config.py line 3. Anyone with source code access can forge valid JWT tokens for any user and any role. This trivially compounds with the /auth/refresh endpoint's verify_signature=False bug.
finding.evidence: config.py line 3: SECRET_KEY = "hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d". Even without the refresh bypass, anyone knowing this secret can forge JWT tokens for any user including admin role.

reason: The finding identifies the hardcoded JWT secret in config.py, and also explicitly references the unsigned-token refresh vulnerability.

finding.title: Account enumeration via distinct login error messages
finding.description: The login endpoint returns different error messages depending on whether the account exists: 'no account with that email' (for unknown emails) versus 'wrong password' (for known emails with incorrect passwords). Both return HTTP 401, but the message difference allows an attacker to enumerate valid email addresses.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/login with nonexistent@test.com returned {'error':'no account with that email'}, while priya.shah@mail.test with wrong password returned {'error':'wrong password'}. Both return 401.

reason: The finding identifies login account enumeration through distinct error messages, which is part of V16.

finding.title: IDOR on order detail endpoint allows viewing other users' orders
finding.description: The GET /orders/<order_id> endpoint delegates to get_order() which only checks whether the order exists. It does not verify that the requesting user owns the order. Any authenticated user can view another user's order details including refund history.
finding.evidence: Confirmed interactively: logged in as priya.shah@mail.test (customer_id=1) and successfully retrieved order 3, which belongs to tom.okafor@mail.test (customer_id=2).

reason: It identifies the IDOR in show_order, where get_order retrieves an order without checking that the requester owns it.

finding.title: Arbitrary code execution via pickle deserialization in basket cookie
finding.description: The basket cookie value is decoded from base64 and passed directly to pickle.loads(). Because the cookie is settable by the browser and stored client-side, an attacker can craft a malicious pickle payload that executes arbitrary code when deserialized by the server.
finding.evidence: Line 20: pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw)). Pickle is inherently unsafe for untrusted data; any user can craft or modify the basket cookie.

reason: The finding correctly identifies unauthenticated pickle deserialization of the client-controlled basket cookie in read_basket, enabling remote code execution.

finding.title: JWT signature verification disabled in token refresh
finding.description: The /auth/refresh endpoint decodes the supplied token with verify_signature=False. An attacker can forge a JWT with any 'sub' claim (user ID), including any admin/staff user, and obtain a valid signed token — effectively hijacking any account without knowing the signing key.
finding.evidence: Line 101: jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False}). Confirmed by inspecting source; the refresh flow accepts a forged token as proof of identity.

reason: It identifies the disabled signature verification in the refresh endpoint, allowing forged tokens to be exchanged for valid signed tokens.

finding.title: Gift card balance check accessible to any authenticated user
finding.description: The GET /giftcards/<code> endpoint at line 11 requires authentication but does not verify that the requesting user owns the gift card or has permission to view its balance. Any authenticated user can check the balance of any gift card code in the system.
finding.evidence: Authenticated as user 23 (test@evil.com, a customer), GET /giftcards/HFDEMO10 returned {balance_pence:1000, code:HFDEMO10}, revealing the balance of a gift card belonging to user 2 (Tom).

reason: The balance endpoint exposes another user’s gift card balance without an ownership check, a real issue distinct from V15’s redemption race condition.

finding.title: SQL injection in admin reviews report
finding.description: The /admin/reports/reviews endpoint uses Python f-string interpolation to embed customer.display_name directly into SQL. Any user whose display_name contains SQL metacharacters can trigger injection when a staff member queries reviews for that customer.
finding.evidence: Line 80: f"WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}' ORDER BY r.id DESC". Display name is user-controlled at registration time.

reason: It identifies the f-string SQL injection in the admin reviews report using a customer-controlled display name.

finding.title: Predictable password-reset tokens
finding.description: Reset tokens are generated with '%08d' % int(random.random() * 10**8), using Python's Mersenne Twister PRNG seeded with system time. With ~2^27 possible values and deterministic seeding, tokens are trivially guessable, enabling brute-force password resets.
finding.evidence: Line 135: token = "%08d" % int(random.random() * 10**8). Only 8-digit numeric codes (00000000–99999999), plus random.seed() defaults to time-based seed.

reason: It identifies the predictable, short password-reset codes generated with random.random(), matching V10.

finding.title: Password hashing without salt
finding.description: Passwords are hashed with plain SHA-256 and no salt. Identical passwords produce identical hashes, making rainbow-table attacks effective. Salt + iterative hashing (e.g., bcrypt, argon2) is required.
finding.evidence: Line 16: hash_password(password) returns hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest(). Seed script confirms all demo accounts use the same password hash.

reason: It identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in hash_password, matching V09.

finding.title: Hardcoded SECRET_KEY
finding.description: The Flask SECRET_KEY is baked into the source file. Anyone with read access to the repo knows the session signing key, allowing forging of session cookies and JWT tokens if the signing algorithm is compromised.
finding.evidence: Line 3: SECRET_KEY = "hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d". Used for both Flask sessions and JWT HS256 signing.

reason: The hardcoded SECRET_KEY in config.py can be used to forge signed tokens.

finding.title: Sensitive data logged in request body
finding.description: All POST, PUT, and PATCH request bodies are written to the log file (up to 2000 bytes). Login attempts, registration, and password-reset requests may contain plaintext passwords or PII.
finding.evidence: Line 31: log.info('%s %s %s', request.method, request.path, request.get_data(as_text=True)[:2000]). Affects /auth/login, /auth/register, /auth/reset/request.

reason: It identifies log_request writing request bodies, including sensitive authentication data, to the logs.

finding.title: Overly permissive CORS configuration
finding.description: The CORS handler reflects the Origin header back as Access-Control-Allow-Origin with Allow-Credentials: true. Combined with wildcard-origin-like behavior, this means any website can make credentialed cross-origin requests to the API.
finding.evidence: Lines 44-51: resp.headers['Access-Control-Allow-Origin'] = origin, combined with CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS = True. For any origin X, browser will send cookies with cross-origin requests.

reason: The after-request handler reflects any Origin and allows credentials, matching the permissive CORS vulnerability.

finding.title: Unauthenticated basket cookie is deserialized with pickle
finding.description: The basket cookie is attacker-controlled but is passed directly to pickle.loads. A remote attacker can submit a crafted cookie that executes arbitrary Python code in the web application's process whenever a basket endpoint reads it.
finding.evidence: read_basket() obtains request.cookies['basket'], base64-decodes it, and calls pickle.loads(raw) without a signature or integrity check; the cookie is created only with base64(pickle.dumps(...)) in with_basket().

reason: It identifies the unsigned, attacker-controlled pickle deserialization in shopapi/basket.py read_basket, which enables remote code execution.

finding.title: Token refresh accepts unsigned attacker-created JWTs
finding.description: The refresh endpoint explicitly disables JWT signature verification and only checks that the token's subject belongs to a user. An attacker can forge a token naming any user, including a staff user, and exchange it for a valid signed access token.
finding.evidence: refresh() calls jwt.decode(token, options={'verify_signature': False}), loads claims.get('sub'), and then returns make_token(user) without validating the original token's signature, issuer, or token type.

reason: The refresh endpoint disables signature verification and exchanges a forged token for a valid signed token.

finding.title: JWT signing key is hard-coded in source
finding.description: The production configuration contains a fixed, source-visible SECRET_KEY. Anyone who obtains the repository can mint valid JWTs for arbitrary user IDs and roles accepted by the application, enabling account and staff impersonation.
finding.evidence: SECRET_KEY is assigned the literal value 'hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d' and is used by auth.make_token() and auth.user_from_request() for HS256 JWT signing and verification.

reason: The finding identifies the hard-coded SECRET_KEY in config.py, which can be used to forge JWTs.

finding.title: Weak and known WEBHOOK_SECRET default
finding.description: The webhook secret falls back to the hardcoded string 'whsec-local'. Anyone who reads the source code can forge valid payment webhooks, potentially changing order statuses fraudulently.
finding.evidence: Line 8: WEBHOOK_SECRET = os.environ.get("WEBHOOK_SECRET", "whsec-local"). Webhook handler trusts its HMAC signature blindly.

reason: A hardcoded default webhook secret can enable forged payment webhooks, but it is distinct from the keyed JWT SECRET_KEY issue and does not identify V19’s body-coverage flaw.

finding.title: Authenticated users can view any order by ID
finding.description: The order detail endpoint authenticates the caller but does not verify that the requested order belongs to that caller. Order status, totals, payment amounts, delivery information, item data, and refunds are exposed by guessing or enumerating order IDs.
finding.evidence: show_order() returns order_json(get_order(order_id)); get_order() selects only by id, while the ownership check exists separately in own_order() and is not used by this endpoint.

reason: The finding identifies the IDOR in show_order, which fetches an order by ID without checking that it belongs to the authenticated user.

finding.title: Product search concatenates the query into SQL
finding.description: The public search endpoint interpolates the q parameter directly into a SQL statement. An unauthenticated attacker can alter the WHERE clause and use UNION-style SQL injection to extract records from other tables, including user and payment-related data.
finding.evidence: The query is built as "SELECT * FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%" + q + "%' OR sku LIKE '%" + q + "%' ORDER BY name LIMIT 50" instead of using a bound parameter.

reason: The finding identifies SQL injection in the product search endpoint caused by concatenating the q parameter into the SQL query.

finding.title: Admin review report is injectable through a display name
finding.description: A display name, which can be set by a normal user, is inserted into the review report SQL using an f-string. A user can choose a SQL fragment as their display name and have it executed when a staff member requests the report for that user.
finding.evidence: reviews_by_customer() executes f"WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}' ORDER BY r.id DESC" with no SQL escaping or parameter binding.

reason: The finding identifies the second-order SQL injection in reviews_by_customer, where a user-controlled display name is interpolated into the report query.

finding.title: Review bodies are stored and rendered as trusted HTML
finding.description: Authenticated users can submit arbitrary review text, and the product template renders it with the safe filter. A malicious review can therefore execute JavaScript for every visitor to the public product page, including staff users.
finding.evidence: add_review() inserts the unescaped body directly into reviews.body, while product.html renders r.body with {{ r.body|safe }}.

reason: The finding identifies stored XSS because raw review bodies are rendered with the template’s |safe filter.

finding.title: Payment status timeouts are treated as successful payments
finding.description: If the payment provider times out, the checkout endpoint assumes the payment is paid and moves the order to processing. A provider outage or targeted request disruption can therefore cause fulfillment of unpaid orders.
finding.evidence: The except requests.Timeout branch sets status = 'paid', after which the normal status == 'paid' branch sets status to processing and paid_pence to total_pence.

reason: It identifies confirm_payment treating a provider timeout as paid and processing the order without payment.

finding.title: Passwords are stored as unsalted fast SHA-256 hashes
finding.description: User passwords are hashed with a single unsalted SHA-256 operation. If the SQLite database or a backup is obtained, the hashes can be cracked quickly with commodity hardware and reused against users elsewhere.
finding.evidence: hash_password() returns hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() with no salt or work factor; this value is stored as users.password_hash.

reason: The finding correctly identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in hash_password.

finding.title: Image importer follows redirects outside the host allowlist
finding.description: The URL is checked before the request, but requests.get follows HTTP redirects by default and the final destination is never validated. A resource on an allowlisted host that redirects to an internal address can make the server fetch internal services.
finding.evidence: check_url(url) validates only the initial parsed hostname, then requests.get(url, timeout=10, stream=True) is called without allow_redirects=False or validation of r.url/history.

reason: The finding identifies the redirect-based SSRF in shopapi/images.py, where only the initial URL is validated before the request follows redirects.

finding.title: Order detail does not enforce ownership
finding.description: The order-detail endpoint calls get_order rather than own_order, so an authenticated customer can retrieve another customer's order details.
finding.evidence: GET /orders/3 with Priya's token returned Tom's order, including items, payment amount, delivery date, and refunds. The vulnerable path is show_order to get_order at shopapi/orders.py:48-49.

reason: It identifies the IDOR in show_order, where get_order allows a customer to retrieve another customer's order.

finding.title: Token refresh accepts unsigned JWT claims
finding.description: The refresh endpoint disables signature verification and uses the unverified sub claim to select an account before issuing a newly signed token. An attacker can forge a token naming another user, including a staff user.
finding.evidence: refresh calls jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False}) at line 101, then load_user and make_token. A forged unsigned JWT with sub=3 was accepted by POST /auth/refresh and returned a valid token for the staff account.

reason: The refresh endpoint disables JWT signature verification and uses the unverified subject to issue a valid token for the named account.

finding.title: Trailing-slash admin refund route bypasses staff authorization
finding.description: The staff hook compares request.path to registered rule strings. The refund route accepts both slash variants with strict_slashes=False, but the alternate trailing-slash path is not matched, so it reaches the staff-only handler without a role check.
finding.evidence: POST /admin/refunds/ without Authorization and with an order_id and amount returned HTTP 200 and performed a refund. The route is declared at shopapi/admin.py:52 with strict_slashes=False, while the hook uses exact request.path membership at line 37.

reason: It identifies the trailing-slash route bypass of the staff check on the admin refund endpoint.

finding.title: Unauthenticated basket cookie permits arbitrary pickle deserialization
finding.description: The basket cookie is client-controlled and has no signature or MAC, but is passed to pickle.loads. A crafted cookie can execute attacker-controlled Python when an endpoint reads the basket.
finding.evidence: read_basket base64-decodes the request cookie and calls pickle.loads at line 20; with_basket creates the cookie without integrity protection at line 27. GET /basket reads the cookie without authentication.

reason: It identifies the unsigned, client-controlled basket pickle deserialization in read_basket, which enables remote code execution.

finding.title: Product search concatenates the query directly into SQL
finding.description: The q parameter is concatenated into a SQL LIKE expression rather than bound as a parameter, allowing an attacker to alter the predicate and retrieve unintended records.
finding.evidence: GET /products/search?q=%27%20OR%201=1-- returned all six products. The statement at lines 40-41 directly concatenates q into both LIKE clauses.

reason: The finding correctly identifies SQL injection in the q parameter of GET /products/search, where it is concatenated into the query.

finding.title: Customer display names enable second-order SQL injection in the staff report
finding.description: The review report interpolates a mutable customer display_name into SQL. A customer can set a display name containing SQL syntax, and a staff member later viewing that customer's report executes the injected query.
finding.evidence: PATCH /account stores display_name at auth.py:116-125, but admin.py:77-80 constructs the author_name predicate with an f-string and no SQL parameterization.

reason: The finding identifies the second-order SQL injection in admin.py’s reviews_by_customer report query using a customer-controlled display name.

finding.title: Signed payment webhook does not validate the paid amount
finding.description: Any accepted paid webhook marks an order as processing using the caller-supplied amount, without requiring it to equal the order total or be positive. A forged or faulty provider event can mark an underpaid or zero-paid order as paid and fulfilled.
finding.evidence: For status == 'paid', the handler executes UPDATE orders SET status = 'processing', paid_pence = int(event.get('amount_pence', 0)) without comparing amount_pence with order.total_pence.

reason: The webhook trusts the caller-supplied amount without binding it to the signed data or validating it against the order total, matching V19.

finding.title: Authentication failures are swallowed, allowing protected handlers to run unauthenticated
finding.description: require_auth catches all exceptions, including the 401 abort it raises when no valid user is present, then invokes the wrapped handler with g.user set to None. Any protected handler that does not immediately dereference g.user can therefore execute without authentication.
finding.evidence: The wrapper catches abort(401) at lines 51-57 and calls the handler at line 58 regardless. GET /orders/3 without an Authorization header returned HTTP 200 and disclosed the order because show_order only uses the path ID.

reason: It identifies require_auth swallowing the 401 abort and continuing into protected handlers, allowing unauthenticated requests.

finding.title: Payment timeout fails open and marks orders paid
finding.description: A timeout while checking the payment provider is treated as a successful payment. The order is changed to processing and paid_pence is set to the full total without provider confirmation.
finding.evidence: confirm_payment catches requests.Timeout at lines 39-42 and sets status to paid; lines 43-45 then update the order to processing and set paid_pence to total_pence.

reason: It identifies the timeout fail-open in confirm_payment, which marks the order paid without provider confirmation.

finding.title: Concurrent gift-card redemptions can double spend a balance
finding.description: The balance check and derived balance update are not protected by a row lock or atomic conditional update. Concurrent requests can both validate against the same balance and create redemptions exceeding the available value.
finding.evidence: The handler checks balance at line 39, computes new_balance at line 41, inserts the redemption at line 42, and updates the card at line 43. There is no transaction locking or conditional balance update.

reason: It identifies the non-atomic balance check and overwrite in gift-card redemption, which allows concurrent requests to overspend the same balance.

finding.title: Payment webhook does not validate the paid amount or sign event contents
finding.description: A webhook signature covers only order_id. If the secret is known or the provider is compromised, an event with status paid and an arbitrary amount, including zero, transitions the order to processing without comparing the amount to the order total.
finding.evidence: webhook_signature at lines 53-55 signs only order_id. Lines 69-71 accept status paid and store amount_pence without comparing it with order total.

reason: The webhook signature covers only the order ID while the handler trusts the event status and amount without validating them against the order.

finding.title: Passwords are stored with unsalted SHA-256
finding.description: Passwords use a single fast unsalted SHA-256 digest instead of a password-specific hashing scheme such as Argon2id, scrypt, or bcrypt. A database compromise enables efficient offline cracking.
finding.evidence: hash_password returns hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() at lines 15-16, and the digest is stored during registration and reset.

reason: The finding identifies the unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in hash_password.

finding.title: External refunds are not atomic with local refund records
finding.description: issue_refund calls the payment provider before inserting the local refund record, and callers commit only afterward. A database failure after provider success leaves local state inconsistent; retrying can issue duplicate refunds.
finding.evidence: payments.py:21-23 calls client().refund before the INSERT, while orders.py:69-71 and admin.py:65-66 commit afterward. No idempotency key or reconciliation path is present.

reason: The finding identifies a real duplicate-refund risk from issuing the external refund before the local record is committed, but it does not match a planted vulnerability.

finding.title: Password reset codes use weak randomness and have no guessing or request limits
finding.description: Reset codes are eight decimal digits generated with the non-cryptographic random module, remain valid for 30 minutes, and have no failed-attempt counter or endpoint throttling.
finding.evidence: Codes are generated with random.random at line 135 and expire after 30 minutes. reset_confirm compares the code at line 153 without recording failures, and neither reset endpoint implements rate limiting.

reason: The reset codes use predictable random.random values and lack attempt limits, matching V10.

finding.title: Review bodies are rendered as trusted HTML
finding.description: Review bodies are accepted without sanitization and rendered with Jinja's safe filter. A malicious authenticated customer can store script markup that executes for visitors viewing the product page.
finding.evidence: POST /products/<product_id>/reviews stores body directly at products.py:90-91, and the product template renders r.body|safe at line 13.

reason: It identifies stored XSS from unsanitized review bodies rendered with |safe in the product template.

finding.title: Concurrent cancellations and returns can issue duplicate refunds
finding.description: Cancellation and return quantities are checked and incremented in separate statements, then refunded. Concurrent requests can both pass the remaining-quantity check and refund more units than the order contains.
finding.evidence: cancel_items checks and updates cancelled_qty at lines 65-67 before refunding at line 70; return_items performs the analogous sequence at lines 91-96. Neither uses row locking or an atomic conditional update.

reason: The finding describes a genuine concurrency flaw in cancellation and return refunds, distinct from V14’s ability to return already-cancelled quantities.

finding.title: JWT signing key is hardcoded and weak
finding.description: The HS256 signing key is a short static repository value. Anyone obtaining the source or deployment artifact can forge access tokens, including staff tokens.
finding.evidence: config.py defines SECRET_KEY = hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d at line 3; auth.py uses it for signing and verification.

reason: It identifies the hardcoded JWT signing secret in config.py, which allows token forgery.

finding.title: Application entry point enables Flask debug mode
finding.description: The executable entry point starts Flask with debug=True. If run.py is used in a reachable deployment, unhandled exceptions expose debug behavior and potentially the interactive debugger.
finding.evidence: run.py line 6 calls app.run with debug=True.

reason: It identifies run.py enabling Flask debug mode, matching V04.

finding.title: Request logging records credentials and sensitive request bodies
finding.description: The global request hook logs every POST, PUT, and PATCH body, including login passwords, reset codes, payment data, and customer information.
finding.evidence: shopapi/__init__.py:29-31 logs request.get_data(as_text=True) before routing. Login and password-reset endpoints send secrets in these bodies.

reason: The finding identifies the request logger recording POST, PUT, and PATCH bodies, including credentials, which is V20.

finding.title: Token refresh accepts unsigned attacker-controlled JWT claims
finding.description: The refresh endpoint disables signature verification and uses the untrusted sub claim to select the account for which it issues a newly signed token. An attacker can submit a token with the sub of another user, including a staff user, and obtain a valid session for that account.
finding.evidence: refresh() calls jwt.decode(token, options={'verify_signature': False}) at line 101, loads the user from claims.get('sub') at line 104, and returns make_token(user) at line 107 without ever verifying the original token.

reason: The refresh endpoint disables signature verification and issues a signed token based on the untrusted subject claim, enabling account takeover.

finding.title: Webhook signing secret has a predictable default
finding.description: When WEBHOOK_SECRET is unset, the application uses the repository-visible value whsec-local. A reachable webhook can therefore be forged in deployments relying on the default.
finding.evidence: config.py line 8 uses os.environ.get with default whsec-local, and payments.py uses this value to verify X-Signature.

reason: A predictable default webhook secret is a real weakness, but it is distinct from the JWT SECRET_KEY issue in V08 and the webhook-signature coverage flaw in V19.

finding.title: Unauthenticated pickle deserialization of the basket cookie
finding.description: The basket cookie is entirely controlled by the client, but it is passed directly to pickle.loads(). A crafted cookie can execute arbitrary Python code in the web application's process whenever a basket endpoint reads it.
finding.evidence: read_basket() obtains request.cookies['basket'] at line 16, base64-decodes it, and calls pickle.loads(raw) at line 20 without a signature or integrity check; /basket is unauthenticated and invokes read_basket() at line 46.

reason: It identifies unauthenticated pickle deserialization of the client-controlled basket cookie in read_basket, enabling remote code execution.

finding.title: Authenticated users can read other customers' orders
finding.description: The order detail endpoint authenticates the caller but does not enforce that the requested order belongs to that caller. Any logged-in user who guesses an order ID can read another customer's order contents, payment totals, delivery information, and refunds.
finding.evidence: show_order() calls order_json(get_order(order_id)) at line 49; unlike own_order(), get_order() only checks that the order exists and never compares customer_id with g.user.

reason: The finding correctly identifies the IDOR in show_order, which retrieves orders without checking ownership.

finding.title: Product search concatenates the query into SQL
finding.description: The unauthenticated search endpoint inserts the q parameter directly into a SQL statement. An attacker can alter the WHERE clause or inject additional SQL syntax, potentially exposing or modifying database data depending on the SQLite statement parser and execution context.
finding.evidence: The query at line 41 is built with "... LIKE '%" + q + "%' ..." rather than a bound parameter.

reason: It identifies SQL injection in the q parameter concatenation in shopapi/products.py’s product search endpoint.

finding.title: Mixed private and public indexes create dependency-confusion risk
finding.description: Installation uses a private index as the primary index and PyPI as an extra index. If a package expected from the private repository is missing or resolution is misconfigured, a public package with the same name can enter the production build.
finding.evidence: requirements.txt lines 1-2 configure an internal index and public extra index; production installation resolves packages across both indexes.

reason: It identifies dependency-confusion risk from resolving an internal package alongside public PyPI via an extra index.

finding.title: Review bodies are rendered as trusted HTML
