finding.description: Authenticated users can submit arbitrary review text, and the product page renders that text with the Jinja safe filter. A malicious review can therefore execute JavaScript in every visitor's browser.
finding.evidence: add_review() stores the submitted body without HTML sanitization at shopapi/products.py:90-91, while product.html renders r.body|safe at line 13.

reason: It identifies stored XSS because unsanitized review bodies are rendered with the |safe filter on the product page.

finding.title: Payment-status timeouts are treated as successful payments
finding.description: If the payment provider times out, the endpoint assumes the payment was paid and moves the order to processing with paid_pence equal to the order total. A transient timeout or provider/network interference can therefore let an unpaid order proceed as paid.
finding.evidence: The requests.Timeout handler at lines 39-42 assigns status = 'paid', and lines 43-45 then set status to processing and paid_pence to total_pence.

reason: It identifies confirm_payment treating a payment-provider timeout as paid and processing the order without payment.

finding.title: Customer review report is injectable through display names
finding.description: The admin report interpolates a customer's mutable display name into SQL. A customer can choose a display name containing SQL syntax, then a staff member viewing that customer's report causes the injected expression to execute.
finding.evidence: update_account() permits user-controlled display_name values, and reviews_by_customer() constructs `WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}'` with an f-string at line 80 instead of binding the value.

reason: It identifies the second-order SQL injection in reviews_by_customer using a customer-controlled display name.

finding.title: Passwords are stored as unsalted fast SHA-256 hashes
finding.description: Password hashes use a single unsalted SHA-256 digest, which is inexpensive to brute-force and enables identical passwords to be identified. A database disclosure would make the application's user passwords substantially easier to crack than with a password-specific KDF.
finding.evidence: hash_password() returns hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() at line 16; no salt or work-factor KDF is used.

reason: The finding identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in hash_password, matching V09.

finding.title: Production JWT signing key is hard-coded in source
finding.description: The application uses a fixed secret embedded in the repository for HS256 JWT signing. Anyone who obtains the source can forge arbitrary access tokens, including staff tokens; the configuration does not require an externally supplied key.
finding.evidence: SECRET_KEY is assigned the literal value "hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d" at line 3 and is used by jwt.encode/jwt.decode in shopapi/auth.py:27 and 42.

reason: It identifies the hard-coded JWT signing secret in config.py, which allows attackers with the source to forge tokens.

finding.title: Authentication failures are swallowed by the auth decorator
finding.description: require_auth catches the abort(401) raised for missing or invalid credentials and continues into the endpoint with g.user set to None. Endpoints that do not independently use g.user can therefore be reached without authentication; the gift-card balance endpoint is one such case and exposes card balances to anonymous callers.
finding.evidence: The decorator catches Exception around abort(401) at lines 52-58 and always calls f(*args, **kwargs) at line 58. giftcards.balance() has only @require_auth and returns the card balance at shopapi/giftcards.py:10-16 without checking g.user.

reason: The require_auth decorator catches the 401 abort and continues into the endpoint, allowing unauthenticated requests through.

finding.title: Payment webhook does not validate the settled amount
finding.description: A signed paid event can mark an order processing with any amount_pence, including zero or an amount below the order total. The signature covers only the order ID, so it does not protect the status or amount fields from tampering by anyone able to produce or replay a valid order-ID signature.
finding.evidence: webhook_signature() signs only str(order_id) at lines 53-55; payment_webhook() accepts event status and amount independently and writes int(event.get('amount_pence', 0)) to paid_pence at lines 69-71 without comparing it to order.total_pence.

reason: The webhook signature covers only the order ID, leaving the status and amount fields unprotected and trusted.

finding.title: Image import follows redirects outside the approved host allowlist
finding.description: The initial URL is restricted to approved public hosts, but requests.get follows redirects by default and the redirected destination is never revalidated. A compromised approved host or redirect can make the staff-only importer fetch internal or otherwise unintended resources.
finding.evidence: check_url() validates only the original URL at lines 28-35, then requests.get(url, timeout=10, stream=True) at line 50 follows redirects without allowlist or destination validation.

reason: It identifies the SSRF in shopapi/images.py: the initial URL is validated, but redirects are followed without revalidating the destination.

finding.title: Passwordless token refresh accepts unsigned attacker-chosen claims
finding.description: The refresh endpoint decodes the supplied JWT with signature verification disabled and only checks that the referenced user exists. An attacker can create an unsigned token naming another user and receive a freshly signed token for that account.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/refresh with token eyJhbGciOiJub25lIiwidHlwIjoiSldUIn0.eyJzdWIiOjF9. returned a valid HS256 token for user id 1. The returned token then authenticates to account/order functionality as that user.

reason: The finding describes the refresh endpoint accepting a token with signature verification disabled and issuing a valid token for the attacker-chosen user.

finding.title: Product search is SQL-injectable
finding.description: The search term is concatenated directly into a SQL statement. SQL metacharacters can alter the WHERE clause and expose arbitrary rows; further database-specific payloads may alter or extract data.
finding.evidence: GET /products/search?q=%27%20OR%201%3D1%20-- returned all six products, including products that do not match the original search term.

reason: The finding identifies SQL injection in the q parameter of GET /products/search, matching V11.

finding.title: Gift-card balance is disclosed without authentication
finding.description: The balance handler is wrapped in require_auth, but that decorator catches its own 401 exception and still invokes the endpoint. Because balance() does not dereference g.user, the request succeeds for an unauthenticated caller.
finding.evidence: GET http://127.0.0.1:52091/giftcards/HFDEMO10 with no Authorization header returned HTTP 200 with {"balance_pence":1000,"code":"HFDEMO10"}.

reason: The finding identifies the fail-open behavior in require_auth, which catches its own 401 and lets unauthenticated requests reach protected routes.

finding.title: Customer display names enable second-order SQL injection in the admin report
finding.description: A customer can set display_name to arbitrary text, and the admin review report later interpolates that stored value into SQL. This lets an ordinary user inject SQL when a staff member views that customer’s report.
finding.evidence: PATCH /account with display_name=' OR 1=1 -- followed by an authenticated GET /admin/reports/reviews?customer_id=1 caused the constructed WHERE clause to become an always-true predicate. The value is written at auth.py:275-277 and later inserted into the f-string at admin.py:141-145.

reason: It identifies the second-order SQL injection in reviews_by_customer, where a customer-controlled display name is interpolated into the admin report query.

finding.title: Unauthenticated pickle deserialization in the basket cookie enables server-side code execution
finding.description: The basket cookie is entirely attacker-controlled and is passed to pickle.loads without a signature or any other integrity check. A crafted cookie can invoke arbitrary callables during deserialization, before the result is type-checked.
finding.evidence: GET /basket reaches read_basket() and pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw)); the cookie is generated by the client and with_basket() provides no MAC or encryption. This is an arbitrary-code-execution path for any request that supplies a basket cookie.

reason: It identifies the unauthenticated pickle deserialization in shopapi/basket.py read_basket that enables remote code execution.

finding.title: Stored review content is rendered as raw HTML
finding.description: Review bodies are accepted from authenticated users and rendered with the Jinja safe filter. A malicious review therefore executes script in every visitor’s product-page browser context.
finding.evidence: POST /products/1/reviews with body <script>alert(document.domain)</script> returned 201. GET /p/MUG-SPECK then contained the same script tag verbatim at the review-body location.

reason: The finding identifies stored review text rendered with Jinja’s |safe filter, matching the stored XSS vulnerability.

finding.title: Order detail endpoint does not enforce ownership
finding.description: show_order() calls get_order() directly instead of own_order(), so any caller who knows or guesses an order ID can read its status, amounts, items, delivery date, and refunds.
finding.evidence: GET http://127.0.0.1:52091/orders/1 with no Authorization header returned HTTP 200 and the complete order, including items, paid_pence, and refunds. The require_auth decorator fails open on its abort and this handler never checks g.user.

reason: The finding identifies the order ownership flaw in show_order (V01) and also describes require_auth failing open on unauthenticated requests (V22).

finding.title: Payment-status timeout fails open as a successful payment
finding.description: A timeout from the payment provider is explicitly converted to status='paid', and the order is moved to processing with paid_pence equal to the order total. A transient provider outage can therefore create unpaid fulfilled orders.
finding.evidence: confirm_payment() catches requests.Timeout at lines 753-756 and immediately takes the paid branch at lines 757-759. No provider confirmation or later rollback is required before fulfillment.

reason: It identifies confirm_payment in shopapi/payments.py treating a provider timeout as paid and fulfilling the order without payment.

finding.title: Passwords are stored as unsalted fast SHA-256 hashes
finding.description: Password hashes use raw SHA-256 with no salt or work factor. A database compromise permits efficient offline dictionary and brute-force recovery of users’ passwords, including the seeded shared demo password.
finding.evidence: hash_password() is hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest(), and both registration and reset store that value directly in password_hash.

reason: The finding identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in shopapi/auth.py’s hash_password function.

finding.title: Payment webhook authentication uses a hardcoded, guessable default secret
finding.description: WEBHOOK_SECRET defaults to the source-visible value whsec-local. Deployments that do not override it allow anyone who knows the application defaults to forge payment events.
finding.evidence: The running application accepted an X-Signature HMAC generated with the literal key whsec-local on POST /webhooks/payments and changed a newly created order to processing.

reason: A source-visible default webhook secret enables forged payment events, which is a real weakness distinct from the key’s webhook-signature coverage flaw and JWT secret issue.

finding.title: Password reset codes use non-cryptographic randomness and have no attempt throttling
finding.description: Reset codes are eight decimal digits generated with random.random(), not a cryptographic generator. reset_confirm has no attempt counter, lockout, or rate limit, so an attacker can make unlimited online guesses during the 30-minute validity window.
finding.evidence: reset_request() creates the code with int(random.random() * 10**8), while reset_confirm() compares a supplied code and changes the password without tracking failed attempts.

reason: The finding identifies predictable random.random() reset codes and the lack of attempt limits in reset_confirm.

finding.title: Login reveals whether an email account exists and has no brute-force protection
finding.description: The login response distinguishes an unknown email from a known email with a wrong password, and the endpoint has no rate limiting, lockout, or progressive delay. This supports account enumeration and password guessing.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/login for nobody@mail.test returned {"error":"no account with that email"}, while the same request for admin@hartleyfinch.co.uk with a wrong password returned {"error":"wrong password"}.

reason: The finding identifies login’s account-enumeration responses and lack of rate limiting or lockout.

finding.title: SQL injection in product search
finding.description: The search query parameter 'q' is concatenated directly into the SQL query string on line 41 without parameterisation or sanitisation. An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL to read, modify, or drop database contents.
finding.evidence: GET /products/search?q=' OR 1=1-- returns all products; GET /products/search?q=' UNION SELECT * FROM users-- would dump the users table.

reason: It identifies the concatenated q parameter in GET /products/search as SQL injection.

finding.title: Token refresh bypasses JWT signature verification
finding.description: The /auth/refresh endpoint decodes the provided JWT with options={'verify_signature': False}, meaning any arbitrarily formatted payload can be accepted. If the referenced user_id exists in the database, the app issues a fresh, legitimately-signed token for that user—including staff members—using the correct secret key.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/refresh with body '{"token": "any.string.payload"}' where the payload contains {"sub": <existing user id>} successfully returns a new signed JWT for that user. Verified against running app: posting a forged payload with sub=1 returned a valid staff-level JWT.

reason: It identifies the refresh endpoint accepting tokens without signature verification and issuing valid signed tokens for the referenced user.

finding.title: Request logging records credentials and other sensitive POST data
finding.description: Every POST body is logged, including login passwords, password-reset payloads, bearer-adjacent application data, and potentially payment or personal information. The 2,000-byte truncation does not prevent secret disclosure to log readers or log storage.
finding.evidence: The before_request hook calls request.get_data(as_text=True)[:2000] for all POST requests. /auth/login and /auth/reset/confirm send passwords in those bodies, so normal authentication traffic is written to application logs.

reason: The request logger records up to 2,000 characters of POST bodies, including passwords and other sensitive data.

finding.title: Payment webhook trusts an attacker-controlled payment amount
finding.description: After signature verification, the webhook stores event.amount_pence without checking it against the order total or a provider-side payment record. A signed or forged paid event can therefore settle an order for less than its price, including zero.
finding.evidence: A webhook for a £35.00 order with status=paid and amount_pence=0 returned 200; GET /orders/4 then showed status=processing, total_pence=3500, and paid_pence=0.

reason: The webhook signature does not cover the event amount, allowing a modified paid event to settle an order for less than its total.

finding.title: Predictable password-reset tokens
finding.description: Reset tokens are generated with '%08d' % int(random.random() * 10**8). Python's random module uses the Mersenne Twister PRNG, which is fully deterministic and predictable. The token space is limited to 10^8 values (~27 bits of entropy), making brute-force feasible. An attacker who observes one token (or knows the algorithm's seed) can predict others.
finding.evidence: The code at auth.py:135 uses random.random() — not secrets.token_urlsafe or os.urandom — to generate reset codes, producing only 8-digit decimal strings from a trivially guessable space.

reason: It identifies predictable, short password-reset codes generated with random.random() in reset_request.

finding.title: Server-Side Request Forgery in image import
finding.description: After checking the hostname against an allowlist and verifying it resolves to a public IP, the app fetches the URL with requests.get(). The hostname-to-IP check can be circumvented via DNS rebinding, and the allowlist only matches hostnames—not subdomains—so registering a controlled subdomain of an approved host (e.g. cdn.hartleyfinch.co.uk.attacker.evil) could reach internal network resources.
finding.evidence: A staff-authenticated POST to /products/<id>/image with a crafted URL will cause the server to make an outbound HTTP request to whatever host is specified.

reason: It identifies the image-import SSRF in check_url, where the server fetches attacker-controlled URLs without validating redirect destinations.

finding.title: Broken object-level authorization on order detail view
finding.description: The /orders/<order_id> endpoint retrieves and returns an order using only its integer id, without verifying that the requesting user owns the order. Any authenticated user can view another user's order details.
finding.evidence: Authenticated user with id=1 (customer) can GET /orders/3 (which belongs to customer id=2) and receives full order data including items, prices, delivery date, and refund history. Verified against running app.

reason: It identifies the IDOR in show_order, where any signed-in customer can retrieve another customer's order by ID.

finding.title: Arbitrary code execution via pickle-deserialized basket cookie
finding.description: The basket cookie value is base64-decoded and passed to pickle.loads(). Because an attacker can set any cookie value, they can craft a malicious pickle payload that executes arbitrary code when the server processes it (on every request, since read_basket is called from both GET /basket and POST /basket/items).
finding.evidence: Line 20 of shopapi/basket.py calls pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw)) on untrusted cookie data. Standard pickle deserialization allows remote code execution through __reduce__ hooks.

reason: The finding identifies the unauthenticated pickle deserialization of the attacker-controlled basket cookie in read_basket, enabling remote code execution.

finding.title: Payment confirmation defaults to 'paid' on timeout
finding.description: When the call to client().payment_status() raises requests.Timeout (line 39), the code unconditionally sets status = 'paid' (line 42) and transitions the order to 'processing'. A slow or unavailable payment provider means genuine unpaid orders may be marked as paid and shipped. There is no retry mechanism or manual reconciliation.
finding.evidence: Line 42 of shopapi/payments.py: on Timeout, status is set to 'paid' and the order transitions to 'processing' immediately. The comment admits 'Reconciliation runs overnight', but the damage (fulfillment) happens before that.

reason: It identifies the timeout in confirm_payment being treated as paid, allowing unpaid orders to be processed.

finding.title: Over-permissive CORS configuration
finding.description: The CORS hook echoes back the request's Origin header as Access-Control-Allow-Origin, sets Access-Control-Allow-Credentials to true, and applies this to every response. This effectively allows any origin to make credentialed cross-origin requests against the API, undermining CSRF protections.
finding.evidence: Lines 44-51 of shopapi/__init__.py set Access-Control-Allow-Origin to the caller's Origin and Allow-Credentials to true for every response. Combined with session-based authentication, any rogue website can perform authenticated requests.

reason: It identifies the CORS hook reflecting arbitrary Origin values while allowing credentials.

finding.title: Trailing-slash admin refund route bypasses staff authorization
finding.description: The global admin check compares request.path to the set of exact route rules. The refund route is registered with strict_slashes=False, so /admin/refunds/ is a valid route but is not equal to the collected /admin/refunds rule; unauthenticated callers can execute the refund operation.
finding.evidence: POST /admin/refunds/ with no Authorization header and body {"order_id":1,"amount_pence":1} returned HTTP 200 and created a refund. The authorization hook is at shopapi/__init__.py:35-41 and only checks exact request.path membership.

reason: The trailing-slash refund route bypasses the exact-path staff authorization check, matching V03.

finding.title: Token refresh accepts unsigned attacker-controlled JWT claims
finding.description: The refresh endpoint decodes the supplied token with verify_signature=False and only checks that the subject maps to a user. An attacker can create an unsigned token naming any user and obtain a valid signed session token for that account.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/refresh with an unsigned JWT whose payload was {"sub":1} returned HTTP 200 and a fresh HS256 token for user 1. No signature or expiration validation is performed before load_user().

reason: It identifies the refresh endpoint accepting unsigned JWT claims and issuing a valid signed token for the named user.

finding.title: SQL injection and stored XSS in admin review report
finding.description: Line 80 constructs the review lookup query with an f-string embedding customer['display_name'] directly into SQL. Since display_name is user-controllable (settable via PATCH /account), an attacker can store a payload like '; DROP TABLE users; --' that injects SQL on subsequent admin queries. The same display_name is later rendered in the JSON response without escaping, enabling stored XSS when admins consume the API.
finding.evidence: Setting display_name to an XSS payload such as causes that payload to appear verbatim in the GET /admin/reports/reviews?customer_id= JSON response. Verified: after registering a user with a script-containing display name and leaving a review, the admin reports endpoint returned the raw XSS payload in the reviews JSON.

reason: It identifies the second-order SQL injection in reviews_by_customer, where the customer-controlled display_name is interpolated into the report query.

finding.title: Hardcoded JWT secret key
finding.description: The JWT signing key SECRET_KEY = 'hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d' is a static literal baked into the source code. Anyone who has access to the repository can sign arbitrary JWTs (e.g. granting themselves admin/staff roles). The key is not read from environment variables or a secrets manager.
finding.evidence: Line 3 of config.py: SECRET_KEY = 'hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d'. Combined with the refresh bypass, an attacker needs only a valid user_id to escalate privileges.

reason: It identifies the hardcoded JWT signing secret in config.py, matching V08; the refresh-bypass mention is contextual rather than a separate finding.

finding.title: Product search is vulnerable to SQL injection
finding.description: The q parameter is concatenated directly into a SQL LIKE expression instead of being bound as a parameter. This permits modification of the query and potentially broader database access through SQLite SQL injection techniques.
finding.evidence: GET /products/search?q=%27%20OR%201%3D1-- returned HTTP 200 with all six products, demonstrating that the input changed the WHERE predicate.

reason: The finding identifies SQL injection in the concatenated query parameter in GET /products/search.

finding.title: Review bodies are stored and rendered as trusted HTML
finding.description: Review body input is stored without sanitization and the product template renders r.body with the safe filter. A logged-in user can persist arbitrary HTML/script markup that executes for anyone viewing the product page.
finding.evidence: POST /products/<product_id>/reviews accepts body without bleach.clean(), and shopapi/templates/product.html:13 renders {{ r.body|safe }}. This is a stored XSS path from the review API to every product-page visitor.

reason: It identifies stored XSS from unsanitized review bodies rendered with the safe filter on product pages.

finding.title: Authentication decorator fails open when authentication is missing or invalid
finding.description: require_auth catches its own abort(401) (and other exceptions), clears g.user, and then still invokes the protected handler. Any protected handler that does not immediately dereference g.user can therefore be reached without authentication, while others produce an avoidable 500 instead of a 401.
finding.evidence: GET /orders/1 with no Authorization header returned the complete order JSON with HTTP 200. The wrapper catches abort(401) at line 54 and calls the endpoint at shopapi/orders.py:46-50, which uses get_order() but never verifies ownership.

reason: The finding identifies require_auth catching abort(401) and continuing, while its evidence also notes that show_order uses get_order without ownership checks.

finding.title: Authenticated users can read other customers' orders
finding.description: show_order calls get_order rather than own_order, so any authenticated user (and, due to the decorator bug, even an unauthenticated request) can retrieve another customer's order, item and refund details.
finding.evidence: GET /orders/1 without credentials returned order 1, including its items, payment totals and refund history. The ownership check exists in own_order() at lines 32-36 but is not used by show_order().

reason: The finding identifies the IDOR in show_order, and also describes the fail-open authentication decorator that lets unauthenticated requests through.

finding.title: CORS reflects arbitrary origins while allowing credentials
finding.description: For every request with an Origin header, the application reflects that origin and enables credentialed CORS. Any hostile website can therefore make credentialed cross-origin requests if the browser has usable authentication state, and the application provides no allowlist.
finding.evidence: GET /health with Origin: https://evil.example returned Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://evil.example and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. config.py:12 enables CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS globally.

reason: The finding identifies the CORS handler in shopapi/__init__.py reflecting arbitrary origins while allowing credentials.

finding.title: Payment-status timeout fails open and marks orders paid
finding.description: When the payment provider times out, the exception handler sets status to paid instead of leaving the order awaiting payment or requiring reconciliation. A provider outage or induced timeout can therefore cause goods to be dispatched without confirmed payment.
finding.evidence: shopapi/payments.py:39-44 catches requests.Timeout, assigns status = "paid", and then updates the order to processing with paid_pence = total_pence.

reason: The finding identifies confirm_payment treating a provider timeout as paid, allowing orders to be processed without confirmed payment.

finding.title: Passwords are stored as unsalted SHA-256 hashes
finding.description: Password hashing uses a single fast SHA-256 digest with no salt or work factor. A database disclosure permits efficient offline cracking and makes equal passwords identifiable; a password KDF such as Argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt should be used.
finding.evidence: hash_password() is hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() at lines 15-16, and the resulting value is stored directly in users.password_hash by registration and reset flows.

reason: It identifies the unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in shopapi/auth.py hash_password.

finding.title: Application entry point enables Flask debug mode
finding.description: The runnable application starts Flask with debug=True. If this entry point is used in a reachable deployment, unhandled exceptions expose interactive debugger functionality and detailed internals; debug mode must not be enabled for production serving.
finding.evidence: run.py:6 calls app.run(..., debug=True). The live app also returned an HTML 500 response for an exception path, demonstrating that this executable is an active deployment entry point.

reason: It identifies debug=True in run.py, which enables the Flask interactive debugger.

finding.title: Request logger records sensitive request bodies
finding.description: All POST, PUT and PATCH bodies are written to application logs, including login passwords, password reset codes, bearer-like secrets submitted in JSON, payment data supplied by clients, and personal information. Logs commonly have broader retention and access than the application and this creates unnecessary credential and privacy exposure.
finding.evidence: before_request log_request() calls request.get_data(as_text=True)[:2000] for every mutating request at lines 30-31; /auth/login and /auth/reset/confirm send passwords and reset codes in those bodies.

reason: It identifies log_request writing request bodies, including credentials, to application logs.

finding.title: Stored review XSS
finding.description: Review bodies are accepted and stored without HTML sanitization, then rendered with Jinja's safe filter. Any customer can persist script markup that executes for every visitor to the product page.
finding.evidence:
POST /products/1/reviews with an authenticated customer and body returned 201; GET /p/MUG-SPECK subsequently contained
. Storage occurs at products.py:90-92 and unsafe rendering is template line 13.

reason: It identifies stored review text rendered with |safe without sanitization, matching the stored XSS vulnerability.

finding.title: JWT and webhook signing secret is hardcoded in source
finding.description: SECRET_KEY is a fixed repository value rather than a required deployment secret. Anyone who obtains the source or reads this value can forge HS256 authentication tokens and, because the webhook uses the same application configuration family of secrets, the deployment's trust boundary is compromised. The default WEBHOOK_SECRET is also predictable at line 8.
finding.evidence: config.py:3 contains SECRET_KEY = "hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d" and config.py:8 defaults WEBHOOK_SECRET to "whsec-local". JWT signing uses SECRET_KEY at shopapi/auth.py:27 and webhook verification uses WEBHOOK_SECRET at shopapi/payments.py:53-64.

reason: It identifies the hardcoded SECRET_KEY in config.py, which enables forged JWTs.

finding.title: Product search is vulnerable to SQL injection
finding.description: The q query parameter is concatenated directly into the LIKE expression. An attacker can alter the WHERE clause and retrieve arbitrary product rows (and potentially use other SQLite expressions).
finding.evidence: GET /products/search?q=%27%20OR%201=1-- returned HTTP 200 with all six products, including products unrelated to the search. The vulnerable concatenation is at products.py:40-42.

reason: It identifies SQL injection in the q parameter of GET /products/search, matching V11.

finding.title: Payment webhook does not validate the paid amount
finding.description: The webhook authenticates only order_id via its signature and accepts any supplied amount_pence, including zero or an amount below the order total, while transitioning the order to processing. A sender possessing the webhook secret can underpay an order, and the application does not enforce the invariant that paid_pence covers total_pence.
finding.evidence: The paid branch at lines 69-71 casts event.amount_pence and writes it directly to paid_pence without comparing it with order.total_pence. The signature at lines 53-55 covers only order_id, not status or amount.

reason: The webhook signature covers only the order_id, leaving amount_pence and status unprotected and allowing the payment event to be altered.

finding.title: Authentication decorator fails open
finding.description: require_auth catches all exceptions, including Flask's abort(401), and then proceeds to execute the protected handler with g.user set to None. Endpoints decorated with it are therefore callable without a valid token, with inconsistent crashes where handlers use g.user.
finding.evidence: GET /orders/1 with no Authorization header returned HTTP 200 and the order contents, despite orders.py:46-49 being decorated with @require_auth. The exception handler at auth.py:55-58 suppresses the authentication failure and calls f anyway.

reason: It identifies require_auth catching abort(401) and continuing with g.user=None, allowing unauthenticated requests through.

finding.title: Admin review report SQL injection through customer display name
finding.description: A customer-controlled display_name is interpolated into the admin review report query. A staff user can set a display name containing SQL syntax and then trigger injection when the report looks up that customer.
finding.evidence: display_name is accepted/updated by auth.py:119-125 and is interpolated into the f-string query at admin.py:77-81 rather than bound as a parameter. The report is staff-protected but staff authorization does not make interpolation safe.

reason: The finding identifies second-order SQL injection in admin.py's reviews_by_customer report query via the customer-controlled display_name.

finding.title: Unsigned pickle basket cookie enables unsafe deserialization and tampering
finding.description: The basket cookie is client-controlled base64-encoded pickle data with no signature or encryption. pickle.loads executes attacker-supplied pickle opcodes on every basket read, allowing server-side code execution; even benign tampering can alter quantities and checkout totals.
finding.evidence: basket.py:15-23 decodes request.cookies['basket'] and directly calls pickle.loads, while with_basket at lines 26-29 issues no MAC/signature. /basket, /basket/items and checkout all call read_basket.

reason: It identifies the unsigned, client-controlled pickle deserialization in shopapi/basket.py, which enables remote code execution.

finding.title: Payment status timeout fails open as paid
finding.description: When the payment provider times out, confirm-payment unconditionally sets status to 'paid' and proceeds to processing. A transient provider failure therefore lets an order be fulfilled without confirmed payment.
finding.evidence: payments.py:37-43 catches requests.Timeout and assigns status = 'paid'; line 44 then marks the order processing and sets paid_pence to the total.

reason: It identifies the payment timeout in confirm_payment being treated as paid, allowing fulfillment without confirmed payment.

finding.title: Order detail does not enforce ownership
finding.description: show_order calls get_order directly instead of own_order, so any caller that reaches the endpoint can read another customer's order, items, payment totals and refunds.
finding.evidence: orders.py:46-49 uses order_json(get_order(order_id)); the ownership check exists separately in own_order at lines 32-36 but is not used. In the running app, GET /orders/1 returned the order data without an Authorization header (also enabled by the fail-open decorator).

reason: The finding identifies the order-ownership IDOR in show_order and also explicitly notes the fail-open authentication decorator that allows unauthenticated access.

finding.title: Passwords are stored as unsalted SHA-256 hashes
finding.description: Password hashing uses a single fast unsalted SHA-256 digest, making database compromise substantially easier to crack than a memory-hard password KDF and reusing the same digest construction for all users.
finding.evidence: hash_password at auth.py:15-17 is hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest(); registration stores this directly at lines 77-78.

reason: It identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in hash_password.

finding.title: Hardcoded JWT signing secret
finding.description: SECRET_KEY is a fixed source-controlled value. Anyone who obtains the code/config can forge HS256 bearer tokens, including staff-role claims, and the same key is used for authentication token verification.
finding.evidence: config.py:3 sets SECRET_KEY = 'hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d'; auth.py:27 signs tokens and auth.py:42 verifies them with this value.

reason: The finding identifies the hardcoded SECRET_KEY in config.py, which enables forged JWTs.

finding.title: Password reset codes use predictable non-cryptographic randomness
finding.description: Reset codes are generated from random.random(), which is not suitable for secrets and produces only an eight-digit value. If the PRNG state or sufficient observations are available, codes can be predicted; the endpoint also provides an online guessing target.
finding.evidence: auth.py:135 generates the code with int(random.random() * 10**8), rather than secrets.SystemRandom/token_bytes.

reason: It identifies the predictable random.random() password-reset code in auth.py, matching V10.

finding.title: SQL Injection in product search endpoint
finding.description: The /products/search endpoint concatenates the user-supplied 'q' query parameter directly into a SQL string without using parameterized queries. An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL to read, modify, or delete data, or potentially execute OS commands via SQLite extensions.
finding.evidence: Line 41: "SELECT * FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%'" + q + "%' OR sku LIKE '%'" + q + "%' ORDER BY name LIMIT 50". Tested with GET /products/search?q=' OR 1=1-- which returned all products instead of zero results.

reason: It identifies SQL injection in the concatenated query parameter in GET /products/search.

finding.title: Server-Side Request Forgery via pickle deserialization in basket cookie
finding.description: The basket cookie stores Python objects serialized with pickle, then unpickled server-side in read_basket(). While there is a try/except around pickle.loads(), an attacker who can craft a malicious pickle payload can achieve remote code execution when the server deserializes it. The cookie is sent with every request.
finding.evidence: Lines 19-21: pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw)) inside read_basket(). Pickle deserialization is inherently unsafe as it executes arbitrary Python code from the deserialized object.

reason: It identifies unsafe unpickling of the attacker-controlled basket cookie in read_basket, which can enable remote code execution.

finding.title: Payment webhook authenticates only an order ID and trusts client amount
finding.description: The signature covers only str(order_id), not status or amount_pence, so a valid signature can be replayed with a modified amount/status. In addition, the built-in default WEBHOOK_SECRET is predictable. The paid transition accepts any supplied amount without checking the order total or provider event identity.
finding.evidence: webhook_signature at payments.py:53-55 hashes only order_id; payment_webhook verifies that value at line 63 but uses event amount directly at lines 69-71. config.py:8 defaults WEBHOOK_SECRET to 'whsec-local'.

reason: The webhook signature covers only the order ID while the handler trusts the supplied status and amount, allowing a captured signature to be replayed with altered payment data.

finding.title: SQL Injection in admin reviews-by-customer endpoint
finding.description: The /admin/reports/reviews endpoint embeds customer['display_name'] directly into a SQL query string via f-string interpolation. Since display_name is stored in the database and controlled by users (set during registration), an authenticated admin can be tricked into querying against malicious input, but more critically, if any external party could influence display_name prior to this query, it would be exploitable. In practice, since only staff can access this, the risk is lower, but the injection vector is present.
finding.evidence: Line 80: f"WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}'". Tested with a crafted display_name containing a quote character causing SQL errors.

reason: It identifies the f-string SQL injection in the admin reviews-by-customer report using a customer-controlled stored display name.

finding.title: Hardcoded secret key
finding.description: The SECRET_KEY used for signing JWT tokens is hardcoded as a static string 'hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d'. This means anyone with access to the source code can forge valid JWT tokens for any user, including admin/staff accounts. It also weakens defense in depth if the token-refresh vulnerability is patched.
finding.evidence: Line 3: SECRET_KEY = 'hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d'. This key is used in make_token() and user_from_request() for JWT encoding/decoding.

reason: It identifies the hardcoded JWT signing secret in config.py, which allows forged tokens.

finding.title: Token refresh endpoint bypasses signature verification
finding.description: The /auth/refresh endpoint calls jwt.decode(token, options={'verify_signature': False}), which accepts any JWT regardless of its signature. An attacker can forge tokens with arbitrary claims (including role: 'staff') to gain authentication and escalate privileges. This completely undermines the security of the session management system.
finding.evidence: Line 101: jwt.decode(token, options={'verify_signature': False}). Verified with POST /auth/refresh using a forged token - the server accepted it and returned a fresh valid token for sub=1 with role='customer'.

reason: The refresh endpoint disables signature verification, allowing forged tokens to be exchanged for valid signed tokens.

finding.title: Incorrect HMAC API usage in webhook signature verification
finding.description: The webhook_signature function uses hmac.new() (with lowercase 'new') instead of hmac.new() -- actually, Python's standard library module is 'hmac' and the function is hmac.new(). However, looking at line 55: hmac.new(secret, str(order_id).encode(), hashlib.sha256). The correct API should use hmac.new() but the actual function name in the hmac module is hmac.new()... wait - the issue is that it uses hmac.new() but the correct function call should use hashlib.sha256 as the digestfunc argument correctly, BUT the real problem is: hmac.new() takes three arguments where the third is the hash function. Actually 'hmac.new()' IS the correct function. The issue here may not be real.
finding.evidence: Need to re-examine this - hmac.new() is actually the correct Python API. The function name is 'new' not 'new'. Actually let me reconsider: in Python the function is indeed hmac.new(secret, msg, digestmod). So this is NOT a finding. Removing.

reason: The finding concludes that hmac.new() is the correct API and retracts the claim, so it does not identify a vulnerability.

finding.title: Request body logged for POST/PUT/PATCH requests
finding.description: The before_request hook logs the full request body for POST, PUT, and PATCH requests up to 2000 characters. If these requests contain sensitive data like passwords, tokens, or personal information, that data will appear in logs. For example, /auth/register and /auth/login send password fields that would be logged.
finding.evidence: Lines 29-31 in __init__.py: log.info('%s %s %s', request.method, request.path, request.get_data(as_text=True)[:2000])

reason: It identifies the request logger recording POST, PUT, and PATCH bodies, including sensitive data such as passwords.

finding.title: Server-Side Request Forgery via pickle deserialization in cache files
finding.description: The cache module uses pickle to serialize and deserialize cached data files on disk. If an attacker can write to the cache directory (or if the filesystem is compromised), they can plant malicious pickle payloads that will be executed upon cache reads. The CACHE_DIR permissions are set to 0700 but within the same process, path traversal or other attacks could compromise safety.
finding.evidence: Line 23: pickle.load(f) inside get(). Line 31: pickle.dump(value, f) inside put(). Deserialization of potentially tampered data.

reason: It flags pickle.load in shopapi/cache.py as unsafe, but the cache files are app-written in a 0700 directory and are not attacker-controlled.

finding.title: Debug mode enabled in application start script
finding.description: The run.py script starts Flask with debug=True. In debug mode, Flask provides an interactive debugger that can be triggered by certain error pages. An attacker could potentially exploit this to execute arbitrary code if they can trigger an exception in the application.
finding.evidence: Line 6: app.run(host='127.0.0.1', port=5000, debug=True)

reason: It correctly identifies debug=True in run.py and the resulting risk of the interactive debugger enabling code execution.

finding.title: CORS configured to reflect any origin with credentials
finding.description: The CORS handler in __init__.py sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin to the value of the requesting Origin header unconditionally, and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials to 'true'. This allows any website to make authenticated cross-origin requests to the application, enabling cross-site request forgery attacks from malicious third-party sites.
finding.evidence: Lines 44-51 in __init__.py: resp.headers['Access-Control-Allow-Origin'] = origin with no allowlist check, combined with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.

reason: The CORS handler reflects any Origin and allows credentials, matching V05.

finding.title: Default webhook secret is easily guessable
finding.description: WEBHOOK_SECRET defaults to 'whsec-local', a trivially guessable value. While it can be overridden via environment variable, running with the default exposes the application to webhook forgery - an attacker can craft fake payment webhook events that pass signature verification, potentially marking unpaid orders as paid.
finding.evidence: Line 8: WEBHOOK_SECRET = os.environ.get('WEBHOOK_SECRET', 'whsec-local'). See payments.py webhook_signature() which uses this to verify incoming webhooks.

reason: The guessable default webhook secret is a distinct weakness in config.py, not V19’s failure to authenticate the webhook body.

finding.title: Weak password hashing using plain SHA-256 without salt
finding.description: Passwords are hashed using plain SHA-256 without a per-password salt. This makes passwords vulnerable to rainbow table attacks and precomputation attacks. Additionally, SHA-256 is too fast for password hashing; slow hashes like bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2 should be used.
finding.evidence: Line 16: return hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() in hash_password(). No salt is used.

reason: It identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in hash_password, matching V09.

finding.title: Order detail view missing ownership check
finding.description: The /orders/<int:order_id> endpoint returns full order details to any authenticated user without verifying that the order belongs to them. While own_order() checks ownership for cancellations and returns, show_order() uses get_order() which only checks existence, not ownership. This allows any authenticated user to view other users' orders.
finding.evidence: Line 49: Returns order_json(get_order(order_id)) without checking g.user['id'] matches order['customer_id']. Verified: User 1 can see User 2's order by forging JWT with sub=2, and also Order 2 visible without auth restrictions beyond general login requirement.

reason: It identifies the order-detail IDOR: show_order uses get_order without checking that the order belongs to the signed-in customer.

finding.title: Passwordless token refresh accepts unsigned JWTs
finding.description: The refresh endpoint decodes the supplied token with signature verification disabled and only checks that its subject maps to a user. An attacker can submit an unsigned JWT naming any existing user and receive a valid signed session token.
finding.evidence: POST /auth/refresh with an unsigned token whose payload is {"sub":1,"exp":1793585872} returned 200 and a fresh HS256 token. The request used a token with header {"alg":"none"} and no signature.

reason: The finding identifies refresh decoding JWTs with signature verification disabled, allowing forged tokens to be exchanged for valid signed tokens.

finding.title: Reset token uses cryptographically weak randomness
finding.description: Password reset tokens are generated using random.random() which produces a float between 0 and 1 with limited precision, then formatted as an 8-digit decimal. This creates only 10^8 possible values, making brute-force recovery of the token feasible.
finding.evidence: Line 135: token = '%08d' % int(random.random() * 10**8). Only 100 million possible tokens, generated using non-cryptographic random.

reason: The finding identifies the predictable, short reset code generated with random.random() in reset_request.

finding.title: Trailing slash bypasses the global admin authorization check
finding.description: The before_request hook compares request.path to a set containing the canonical admin rules. The refunds route explicitly accepts a trailing slash, but /admin/refunds/ is not in that set, so the route executes without the staff check.
finding.evidence: Unauthenticated POST /admin/refunds/ with {"order_id":3,"amount_pence":1} returned 200 and created a refund. The canonical POST /admin/refunds with the same unauthenticated request returned 403.

reason: It identifies the trailing-slash bypass of the staff authorization check on /admin/refunds/.

finding.title: Hardcoded JWT signing key permits account and staff-token forgery
finding.description: The application uses a fixed source-controlled SECRET_KEY for all JWTs. Anyone who obtains the source or the distributed application can mint tokens for any user ID, including the staff account.
finding.evidence: Signing a JWT with sub=3 and role=staff using the literal key hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d allowed GET /admin/users to return 200, without logging in as the staff account. Token validation is in shopapi/auth.py:42.

reason: The hardcoded SECRET_KEY in config.py allows attackers with the source to forge JWTs, including staff tokens.

finding.title: Order detail endpoint exposes any customer’s order
finding.description: show_order calls get_order directly rather than own_order, so the authenticated user is never compared with the order customer. The route also becomes publicly readable because the authentication decorator fails open for this handler.
finding.evidence: GET /orders/3 with Priya’s bearer token returned Tom’s delivered order. GET /orders/1 with no Authorization header also returned 200 and the complete order JSON.

reason: The finding identifies the order IDOR in show_order and also describes the fail-open authentication decorator that lets unauthenticated requests reach the route.

finding.title: Product search is vulnerable to SQL injection
finding.description: The search query concatenates q directly into a SQL statement. A caller can alter the query and use UNION results to read arbitrary database fields exposed through the product JSON mapping.
finding.evidence: GET /products/search?q=%27%20UNION%20SELECT%20id,email,password_hash,role,created,reset_token,reset_expires%20FROM%20users-- returned user rows, including email addresses and password hashes, in the product name/price/sku fields.

reason: The finding identifies the concatenated search parameter in GET /products/search as SQL injection, matching V11.

finding.title: Review bodies are stored and rendered as trusted HTML
finding.description: Review text is inserted without sanitization and the product template renders it with the safe filter. Any authenticated user can persist script markup that executes for visitors to the affected product page.
finding.evidence: POST /products/1/reviews as Priya with body <script>document.body.dataset.pwned=1</script> returned 201. GET /p/MUG-SPECK then contained that exact script in the response HTML. The sink is shopapi/templates/product.html:13.

reason: It identifies stored XSS from raw review text rendered with the template’s safe filter.

finding.title: Unauthenticated basket cookie is unsafe pickle data
finding.description: The basket cookie is only base64 encoded, not authenticated, and is passed to pickle.loads. An attacker can submit a crafted cookie to execute arbitrary Python pickle globals in the application process when any basket endpoint reads it.
finding.evidence: GET /basket accepts a client-supplied basket cookie and invokes pickle.loads before any authentication. The cookie is generated with plain pickle.dumps at shopapi/basket.py:27 and has no MAC or signing key.

reason: The finding correctly identifies unauthenticated pickle deserialization of the client-controlled basket cookie in read_basket, enabling remote code execution.

finding.title: Payment-provider timeout fails open as a successful payment
finding.description: When payment_status raises requests.Timeout, the exception handler unconditionally substitutes paid and moves the order to processing. A provider outage or request timeout therefore grants fulfillment without payment confirmation.
finding.evidence: The confirm-payment path catches requests.Timeout at lines 39-42 and then executes the paid transition at lines 43-45; no provider confirmation or reconciliation result is required.

reason: It identifies the payment timeout in confirm_payment being treated as paid, allowing an order to be processed without payment.

finding.title: Editable package install without checksum verification
finding.description: requirements-dev.txt installs hf-payments as an editable package (-e packages/hf_payments) without any dependency hash or pinning verification. Combined with requirements.txt pulling from an internal PyPI index (pypi.hartleyfinch.internal), this means that if the internal index or hf-payments source is compromised, arbitrary code can be injected into the build.
finding.evidence: Line 6 of requirements-dev.txt: -e packages/hf_payments. The pyproject.toml has no constraints on dependencies and pip editable installs don't verify checksums.

reason: The finding describes a generic source or internal-index compromise, not the public-index dependency-confusion issue in V07, and an editable install of the repository’s local package without hashes is not by itself a vulnerability.

finding.title: Request logging records passwords and other secrets
finding.description: Every POST body is logged verbatim up to 2,000 bytes. Login passwords, registration passwords, password-reset codes, reset passwords, bearer-like application data, and payment-related fields can therefore enter application logs.
finding.evidence: The before_request hook calls request.get_data(as_text=True) for every POST. The login and reset endpoints send password/code fields in POST JSON, so those values are included in the logged body.

reason: The request logger records POST bodies, including passwords and reset credentials, in the application logs.

finding.title: Payment webhook does not validate the settled amount
finding.description: A signed paid event writes the caller-provided amount directly to paid_pence without comparing it to the order total or a provider-side amount. This corrupts payment accounting and can enable over-refunds or fulfillment based on an invalid amount.
finding.evidence: The forged-event test submitted amount_pence=999999 for an order whose total_pence was 2800; the resulting order had paid_pence=999999 and status=processing.

reason: The payment webhook trusts caller-supplied amount_pence without authenticating it, matching V19’s webhook integrity flaw.

finding.title: Passwords are stored as unsalted fast SHA-256 hashes
finding.description: Password hashing uses a single unsalted SHA-256 digest with no work factor. A database disclosure therefore permits efficient dictionary and password-reuse cracking, and identical passwords produce identical hashes.
finding.evidence: hash_password is hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest(), and the SQL injection response exposed these 64-character hashes from users.password_hash.

reason: It identifies the unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in hash_password.

finding.title: Authentication failures are swallowed, allowing protected handlers to run
finding.description: The require_auth decorator catches the 401 exception raised by abort(), clears g.user, and still invokes the protected handler. As a result, endpoints intended to require authentication can disclose data or fail with an unrelated server error instead of rejecting the request.
finding.evidence: shopapi/auth.py:51-58 catches every exception and returns f(*args, **kwargs). GET /orders/1 without an Authorization header returned HTTP 200 with the complete order contents; GET /account without authentication proceeded to a 500 response.

reason: The finding identifies require_auth swallowing abort(401) and allowing unauthenticated requests to reach protected handlers.

finding.title: Password reset codes use weak non-cryptographic randomness without attempt limits
finding.description: Reset codes are generated from random.random and truncated to an eight-digit decimal value. Confirmation has no per-account or per-IP attempt limit, so online guessing can continue for the full 30-minute validity period.
finding.evidence: The request path generates codes with int(random.random() * 10**8), stores them directly, and reset_confirm compares the submitted code without recording or limiting failures.

reason: It identifies the predictable, eight-digit password-reset code and lack of attempt limits in reset_request/reset_confirm.

finding.title: Image import can follow redirects to an unvalidated destination
finding.description: The code validates only the initial URL hostname against the allowlist and then uses requests.get with its default redirect behavior. An approved host that redirects to an internal address can make the staff import endpoint fetch internal services, with the response copied into the application filesystem.
finding.evidence: check_url validates u.hostname before requests.get, but requests.get(url, timeout=10, stream=True) follows redirects and there is no validation of the final response URL or each redirect hop.

reason: It identifies the SSRF in import_image/check_url, where redirect-following fetches can reach an unvalidated internal destination.

finding.title: Order details do not verify ownership
finding.description: show_order retrieves an order with get_order() rather than own_order(), so it never compares customer_id with the authenticated user. A requester who reaches the endpoint can read another customer's order contents, payment amounts, refunds, and delivery information.
finding.evidence: shopapi/orders.py:46-49 calls order_json(get_order(order_id)) without an ownership check. GET /orders/1 without authentication returned HTTP 200 and the full order JSON because the authentication decorator also fails open.

reason: It identifies the order ownership flaw in show_order, and also explicitly notes the authentication decorator’s fail-open behavior.

finding.title: Product search is vulnerable to SQL injection
finding.description: The search value is concatenated into the SQL statement rather than passed as a parameter. An unauthenticated requester can alter the query and retrieve unintended rows or potentially manipulate the database depending on the database driver and statement handling.
finding.evidence: shopapi/products.py:40-42 concatenates q into the SQL string. GET /products/search?q=%27%20UNION%20SELECT%201,2,3,4,5,6,7%20-- returned an extra product row containing the injected values.

reason: It identifies SQL injection in the concatenated q parameter in GET /products/search.

finding.title: Default webhook secret is public and allows forged payment events
finding.description: WEBHOOK_SECRET defaults to the source-visible value whsec-local. The webhook trusts an HMAC made with that value, so anyone who can inspect the application or its source can mark arbitrary orders as paid.
finding.evidence: For a newly created awaiting_payment order, POST /webhooks/payments with X-Signature=HMAC-SHA256(whsec-local, order_id), status=paid, and amount_pence=999999 returned 200 and changed the order to processing.

reason: The finding identifies the payment webhook’s signature weakness, allowing forged payment events to mark orders as paid.

finding.title: Token refresh accepts unsigned attacker-controlled JWT claims
finding.description: The refresh endpoint disables JWT signature verification and uses the unverified sub claim to select a user before issuing a newly signed token. Anyone can name another existing user, including a staff user, and obtain a valid token for that account.
finding.evidence: shopapi/auth.py:99-107 calls jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False}), loads claims.get("sub"), and signs a fresh token. POST /auth/refresh with an unsigned JWT containing {"sub":1} returned HTTP 200 and a valid signed token.

reason: It identifies the unsigned-token vulnerability in the refresh endpoint, which lets an attacker obtain a signed token for another user.

finding.title: Trailing-slash refund route bypasses the staff authorization check
finding.description: Global admin authorization compares request.path to exact registered rules. The refund route accepts both slash forms with strict_slashes=False, but the trailing-slash path is not equal to the registered rule and the handler has no local authorization check. Unauthenticated users can therefore create goodwill refunds.
finding.evidence: shopapi/__init__.py:26-41 performs the exact path comparison; shopapi/admin.py:51-53 registers /admin/refunds with strict_slashes=False. POST /admin/refunds/ without credentials and {"order_id":1,"amount_pence":1} returned HTTP 200 with {"ok":true} and created a refund.

reason: It identifies the trailing-slash /admin/refunds route bypassing the exact-path staff authorization check.

finding.title: Unsigned basket cookie is deserialized with pickle
finding.description: The basket cookie is entirely client-controlled and is passed to pickle.loads without an integrity check. A crafted cookie can execute arbitrary Python code in the application process whenever a basket endpoint reads it.
finding.evidence: shopapi/basket.py:15-23 base64-decodes request.cookies['basket'] and calls pickle.loads; shopapi/basket.py:26-28 creates the cookie without signing it. The exception handler only handles errors after deserialization and does not prevent pickle gadget execution.

reason: The finding correctly identifies the unsigned, client-controlled basket cookie being unpickled in shopapi/basket.py, enabling remote code execution.

finding.title: Review bodies are rendered as stored HTML
finding.description: Review text supplied by customers is rendered with Jinja's safe filter. A customer can submit markup or script content that executes for anyone viewing the product page, causing stored cross-site scripting.
finding.evidence: shopapi/products.py:82-91 stores the submitted body without sanitization, while shopapi/templates/product.html:13 renders r.body using {{ r.body|safe }}.

reason: It identifies stored XSS because customer review bodies are stored unsanitized and rendered with the safe filter.

finding.title: Payment provider timeouts fail open as successful payments
finding.description: When payment_status times out, confirm_payment treats the result as paid and transitions the order to processing, setting paid_pence to the order total. A provider outage or transient network failure can therefore result in fulfillment without confirmed payment.
finding.evidence: shopapi/payments.py:37-45 catches requests.Timeout, assigns status = "paid", and then updates the order to processing with paid_pence = total_pence.

reason: The finding identifies confirm_payment treating a provider timeout as successful payment and fulfilling the order without confirmed payment.

finding.title: JWT signing key is hardcoded in source
finding.description: JWTs are signed with a fixed source-controlled SECRET_KEY. Anyone who obtains the repository or this reusable deployment value can forge tokens with arbitrary user IDs and roles.
finding.evidence: config.py:3 sets SECRET_KEY = "hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d" instead of requiring a deployment-specific secret.

reason: The finding identifies the hardcoded JWT signing secret in config.py, which allows forged tokens.

finding.title: Customer-controlled display names are interpolated into the admin SQL report
finding.description: The review report embeds a customer's display_name directly in a SQL WHERE clause. A customer can set a display name containing SQL syntax, and a staff request for that customer's report then executes the injected expression.
finding.evidence: shopapi/admin.py:77-81 uses an f-string for r.author_name instead of a parameter. Customer display names are accepted by shopapi/auth.py:116-125 and are copied into review.author_name by shopapi/products.py:90-91.

reason: The admin reviews report interpolates customer-controlled display names into SQL, matching the second-order SQL injection in reviews_by_customer.

finding.title: Passwords are stored with unsalted SHA-256
finding.description: Password hashes use a fast, unsalted general-purpose hash rather than a password-specific KDF with a unique salt. A database compromise enables efficient offline dictionary and brute-force cracking.
finding.evidence: shopapi/auth.py:15-16 computes hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() and stores no salt or work factor.

reason: The finding identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password hashing in shopapi/auth.py, matching V09.

finding.title: Payment webhook signature does not authenticate event contents
finding.description: The webhook MAC covers only order_id, not status or amount_pence. A party able to obtain or replay a valid order signature can change the event status or amount, and the handler accepts any supplied amount without checking it against the order total.
finding.evidence: shopapi/payments.py:53-55 computes the HMAC over only str(order_id). Lines 69-71 trust event.status and int(event.amount_pence), writing the supplied amount to paid_pence without validation.

reason: The webhook signature authenticates only the order ID, allowing the status and amount to be altered or replayed.

finding.title: Password reset codes have no online brute-force protection
finding.description: Reset codes are eight decimal digits and remain valid for 30 minutes. The confirmation endpoint records no failed attempts and applies no rate limit or lockout, allowing unlimited guesses for a known email address during the validity period.
finding.evidence: shopapi/auth.py:135 generates the code with random.random() and an eight-digit decimal format; lines 143-161 compare guesses without attempt tracking or throttling.

reason: The reset confirmation endpoint allows unlimited guesses of a short code, matching V10’s brute-forceable password-reset code weakness.

finding.title: Mutating request bodies containing credentials are logged
finding.description: The global request logger writes POST, PUT, and PATCH bodies before handlers run. Login passwords, registration passwords, reset codes, and other sensitive personal data can therefore be persisted in application logs.
finding.evidence: shopapi/__init__.py:29-31 logs request.get_data(as_text=True)[:2000] for every mutating request, while shopapi/auth.py accepts passwords and reset data in JSON bodies.

reason: The finding identifies the request logger in shopapi/__init__.py logging mutating request bodies that can contain credentials.

finding.title: Application entry point enables Flask debug mode
finding.description: The provided run entry point starts Flask with debug=True. If deployed beyond a strictly local development environment, unhandled exceptions can expose source and configuration through the interactive debugger and may expose its code execution console.
finding.evidence: run.py:6 calls app.run(..., debug=True).

reason: The finding identifies run.py enabling Flask debug mode, matching the planted vulnerability.

finding.title: Client-controlled basket cookie is deserialized with pickle
finding.description: The basket cookie is only base64 encoded, not authenticated or otherwise constrained. An unauthenticated attacker can supply a crafted pickle and have the server execute its pickle payload on any endpoint that calls read_basket().
finding.evidence: read_basket() passes the decoded request cookie directly to pickle.loads().

reason: It identifies the unauthenticated pickle deserialization of the client-controlled basket cookie in read_basket, enabling remote code execution.

finding.title: Refresh accepts unsigned attacker-supplied JWT claims
finding.description: The refresh endpoint explicitly disables signature verification and then issues a new signed token for the claimed subject. Anyone can submit an unsigned token containing another user's id and obtain a valid session token for that account, including a staff account.
finding.evidence: jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False}) is followed by load_user(claims.get("sub")) and make_token(user).

reason: The refresh endpoint disables signature verification and issues a valid token for the claimed subject, enabling account takeover.

finding.title: Unauthenticated product search concatenates the query into SQL
finding.description: The public search parameter is interpolated into a SQL statement without parameterization. An attacker can alter the WHERE clause or inject additional SQLite expressions through q.
finding.evidence: The execute() argument is built as "... LIKE '%" + q + "%' ..." instead of using a bound parameter.

reason: The finding identifies SQL injection in the q parameter of product search, matching V11.

finding.title: JWT signing key is hardcoded and publicly recoverable
finding.description: The application uses a fixed secret committed in source for HS256 JWTs. Anyone who can read the repository can forge authentication tokens for arbitrary users and roles; the fallback also remains active unless deployment explicitly overrides it.
finding.evidence: SECRET_KEY = "hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d" and auth.py uses it to sign and verify all bearer tokens.

reason: It identifies the hardcoded JWT signing secret in config.py, which enables token forgery.

finding.title: Webhook signing secret has a known source-controlled default
finding.description: If WEBHOOK_SECRET is not configured, the application uses the publicly visible value whsec-local. Any deployment omitting the environment variable therefore permits anyone familiar with the source to forge payment webhook signatures.
finding.evidence: config.py:8 defaults WEBHOOK_SECRET to whsec-local; shopapi/payments.py:53-55 uses it to authenticate webhooks.

reason: The source-controlled default WEBHOOK_SECRET enables forged payment webhooks, but it is distinct from V08’s hardcoded JWT signing secret.

finding.title: Authenticated users can read any order by numeric id
finding.description: The order detail endpoint authenticates the caller but calls get_order() directly rather than own_order(). Any signed-in customer can enumerate order ids and retrieve another customer's order status, totals, items, and refund history.
finding.evidence: show_order() returns order_json(get_order(order_id)); the ownership check exists only in own_order(), used by mutation endpoints.

reason: The finding identifies the IDOR in show_order, which lets authenticated customers read other customers’ orders.

finding.title: Payment-status timeout is treated as a successful payment
finding.description: A network timeout from the payment provider causes the order to be marked processing and paid for its full total without confirmation. A customer can exploit provider unavailability or an induced timeout to receive goods without a settled payment.
finding.evidence: The requests.Timeout handler sets status = "paid", and the following branch writes paid_pence = total_pence.

reason: The finding identifies the payment confirmation timeout being treated as paid, allowing an order to be processed without payment.

finding.title: Staff review report interpolates a user-controlled display name into SQL
finding.description: A customer's display name is user-controlled, but it is inserted into the report query with an f-string. A staff member viewing the report for that customer can trigger SQL injection, allowing manipulation of the query and potentially disclosure of database contents.
finding.evidence: The query ends with f"WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}' ORDER BY r.id DESC".

reason: The report query interpolates a customer-controlled display name into SQL, matching the second-order SQL injection in reviews_by_customer.

finding.title: Request bodies containing credentials and payment data are logged
finding.description: Every POST, PUT, and PATCH body is written to application logs. This includes login passwords, reset codes, bearer-token-bearing client payloads, and potentially payment information, creating a persistent credential disclosure path to anyone with log access.
finding.evidence: log_request() logs request.get_data(as_text=True)[:2000] without endpoint- or field-based redaction.

reason: It identifies log_request writing request bodies, including credentials, to application logs.

finding.title: Passwords are stored as unsalted fast SHA-256 hashes
finding.description: A database disclosure exposes passwords as single-round unsalted SHA-256 digests, which are inexpensive to crack at scale and enable password reuse attacks. A password-specific KDF such as Argon2id, scrypt, or bcrypt is required for safe password storage.
finding.evidence: hash_password() returns hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() with no salt or work factor.

reason: It identifies unsalted, fast SHA-256 password storage in hash_password, matching V09.

finding.title: Payment webhook signature does not cover payment status or amount
finding.description: The HMAC is calculated only over order_id. Anyone able to replay a valid signature for an order can change status and amount_pence while retaining the same signature; the handler accepts the supplied amount without checking it against the order total or provider payment.
finding.evidence: webhook_signature() hashes only str(order_id), while payment_webhook() trusts event status and int(event.get("amount_pence", 0)).

reason: The webhook HMAC covers only the order ID while the handler trusts the supplied status and amount, allowing a valid signature to be replayed with altered payment details.

finding.title: Cancellation and return accounting permits refunds above the amount paid
finding.description: Cancellation and return quantities are tracked independently and neither path checks existing refunds, the other quantity, or paid_pence. The same item can therefore be cancelled and returned (or repeated duplicate lines can pass validation) and issue_refund() sends each computed amount to the provider without a cumulative cap.
finding.evidence: cancel_items() validates only cancelled_qty and return_items() validates only returned_qty; both call issue_refund() with their full line total, and issue_refund() has no paid/refunded limit.

reason: The finding identifies that return_items ignores quantities already cancelled and refunded, allowing the same order items to be refunded again.

finding.title: Trailing slash bypasses the admin authorization hook for refunds
finding.description: Admin protection compares request.path to the set of exact route rules. The refund route is registered with strict_slashes=False, so /admin/refunds/ reaches the handler but is not equal to the stored /admin/refunds rule. The handler performs the refund without its own authorization check.
finding.evidence: POST /admin/refunds/ without credentials with {"order_id":1,"amount_pence":1} returned HTTP 200 and recorded the refund; POST /admin/refunds with the same request returned HTTP 403. Relevant code is shopapi/__init__.py:35-41 and shopapi/admin.py:51-67.

reason: It describes the trailing-slash path bypass of the staff authorization hook on /admin/refunds.

finding.title: Password-reset codes are brute-forceable without rate limiting
finding.description: Reset codes are only eight decimal digits, are generated with the non-cryptographic random module, and confirmation has no attempt limit, lockout, or request throttling. An attacker can repeatedly try codes during the 30-minute validity window and reset a known user's password.
finding.evidence: reset_request() creates a decimal code with random.random(), while reset_confirm() compares the submitted code and has no rate-limit or failed-attempt state.

reason: It identifies the predictable random.random() reset codes and lack of attempt limits in reset_request/reset_confirm.

finding.title: Client-controlled basket cookie is deserialized with pickle
finding.description: The basket cookie is only base64 encoded, not authenticated or signed. pickle.loads executes attacker-controlled pickle reducers in the application process before the resulting value is checked for being a dict, allowing arbitrary code execution from a request cookie.
finding.evidence: shopapi/basket.py:15-23 calls pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw)) on the client-supplied basket cookie; with_basket at lines 26-29 writes the same unsigned format. A request can therefore supply an arbitrary pickle payload in Cookie: basket=... .

reason: It identifies the unsigned, client-controlled pickle deserialization in shopapi/basket.py that enables remote code execution.

finding.title: Review bodies are rendered as stored XSS
finding.description: Authenticated users can submit arbitrary review text and the product template marks it safe without sanitizing it. A malicious review executes in every visitor's browser on the product page.
finding.evidence: POST /products/1/reviews with body returned 201; GET /p/MUG-SPECK then contained the literal . The write path is shopapi/products.py:79-93 and the unsafe sink is product.html:13.

reason: It identifies unsanitized review text rendered with |safe in the product template, matching the stored XSS vulnerability.

finding.title: Product search is SQL-injectable
finding.description: The q query parameter is concatenated directly into a SQL string instead of being bound as a parameter.
finding.evidence: GET /products/search?q=%27%20OR%201%3D1-- returned all six products, including products that do not match the search term. The vulnerable concatenation is shopapi/products.py:40-43.

reason: It identifies the concatenated q parameter in shopapi/products.py search as SQL injection.

finding.title: Any authenticated or unauthenticated caller can read any order by ID
finding.description: The show_order handler requires a token but calls get_order(), which only looks up the numeric ID and never checks customer_id.
